sentences.en: Finally, after a few attempts, Elsa mounted.
sentences.zh: 试了几下，艾莎终于骑稳了。

sentences.en: Together, they trotted out of the stables and left the courtyard, with Anna waving to Kristoff, who smiled from under a pile of kittens batting at his face.
sentences.zh: 她们一同小跑出马厩，离开庭院，安娜朝克斯托夫挥手，他正埋在一堆扑他脸的小猫崽下笑着。

sentences.en: The sisters crossed the Bridge of Arches and took in the wild, fresh autumn air.
sentences.zh: 姐妹俩越过拱桥，呼吸着旷野里清新的秋日空气。

sentences.en: Behind them, nestled in the shadow of soaring mountains, the castle sparkled and shone with the decorative touches of Elsa’s ice magic.
sentences.zh: 身后，城堡依偎在高耸群山的阴影里，因艾莎冰魔法的点缀而熠熠生辉。

sentences.en: Anna kicked her horse into a canter, and Elsa did the same.
sentences.zh: 安娜催马小跑，艾莎也照做。

sentences.en: Arendelle was a kingdom of wilderness, of rugged coasts, deep blue waters, and towering ships.
sentences.zh: 阿伦黛尔是个荒野之国，有崎岖的海岸、深蓝的海水，和高耸的船舶。

sentences.en: Lots and lots of ships.
sentences.zh: 许许多多的船。

sentences.en: They came from everywhere, bringing people from all over the world who were happy to settle down in the picturesque kingdom—people who were happy to answer Anna’s invitation to share memories of their own countries so she could learn about their customs.
sentences.zh: 它们来自四方，带来世界各地乐意在这如画王国定居的人——这些人也乐意响应安娜的邀请，分享祖国的记忆，好让她了解各地的风土人情。

sentences.en: Memories that could help Anna prepare Elsa for the grand tour…if only Elsa would let her.
sentences.zh: 这些记忆能帮安娜为巡游给艾莎做准备……只要艾莎肯让她来。

sentences.en: Because while ships brought people to the kingdom, they also left with people.
sentences.zh: 因为船既把人送来王国，也载着人离开。

sentences.en: The royal ship currently sat in the harbor, loaded with goods and waiting for Elsa to board.
sentences.zh: 那艘皇家船如今停在港湾，装满了货物，等着艾莎登船。

sentences.en: As they rode past the expanding village and people waving excitedly at them, a delighted fizziness filled Anna’s body.
sentences.zh: 她们骑马经过不断扩张的村庄，人们兴奋地向她们挥手，安娜浑身涌起一股雀跃的酥痒感。

sentences.en: This was the best part of opening the kingdom gates three years ago—all the new people and new ideas that had trickled in.
sentences.zh: 这是三年前敞开王国大门最棒的部分——所有新人和新思想如细流般涌入。

sentences.en: Although the village was more populous than ever before, with more and more people having moved there, Arendelle would always be Anna’s heart and home.
sentences.zh: 尽管村庄比以往任何时候都更热闹，搬来的人越来越多，阿伦黛尔永远是安娜的心之所系与家园。

sentences.en: That was one thing that would never change.
sentences.zh: 这是永不会变的一点。

sentences.en: As they moved beyond the houses and shops, the forest of Arendelle flourished around them, showing off in bright yellows, deep reds, and burnt oranges that reminded Anna of bonfires and melted caramels.
sentences.zh: 她们越过房舍与店铺，阿伦黛尔的森林在四周繁茂生长，炫耀着明黄、深红与焦橙，让安娜想起篝火和融化的焦糖。

sentences.en: A happy sigh slipped from Anna.
sentences.zh: 安娜轻轻舒了口气，满是欢喜。

sentences.en: The autumn leaves had just begun to turn and change, and the living things of the forest seemed to be settling into themselves, the same way Elsa had settled into being queen.
sentences.zh: 秋叶刚开始变幻颜色，森林里的生灵似乎也安顿下来，正如艾莎安顿于女王之位。

sentences.en: Anna didn’t particularly like change.
sentences.zh: 安娜并不怎么喜欢变化。

sentences.en: She always wanted things to stay the same.
sentences.zh: 她总希望一切如常。

sentences.en: These days, Anna barely got to see Elsa, who was constantly cooped up in the council chambers poring over paperwork, or else leading important meetings that Anna also attended.
sentences.zh: 这些日子，安娜几乎见不到艾莎，她不是成天闷在议事厅里钻研文件，就是主持安娜也参加的重要会议。

sentences.en: But she was happy watching Elsa come into her own, even if it meant their relationship was evolving as a side effect of it.
sentences.zh: 可她乐于看艾莎找到自我，即便这意味着她们的关系正随之悄然改变。

sentences.en: The horses slowed, picking up an easy trot side by side.
sentences.zh: 马儿慢下来，并肩踏起轻快的小步。

sentences.en: Wondering if now was the moment, Anna glanced over at Elsa.
sentences.zh: 安娜想着此刻是不是时机，瞥了一眼艾莎。

sentences.en: Her sister wore a far-off and pensive look on her face. “What are you thinking about?” Anna asked. “Oh.” Elsa looked up from her reins. “Nothing…just, you know, work.” “Want to tell me?” Anna said, trying to keep her eagerness down to about a level eight, instead of her usual level ten. “You remember what Father always said, right?” Elsa tilted her head. “What, that ‘burdens should be shared’?” Something scraped in Anna, like a rough crumb caught in her throat.
sentences.zh: 姐姐脸上浮着一种出神而若有所思的神情。“你在想什么？”安娜问。“哦。”艾莎从缰绳上抬起眼。“没什么……就是，你知道的，公事。”“想跟我说说吗？”安娜说，努力把热切压到八分，而不是平素的十分。“你记得父亲总说的话吧？”艾莎偏了偏头。“什么，‘重担应当共担’？”安娜心里咯噔一下，像有颗粗粝的面包屑卡在喉咙。

sentences.en: Because…well, her family’s burdens and secrets hadn’t been for everyone.
sentences.zh: 因为……嗯，家里的重担和秘密，并非人尽可知。

sentences.en: Or at least, they hadn’t been for Anna.
sentences.zh: 至少，对安娜就不是。

sentences.en: Her father had let a mountain troll bundle away Anna’s memories of Elsa’s ice magic, and he, her mother, and Elsa had all worked together to keep it a secret from Anna.
sentences.zh: 父亲曾让一只山地地精把安娜关于艾莎冰魔法的记忆一并卷走，而他、母亲和艾莎齐心合力，对安娜瞒下了这个秘密。

sentences.en: And it had stayed a very, very big secret, until Elsa’s coronation day, when Anna had pushed the new queen a little too far and Elsa had lost control of her temper—and her ice powers.
sentences.zh: 这个秘密一直藏得很深很深，直到艾莎加冕那天，安娜把新女王逼得太过，艾莎才失控了脾气——也失控了冰力。

sentences.en: Which, at the time, had seemed as terrible as the vast and eternal winter that had taken root in the kingdom, but in hindsight had been the best thing to ever happen to Anna.
sentences.zh: 当时看来，这就像在王国扎根的无垠永冬一样可怕，可事后想来，却是发生在安娜身上最好的事。

sentences.en: Not only had it marked the beginning of a new era with her sister, but Anna had also narrowly managed to avoid a very… hasty …marriage with a prince who had deceived her. “Nope!
sentences.zh: 它不光标志了与姐姐新纪元的开端，安娜还险险避开了与一位骗了她王子的、极其……仓促……的婚姻。“不！

sentences.en: Not that one!” Anna shook her head, wishing she could shake away the uncomfortable feeling. “The other saying—the one about ‘many hands make light work.’” “Oh.” Elsa laughed. “He had a lot of sayings, didn’t he?” Anna waited for Elsa to keep talking, but she seemed to have forgotten Anna was there again even though she was trotting alongside her. “Hey, Elsa?” she tried again. “Hmm?” “Bet I can beat you to the clearing!” “What?” But Anna had already kicked Havski back into a gallop.
sentences.zh: 不是那句！”安娜摇头，恨不得把那股不舒服的感觉也甩掉。“是另一句——‘众人拾柴火焰高’那句。”“哦。”艾莎笑了。“他的格言可真多，是不是？”安娜等着艾莎接着说，可她似乎又把安娜忘了，尽管正并肩小跑着。“嘿，艾莎？”她又试了一次。“嗯？”“打赌我能比你先到空地！”“什么？”可安娜早已催动哈夫斯基重新飞奔起来。

sentences.en: Havski surged forward, setting Anna’s heart free.
sentences.zh: 哈夫斯基向前一窜，安娜的心也自由了。

sentences.en: Riding the gray horse was like riding an avalanche: fast, thrilling, and powerful.
sentences.zh: 骑这匹灰马，就像骑着一场雪崩：飞快、刺激而有力。

sentences.en: Adrenaline rushed through her, and without thinking, she let go of the reins. “What are you doing?” Elsa shouted from behind her. “Flying!” Anna shouted back.
sentences.zh: 肾上腺素在她体内奔涌，她想都没想就松开了缰绳。“你在干什么？”艾莎在身后喊。“飞！”安娜喊回去。

sentences.en: She flung out her arms.
sentences.zh: 她张开双臂。

sentences.en: Cool wind flowed over her face, and it seemed to blow away that tight feeling that had settled on her chest since Elsa had announced she was leaving.
sentences.zh: 凉风拂过她的脸，仿佛吹散了自艾莎宣布离开以来压在她胸口的那种紧绷感。

sentences.en: Elsa yelled something, but the wind swept her words away. “What?” Anna glanced over her shoulder. “BRANCH!” Elsa yelled again.
sentences.zh: 艾莎喊了句什么，却被风卷走了。“什么？”安娜回头瞥了一眼。“树枝！”艾莎又喊。

sentences.en: Anna swung forward just in time to duck beneath a birch tree’s low-hanging branch.
sentences.zh: 安娜及时向前一伏，从一棵桦树低垂的枝下闪过。

sentences.en: Giggling, she hugged Havski’s neck and the horse snorted in response, never missing a stride.
sentences.zh: 她咯咯笑着搂住哈夫斯基的脖子，马儿喷了喷鼻息回应，步子丝毫没乱。

sentences.en: And why should he?
sentences.zh: 他何必乱呢？

sentences.en: They’d grown up together, and for a long time, he’d been the closest thing Anna had had to a best friend.
sentences.zh: 他们一起长大，很长一段时间里，他几乎是安娜最亲近的“最好朋友”。

sentences.en: They’d dodged thicker branches and jumped across wider rivers together.
sentences.zh: 他们一起闪过更密的枝，一起跃过更宽的河。

sentences.en: Picking up the reins again, she kept them loose and let Havski settle into a breathless canter.
sentences.zh: 她重新拾起缰绳，松松握着，让哈夫斯基转入一阵畅快的奔驰。

sentences.en: Gradually, his strides shortened and he transitioned into an easy trot before reaching a mossy clearing.
sentences.zh: 渐渐地，他的步幅缩短，在进入一片长满青苔的空地前转为轻快的小跑。

sentences.en: There was a crunch and the sound of twigs snapping, and Anna twisted in her saddle just in time to see Elsa and Fjøra blunder into the clearing.
sentences.zh: 一阵嘎吱声和细枝折断的脆响传来，安娜在鞍上扭身，正好看见艾莎和弗约拉跌跌撞撞冲进空地。

sentences.en: A single scarlet leaf had snagged on Elsa’s hair, and it looked almost as though the forest had crowned her its autumn queen.
sentences.zh: 一片猩红的叶子挂在了艾莎发间，看起来几乎像森林为她加冕，封她为秋之女王。

sentences.en: Anna grinned. “Isn’t this fun?” Sweeping away loose strands of her blond hair, Elsa plucked the leaf off her head, looked at it, and began to laugh. “It is,” she agreed.
sentences.zh: 安娜咧嘴一笑。“这不好玩吗？”艾莎拂开散落的金发，把那片叶子从头上摘下，看了看，笑了起来。“好玩，”她表示赞同。

sentences.en: Anna felt like a miniature sun had ignited in her chest.
sentences.zh: 安娜觉得胸口里点亮了一颗小小的太阳。

sentences.en: Eventually, they neared the tamed, bountiful farmlands, and Anna, sneaking glances at Elsa, saw that her sister had finally settled into her saddle and was looking around the landscape with curious eyes.
sentences.zh: 终于，她们接近了被驯服而丰饶的农田，安娜偷瞄艾莎，见姐姐终于安稳坐进鞍里，好奇地环顾四周景色。

sentences.en: She seemed at ease.
sentences.zh: 她显得自在。

sentences.en: She seemed relaxed.
sentences.zh: 她显得放松。

sentences.en: Maybe it was time for Anna to finally ask her burning question.
sentences.zh: 也许是时候，让安娜终于问出那个憋了很久的问题了。

sentences.en: As they turned left, they passed a beautiful orchard with bright red apples and autumn leaves so orange that the world looked like it had been set aflame.
sentences.zh: 她们向左转，经过一座美丽的果园，红艳艳的苹果和橙得发亮的秋叶，让世界仿佛着了火。

sentences.en: Apples.
sentences.zh: 苹果。

sentences.en: Perfect.
sentences.zh: 完美。

sentences.en: Anna pointed at them. “Did you know that there’s an apple on the royal flag of Zaria?” she said oh-so-casually. “And that’s because it’s always customary for a guest to present an apple to the host.” A worry pricked Anna’s thoughts. “Your ship does have apples on board, right?” Elsa shook her head. “Yes, Anna—you’ve made sure of it!
sentences.zh: 安娜指向它们。“你知道扎利亚的皇家旗帜上有一只苹果吗？”她故作随意地说。“那是因为客人向来要给主人献一只苹果，这是惯例。”一丝担忧刺进安娜的心思。“你的船上备了苹果吧，对吧？”艾莎摇摇头。“备了，安娜——这可是你盯着的！

sentences.en: If I have any more barrels of gifts you’ve suggested for everyone, my ship will be too heavy to leave the harbor!” Anna swept her bangs out of her eyes and laughed. “What would you do without me?” She tugged on the reins, gently pulling Havski to a halt. “Elsa, I wanted to ask you something.
sentences.zh: 要是再装上你给每个人都建议的成桶礼物，我的船怕是重得开不出港湾了！”安娜把刘海从眼前拨开，笑了。“没我你怎么办？”她轻拉缰绳，缓缓让哈夫斯基停下。“艾莎，我想问你点事。

sentences.en: I was wondering if I could join—” But before she could finish, Havski’s ears flattened as a rustling came from nearby.
sentences.zh: 我在想我能不能一起——”可没等她说完，附近一阵窸窣声让哈夫斯基的耳朵向后贴平。

sentences.en: A villager burst from the underbrush, panting heavily as she lifted her green skirts high so she could run.
sentences.zh: 一个村民从灌木丛里冲出来，气喘吁吁，高高提起绿裙以便奔跑。

sentences.en: It took Anna a moment to place her—there were so many new villagers in Arendelle these days—but then she recognized SoYun Lim, a girl Anna’s own age who’d recently started to herd cattle on a farm not far from there.
sentences.zh: 安娜愣了一下才认出她——如今阿伦黛尔的新村民太多了——但随即她认出了林小允，一个和安娜同龄的姑娘，最近开始在附近一座农场放牛。

sentences.en: Anna had talked to her over the summer, during one of the castle’s hosted bonfire nights, and had asked her about her native country of Chatho.
sentences.zh: 安娜夏天曾在城堡举办的一场篝火夜谈上和她聊过，问起她的故国查索。

sentences.en: Research, of course, for the grand tour.
sentences.zh: 当然是为其巡游做准备的研究。

sentences.en: In fact, SoYun had been the one to help Anna perfect her Chathoanese accent.
sentences.zh: 事实上，正是小允帮安娜打磨了查索口音。

sentences.en: But that girl always seemed as calm as a lake on a windless morning, her quiet nature soothing the animals she tended.
sentences.zh: 可那姑娘向来像无风清晨的湖面般平静，她安静的性子安抚着照料的动物。

sentences.en: The girl standing in front of her now was disheveled.
sentences.zh: 此刻站在她面前的姑娘却是一副狼狈相。

sentences.en: Her jet-black braid, which usually hung as straight and tidy as a clothesline, was a series of escaping loops, and she had on two different boots—the left foot was clad in a tall black boot, while the right foot wore a soft brown leather one.
sentences.zh: 她那乌黑的辫子平时直挺挺、整齐得像晾衣绳，此刻却散成一串乱环，而且她穿了两只不一样的靴子——左脚是只高筒黑靴，右脚却是只柔软的棕色皮靴。

sentences.en: But it wasn’t the strange state of her clothes or hair that sent warning bells tolling through Anna.
sentences.zh: 可让安娜警铃大作的，不是她衣衫或头发这副怪相。

sentences.en: It was the girl’s expression—wide-eyed, as though she’d seen a ghost—and the frantic way in which she flailed her arms to catch their attention. “Your Majesty!” SoYun bobbed her head toward Elsa in a slight bow. “Thank goodness I caught up with you—something terrible has happened!”
sentences.zh: 而是那姑娘的表情——瞪大双眼，仿佛见了鬼——以及她拼命挥臂、想引起她们注意的慌张模样。“陛下！”小允朝艾莎微微低头行礼。“谢天谢地追上您了——出大事了！”

chapters.title: 第2章
chapters.en:
“SOYUN! WHAT’S WRONG?” Anna swung off Havski, landing in a pile of leaves before hurrying toward her.

“It’s my cattle,” SoYun said, looking from Elsa, who was cautiously dismounting from Fjøra, to Anna. “They’re—oh!” SoYun shook her head. “I don’t even know where to begin!” Tears formed in her eyes.

Anna opened her mouth to respond, but stopped herself to give Elsa a chance.

Elsa stepped a little closer. “How about if you take us to your cattle, and you can tell us all about it on the way? Say whatever comes first, and we’ll piece it together, all right?”

SoYun blew her nose, then nodded. “I’m just up that way,” she said, and broke into such a fast walk that it almost could have been a jog. Holding on to the horses’ reins, the sisters followed, trying to catch SoYun’s story as she told it.

“It started a few days ago,” SoYun said, her voice ragged, “when I tried to call the cattle in—you know how it usually works like a charm.”

Anna did. Calling cattle was an old Arendellian custom of singing high notes to summon the animals home. Much practice and control was required in order to do it properly, as it was so much more than a simple call. It was a fairy-like sound. A sound that raised the hair on the back of Anna’s neck and let her know—really, truly, deeply know—for one single instant that any difference between her and the earth and wind and sky was only an illusion. SoYun was now one of the best cattle callers in the village. She never had any trouble. In fact, when the cows wouldn’t come home, people always went to SoYun for help.

“And so, I went out into the fields,” SoYun continued, “and tried to sing them home. But…” Her shoulders slumped. “They never came. Not even when I pulled out my bukkehorn. I went out looking, and when I finally found them…” SoYun’s voice broke off.

“What happened?” Elsa pressed as they cleared a copse of maple trees and entered into a meadow nestled at the foothill of a blue mountain, where Anna could just make out a neat farmhouse among even neater rows of golden fields, and a herd of cattle circled around a large white boulder.

“This is what happened.” SoYun led them forward. As they got closer to the herd, Anna realized the cows weren’t ringing a white boulder after all, but a sleeping bull.

“That’s Hebert,” SoYun said. “The leader of my herd.”

Hebert. The name struck a familiar chord in Anna, and she remembered that a year before, during the harvest festival best-in-show competition, a large energetic bull with that name had won first place. But that bull’s hide had been as black as a raven’s wing, while this one was entirely white.

SoYun took a shuddery breath. “A few days ago, I noticed he had a sprinkle of white hairs, which wasn’t too strange. He’s getting up there in age. But then, the next morning, the white increased pretty dramatically, until he was as you see him now.”

Elsa raised her eyebrows, as if to say, That’s it? Some white hair?

But Anna remembered when a lock of her own hair had turned white as a result of an accidental strike from Elsa’s ice magic when they were children.

SoYun tugged on the end of her long braid and bit her bottom lip. “But I wouldn’t have bothered you just because of that, Your Majesty. There’s…there’s more.”

“Like…?” Anna didn’t take her eyes off the figure of the sleeping bull, his great horns curved up to the sky in twin points.

“He’d been acting funny for a few days, too—at first it seemed like he was scared of something he couldn’t see, like a draug,” SoYun said, referencing a terrifying mythological zombie Anna had heard spoken of around castle bonfires. “And then,” SoYun continued, “he ran around the field until he broke into a panicked sweat, which seemed to turn his fur white. And finally, his pupils grew wide, huge, until his eyes were completely swallowed by inky black.” SoYun made her eyes wide as she looked at them. “And then he started groaning like he was in horrible pain, and fell down, until, at last, he slept.”

Anna exchanged a confused look with Elsa. Anna didn’t usually think of sleep as a bad thing. In fact, the more sleep she got, the better.

Elsa’s eyebrow quirked again. “Slept?” she asked.

“Yes,” SoYun nodded vigorously. “But not a usual sleep. A deep sleep. No matter what we do—yell, shake him, splash water on him—he won’t wake up. It’s been days. Which means he also hasn’t been eating.”

Now that SoYun had mentioned it, Anna could see the bull’s ribs jutting from its sides, the white fur making it far too easy to imagine him as a pile of bones bleached by the sun. Anna wrapped her fingers in Havski’s long silky mane—she didn’t know what she would do if something like that happened to him. At the same time, any thoughts Anna had about a connection between her once-white streak of hair and the blanched bull fell away. After all, when Elsa had turned her hair white, Anna had been in danger of turning to ice, not falling asleep.

SoYun looked from the bull to the girls, and a tear rolled down her cheek. “He’s fading away right in front of us—and the other cattle are showing similar symptoms, too!” SoYun gestured to a sweet-looking cow with long lashes, and eyes that moved back and forth like the pendulum in a grandfather clock. It was as if the cow was tracking something that wasn’t there. Or rather, tracking something invisible that only the cow could see.

“What if,” SoYun continued, “they all fall into the deep sleep, and then…” The fear in the girl’s voice was tangible and sharp.

Anna reached out and hugged her close. “They’ll be okay,” Anna said. “Don’t worry. We’ll find a way to help, won’t we, Elsa?”

Elsa reached out and patted SoYun’s shoulder a few times. “Yes. You did exactly right by coming to tell me.”

Me. That small word echoed through Anna’s whole body. There had been a time, she was sure, when Elsa would have said us.

Anna spun to Elsa. “I have an idea,” she whispered. “We should visit the trolls.” Though only as tall as Anna’s waist and covered in moss, the tiny mountain trolls were the most powerful creatures Anna knew. Grand Pabbie, the oldest and arguably the wisest troll, would sometimes use the aurora’s glow to show glimpses of what might be or, occasionally, to deal with all matters that could involve magic. If anyone could help SoYun and her cattle, Anna knew it was the trolls. Because as she had learned, when mysterious happenings occurred that raised questions, it was best to visit mystical creatures for answers.

Elsa smiled. “That’s a great idea, but I think we may only have time to look in the castle library. Why don’t we try that first? Remember what Father used to say.”

Anna scrunched up her face, trying to remember which of Father’s many sayings Elsa could be referring to. “‘Anna and Elsa, always lean on each other for help’?” she guessed.

A slight smile appeared on Elsa’s lips, though it was tinged with sadness. “He did say that. But he also said, ‘The past has a way of returning.’ We should find out if this has happened before, and at the very least, gather information that might be of use for the trolls.”

Elsa made an excellent point, and Anna was suddenly excited to check the library together. Both sisters enjoyed curling up with a good storybook there, but the library also held books about the histories of the kingdom, the royal family, and the townspeople. If any place in the castle had answers, it would be there.

“Does anything help with the symptoms?” Elsa asked SoYun.

SoYun, who’d knelt down to stroke Hebert’s nose, glanced up. “Mint seems to help them stay alert. The smell is sharp for their noses, but it doesn’t last for long.”

“Mint,” Elsa repeated. “I’ll make sure to write that down in the report. Remind me, Anna, won’t you?” After making sure they had taken in all there was to know regarding the symptoms, they bade their farewells to SoYun, Hebert, and the rest of the cattle.

As Anna hauled herself onto Havski, she called back, “Don’t worry, SoYun! We’ll fix this. I promise.”

——

Anna and Elsa spent the rest of the afternoon in the castle library. So far, absolutely nothing mentioned sick cattle ever falling into seemingly endless sleeps in all of Arendelle’s history. Which meant that there were no suggestions for a cure for the Blight, as Elsa had decided to call the sleeping sickness.

Elsa sat in the window seat, flipping through a book, while Anna sprawled out on the couch in front of the fire, lifting a book overhead to read. A sharp knock resounded throughout the library, followed by Kai’s urgent voice. “Your Majesty, are you in there?”

“I’m here, Kai!” Elsa called.

The ornate door slammed open, and the usually calm man entered looking flustered, his scarf undone instead of knotted neatly at his neck and his ruddy eyebrows knitted together. Anna’s heart sped up. As steward of the castle, Kai was a man of decorum and protocol. He always bowed when he greeted them, no matter how many times the sisters had begged him to stop. But not now.

“What’s wrong, Kai?” Elsa stood up from the window alcove and hurried toward him as Anna set down her book and bolted up from the couch.

“Grave news,” Kai gasped out, sounding as though he’d run to get there. “The Westens’ entire herd of goats have seemingly dropped down in the middle of the field, and they simply won’t wake up. The family is asking for you to come quickly, Your Majesty.”

Dread crept over Anna, and she turned to Elsa. “Do you think…?”

Elsa nodded. “It’s certainly possible. But we still haven’t found an answer.” She looked from the tall piles of books to the high, full bookcases, then back at Kai, clearly torn about what she should do next.

“You should go,” Anna urged her. “Just to make sure it’s the same thing.”

Elsa tugged at her fingers, a habit Anna knew was left over from the days when Elsa always wore silk gloves to repress her powers. Anna reached out to rest a hand on Elsa’s forearm. Startled, Elsa looked down and, realizing what she had been doing, gave Anna a small smile as if to thank her. She folded her hands neatly in front of her.

“If you’re worried,” Anna said, “we should divide and conquer. Send Kristoff and Sven to the trolls, since we haven’t found anything useful, and I’ll stay here to keep looking for answers. I can handle it.”

Still, Elsa hesitated, and Anna wondered why. Did Elsa not like her recommendation? Or did Elsa not trust her to handle this job? But at last, Elsa nodded, and relief settled over Anna as her sister said, “That’s a good idea. I’ll let Kristoff know before I go, but I promise I’ll come right back.” And with that, Elsa hurried out after Kai, leaving Anna to search for solutions on her own.

Hours passed, and the wax from the candles cascaded onto the table in little pools, but Anna hardly noticed—she kept bouncing from book to book, trying to find answers…and failing. A gentle breeze twirled in from the open window, sending many of the open books’ pages fluttering, as well as scattering a sprinkle of goosebumps across Anna’s arm and stirring up the ash in the fireplace. Soon, that very same breeze would be filling Elsa’s sails to take her far, far away.

Travel by ship made Anna nervous. Seven years had passed since their parents had set out on a voyage to the Southern Sea that had been meant to last only two weeks, but had turned into forever. The days following the news had been the darkest of Anna’s life, and the nights had been worse. Sleep had been impossible. The insides of her eyelids were the color of the fathomless waves that she imagined took her parents. Sometimes, even now, her parents’ absence would startle her all over again, fresh and sudden as a bee sting. But as the years went by, the pain had become less immediate, old childhood nightmares faded, and she could remember her parents—her mother’s loving lullabies, her father’s teasing humor and tall tales—with joy.

Her reunion with Elsa had helped. When Elsa had shut herself away as a little girl, Anna was left with only her own memories of their parents. But since Elsa’s bedroom door had opened, Anna’s collection of stories about their parents had multiplied. And while the stories didn’t fill the hole in her heart, they did help smooth out the jagged edges.

She may not have her parents anymore, but she had her sister, and that was enough. Enough to make her wish Elsa wasn’t leaving her behind. She would be leaving her…unless Anna could prove her worth. Unless she could prove she was more than just the silly little girl who had talked to the portraits in the gallery and said yes to an offer of marriage to the evil (and thankfully now exiled) Prince Hans after less than twenty-four hours of knowing him. Anna knew Elsa valued her despite those things, but she still felt lingering insecurity.

Anna glanced at the stone statue of the horse that stood in the corner of the library as if it would have the answers they needed. But all it had were delicate stone seashells and starfish carved into its mane, and an angry expression on its face. It was an old statue, and Anna had been afraid of its bared teeth, its two front hooves furiously out in the air, and its blank eyes. Once, when she was four, she’d used up all of her mother’s cosmetics trying to make the horse look happier before her mother had discovered her and carried her out of the room, warning her not to touch the statue again. Young Anna was always being told not to touch things, like guitar strings, and oil paintings, and her father’s swords, and…

“Wow, what happened in here?”

Anna startled at the sound of the voice. Dragging her eyes away from the statue, she looked up to see the round shape of Olaf standing in the doorway.

As children, Elsa and Anna had made up stories about a snowman named Olaf with branches for arms and a carrot for a nose. Years later, on the day of Elsa’s coronation, Elsa had accidentally lost control of her ice powers and brought Olaf to life. Since then, he’d become the castle’s resident snowman and a member of the sisters’ family. He used to have a snow flurry hovering over his head that prevented him from melting, but since Elsa’s powers had grown and changed, she was able to do away with it and instead enchant him with a permafrost that served the same purpose. Now, Olaf’s eyes widened as he took in the library. Or rather, the mess in the library.

“It’s easier for me if I sort things into piles,” Anna explained, following his gaze to the towers of books scattered across the floor. She hadn’t realized how…enthusiastic she’d been when she’d pulled titles. There might actually have been more books on the floor than there were left on the shelves. It certainly wasn’t Elsa’s neat and methodical system, judging by the volumes Elsa had left standing in perfect stacks in the window alcove.

Olaf nodded. “That makes sense. When you build a snowman, you always have to start with piles. Unless you’re Elsa, of course.” He pointed. “Which ones are those?”

“Books about sicknesses,” Anna said. “The pile next to that is about animal anatomy, and the one next to that is about sleep.” Each title was bursting with possibilities.

Olaf moved to the last pile, his twiggy hair just visible over the stack. “And this massive one?”

“That’s my ‘to be read’ pile.”

“Oooh, it’s so much bigger than all the rest,” he observed.

Anna shrugged. She had set aside these books as not currently useful but interesting enough that she wanted to check them out later. Poems were great because of their beautiful imagery and brevity, but she also loved the thick tomes of artists through the ages. And, of course, there were novels where people found true love, or undertook a dangerous quest, or were reunited with loved ones lost.

Anna rubbed her eyes and adjusted the skirt of her dress, which had begun to bunch around her uncomfortably. “Where have you been?” she asked.

Olaf wandered from pile to pile. “The village library, listening to a lecture on Dante’s Inferno—the hotter the tale, the better.”

Anna smiled. After her first birthday party following Elsa’s eternal winter, Anna had taught Olaf how to read, and ever since, the snowman had become obsessed. He liked books of all sizes, but his favorites were the thick tomes on philosophy—and beach reads, which he so often insisted were just as important as the classics. Anna didn’t disagree.

“So, why are you rearranging the library, anyway?” Olaf asked.

Taking a deep breath, Anna quickly explained about SoYun and her cattle and how Elsa was out now, checking on the Westens’ goats.

“It seems that you could use some help,” Olaf said, straightening a coal button. “And in the wise words of many a philosopher, four eyeballs are better than three.”

“Is that what they say?” Anna asked, resting her head on her palm.

Olaf whipped out his favorite pair of ice spectacles, specially made for him by Elsa. “Indeed,” he said. “They also say to ‘start at the beginning.’ So, we’ll start with the letter B, for beginning.” He pointed, and Anna followed his scraggly finger to the middle shelf of the nearest bookshelf behind the horse statue.

“Sure,” Anna said. “You look at that while I finish this one.”

Olaf clambered onto a table beneath a portrait of King Agnarr’s coronation, then jumped onto the stone horse’s back. Carefully, he shimmied onto one of the rearing legs and pulled himself up, wobbling precariously from side to side. “Almost…” he said, reaching out.

Anna could see he was struggling, so she leapt up and hurried over to him.

“Just a little bit further—whoops!” There was a click followed by a great grinding, like the sound of gears turning on each other, as the horse’s rearing leg that Olaf stood on sank down like a lever. Dust swirled into the air, and Anna squeezed her eyes shut, turning her head away to avoid swallowing any more of the grime. And then…everything was still.

Everything was silent.

“Wow,” Olaf breathed. “Now that’s something you don’t see every day.”

Anna’s eyes flew open, and she gasped.

The bookcase behind the statue had swung inward like a door. No, not like a door. It was an actual door, opening to reveal an arched entryway and, beyond it, darkness. And maybe—just maybe—something that would hold answers and help Elsa figure out how to cure the Blight.

Squealing, Anna plunged into the secret room—and immediately crashed her shins against something. She winced. Whatever she’d hit was definitely going to leave a bruise. Why hadn’t she thought to grab a candle? Turning to head back, she saw Olaf waddling toward her, a candle in his hand. He stopped in front of her, the flame casting a creamy orange glow across his concerned face.

He raised a skeptical eyebrow. “I thought you couldn’t see in the dark.”

“I can’t,” Anna said. “Do you mind sharing the light?”

“Nope!” Olaf handed it to her. “You’ll need it to see that person standing right behind you.”
chapters.zh:
“小允！

怎么了？”安娜翻身下了哈夫斯基，落进一堆落叶里，随即朝她奔去。“是我的牛，”小允说，目光从正小心下弗约拉的艾莎身上移到安娜身上。“它们——噢！”小允摇摇头。“我都不知道从哪儿说起！”她眼里泛起泪花。

安娜张嘴想回应，却停住，把机会留给艾莎。

艾莎走近了些。“你带我们去看看你的牛，路上再全讲给我们听，怎么样？

想到什么先说什么，我们拼起来就行，好吗？”小允擤了擤鼻子，点点头。“就在那边，”她说，然后迈开飞快的步子，几乎要跑起来。

姐妹俩牵着缰绳跟上，努力听清小允讲述的故事。“几天前开始的，”小允声音沙哑，“我试着把牛唤回来——你知道那法子平时特别灵。”安娜知道。

唤牛是阿伦黛尔古老的风俗，用高音歌唱把牲口召唤回家。

要做得好，需大量练习与控制，因为这远不止一声简单的呼唤。

那是一种如精灵般的声音。

那声音让安娜颈后的汗毛竖起，让她在那一瞬——真切地、深深地、彻底地——明白，她与大地、风与天空之间的一切分别，都只是幻象。

小允如今是村中最出色的唤牛人之一。

她从来没有麻烦。

事实上，牛不肯回家时，人们总去找小允帮忙。“于是，我走到田里，”小允继续说，“想唱它们回家。

可……”她肩膀塌了下来。“它们再也没回来。

连我拿出牧羊号角也不行。

我出去找，终于找到它们时……”小允的声音断了。“怎么了？”艾莎追问道。她们穿过一片枫树林，进入一片偎在蓝山山脚下的草甸，安娜隐约辨认出整齐农舍立于更整齐的金色田垄间，一群牛正围着一块白色大圆石。“就是这般光景。”小允引着她们上前。

越靠近牛群，安娜才看清，牛们围着的并非白石，而是一头熟睡的公牛。“那是赫伯特，”小允说。“我牛群的首领。”赫伯特。

这名字在安娜心里拨动熟悉的一弦，她记起一年前丰收节的“最佳展示”比赛上，一头叫这名字、精力充沛的大公牛得了头名。

可那头牛的皮毛黑如乌鸦翅，而这头却通体雪白。

小允颤着吸了口气。“几天前，我注意到他冒出几根白毛，倒也不算怪。

他年岁不小了。

可第二天一早，白毛剧增，直到变成你如今看到的样子。”艾莎挑了挑眉，仿佛在说：就这？

几根白毛？

可安娜记得，小时候因艾莎冰力意外击中，自己也曾有一绺头发变白。

小允扯了扯长辫的末梢，咬住下唇。“可我不会因为这点就打扰您，陛下。

还有……还有别的。”“比如……？”安娜目不转睛地盯着那头熟睡公牛的身形，他巨大的双角如双尖朝天弯起。“他这几天举止也古怪——起初像在怕什么看不见的东西，比如draug（一种恐怖的神话僵尸，安娜在城堡篝火边听人讲过），”小允说。“然后，”小允继续，“他在场上乱跑，直到吓出一身冷汗，那汗仿佛把他的毛变白了。

最后，他的瞳孔放大、变得巨大，直到眼睛完全被墨黑吞没。”小允瞪大眼睛看着她们。“然后他开始呻吟，像在忍受剧痛，倒下，终于，睡着了。”安娜与艾莎交换了一个困惑的眼神。

安娜平时不觉得睡觉是坏事。

事实上，她睡得越多越好。

艾莎的眉又挑了一下。“睡着了？”她问。“对，”小允用力点头。“但不是寻常的睡。

是沉睡。

不管我们做什么——喊、摇、泼水——他都醒不过来。

已经好几天了。

也就是说，他也没吃东西了。”经小允一提，安娜才看见公牛的肋骨从体侧凸出，那白毛太容易让人把他想成一堆被太阳漂白的骨头。

安娜把手指缠进哈夫斯基长长的丝滑鬃毛里——她不敢想，若这事发生在他身上该怎么办。

同时，安娜任何关于自己那缕曾变白的头发与这头褪色公牛之间关联的念头，也都消散了。

毕竟，当初艾莎把她的头发变白时，安娜面临的是冻成冰的危险，而非昏睡。

小允把目光从公牛移到姐妹俩身上，一滴泪滑下脸颊。“他就在我们眼前一点点消逝——别的牛也出现类似症状了！”小允指向一头模样温顺、睫毛长长、眼睛像落地大摆钟的钟摆般来回转动的母牛。

仿佛那牛在追踪什么并不存在之物。

更确切地说，在追踪只有那牛能看见的隐形之物。“倘若，”小允继续，“它们全陷入沉睡，然后……”女孩声音里的恐惧真切而尖锐。

安娜伸出手，把她搂近。“会没事的，”安娜说。“别担心。

我们会找到办法帮忙的，对吧，艾莎？”艾莎伸手轻拍了小允肩膀几下。“对。

你来告诉我，做得完全对。”我。

这个小小的字眼在安娜全身回荡。

她确信，曾几何时，艾莎会说“我们”。

安娜转向艾莎。“我有个主意，”她低声说。“我们该去见地精。”那些山地小地精虽只到安娜腰高、满身青苔，却是安娜所知最强大的生灵。

最年长、或许也最睿智的地精皮比，有时会借极光的光晕，显现未来可能的片段，偶尔也处理一切与魔法相关的事务。

若谁能帮小允和她的牛，安娜知道，那便是地精。

因为她已懂得，当神秘之事发生、引人疑问时，最好去拜访神异生灵寻求答案。

艾莎笑了。“这主意很棒，可我想我们或许只够时间去城堡图书馆查查。

我们何不先试试那儿？

记得父亲以前常说的话吗。”安娜皱起脸，努力回想艾莎指的是父亲哪句格言。“‘安娜与艾莎，永远互相依靠’？”她猜。

艾莎唇边浮起一丝微笑，却带着些许哀伤。“他的确说过。

可他也说过，‘过去总会有回来的方式。’我们该弄清这事是否发生过，至少，收集些对地精有用的信息。”艾莎说得极是，安娜忽然兴奋起来，想一起去图书馆查。

姐妹俩都爱在那里裹着好书窝着读，可图书馆还藏着关于王国史、王室与镇民的书。

若城堡里哪处藏有答案，必是那儿。“有什么能缓解这些症状吗？”艾莎问小允。

跪下轻抚赫伯特鼻子的小允抬起眼。“薄荷似乎能帮它们保持清醒。

那气味对它们的鼻子很冲，但持续不久。”“薄荷，”艾莎重复。“我定会写进报告里。

提醒我，安娜，好吗？”确认已记下所有关于症状该知的之后，她们向小允、赫伯特和其余的牛道了别。

安娜爬上哈夫斯基时回头喊道，“别担心，小允！

我们会解决的。

我保证。”——安娜和艾莎在城堡图书馆度过了那天下午余下的时光。

到目前为止，阿伦黛尔所有历史中，绝无任何记载说病牛曾陷入看似无尽的沉睡。

这意味着，对于艾莎命名的这种昏睡症“枯萎病”，毫无治疗建议。

艾莎坐在窗边座翻书，安娜则瘫在炉前沙发上，把书举过头顶读。

一声急促的敲门响彻图书馆，接着是凯伊急切的声音。“陛下，您在里头吗？”“我在，凯伊！”艾莎喊。

那扇华丽的门猛地被推开，平日镇定的男人神色慌张地进来，围巾没在颈上系好而是松着，红润的眉毛拧成一团。

安娜的心加速跳了起来。

作为城堡管家，凯伊是个讲究礼节与规矩的人。

无论姐妹俩恳求过多少次让他别鞠躬，他每次问候必鞠躬。

可现在没有。“怎么了，凯伊？”艾莎从窗凹处站起，朝他奔去，安娜也放下书从沙发上弹起。“坏消息，”凯伊喘着气，像是一路跑来的。“韦斯顿家整群山羊似乎在田中央倒了下去，怎么都叫不醒。

那家人请您快去，陛下。”恐惧爬上安娜，她转向艾莎。“你觉得……？”艾莎点头。“很有可能是。

可我们还没找到答案。”她从高高叠起的书堆望向满当当的大书架，又回头看凯伊，显然对下一步拿不定主意。“你该去，”安娜催她。“就去确认是不是同一回事。”艾莎拽着手指——安娜认得，这是她从前总戴丝手套压抑魔力时留下的习惯。

安娜伸手，把手搭在艾莎前臂上。

艾莎一惊，低头看见自己在做什么，给了安娜一个浅浅的微笑，像在道谢。

她把双手整齐交叠身前。“你若担心，”安娜说，“我们不如分头行动。

既然我们没找到有用的，就派克斯托夫和斯文去见地精，我留在这儿继续找答案。

我应付得来。”可艾莎仍犹豫，安娜疑惑为何。

是艾莎不喜欢她的建议？

还是艾莎不放心她来做这事？

但终于，艾莎点头，安娜松了口气，姐姐说：“这主意不错。

我走前会知会克斯托夫，但我保证马上回来。”说罢，艾莎随凯伊匆匆离去，留下安娜独自寻找对策。

几小时过去，蜡烛的蜡在小水洼般淌到桌上，安娜却几乎没注意——她不停从一本书跳到另一本，想找答案……却徒劳。

一阵和风从敞开的窗旋入，吹得许多摊开的书页翻飞，也把一层鸡皮疙瘩撒在安娜臂上，搅起壁炉里的灰。

很快，这同一阵风就要鼓满艾莎的帆，送她去很远、很远的地方。

乘船旅行让安娜不安。

自父母启程前往南海——本只该为期两周，却成了永别——已过去了七年。

噩耗之后的那些白昼，是安娜一生最黑暗的，而夜晚更糟。

那时根本无法入睡。

她眼皮内侧，是她想象中带走父母的、那无底海浪的颜色。

有时，即便现在，父母的缺席仍会像蜂蜇般新鲜而骤然地惊她一下。

可随着岁月流逝，痛苦不再那么切近，童年旧噩梦淡去，她已能欢喜地记起父母——母亲温柔的摇篮曲，父亲戏谑的幽默与奇谈。

她与艾莎的重逢帮了忙。

当艾莎小时候把自己关起来时，安娜只剩自己对父母的记忆。

可自艾莎的卧室门打开后，安娜关于父母的故事收藏翻了倍。

故事虽填不满她心里的洞，却帮她磨平了尖锐的边缘。

她或许不再有父母，但她有姐姐，这就够了。

够让她但愿艾莎别把她抛下。

艾莎要丢下她了……除非安娜能证明自己的价值。

除非她能证明，自己不只是那个对着画廊画像说话、认识邪恶（所幸现已流放）的汉斯王子不到二十四小时就答应婚事的小傻瓜。

安娜知道艾莎看重她，尽管有那些事，她仍残留着不安。

安娜瞥了眼立在图书馆角落的石马像，仿佛它能给出所需答案。

可它有的，只是雕在鬃毛里的精致石贝壳与海星，以及一脸怒容。

那是座老雕像，安娜曾怕它龇出的牙、腾在空中的两只前蹄，和那双空洞的眼。

有一次，她四岁时，曾用光母亲所有的化妆品想让马显得开心些，直到母亲发现，把她抱出房间，警告她别再碰雕像。

小安娜总被叮嘱别碰东西，比如吉他弦、油画、父亲的剑，还有……“哇，这儿怎么了？”那声音吓了安娜一跳。

她把目光从雕像上扯开，抬头看见奥拉夫圆滚滚的身影立在门口。

小时候，艾莎和安娜编过关于一个叫奥拉夫的雪人的故事，那雪人用树枝当手臂、胡萝卜当鼻子。

多年后，在艾莎加冕那天，艾莎意外失控冰力，把奥拉夫变活了。

自那以后，他成了城堡的常驻雪人，也成了姐妹一家的一员。

他头顶曾有一团雪霰悬着防止融化，可随着艾莎魔力增长变化，她去掉了那团雪，改用永冻术为他施咒，作用相同。

此刻，奥拉夫睁大眼，打量着图书馆。

更确切地说，打量着图书馆的乱象。“我把它分成堆，方便些，”安娜解释，顺着他的目光看向散落一地的书塔。

她没意识到自己抽书时有多……起劲。

地上的书，说不定比架上剩下的还多。

看艾莎留在窗凹处码得齐整的书堆，这绝非艾莎那套整齐而系统的方法。

奥拉夫点头。“说得通。

堆雪人时，总得从一堆堆开始。

除非你是艾莎，当然。”他指了指。“那些是哪堆？”“讲疾病的书，”安娜说。“旁边那堆是动物解剖，再旁边是讲睡眠的。”每本书名都充满可能。

奥拉夫挪到最后一堆，枝丫般的头发刚从书堆上露出来。“这巨堆呢？”“那是我的‘待读’堆。”“噢，比其余所有都大得多，”他评论道。

安娜耸耸肩。

这些书她先搁在一边，眼下没用，却有趣得让她想日后翻翻。

诗极好，因其意象优美而简短，可她也爱历代艺术家的厚重大部头。

当然，还有那些小说：有人寻得真爱，有人踏上险途，有人与失散的所爱重逢。

安娜揉揉眼，整了整开始不舒服地缠在身上的裙摆。“你刚在哪儿？”她问。

奥拉夫在书堆间晃悠。“在村里的图书馆，听一场但丁《神曲·地狱篇》的讲座——故事越火热越好。”安娜笑了。

在艾莎永冬后的第一次生日宴上，安娜教会了奥拉夫识字，自那以后，这雪人就痴迷上了。

他爱各种开本的书，最爱的却是哲学厚本——还有海滩读物，他常坚称它们与经典同样重要。

安娜不反对。“话说，你到底为什么在重排图书馆？”奥拉夫问。

安娜深吸一口气，飞快讲了小允和她的牛，以及艾莎此刻外出查看韦斯顿家的山羊。“看来你需要帮手，”奥拉夫说，正了正一颗煤纽扣。“用许多哲学家明智的话说，四只眼胜三只眼。”“他们真这么说的？”安娜问，把头枕在掌心。

奥拉夫抽出他最爱的那副冰眼镜——艾莎特意为他做的。“确实，”他说。“他们还说‘从头开始’。所以，我们从字母B、代表beginning开始。”他一指，安娜顺着他毛糙的手指看向石马像后最近书架的中层。“行，”安娜说。“你看那层，我把这堆看完。”奥拉夫爬上阿格瑞国王加冕画像下的桌子，又跳上石马背。

他小心地挪到一只腾空的前腿上，攀上去，左右危险地晃。“快了……”他伸出手说。

安娜见他吃力，便跳起奔过去。“再差一点点——哎呀！”一声咔哒后跟着巨大的研磨声，像齿轮互相咬合转动，奥拉夫所站的马腿如杠杆般沉了下去。

灰尘打着旋腾起，安娜紧闭双眼，别过头去，免得再吞下更多污垢。

然后……一切静止。

一切寂然。“哇，”奥拉夫轻叹。“这可真不是天天能见到的。”安娜猛地睁眼，倒吸一口气。

雕像后的书柜像门一样向内转开了。

不，不像门。

它就是一扇真正的门，敞开露出拱形入口，入口之后是黑暗。

而也许——只是也许——那里藏着答案，能帮艾莎想出治愈枯萎病的法子。

安娜尖叫着冲进密室——立刻把小腿撞上了什么。

她龇牙一缩。

不管撞到的是什么，准会留块淤青。

她怎么就没想到抓支蜡烛？

她转身要回去，却见奥拉夫摇摇摆摆朝她走来，手里拿着一支蜡烛。

他在她面前停下，火苗在他担忧的脸上投下乳橙色的光。

他挑起一只怀疑的眉。“我以为你在黑暗里看不见。”“我是看不见，”安娜说。“介意分享一下光吗？”“不介意！”奥拉夫把蜡烛递给她。“你正需要它，好看清就站在你身后的那个人。”

sentences.en: A sound that raised the hair on the back of Anna’s neck and let her know—really, truly, deeply know —for one single instant that any difference between her and the earth and wind and sky was only an illusion.
sentences.zh: 那声音让安娜颈后的汗毛竖起，让她在那一瞬——真切地、深深地、彻底地——明白，她与大地、风与天空之间的一切分别，都只是幻象。

sentences.en: SoYun was now one of the best cattle callers in the village.
sentences.zh: 小允如今是村中最出色的唤牛人之一。

sentences.en: She never had any trouble.
sentences.zh: 她从来没有麻烦。

sentences.en: But…” Her shoulders slumped. “They never came.
sentences.zh: 可……”她肩膀塌了下来。“它们再也没回来。

sentences.en: I went out looking, and when I finally found them…” SoYun’s voice broke off. “What happened?” Elsa pressed as they cleared a copse of maple trees and entered into a meadow nestled at the foothill of a blue mountain, where Anna could just make out a neat farmhouse among even neater rows of golden fields, and a herd of cattle circled around a large white boulder. “ This is what happened.” SoYun led them forward.
sentences.zh: 我出去找，终于找到它们时……”小允的声音断了。“怎么了？”艾莎追问道。她们穿过一片枫树林，进入一片偎在蓝山山脚下的草甸，安娜隐约辨认出整齐农舍立于更整齐的金色田垄间，一群牛正围着一块白色大圆石。“就是这般光景。”小允引着她们上前。

sentences.en: As they got closer to the herd, Anna realized the cows weren’t ringing a white boulder after all, but a sleeping bull. “That’s Hebert,” SoYun said. “The leader of my herd.” Hebert.

sentences.en: The name struck a familiar chord in Anna, and she remembered that a year before, during the harvest festival best-in-show competition, a large energetic bull with that name had won first place.
sentences.zh: 这名字在安娜心里拨动熟悉的一弦，她记起一年前丰收节的“最佳展示”比赛上，一头叫这名字、精力充沛的大公牛得了头名。

sentences.en: But then, the next morning, the white increased pretty dramatically, until he was as you see him now.” Elsa raised her eyebrows, as if to say, That’s it?
sentences.zh: 可第二天一早，白毛剧增，直到变成你如今看到的样子。”艾莎挑了挑眉，仿佛在说：就这？

sentences.zh: 几根白毛？

sentences.zh: 可安娜记得，小时候因艾莎冰力意外击中，自己也曾有一绺头发变白。

sentences.en: SoYun tugged on the end of her long braid and bit her bottom lip. “But I wouldn’t have bothered you just because of that, Your Majesty.
sentences.zh: 小允扯了扯长辫的末梢，咬住下唇。“可我不会因为这点就打扰您，陛下。

sentences.en: There’s…there’s more.” “Like…?” Anna didn’t take her eyes off the figure of the sleeping bull, his great horns curved up to the sky in twin points. “He’d been acting funny for a few days, too—at first it seemed like he was scared of something he couldn’t see, like a draug,” SoYun said, referencing a terrifying mythological zombie Anna had heard spoken of around castle bonfires. “And then,” SoYun continued, “he ran around the field until he broke into a panicked sweat, which seemed to turn his fur white.
sentences.zh: 还有……还有别的。”“比如……？”安娜目不转睛地盯着那头熟睡公牛的身形，他巨大的双角如双尖朝天弯起。“他这几天举止也古怪——起初像在怕什么看不见的东西，比如draug（一种恐怖的神话僵尸，安娜在城堡篝火边听人讲过），”小允说。“然后，”小允继续，“他在场上乱跑，直到吓出一身冷汗，那汗仿佛把他的毛变白了。

sentences.en: And finally, his pupils grew wide, huge , until his eyes were completely swallowed by inky black.” SoYun made her eyes wide as she looked at them. “And then he started groaning like he was in horrible pain, and fell down, until, at last, he slept.” Anna exchanged a confused look with Elsa.
sentences.zh: 最后，他的瞳孔放大、变得巨大，直到眼睛完全被墨黑吞没。”小允瞪大眼睛看着她们。“然后他开始呻吟，像在忍受剧痛，倒下，终于，睡着了。”安娜与艾莎交换了一个困惑的眼神。

sentences.en: Anna didn’t usually think of sleep as a bad thing.
sentences.zh: 安娜平时不觉得睡觉是坏事。

sentences.en: In fact, the more sleep she got, the better.
sentences.zh: 事实上，她睡得越多越好。

sentences.en: Elsa’s eyebrow quirked again. “Slept?” she asked. “Yes,” SoYun nodded vigorously. “But not a usual sleep.
sentences.zh: 艾莎的眉又挑了一下。“睡着了？”她问。“对，”小允用力点头。“但不是寻常的睡。

sentences.en: A deep sleep.
sentences.zh: 是沉睡。

sentences.en: No matter what we do—yell, shake him, splash water on him—he won’t wake up.
sentences.zh: 不管我们做什么——喊、摇、泼水——他都醒不过来。

sentences.en: It’s been days.
sentences.zh: 已经好几天了。

sentences.en: Which means he also hasn’t been eating.” Now that SoYun had mentioned it, Anna could see the bull’s ribs jutting from its sides, the white fur making it far too easy to imagine him as a pile of bones bleached by the sun.
sentences.zh: 也就是说，他也没吃东西了。”经小允一提，安娜才看见公牛的肋骨从体侧凸出，那白毛太容易让人把他想成一堆被太阳漂白的骨头。

sentences.en: Anna wrapped her fingers in Havski’s long silky mane—she didn’t know what she would do if something like that happened to him.
sentences.zh: 安娜把手指缠进哈夫斯基长长的丝滑鬃毛里——她不敢想，若这事发生在他身上该怎么办。

sentences.en: At the same time, any thoughts Anna had about a connection between her once-white streak of hair and the blanched bull fell away.
sentences.zh: 同时，安娜任何关于自己那缕曾变白的头发与这头褪色公牛之间关联的念头，也都消散了。

sentences.en: After all, when Elsa had turned her hair white, Anna had been in danger of turning to ice, not falling asleep.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，当初艾莎把她的头发变白时，安娜面临的是冻成冰的危险，而非昏睡。

sentences.en: SoYun looked from the bull to the girls, and a tear rolled down her cheek. “He’s fading away right in front of us—and the other cattle are showing similar symptoms, too!” SoYun gestured to a sweet-looking cow with long lashes, and eyes that moved back and forth like the pendulum in a grandfather clock.
sentences.zh: 小允把目光从公牛移到姐妹俩身上，一滴泪滑下脸颊。“他就在我们眼前一点点消逝——别的牛也出现类似症状了！”小允指向一头模样温顺、睫毛长长、眼睛像落地大摆钟的钟摆般来回转动的母牛。

sentences.en: It was as if the cow was tracking something that wasn’t there.
sentences.zh: 仿佛那牛在追踪什么并不存在之物。

sentences.en: Or rather, tracking something invisible that only the cow could see. “What if,” SoYun continued, “they all fall into the deep sleep, and then…” The fear in the girl’s voice was tangible and sharp.
sentences.zh: 更确切地说，在追踪只有那牛能看见的隐形之物。“倘若，”小允继续，“它们全陷入沉睡，然后……”女孩声音里的恐惧真切而尖锐。

sentences.en: Anna reached out and hugged her close. “They’ll be okay,” Anna said. “Don’t worry.
sentences.zh: 安娜伸出手，把她搂近。“会没事的，”安娜说。“别担心。

sentences.en: We’ll find a way to help, won’t we, Elsa?” Elsa reached out and patted SoYun’s shoulder a few times. “Yes.
sentences.zh: 我们会找到办法帮忙的，对吧，艾莎？”艾莎伸手轻拍了小允肩膀几下。“对。

sentences.en: You did exactly right by coming to tell me.” Me.
sentences.zh: 你来告诉我，做得完全对。”我。

sentences.en: That small word echoed through Anna’s whole body.
sentences.zh: 这个小小的字眼在安娜全身回荡。

sentences.en: There had been a time, she was sure, when Elsa would have said us .
sentences.zh: 她确信，曾几何时，艾莎会说“我们”。

sentences.en: Anna spun to Elsa. “I have an idea,” she whispered. “We should visit the trolls.” Though only as tall as Anna’s waist and covered in moss, the tiny mountain trolls were the most powerful creatures Anna knew.
sentences.zh: 安娜转向艾莎。“我有个主意，”她低声说。“我们该去见地精。”那些山地小地精虽只到安娜腰高、满身青苔，却是安娜所知最强大的生灵。

sentences.en: Grand Pabbie, the oldest and arguably the wisest troll, would sometimes use the aurora’s glow to show glimpses of what might be or, occasionally, to deal with all matters that could involve magic.
sentences.zh: 最年长、或许也最睿智的地精皮比，有时会借极光的光晕，显现未来可能的片段，偶尔也处理一切与魔法相关的事务。

sentences.en: If anyone could help SoYun and her cattle, Anna knew it was the trolls.
sentences.zh: 若谁能帮小允和她的牛，安娜知道，那便是地精。

sentences.en: Because as she had learned, when mysterious happenings occurred that raised questions, it was best to visit mystical creatures for answers.
sentences.zh: 因为她已懂得，当神秘之事发生、引人疑问时，最好去拜访神异生灵寻求答案。

sentences.en: Elsa smiled. “That’s a great idea, but I think we may only have time to look in the castle library.
sentences.zh: 艾莎笑了。“这主意很棒，可我想我们或许只够时间去城堡图书馆查查。

sentences.en: Why don’t we try that first?
sentences.zh: 我们何不先试试那儿？

sentences.en: Remember what Father used to say.” Anna scrunched up her face, trying to remember which of Father’s many sayings Elsa could be referring to. “‘Anna and Elsa, always lean on each other for help’?” she guessed.
sentences.zh: 记得父亲以前常说的话吗。”安娜皱起脸，努力回想艾莎指的是父亲哪句格言。“‘安娜与艾莎，永远互相依靠’？”她猜。

sentences.en: A slight smile appeared on Elsa’s lips, though it was tinged with sadness. “He did say that.
sentences.zh: 艾莎唇边浮起一丝微笑，却带着些许哀伤。“他的确说过。

sentences.en: But he also said, ‘The past has a way of returning.’ We should find out if this has happened before, and at the very least, gather information that might be of use for the trolls.” Elsa made an excellent point, and Anna was suddenly excited to check the library together.
sentences.zh: 可他也说过，‘过去总会有回来的方式。’我们该弄清这事是否发生过，至少，收集些对地精有用的信息。”艾莎说得极是，安娜忽然兴奋起来，想一起去图书馆查。

sentences.en: Both sisters enjoyed curling up with a good storybook there, but the library also held books about the histories of the kingdom, the royal family, and the townspeople.
sentences.zh: 姐妹俩都爱在那里裹着好书窝着读，可图书馆还藏着关于王国史、王室与镇民的书。

sentences.en: If any place in the castle had answers, it would be there. “Does anything help with the symptoms?” Elsa asked SoYun.
sentences.zh: 若城堡里哪处藏有答案，必是那儿。“有什么能缓解这些症状吗？”艾莎问小允。

sentences.en: SoYun, who’d knelt down to stroke Hebert’s nose, glanced up. “Mint seems to help them stay alert.
sentences.zh: 跪下轻抚赫伯特鼻子的小允抬起眼。“薄荷似乎能帮它们保持清醒。

sentences.en: The smell is sharp for their noses, but it doesn’t last for long.” “Mint,” Elsa repeated. “I’ll make sure to write that down in the report.
sentences.zh: 那气味对它们的鼻子很冲，但持续不久。”“薄荷，”艾莎重复。“我定会写进报告里。

sentences.en: Remind me, Anna, won’t you?” After making sure they had taken in all there was to know regarding the symptoms, they bade their farewells to SoYun, Hebert, and the rest of the cattle.
sentences.zh: 提醒我，安娜，好吗？”确认已记下所有关于症状该知的之后，她们向小允、赫伯特和其余的牛道了别。

sentences.en: As Anna hauled herself onto Havski, she called back, “Don’t worry, SoYun!
sentences.zh: 安娜爬上哈夫斯基时回头喊道，“别担心，小允！

sentences.en: We’ll fix this.
sentences.zh: 我们会解决的。

sentences.en: I promise.” —— Anna and Elsa spent the rest of the afternoon in the castle library.
sentences.zh: 我保证。”——安娜和艾莎在城堡图书馆度过了那天下午余下的时光。

sentences.en: So far, absolutely nothing mentioned sick cattle ever falling into seemingly endless sleeps in all of Arendelle’s history.
sentences.zh: 到目前为止，阿伦黛尔所有历史中，绝无任何记载说病牛曾陷入看似无尽的沉睡。

sentences.en: Which meant that there were no suggestions for a cure for the Blight, as Elsa had decided to call the sleeping sickness.
sentences.zh: 这意味着，对于艾莎命名的这种昏睡症“枯萎病”，毫无治疗建议。

sentences.en: Elsa sat in the window seat, flipping through a book, while Anna sprawled out on the couch in front of the fire, lifting a book overhead to read.
sentences.zh: 艾莎坐在窗边座翻书，安娜则瘫在炉前沙发上，把书举过头顶读。

sentences.en: A sharp knock resounded throughout the library, followed by Kai’s urgent voice. “Your Majesty, are you in there?” “I’m here, Kai!” Elsa called.
sentences.zh: 一声急促的敲门响彻图书馆，接着是凯伊急切的声音。“陛下，您在里头吗？”“我在，凯伊！”艾莎喊。

sentences.en: The ornate door slammed open, and the usually calm man entered looking flustered, his scarf undone instead of knotted neatly at his neck and his ruddy eyebrows knitted together.
sentences.zh: 那扇华丽的门猛地被推开，平日镇定的男人神色慌张地进来，围巾没在颈上系好而是松着，红润的眉毛拧成一团。

sentences.en: Anna’s heart sped up.
sentences.zh: 安娜的心加速跳了起来。

sentences.en: As steward of the castle, Kai was a man of decorum and protocol.
sentences.zh: 作为城堡管家，凯伊是个讲究礼节与规矩的人。

sentences.en: He always bowed when he greeted them, no matter how many times the sisters had begged him to stop.
sentences.zh: 无论姐妹俩恳求过多少次让他别鞠躬，他每次问候必鞠躬。

sentences.en: But not now. “What’s wrong, Kai?” Elsa stood up from the window alcove and hurried toward him as Anna set down her book and bolted up from the couch. “Grave news,” Kai gasped out, sounding as though he’d run to get there. “The Westens’ entire herd of goats have seemingly dropped down in the middle of the field, and they simply won’t wake up.
sentences.zh: 可现在没有。“怎么了，凯伊？”艾莎从窗凹处站起，朝他奔去，安娜也放下书从沙发上弹起。“坏消息，”凯伊喘着气，像是一路跑来的。“韦斯顿家整群山羊似乎在田中央倒了下去，怎么都叫不醒。

sentences.en: The family is asking for you to come quickly, Your Majesty.” Dread crept over Anna, and she turned to Elsa. “Do you think…?” Elsa nodded. “It’s certainly possible.
sentences.zh: 那家人请您快去，陛下。”恐惧爬上安娜，她转向艾莎。“你觉得……？”艾莎点头。“很有可能是。

sentences.en: But we still haven’t found an answer.” She looked from the tall piles of books to the high, full bookcases, then back at Kai, clearly torn about what she should do next. “You should go,” Anna urged her. “Just to make sure it’s the same thing.” Elsa tugged at her fingers, a habit Anna knew was left over from the days when Elsa always wore silk gloves to repress her powers.
sentences.zh: 可我们还没找到答案。”她从高高叠起的书堆望向满当当的大书架，又回头看凯伊，显然对下一步拿不定主意。“你该去，”安娜催她。“就去确认是不是同一回事。”艾莎拽着手指——安娜认得，这是她从前总戴丝手套压抑魔力时留下的习惯。

sentences.en: Anna reached out to rest a hand on Elsa’s forearm.
sentences.zh: 安娜伸手，把手搭在艾莎前臂上。

sentences.en: Startled, Elsa looked down and, realizing what she had been doing, gave Anna a small smile as if to thank her.
sentences.zh: 艾莎一惊，低头看见自己在做什么，给了安娜一个浅浅的微笑，像在道谢。

sentences.en: She folded her hands neatly in front of her. “If you’re worried,” Anna said, “we should divide and conquer.
sentences.zh: 她把双手整齐交叠身前。“你若担心，”安娜说，“我们不如分头行动。

sentences.en: Send Kristoff and Sven to the trolls, since we haven’t found anything useful, and I’ll stay here to keep looking for answers.
sentences.zh: 既然我们没找到有用的，就派克斯托夫和斯文去见地精，我留在这儿继续找答案。

sentences.en: I can handle it.” Still, Elsa hesitated, and Anna wondered why.
sentences.zh: 我应付得来。”可艾莎仍犹豫，安娜疑惑为何。

sentences.en: Did Elsa not like her recommendation?
sentences.zh: 是艾莎不喜欢她的建议？

sentences.en: Or did Elsa not trust her to handle this job?
sentences.zh: 还是艾莎不放心她来做这事？

sentences.en: But at last, Elsa nodded, and relief settled over Anna as her sister said, “That’s a good idea.
sentences.zh: 但终于，艾莎点头，安娜松了口气，姐姐说：“这主意不错。

sentences.en: I’ll let Kristoff know before I go, but I promise I’ll come right back.” And with that, Elsa hurried out after Kai, leaving Anna to search for solutions on her own.
sentences.zh: 我走前会知会克斯托夫，但我保证马上回来。”说罢，艾莎随凯伊匆匆离去，留下安娜独自寻找对策。

sentences.en: Hours passed, and the wax from the candles cascaded onto the table in little pools, but Anna hardly noticed—she kept bouncing from book to book, trying to find answers…and failing.
sentences.zh: 几小时过去，蜡烛的蜡在小水洼般淌到桌上，安娜却几乎没注意——她不停从一本书跳到另一本，想找答案……却徒劳。

sentences.en: A gentle breeze twirled in from the open window, sending many of the open books’ pages fluttering, as well as scattering a sprinkle of goosebumps across Anna’s arm and stirring up the ash in the fireplace.
sentences.zh: 一阵和风从敞开的窗旋入，吹得许多摊开的书页翻飞，也把一层鸡皮疙瘩撒在安娜臂上，搅起壁炉里的灰。

sentences.en: Soon, that very same breeze would be filling Elsa’s sails to take her far, far away.
sentences.zh: 很快，这同一阵风就要鼓满艾莎的帆，送她去很远、很远的地方。

sentences.en: Travel by ship made Anna nervous.
sentences.zh: 乘船旅行让安娜不安。

sentences.en: Seven years had passed since their parents had set out on a voyage to the Southern Sea that had been meant to last only two weeks, but had turned into forever.
sentences.zh: 自父母启程前往南海——本只该为期两周，却成了永别——已过去了七年。

sentences.en: The days following the news had been the darkest of Anna’s life, and the nights had been worse.
sentences.zh: 噩耗之后的那些白昼，是安娜一生最黑暗的，而夜晚更糟。

sentences.en: Sleep had been impossible.
sentences.zh: 那时根本无法入睡。

sentences.en: The insides of her eyelids were the color of the fathomless waves that she imagined took her parents.
sentences.zh: 她眼皮内侧，是她想象中带走父母的、那无底海浪的颜色。

sentences.en: Sometimes, even now, her parents’ absence would startle her all over again, fresh and sudden as a bee sting.
sentences.zh: 有时，即便现在，父母的缺席仍会像蜂蜇般新鲜而骤然地惊她一下。

sentences.en: But as the years went by, the pain had become less immediate, old childhood nightmares faded, and she could remember her parents—her mother’s loving lullabies, her father’s teasing humor and tall tales—with joy.
sentences.zh: 可随着岁月流逝，痛苦不再那么切近，童年旧噩梦淡去，她已能欢喜地记起父母——母亲温柔的摇篮曲，父亲戏谑的幽默与奇谈。

sentences.en: Her reunion with Elsa had helped.
sentences.zh: 她与艾莎的重逢帮了忙。

sentences.en: When Elsa had shut herself away as a little girl, Anna was left with only her own memories of their parents.
sentences.zh: 当艾莎小时候把自己关起来时，安娜只剩自己对父母的记忆。

sentences.en: But since Elsa’s bedroom door had opened, Anna’s collection of stories about their parents had multiplied.
sentences.zh: 可自艾莎的卧室门打开后，安娜关于父母的故事收藏翻了倍。

sentences.en: And while the stories didn’t fill the hole in her heart, they did help smooth out the jagged edges.
sentences.zh: 故事虽填不满她心里的洞，却帮她磨平了尖锐的边缘。

sentences.en: She may not have her parents anymore, but she had her sister, and that was enough.
sentences.zh: 她或许不再有父母，但她有姐姐，这就够了。

sentences.en: Enough to make her wish Elsa wasn’t leaving her behind.
sentences.zh: 够让她但愿艾莎别把她抛下。

sentences.en: She would be leaving her… unless Anna could prove her worth.
sentences.zh: 艾莎要丢下她了……除非安娜能证明自己的价值。

sentences.en: Unless she could prove she was more than just the silly little girl who had talked to the portraits in the gallery and said yes to an offer of marriage to the evil (and thankfully now exiled) Prince Hans after less than twenty-four hours of knowing him.
sentences.zh: 除非她能证明，自己不只是那个对着画廊画像说话、认识邪恶（所幸现已流放）的汉斯王子不到二十四小时就答应婚事的小傻瓜。

sentences.en: Anna knew Elsa valued her despite those things, but she still felt lingering insecurity.
sentences.zh: 安娜知道艾莎看重她，尽管有那些事，她仍残留着不安。

sentences.en: Anna glanced at the stone statue of the horse that stood in the corner of the library as if it would have the answers they needed.
sentences.zh: 安娜瞥了眼立在图书馆角落的石马像，仿佛它能给出所需答案。

sentences.en: But all it had were delicate stone seashells and starfish carved into its mane, and an angry expression on its face.
sentences.zh: 可它有的，只是雕在鬃毛里的精致石贝壳与海星，以及一脸怒容。

sentences.en: It was an old statue, and Anna had been afraid of its bared teeth, its two front hooves furiously out in the air, and its blank eyes.
sentences.zh: 那是座老雕像，安娜曾怕它龇出的牙、腾在空中的两只前蹄，和那双空洞的眼。

sentences.en: Once, when she was four, she’d used up all of her mother’s cosmetics trying to make the horse look happier before her mother had discovered her and carried her out of the room, warning her not to touch the statue again.
sentences.zh: 有一次，她四岁时，曾用光母亲所有的化妆品想让马显得开心些，直到母亲发现，把她抱出房间，警告她别再碰雕像。

sentences.en: Young Anna was always being told not to touch things, like guitar strings, and oil paintings, and her father’s swords, and… “Wow, what happened in here?” Anna startled at the sound of the voice.
sentences.zh: 小安娜总被叮嘱别碰东西，比如吉他弦、油画、父亲的剑，还有……“哇，这儿怎么了？”那声音吓了安娜一跳。

sentences.en: Dragging her eyes away from the statue, she looked up to see the round shape of Olaf standing in the doorway.
sentences.zh: 她把目光从雕像上扯开，抬头看见奥拉夫圆滚滚的身影立在门口。

sentences.en: As children, Elsa and Anna had made up stories about a snowman named Olaf with branches for arms and a carrot for a nose.
sentences.zh: 小时候，艾莎和安娜编过关于一个叫奥拉夫的雪人的故事，那雪人用树枝当手臂、胡萝卜当鼻子。

sentences.en: Years later, on the day of Elsa’s coronation, Elsa had accidentally lost control of her ice powers and brought Olaf to life.
sentences.zh: 多年后，在艾莎加冕那天，艾莎意外失控冰力，把奥拉夫变活了。

sentences.en: Since then, he’d become the castle’s resident snowman and a member of the sisters’ family.
sentences.zh: 自那以后，他成了城堡的常驻雪人，也成了姐妹一家的一员。

sentences.en: He used to have a snow flurry hovering over his head that prevented him from melting, but since Elsa’s powers had grown and changed, she was able to do away with it and instead enchant him with a permafrost that served the same purpose.
sentences.zh: 他头顶曾有一团雪霰悬着防止融化，可随着艾莎魔力增长变化，她去掉了那团雪，改用永冻术为他施咒，作用相同。

sentences.en: Now, Olaf’s eyes widened as he took in the library.
sentences.zh: 此刻，奥拉夫睁大眼，打量着图书馆。

sentences.en: Or rather, the mess in the library. “It’s easier for me if I sort things into piles,” Anna explained, following his gaze to the towers of books scattered across the floor.
sentences.zh: 更确切地说，打量着图书馆的乱象。“我把它分成堆，方便些，”安娜解释，顺着他的目光看向散落一地的书塔。

sentences.en: She hadn’t realized how… enthusiastic she’d been when she’d pulled titles.
sentences.zh: 她没意识到自己抽书时有多……起劲。

sentences.en: There might actually have been more books on the floor than there were left on the shelves.
sentences.zh: 地上的书，说不定比架上剩下的还多。

sentences.en: It certainly wasn’t Elsa’s neat and methodical system, judging by the volumes Elsa had left standing in perfect stacks in the window alcove.
sentences.zh: 看艾莎留在窗凹处码得齐整的书堆，这绝非艾莎那套整齐而系统的方法。

sentences.en: Olaf nodded. “That makes sense.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫点头。“说得通。

sentences.en: When you build a snowman, you always have to start with piles.
sentences.zh: 堆雪人时，总得从一堆堆开始。

sentences.en: Unless you’re Elsa, of course.” He pointed. “Which ones are those?” “Books about sicknesses,” Anna said. “The pile next to that is about animal anatomy, and the one next to that is about sleep.” Each title was bursting with possibilities.
sentences.zh: 除非你是艾莎，当然。”他指了指。“那些是哪堆？”“讲疾病的书，”安娜说。“旁边那堆是动物解剖，再旁边是讲睡眠的。”每本书名都充满可能。

sentences.en: Olaf moved to the last pile, his twiggy hair just visible over the stack. “And this massive one?” “That’s my ‘to be read’ pile.” “Oooh, it’s so much bigger than all the rest,” he observed.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫挪到最后一堆，枝丫般的头发刚从书堆上露出来。“这巨堆呢？”“那是我的‘待读’堆。”“噢，比其余所有都大得多，”他评论道。

sentences.en: Anna shrugged.
sentences.zh: 安娜耸耸肩。

sentences.en: She had set aside these books as not currently useful but interesting enough that she wanted to check them out later.
sentences.zh: 这些书她先搁在一边，眼下没用，却有趣得让她想日后翻翻。

sentences.en: Poems were great because of their beautiful imagery and brevity, but she also loved the thick tomes of artists through the ages.
sentences.zh: 诗极好，因其意象优美而简短，可她也爱历代艺术家的厚重大部头。

sentences.en: And, of course, there were novels where people found true love, or undertook a dangerous quest, or were reunited with loved ones lost.
sentences.zh: 当然，还有那些小说：有人寻得真爱，有人踏上险途，有人与失散的所爱重逢。

sentences.en: Anna rubbed her eyes and adjusted the skirt of her dress, which had begun to bunch around her uncomfortably. “Where have you been?” she asked.
sentences.zh: 安娜揉揉眼，整了整开始不舒服地缠在身上的裙摆。“你刚在哪儿？”她问。

sentences.en: Olaf wandered from pile to pile. “The village library, listening to a lecture on Dante’s Inferno —the hotter the tale, the better.” Anna smiled.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫在书堆间晃悠。“在村里的图书馆，听一场但丁《神曲·地狱篇》的讲座——故事越火热越好。”安娜笑了。

sentences.en: After her first birthday party following Elsa’s eternal winter, Anna had taught Olaf how to read, and ever since, the snowman had become obsessed.
sentences.zh: 在艾莎永冬后的第一次生日宴上，安娜教会了奥拉夫识字，自那以后，这雪人就痴迷上了。

sentences.en: He liked books of all sizes, but his favorites were the thick tomes on philosophy—and beach reads, which he so often insisted were just as important as the classics.
sentences.zh: 他爱各种开本的书，最爱的却是哲学厚本——还有海滩读物，他常坚称它们与经典同样重要。

sentences.en: Anna didn’t disagree. “So, why are you rearranging the library, anyway?” Olaf asked.
sentences.zh: 安娜不反对。“话说，你到底为什么在重排图书馆？”奥拉夫问。

sentences.en: Taking a deep breath, Anna quickly explained about SoYun and her cattle and how Elsa was out now, checking on the Westens’ goats. “It seems that you could use some help,” Olaf said, straightening a coal button. “And in the wise words of many a philosopher, four eyeballs are better than three.” “Is that what they say?” Anna asked, resting her head on her palm.
sentences.zh: 安娜深吸一口气，飞快讲了小允和她的牛，以及艾莎此刻外出查看韦斯顿家的山羊。“看来你需要帮手，”奥拉夫说，正了正一颗煤纽扣。“用许多哲学家明智的话说，四只眼胜三只眼。”“他们真这么说的？”安娜问，把头枕在掌心。

sentences.en: Olaf whipped out his favorite pair of ice spectacles, specially made for him by Elsa. “Indeed,” he said. “They also say to ‘start at the beginning.’ So, we’ll start with the letter B, for beginning .” He pointed, and Anna followed his scraggly finger to the middle shelf of the nearest bookshelf behind the horse statue. “Sure,” Anna said. “You look at that while I finish this one.” Olaf clambered onto a table beneath a portrait of King Agnarr’s coronation, then jumped onto the stone horse’s back.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫抽出他最爱的那副冰眼镜——艾莎特意为他做的。“确实，”他说。“他们还说‘从头开始’。所以，我们从字母B、代表beginning开始。”他一指，安娜顺着他毛糙的手指看向石马像后最近书架的中层。“行，”安娜说。“你看那层，我把这堆看完。”奥拉夫爬上阿格瑞国王加冕画像下的桌子，又跳上石马背。

sentences.en: Carefully, he shimmied onto one of the rearing legs and pulled himself up, wobbling precariously from side to side. “Almost…” he said, reaching out.
sentences.zh: 他小心地挪到一只腾空的前腿上，攀上去，左右危险地晃。“快了……”他伸出手说。

sentences.en: Anna could see he was struggling, so she leapt up and hurried over to him. “Just a little bit further—whoops!” There was a click followed by a great grinding, like the sound of gears turning on each other, as the horse’s rearing leg that Olaf stood on sank down like a lever.
sentences.zh: 安娜见他吃力，便跳起奔过去。“再差一点点——哎呀！”一声咔哒后跟着巨大的研磨声，像齿轮互相咬合转动，奥拉夫所站的马腿如杠杆般沉了下去。

sentences.en: Dust swirled into the air, and Anna squeezed her eyes shut, turning her head away to avoid swallowing any more of the grime.
sentences.zh: 灰尘打着旋腾起，安娜紧闭双眼，别过头去，免得再吞下更多污垢。

sentences.en: And then…everything was still.
sentences.zh: 然后……一切静止。

sentences.en: Everything was silent. “Wow,” Olaf breathed. “Now that’s something you don’t see every day.” Anna’s eyes flew open, and she gasped.
sentences.zh: 一切寂然。“哇，”奥拉夫轻叹。“这可真不是天天能见到的。”安娜猛地睁眼，倒吸一口气。

sentences.en: The bookcase behind the statue had swung inward like a door.
sentences.zh: 雕像后的书柜像门一样向内转开了。

sentences.en: No, not like a door.
sentences.zh: 不，不像门。

sentences.en: It was an actual door, opening to reveal an arched entryway and, beyond it, darkness.
sentences.zh: 它就是一扇真正的门，敞开露出拱形入口，入口之后是黑暗。

sentences.en: And maybe—just maybe—something that would hold answers and help Elsa figure out how to cure the Blight.
sentences.zh: 而也许——只是也许——那里藏着答案，能帮艾莎想出治愈枯萎病的法子。

sentences.en: Squealing, Anna plunged into the secret room—and immediately crashed her shins against something.
sentences.zh: 安娜尖叫着冲进密室——立刻把小腿撞上了什么。

sentences.en: She winced.
sentences.zh: 她龇牙一缩。

sentences.en: Whatever she’d hit was definitely going to leave a bruise.
sentences.zh: 不管撞到的是什么，准会留块淤青。

sentences.en: Why hadn’t she thought to grab a candle?
sentences.zh: 她怎么就没想到抓支蜡烛？

sentences.en: Turning to head back, she saw Olaf waddling toward her, a candle in his hand.
sentences.zh: 她转身要回去，却见奥拉夫摇摇摆摆朝她走来，手里拿着一支蜡烛。

sentences.en: He stopped in front of her, the flame casting a creamy orange glow across his concerned face.
sentences.zh: 他在她面前停下，火苗在他担忧的脸上投下乳橙色的光。

sentences.en: He raised a skeptical eyebrow. “I thought you couldn’t see in the dark.” “I can’t,” Anna said. “Do you mind sharing the light?” “Nope!” Olaf handed it to her. “You’ll need it to see that person standing right behind you.”
sentences.zh: 他挑起一只怀疑的眉。“我以为你在黑暗里看不见。”“我是看不见，”安娜说。“介意分享一下光吗？”“不介意！”奥拉夫把蜡烛递给她。“你正需要它，好看清就站在你身后的那个人。”

chapters.title: 第3章
chapters.en:
ANNA WHIRLED AROUND, stifling a shout.

But as she held up the candle, she realized it wasn’t a person at all, but a metal helmet expertly forged to create the illusion of a fearsome grimace and sharp teeth. It had thrown her off at first, out of sheer surprise and because it was different from the helmets that Arendellian soldiers wore. In fact, the more she looked at it, the more Anna was certain that this helmet came from the same era as Aren of Arendelle, from that long-ago age of heroes that was now more legend than history.

As she raised the candle higher, the sphere of light widened to reveal the rest of what they had found: a windowless room filled from flagstone floor to vaulted ceiling with sparkling shelves.

The shelves had been carved into the stone walls, and unlike the rest of the castle, these walls hadn’t been papered or painted over or decorated with rosemaling. They were left bare, and the tiny crystals embedded in the rock seemed to wink a friendly greeting as the candle’s light passed over them. It wasn’t just the rock that glittered underneath a layer of dust, but also the many strange and wondrous objects that sat on the shelves: a gleaming pair of silver scales, schematics of what looked like a dam, glass beakers and bottles filled with fascinating specimens of flora and fauna suspended in brackish water.

And there were books. They spiraled upward into the rafters of the ceiling, the only surface that had been painted and resembled a sky alive with the northern lights along with familiar constellations: Ulf the Wolf, Frigg the Fisherman, and many others. There were wide books with thick leather spines, tall books with thin spines, books with yellow pages, books with ragged pages, squat books, medium-sized books, and tiny books no bigger than a thumb. Anna’s mouth dropped open. No matter how different they looked, each book had the possibility of containing the answers that she so desperately needed.

Olaf teetered forward into the room. “Oooh, more books! Secret books!”

“Secret books…” Anna mused, and her initial excitement dimmed. She knew she should have been more excited at the discovery of the secret room, but something about the secretness of it all pinched, leaving her feeling slightly bruised. She slowly made her way to the shelves. She wondered who had used this room. Arendelle’s royal family had lived in the castle for decades—ever since her grandfather King Runeard had overseen its construction when her father was just a boy. Perhaps this room had been a place of solace for a long-ago aunt or uncle.

Anna skimmed the titles. Some were written in languages that she didn’t know but recognized from her research for the grand tour. Others were in indecipherable symbols. But the ones that she could read made her heart backflip: Hulda’s Hideout; Scrolls of Trolls; Of Nightmares and Nixies; Quests of Yore; Sorcerer’s Craft and Games; Legends of Magic; Deciphering Magic…

Magic. Anna’s thoughts pulsed with the thump of her heart. Magic. Magic. Magic!

Magic was not unknown in Arendelle. After all, Elsa had magical abilities that no one in the kingdom had ever seen before. Or at least, no one alive had ever seen. In some of the old stories that were favorites of Queen Iduna’s, magic abounded. She’d told tales about tablecloths that could produce banquet-sized feasts in the blink of an eye, and boots that could travel seven leagues in a single step—of shape-shifters who lived in an enchanted forest, and stones that could turn lead into gold…but those were made up. Make believe. Pretend.

However, in the last three years, Anna had seen incredible things, impossible things, come to be. A sister who could be one with the earth and sky and build ice palaces with a few breaths and some nimble flicks of her wrist. A queen who could harness the cold. If Elsa could exist, as Anna very much knew she did, then why couldn’t other impossibilities exist as well?

Why couldn’t there be a spell of sorts, or an enchantment, that could fix whatever was happening with the Blight? Sure, Anna was hoping to find something in this room to help with the problem at hand, but after that, who knew? Maybe there was knowledge somewhere in there that could stop horseshoes from ever rusting, bread from ever going stale, or candles from ever melting down to stubs and going out. She’d be a hero.

“Aha.” Anna pulled a thick volume from a shelf and plopped it down onto a bare worktable in the center of the room alongside the candle. “This one might have something helpful.” She tapped at the title and read it out loud to Olaf. “‘The Alchemist’s Almanac: A Guide to the Care and Keeping of Fields, Accurate Accounting of the Weather, and Wheat.’”

Olaf looked down his pair of ice spectacles at Anna. “Not exactly my genre.”

Anna smiled.

“Ooh, this one seems cryptic and dense!” Olaf said, tugging out another thick book. “Here! You might like it, too!” He held it up for Anna to see. Its cover was a beautiful brown with black lettering. The title wasn’t written in an alphabet Anna recognized, but as she squinted at the book, a forgotten memory—more of an impression of sound and color, really—coalesced: The soft fabric of her mother’s dress beneath her cheek as Anna snuggled into her lap. A warm pressure at her side—Elsa, who’d climbed up to join. Words, low and gentle and hazy as her mother read out loud from a book, its cover the color of Anna’s new riding boots. Lullabies about secret white rivers and Earth Giants and lost legends of yore…Could it be?

Setting the almanac back on the shelf, Anna cracked open the new book and saw the title again written in runes. Someone had written next to them, in pencil, the words Secrets of the Magic Makers.

Anna’s breath caught.

It was her mother’s handwriting.

Anna would know it anywhere.

This book. This room: her mother had known about it; she had been here. These books and objects about magic were hers. Suddenly, Anna’s chest felt too small for her heart. Or maybe her heart was too big for her chest. Secrets. This castle was full of secrets she had not known—was not allowed to know. Questions rattled through her: Why was Anna always shut out? Why had her mother collected all these books about magic? And…did Elsa already know about this room? Like when they were children, was Anna the last to know again?

“Anna?” She felt a gentle pat on her shoulder. “Don’t judge a book by its cover.”

At Olaf’s words, Anna felt her ribcage loosen, just a tad, but it was enough that she could breathe again. Olaf had been the friend of both sisters; he was a little bit of Elsa and a little bit of Anna, created by them together. And looking around, Anna didn’t think Elsa knew about this secret room. After all, Elsa had been so good about filling Anna in on everything she had missed during the time when her head had been under the troll’s persuasion, when she’d been made to forget Elsa’s magic even existed. Elsa didn’t keep things from Anna, not anymore.

“I’m not, Olaf.” Anna flung back a braid. “This book…it was my mother’s.”

“Oh.” Olaf peered down through his spectacles. “Her reading selection appears to have been very specific. I’d rather check out this book.” He waved a slender black volume in his hand. “It’s about dangerous shape-shifters living in a cursed forest.”

“Why don’t you give it a read?” Anna asked. “Who knows—maybe it’ll mention cursed animals, too.”

“Holler if you need me!” Olaf plopped down at the worktable to page through it.

Meanwhile, Anna’s eyes prickled. Her mother’s book. She flipped through the rest of the thick pages. The runes looked like meaningless constellations, but the translations next to them had been made by her mother, and she would follow her mother’s footprints, or fingerprints, as they were, anywhere.

Secrets of the Magic Makers seemed to be a book of old tales, brief histories, and maps showing the way to the Valley of the Living Rock, but also a glossary of sorts, naming all kinds of creatures that only existed in lore. Spirits of wind, water, and fire. Earth Giants. Nattmara. Huldrefólk. They all sounded so familiar, but it was like Anna was trying to stare through a bedsheet hung out to dry. At some point in her life, she’d known what these bedtime-story words had meant in crystal-clear detail, but now she could not make out any more than the slightest shape. Sadness crept over her.

Mother would have known. Anna hadn’t just lost her mother when the ship sank beneath the Southern Sea’s waves. The world had lost Queen Iduna’s stories and lullabies, and there was no way to recover them. Or was there? Anna kept turning the pages. There were too many emotions at war within her to settle on any one page, on any one definition. Faster and faster she flipped through the book until fragile pages slipped out and flitted to the floor.

Anna froze. As carefully as she could, she picked up the papers to realize with relief that they weren’t pages from Secrets of the Magic Makers at all, but scraps of research that had not yet been bound in. One page displayed some familiar-looking blueprints: it was Arendelle Castle. Anna squinted at the page. She, like Gerda, already knew all the secret passages and places that were marked, except for one that drew her attention now and the one she was currently in.

Below the castle, something called the Earth Giant’s Passage seemed to run from somewhere beneath the ice room next to the kitchen and then turn south, under the waters of Arenfjord, to…to somewhere. Anna couldn’t tell. The black ink ran off the page, unfinished. But instructions had been printed in the margins. Three flagstones in, two across.

“Fascinating,” Anna whispered and set aside the blueprints. As soon as she found something to help the animals, she would definitely be taking a trip to the ice room. She shuffled to the next piece of paper. It was a map of Arendelle and the land that surrounded it. Markings circled a black sandy beach and a place called the Dark Sea, and scrawled across it in that same clean flourish that distinguished her mother’s handwriting was one of her father’s many sayings.

The past has a way of returning.

It was underlined twice, as if it meant something important. Anna squinted at the words, trying to make sense of them. But she was confused. The past was the past, so how could it ever come back? And why would her mother have written it on a map…a map that was stored in this particular book in this secret room? Was it supposed to mean something?

Anna yawned. Maybe the words didn’t mean anything special at all. Most likely, she was only looking for meaning because she so badly wanted meaning to exist. And because she dearly missed her mother and, for a moment, had felt close to her again as she read her book. Or maybe it was because she was tired. So very, very tired.

Anna had no idea how much time had passed since she and Olaf had entered the secret room, and with no window, it was impossible to tell. Tucking the map back inside the tome, she looked up to find Olaf balancing on a dusty wooden chair as he pulled a snow globe from a shelf.

“Hey, look what I found!” Olaf called. “Snow that can exist in summer—just like me!” He plopped a kiss on the globe. “Hello, little pocket flurry.” Giving it a shake, he sent the glittering snow swirling around a miniature of Arendelle Castle carved from a seashell. It was pretty, and Anna had definitely seen that snow globe before: not the actual snow globe, but a sketch of it in her father’s sketchbook she still kept in a place of honor on her dressing table.

“I think my father also knew about this secret room,” Anna said, “which means that there’s only one family member who might not know about it yet.” She snapped Secrets of the Magic Makers shut. “We have to go tell Elsa!”

“Tell me what?”
chapters.zh:
安娜猛地转身，把一声惊叫咽了回去。

可当她举起蜡烛，才看清那根本不是人，而是一顶金属头盔，锻造得极具巧思，营造出狰狞的怪相与尖牙的错觉。

起初它把她唬住了，一来纯属意外，二来它和阿伦黛尔士兵戴的头盔不同。

事实上，她越看越确信，这头盔与“阿伦黛尔的阿伦”同属一个时代，来自那个久远的英雄年代——如今与其说成历史，不如说成传说。

她把蜡烛举高，光球扩大，显出他们发现之物的其余部分：一间无窗的房间，从石板地到拱顶，塞满了闪闪发光的架子。

架子是凿进石壁的，而且与城堡其余部分不同，这些墙没贴壁纸、没刷漆，也没用玫瑰彩绘装饰。

它们赤裸着，岩中嵌着的小水晶仿佛在烛光掠过时眨着友好的问候。

在尘埃下熠熠生辉的，不止是岩石，还有架上许多奇异而美妙之物：一对闪亮的银秤、貌似水坝的示意图、盛着悬浮于咸水中的动植物标本的玻璃烧杯与瓶子。

还有书。

它们螺旋着升向天花板的椽木——那是唯一被涂绘的表面，宛如一片活着的极光天空，缀着熟悉的星座：狼神乌尔夫、渔夫弗丽格，以及许多其他。

有宽厚的皮脊大书，有瘦高的薄脊书，有黄页书、毛边书，有矮胖书、中型书，还有不比拇指大的小书。

安娜惊讶得张开了嘴。

无论它们多不同，每本书都可能藏着她急切所需的答案。

奥拉夫摇摇晃晃迈进房间。“噢，更多的书！

秘密的书！”“秘密的书……”安娜若有所思，最初的兴奋淡了下去。

她知道自己本该为发现密室更兴奋些，可这“秘密”的某处掐了她一下，让她觉得微微刺痛。

她缓缓走向书架。

她想知道谁用过这房间。

阿伦黛尔王室在城堡里住了几十年——自她祖父鲁内尔德国王督建此城、那时她父亲还是个孩子起。

或许这房间曾是某位远古姑姨或叔伯的慰藉之所。

安娜掠过那些书名。

有些用她不懂、却因巡游研究而认得的文字写成。

另一些是难以辨认的符号。

可她读得懂的那些，让她的心脏翻了个跟头：《胡尔达的藏身处》；《地精卷轴》；《梦魇与水中精灵》；《远古征途》；《巫师的技艺与游戏》；《魔法传奇》；《破解魔法》……魔法。

安娜的思绪随心跳砰砰跳动。

魔法。

魔法。

魔法！

魔法在阿伦黛尔并非陌生。

毕竟，艾莎拥有的魔力，王国里无人曾见。

至少，在世之人从未见过。

在伊杜娜王后钟爱的某些古老故事里，魔法比比皆是。

她讲过这样的故事：桌布能眨眼间变出一桌宴席，靴子一步能行七里格——还有住在魔法森林里的变形者，能把铅变金的石头……可那些都是编的。

是假想。

是假装。

然而，过去三年里，安娜见过不可思议、不可能之事成真。

一个能与天地合一、几口呼气加几次灵巧的手腕翻转便筑起冰宫的姐姐。

一位能驾驭严寒的女王。

既然艾莎存在——安娜再清楚不过——那为何其他不可能之事不能也存在？

为何不能有某种咒语或魔魅，治愈枯萎病所发生的一切？

当然，安娜盼着在这房间找到应对眼前之困的东西，可那之后，谁知道呢？

也许其中某处藏着知识，能让马掌永不生锈、面包永不发霉、蜡烛永不烧成残根熄灭。

她就成了英雄。“啊哈。”安娜从架上抽下一册厚书，啪地放到房间中央一张光桌面上，挨着蜡烛。“这本或许有用。”她敲着书名念给奥拉夫听。“《炼金术士年鉴：田地养护、天气精算与小麦指南》。”奥拉夫从冰眼镜上方俯视安娜。“不太合我口味。”安娜笑了。“噢，这本好像隐晦又深奥！”奥拉夫抽出另一本厚书说。“给！

你或许也会喜欢！”他举起来给安娜看。

封面是美丽的棕色，配黑字。

书名用的不是安娜认得的字母，可当她眯眼盯着书，一段被遗忘的记忆——更确切说，是声音与色彩的印象——凝聚起来：安娜偎在母亲膝头时，脸颊下母亲衣裙柔软的布料。

身侧一股温暖的压迫——是艾莎，爬上来凑在一起。

话语低沉、温柔而朦胧，是母亲在念一本书，那书的封面是安娜新马靴的颜色。

关于秘密白河、大地巨人、失落的远古传说的摇篮曲……会是它吗？

安娜把年鉴放回架，翻开那本新书，见书名又一次以如尼文写成。

有人在旁用铅笔写着：《魔法创造者之秘》。

安娜屏住了呼吸。

那是她母亲的字迹。

安娜到哪儿都认得。

这本书。

这房间：母亲知道它；她曾来过。

这些关于魔法的书与物，是她的。

忽然，安娜觉得胸口装不下自己的心。

或许，是她的心对胸口来说太大了。

秘密。

这城堡满是她不知、也不被允许知的秘密。

一串问题在她脑中翻腾：为何安娜总被排除在外？

母亲为何收藏所有这些关于魔法的书？

还有……艾莎是否已知道这房间？

就像小时候那样，安娜又是最后一个知道的吗？“安娜？”她感到肩头被轻轻一拍。“别以貌取书。”奥拉夫的话让安娜的胸腔松了松，只一点点，却足以让她重新呼吸。

奥拉夫是两姐妹共同的朋友；他有一点艾莎、有一点安娜，是她们一起创造的。

环顾四周，安娜觉得艾莎并不知道这密室。

毕竟，在安娜被地精施法、被迫忘掉艾莎魔力存在的那段日子里，艾莎总把安娜错过的全都补给她。

艾莎不再对安娜隐瞒，再也不了。“我没有，奥拉夫。”安娜甩了甩辫子。“这本书……是我母亲的。”“噢。”奥拉夫透过眼镜俯视。“她的阅读品味似乎非常专一。

我倒想翻翻这本。”他挥着手里一本细长的黑皮书。“讲的是住在被诅咒森林里的危险变形者。”“你何不读读看？”安娜问。“谁知道——也许它也会提到被诅咒的动物。”“需要就叫我校！”奥拉夫啪地坐到工作台前翻起来。

与此同时，安娜的眼睛刺痛起来。

母亲的书。

她翻过其余厚页。

如尼文看似无意义的星座，可旁边的译文是母亲做的，她愿循着母亲的足迹——或说指纹——去任何地方。

《魔法创造者之秘》似乎是一本旧故事、简史与通往活石谷之路地图的集合，也是某种词汇表，列出了只存在于传说中的各类生灵。

风、水、火之灵。

大地巨人。

夜魇（Nattmara）。

胡尔德民。

它们听来都那么耳熟，可安娜像在透过晾着的床单使劲看。

在她生命的某时，她曾清清楚楚知道这些睡前故事词汇的含义，可如今她连最模糊的轮廓都辨不出。

悲伤悄悄爬上她。

母亲本会知道。

当船沉入南海波涛下时，安娜失去的不只是母亲。

世界失去了伊杜娜王后的故事与摇篮曲，且无从挽回。

还是说，有办法？

安娜继续翻页。

太多情绪在她心中交战，让她无法停驻于任何一页、任何一个定义。

她越翻越快，直到脆页滑脱，飘落地面。

安娜僵住。

她尽可能小心地拾起那些纸，松了口气：它们根本不是《魔法创造者之秘》的书页，而是尚未装订的研究残片。

一页上有些眼熟的蓝图：是阿伦黛尔城堡。

安娜眯眼细看。

她和格尔达一样，早已熟知图上标出的所有密道与密地，除了一处此刻吸引她注意的，以及她正身处的这一处。

城堡之下，有条叫“大地巨人通道”的线路，似乎从厨房旁冰室下方的某处起，向南拐，钻过阿伦峡湾的水下，通往……某处。

安娜看不出来。

黑墨在页边断了，没画完。

但页边印着说明。

进三块石板，横过两块。“有趣，”安娜轻声说，把蓝图放到一边。

一旦找到帮动物的东西，她定要去冰室一探究竟。

她拖着脚走向下一张纸。

那是阿伦黛尔及其四围之地的地图。

标记圈出一片黑沙海滩和一处叫“暗海”的地方，上面以她母亲特有的、干净利落的笔锋草草写着一个父亲常说的格言。

过去总会有回来的方式。

它被划了两次下划线，仿佛意味深重。

安娜眯眼盯着那些字，想弄懂它们。

可她困惑了。

过去就是过去，又怎会回来？

母亲为何要把它写在一张地图——一张藏在密室里这本特定书中的地图上？

它该有什么含义吗？

安娜打了个哈欠。

也许这些字根本没什么特别含义。

多半，她只是在寻找含义，因为她太渴望含义存在。

也因为她是那么思念母亲，且有那么一刻，在读母亲的书时又感到贴近了她。

抑或，是因为她累了。

如此、如此疲惫。

安娜不知她和奥拉夫进密室已过多久，没有窗，根本无从判断。

把地图塞回书里，她抬头，见奥拉夫正立在一把积灰的木椅上，从架上取下一个雪景球。“嘿，看我找到了什么！”奥拉夫喊。“夏天也能存在的雪——就像我！”他往球上啵了一口。“你好啊，小口袋雪。”他摇了摇，让闪亮的雪绕着贝壳雕的阿伦黛尔城堡小模型打旋。

它很美，而安娜肯定见过那雪景球：不是真球，而是父亲素描本里的一幅速写——那本子她仍摆在梳妆台上尊贵的位置。“我想我父亲也知道这密室，”安娜说，“也就是说，只有一个家人或许还不知道它。”“我们得去告诉艾莎！”“告诉我什么？”

sentences.en: ANNA WHIRLED AROUND, stifling a shout.
sentences.zh: 安娜猛地转身，把一声惊叫咽了回去。

sentences.en: But as she held up the candle, she realized it wasn’t a person at all, but a metal helmet expertly forged to create the illusion of a fearsome grimace and sharp teeth.
sentences.zh: 可当她举起蜡烛，才看清那根本不是人，而是一顶金属头盔，锻造得极具巧思，营造出狰狞的怪相与尖牙的错觉。

sentences.en: It had thrown her off at first, out of sheer surprise and because it was different from the helmets that Arendellian soldiers wore.
