sentences.en: In fact, the more she looked at it, the more Anna was certain that this helmet came from the same era as Aren of Arendelle, from that long-ago age of heroes that was now more legend than history.
sentences.zh: 事实上，她越看越确信，这头盔与“阿伦黛尔的阿伦”同属一个时代，来自那个久远的英雄年代——如今与其说成历史，不如说成传说。

sentences.en: As she raised the candle higher, the sphere of light widened to reveal the rest of what they had found: a windowless room filled from flagstone floor to vaulted ceiling with sparkling shelves.
sentences.zh: 她把蜡烛举高，光球扩大，显出他们发现之物的其余部分：一间无窗的房间，从石板地到拱顶，塞满了闪闪发光的架子。

sentences.en: The shelves had been carved into the stone walls, and unlike the rest of the castle, these walls hadn’t been papered or painted over or decorated with rosemaling.
sentences.zh: 架子是凿进石壁的，而且与城堡其余部分不同，这些墙没贴壁纸、没刷漆，也没用玫瑰彩绘装饰。

sentences.en: They were left bare, and the tiny crystals embedded in the rock seemed to wink a friendly greeting as the candle’s light passed over them.
sentences.zh: 它们赤裸着，岩中嵌着的小水晶仿佛在烛光掠过时眨着友好的问候。

sentences.en: It wasn’t just the rock that glittered underneath a layer of dust, but also the many strange and wondrous objects that sat on the shelves: a gleaming pair of silver scales, schematics of what looked like a dam, glass beakers and bottles filled with fascinating specimens of flora and fauna suspended in brackish water.
sentences.zh: 在尘埃下熠熠生辉的，不止是岩石，还有架上许多奇异而美妙之物：一对闪亮的银秤、貌似水坝的示意图、盛着悬浮于咸水中的动植物标本的玻璃烧杯与瓶子。

sentences.en: And there were books.
sentences.zh: 还有书。

sentences.en: They spiraled upward into the rafters of the ceiling, the only surface that had been painted and resembled a sky alive with the northern lights along with familiar constellations: Ulf the Wolf, Frigg the Fisherman, and many others.
sentences.zh: 它们螺旋着升向天花板的椽木——那是唯一被涂绘的表面，宛如一片活着的极光天空，缀着熟悉的星座：狼神乌尔夫、渔夫弗丽格，以及许多其他。

sentences.en: There were wide books with thick leather spines, tall books with thin spines, books with yellow pages, books with ragged pages, squat books, medium-sized books, and tiny books no bigger than a thumb.
sentences.zh: 有宽厚的皮脊大书，有瘦高的薄脊书，有黄页书、毛边书，有矮胖书、中型书，还有不比拇指大的小书。

sentences.en: Anna’s mouth dropped open.
sentences.zh: 安娜惊讶得张开了嘴。

sentences.en: No matter how different they looked, each book had the possibility of containing the answers that she so desperately needed.
sentences.zh: 无论它们多不同，每本书都可能藏着她急切所需的答案。

sentences.en: Olaf teetered forward into the room. “Oooh, more books!
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫摇摇晃晃迈进房间。“噢，更多的书！

sentences.en: Secret books!” “Secret books…” Anna mused, and her initial excitement dimmed.
sentences.zh: 秘密的书！”“秘密的书……”安娜若有所思，最初的兴奋淡了下去。

sentences.en: She knew she should have been more excited at the discovery of the secret room, but something about the secretness of it all pinched, leaving her feeling slightly bruised.
sentences.zh: 她知道自己本该为发现密室更兴奋些，可这“秘密”的某处掐了她一下，让她觉得微微刺痛。

sentences.en: She slowly made her way to the shelves.
sentences.zh: 她缓缓走向书架。

sentences.en: She wondered who had used this room.
sentences.zh: 她想知道谁用过这房间。

sentences.en: Arendelle’s royal family had lived in the castle for decades—ever since her grandfather King Runeard had overseen its construction when her father was just a boy.
sentences.zh: 阿伦黛尔王室在城堡里住了几十年——自她祖父鲁内尔德国王督建此城、那时她父亲还是个孩子起。

sentences.en: Perhaps this room had been a place of solace for a long-ago aunt or uncle.
sentences.zh: 或许这房间曾是某位远古姑姨或叔伯的慰藉之所。

sentences.en: Anna skimmed the titles.
sentences.zh: 安娜掠过那些书名。

sentences.en: Some were written in languages that she didn’t know but recognized from her research for the grand tour.

sentences.en: Others were in indecipherable symbols.

sentences.en: But the ones that she could read made her heart backflip: Hulda’s Hideout ; Scrolls of Trolls ; Of Nightmares and Nixies ; Quests of Yore ; Sorcerer’s Craft and Games ; Legends of Magic ; Deciphering Magic… Magic.
sentences.zh: 可她读得懂的那些，让她的心脏翻了个跟头：《胡尔达的藏身处》；《地精卷轴》；《梦魇与水中精灵》；《远古征途》；《巫师的技艺与游戏》；《魔法传奇》；《破解魔法》……魔法。

sentences.en: Anna’s thoughts pulsed with the thump of her heart.
sentences.zh: 安娜的思绪随心跳砰砰跳动。

sentences.en: Anna’s breath caught.
sentences.zh: 安娜屏住了呼吸。

sentences.en: It was her mother’s handwriting.
sentences.zh: 那是她母亲的字迹。

sentences.en: Anna would know it anywhere.
sentences.zh: 安娜到哪儿都认得。

sentences.en: This book.
sentences.zh: 这本书。

sentences.en: This room : her mother had known about it; she had been here.
sentences.zh: 这房间：母亲知道它；她曾来过。

sentences.en: These books and objects about magic were hers .
sentences.zh: 这些关于魔法的书与物，是她的。

sentences.en: Suddenly, Anna’s chest felt too small for her heart.
sentences.zh: 忽然，安娜觉得胸口装不下自己的心。

sentences.en: Or maybe her heart was too big for her chest.
sentences.zh: 或许，是她的心对胸口来说太大了。

sentences.en: Secrets.
sentences.zh: 秘密。

sentences.en: This castle was full of secrets she had not known—was not allowed to know.
sentences.zh: 这城堡满是她不知、也不被允许知的秘密。

sentences.en: Questions rattled through her: Why was Anna always shut out?
sentences.zh: 一串问题在她脑中翻腾：为何安娜总被排除在外？

sentences.en: Why had her mother collected all these books about magic?
sentences.zh: 母亲为何收藏所有这些关于魔法的书？

sentences.en: And…did Elsa already know about this room?
sentences.zh: 还有……艾莎是否已知道这房间？

sentences.en: Like when they were children, was Anna the last to know again? “Anna?” She felt a gentle pat on her shoulder. “Don’t judge a book by its cover.” At Olaf’s words, Anna felt her ribcage loosen, just a tad, but it was enough that she could breathe again.
sentences.zh: 就像小时候那样，安娜又是最后一个知道的吗？“安娜？”她感到肩头被轻轻一拍。“别以貌取书。”奥拉夫的话让安娜的胸腔松了松，只一点点，却足以让她重新呼吸。

sentences.en: Olaf had been the friend of both sisters; he was a little bit of Elsa and a little bit of Anna, created by them together.
sentences.zh: 奥拉夫是两姐妹共同的朋友；他有一点艾莎、有一点安娜，是她们一起创造的。

sentences.en: And looking around, Anna didn’t think Elsa knew about this secret room.
sentences.zh: 环顾四周，安娜觉得艾莎并不知道这密室。

sentences.en: After all, Elsa had been so good about filling Anna in on everything she had missed during the time when her head had been under the troll’s persuasion, when she’d been made to forget Elsa’s magic even existed.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，在安娜被地精施法、被迫忘掉艾莎魔力存在的那段日子里，艾莎总把安娜错过的全都补给她。

sentences.en: Elsa didn’t keep things from Anna, not anymore. “I’m not, Olaf.” Anna flung back a braid. “This book…it was my mother’s.” “Oh.” Olaf peered down through his spectacles. “Her reading selection appears to have been very specific .
sentences.zh: 艾莎不再对安娜隐瞒，再也不了。“我没有，奥拉夫。”安娜甩了甩辫子。“这本书……是我母亲的。”“噢。”奥拉夫透过眼镜俯视。“她的阅读品味似乎非常专一。

sentences.en: I’d rather check out this book.” He waved a slender black volume in his hand. “It’s about dangerous shape-shifters living in a cursed forest.” “Why don’t you give it a read?” Anna asked. “Who knows—maybe it’ll mention cursed animals, too.” “Holler if you need me!” Olaf plopped down at the worktable to page through it.
sentences.zh: 我倒想翻翻这本。”他挥着手里一本细长的黑皮书。“讲的是住在被诅咒森林里的危险变形者。”“你何不读读看？”安娜问。“谁知道——也许它也会提到被诅咒的动物。”“需要就叫我校！”奥拉夫啪地坐到工作台前翻起来。

sentences.en: Meanwhile, Anna’s eyes prickled.
sentences.zh: 与此同时，安娜的眼睛刺痛起来。

sentences.en: Her mother’s book.
sentences.zh: 母亲的书。

sentences.en: She flipped through the rest of the thick pages.
sentences.zh: 她翻过其余厚页。

sentences.en: The runes looked like meaningless constellations, but the translations next to them had been made by her mother, and she would follow her mother’s footprints, or fingerprints, as they were, anywhere.
sentences.zh: 如尼文看似无意义的星座，可旁边的译文是母亲做的，她愿循着母亲的足迹——或说指纹——去任何地方。

sentences.en: Secrets of the Magic Makers seemed to be a book of old tales, brief histories, and maps showing the way to the Valley of the Living Rock, but also a glossary of sorts, naming all kinds of creatures that only existed in lore.
sentences.zh: 《魔法创造者之秘》似乎是一本旧故事、简史与通往活石谷之路地图的集合，也是某种词汇表，列出了只存在于传说中的各类生灵。

sentences.en: Spirits of wind, water, and fire.
sentences.zh: 风、水、火之灵。

sentences.en: Earth Giants.
sentences.zh: 大地巨人。

sentences.en: Nattmara.
sentences.zh: 夜魇（Nattmara）。

sentences.en: Huldrefólk.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德民。

sentences.en: They all sounded so familiar, but it was like Anna was trying to stare through a bedsheet hung out to dry.
sentences.zh: 它们听来都那么耳熟，可安娜像在透过晾着的床单使劲看。

sentences.en: At some point in her life, she’d known what these bedtime-story words had meant in crystal-clear detail, but now she could not make out any more than the slightest shape.
sentences.zh: 在她生命的某时，她曾清清楚楚知道这些睡前故事词汇的含义，可如今她连最模糊的轮廓都辨不出。

sentences.en: Sadness crept over her.
sentences.zh: 悲伤悄悄爬上她。

sentences.en: Mother would have known.
sentences.zh: 母亲本会知道。

sentences.en: Anna hadn’t just lost her mother when the ship sank beneath the Southern Sea’s waves.
sentences.zh: 当船沉入南海波涛下时，安娜失去的不只是母亲。

sentences.en: The world had lost Queen Iduna’s stories and lullabies, and there was no way to recover them.
sentences.zh: 世界失去了伊杜娜王后的故事与摇篮曲，且无从挽回。

sentences.en: Or was there?
sentences.zh: 还是说，有办法？

sentences.en: Anna kept turning the pages.
sentences.zh: 安娜继续翻页。

sentences.en: There were too many emotions at war within her to settle on any one page, on any one definition.
sentences.zh: 太多情绪在她心中交战，让她无法停驻于任何一页、任何一个定义。

sentences.en: Faster and faster she flipped through the book until fragile pages slipped out and flitted to the floor.
sentences.zh: 她越翻越快，直到脆页滑脱，飘落地面。

sentences.en: Anna froze.
sentences.zh: 安娜僵住。

sentences.en: As carefully as she could, she picked up the papers to realize with relief that they weren’t pages from Secrets of the Magic Makers at all, but scraps of research that had not yet been bound in.
sentences.zh: 她尽可能小心地拾起那些纸，松了口气：它们根本不是《魔法创造者之秘》的书页，而是尚未装订的研究残片。

sentences.en: One page displayed some familiar-looking blueprints: it was Arendelle Castle.
sentences.zh: 一页上有些眼熟的蓝图：是阿伦黛尔城堡。

sentences.en: Anna squinted at the page.
sentences.zh: 安娜眯眼细看。

sentences.en: She, like Gerda, already knew all the secret passages and places that were marked, except for one that drew her attention now and the one she was currently in .
sentences.zh: 她和格尔达一样，早已熟知图上标出的所有密道与密地，除了一处此刻吸引她注意的，以及她正身处的这一处。

sentences.en: Below the castle, something called the Earth Giant’s Passage seemed to run from somewhere beneath the ice room next to the kitchen and then turn south, under the waters of Arenfjord, to…to somewhere.
sentences.zh: 城堡之下，有条叫“大地巨人通道”的线路，似乎从厨房旁冰室下方的某处起，向南拐，钻过阿伦峡湾的水下，通往……某处。

sentences.en: Anna couldn’t tell.
sentences.zh: 安娜看不出来。

sentences.en: The black ink ran off the page, unfinished.
sentences.zh: 黑墨在页边断了，没画完。

sentences.en: But instructions had been printed in the margins.
sentences.zh: 但页边印着说明。

sentences.en: Three flagstones in, two across. “ Fascinating ,” Anna whispered and set aside the blueprints.
sentences.zh: 进三块石板，横过两块。“有趣，”安娜轻声说，把蓝图放到一边。

sentences.en: As soon as she found something to help the animals, she would definitely be taking a trip to the ice room.
sentences.zh: 一旦找到帮动物的东西，她定要去冰室一探究竟。

sentences.en: She shuffled to the next piece of paper.
sentences.zh: 她拖着脚走向下一张纸。

sentences.en: It was a map of Arendelle and the land that surrounded it.
sentences.zh: 那是阿伦黛尔及其四围之地的地图。

sentences.en: Markings circled a black sandy beach and a place called the Dark Sea, and scrawled across it in that same clean flourish that distinguished her mother’s handwriting was one of her father’s many sayings.
sentences.zh: 标记圈出一片黑沙海滩和一处叫“暗海”的地方，上面以她母亲特有的、干净利落的笔锋草草写着一个父亲常说的格言。

sentences.en: The past has a way of returning.
sentences.zh: 过去总会有回来的方式。

sentences.en: It was underlined twice, as if it meant something important.
sentences.zh: 它被划了两次下划线，仿佛意味深重。

sentences.en: Anna squinted at the words, trying to make sense of them.
sentences.zh: 安娜眯眼盯着那些字，想弄懂它们。

sentences.en: But she was confused.
sentences.zh: 可她困惑了。

sentences.en: The past was the past, so how could it ever come back?
sentences.zh: 过去就是过去，又怎会回来？

sentences.en: And why would her mother have written it on a map…a map that was stored in this particular book in this secret room?
sentences.zh: 母亲为何要把它写在一张地图——一张藏在密室里这本特定书中的地图上？

sentences.en: Was it supposed to mean something?
sentences.zh: 它该有什么含义吗？

sentences.en: Anna yawned.
sentences.zh: 安娜打了个哈欠。

sentences.en: Maybe the words didn’t mean anything special at all.
sentences.zh: 也许这些字根本没什么特别含义。

sentences.en: Most likely, she was only looking for meaning because she so badly wanted meaning to exist.
sentences.zh: 多半，她只是在寻找含义，因为她太渴望含义存在。

sentences.en: And because she dearly missed her mother and, for a moment, had felt close to her again as she read her book.
sentences.zh: 也因为她是那么思念母亲，且有那么一刻，在读母亲的书时又感到贴近了她。

sentences.en: Or maybe it was because she was tired.
sentences.zh: 抑或，是因为她累了。

sentences.en: So very, very tired.
sentences.zh: 如此、如此疲惫。

sentences.en: Anna had no idea how much time had passed since she and Olaf had entered the secret room, and with no window, it was impossible to tell.
sentences.zh: 安娜不知她和奥拉夫进密室已过多久，没有窗，根本无从判断。

sentences.en: Tucking the map back inside the tome, she looked up to find Olaf balancing on a dusty wooden chair as he pulled a snow globe from a shelf. “Hey, look what I found!” Olaf called. “Snow that can exist in summer—just like me!” He plopped a kiss on the globe. “Hello, little pocket flurry.” Giving it a shake, he sent the glittering snow swirling around a miniature of Arendelle Castle carved from a seashell.
sentences.zh: 把地图塞回书里，她抬头，见奥拉夫正立在一把积灰的木椅上，从架上取下一个雪景球。“嘿，看我找到了什么！”奥拉夫喊。“夏天也能存在的雪——就像我！”他往球上啵了一口。“你好啊，小口袋雪。”他摇了摇，让闪亮的雪绕着贝壳雕的阿伦黛尔城堡小模型打旋。

sentences.en: It was pretty, and Anna had definitely seen that snow globe before: not the actual snow globe, but a sketch of it in her father’s sketchbook she still kept in a place of honor on her dressing table. “I think my father also knew about this secret room,” Anna said, “which means that there’s only one family member who might not know about it yet.” She snapped Secrets of the Magic Makers shut. “We have to go tell Elsa!” “Tell me what?”
sentences.zh: 它很美，而安娜肯定见过那雪景球：不是真球，而是父亲素描本里的一幅速写——那本子她仍摆在梳妆台上尊贵的位置。“我想我父亲也知道这密室，”安娜说，“也就是说，只有一个家人或许还不知道它。”“我们得去告诉艾莎！”“告诉我什么？”

chapters.title: 第4章
chapters.en:
ELSA HAD RETURNED.

And though Anna knew her sister had been up since way before her, had held a meeting for the villagers, visited a farm, scoured the library, then visited another farm, she was still crisp and clean, her blond braid a streak of sunshine against the burgundy of their mother’s cozy scarf, which was now wrapped around her shoulders. Elsa stood still, her mouth open, staring in what could only be called astonishment at Anna and Olaf inside the secret room.

“H-how? I mean, did you…” Elsa sputtered. “What is this place?”

Happiness and relief washed over Anna. From the expression on Elsa’s face and the way her voice shook, Anna knew—the same way she knew that ice was cold and fire was hot—that Elsa had not known about this particular secret. For once, Anna had not been the last to know.

“We found a clandestine room,” Olaf said. “Clandestine means secret. But I guess now it’s not so clandestine. Unless you can keep a…what’s the noun form of clandestine? Keep a clandestiny?” He still held the snow globe in his hands. “Do you mind if I show this to Sven?” And before the sisters could reply, he skipped out of the room.

“I don’t know, exactly,” Anna said in reply to Elsa’s question. “But isn’t it wonderful?” She gestured to the secret room’s shelves and fought the urge to giggle as Elsa took a few steps into the room and looked around, her eyes wide, taking in the dried herbs, the gleaming copper spyglass, and the creamy swirl of what appeared to be a narwhal tusk. Elsa moved closer to the shelves.

“How did you find this place?” Elsa asked.

“Olaf,” Anna said. She filled Elsa in on the items, the map, the notes, and the book she felt could hold the answers to their problems. At the mention of their parents having been in this room, Elsa gasped.

“And so,” Anna concluded, “I bet we can find something in here about the Blight.”

“I don’t know about that,” Elsa said. “But whatever is affecting SoYun’s cows is also affecting the Westens’ goats. I couldn’t wake them up. I tried everything.”

“I mean, look at this title!” Anna plucked the Alchemist’s Almanac from the shelf and turned back to Elsa, but Elsa’s attention seemed to have snagged elsewhere, onto an old golden frame that had been carefully leaning against a wall. The painting inside of it was muddied by grime, but Anna thought she could just make out a pair of eyes and a strong jaw: a portrait.

Picking it up, Elsa blew, and a puff of dust ballooned into the air, settling on Anna’s face. Anna sneezed while Elsa held out the painting at arm’s length and squinted. “I think this is supposed to be Aren of Arendelle. The painting is so dirty, though, it’s hard to tell.”

Anna placed the almanac back on the shelf and peered over Elsa’s shoulder. “What makes you think it’s Aren?”

Aren was a legendary leader from times of old—the very, very old, before the last ice age, even. So old, in fact, that it was most likely the famous warrior had never even existed.

“See that?” Elsa pointed at a dark smudge. “I think that’s supposed to be Revolute, his sword with a ‘yellow diamond, bright as an eye.’”

Anna stared at her sister. “Are you…quoting something?”

“Yeah,” Elsa admitted. “That’s a line from the Saga of Aren, written by an unknown poet whom some claimed was actually Aren’s true love.”

It sounded kind of familiar to Anna. While she knew everything that there was to know about Arendelle, there were still some things, like these fine details, that she knew she’d once known but had forgotten. The things that she’d forgotten were usually stories her parents had shared. Embarrassment crept through her. She hated when she forgot things!

She tried to remember everything she could about Aren. There were endless stories and epic poems about his brave deeds—from helping the Huldrefólk hide their tails to journeying under the sea to sing with mermaids or questing to mountaintops to meet the sun. According to that particular story, Anna recalled, the sun had been so impressed with Aren that she’d given him a sword called the Revolute Blade. With the sun’s sword in his hand, Aren had carved the fjord between the mountains. And not just any fjord, but this fjord: Arenfjord, the backbone of the kingdom of Arendelle.

“Is that the one that goes, ‘Revolving moon and spinning sun, forged a crescent blade,’ and…something, something, something, ‘May the flags of Arendelle ever wave’?” Anna asked.

Elsa nodded. “Exactly.” Anna’s embarrassment subsided as Elsa pointed a little above the smudge to a blur. “I think that might be the yellow diamond in the pommel, and then there”—she moved her hand—“see how the blade curves? According to myth, the curve is where the sword first struck the earth. That’s how the sword got its name. ‘Revolute’ means ‘curved.’”

“Magic swords are nice and all,” Anna said, tilting her head and fanning herself with her hand. It was getting hot in the windowless room. “But I don’t really see why it would be helpful to be able to make cuts into the earth.”

Elsa fiddled with her braid as she looked at the painting. “Apparently, the sun bestowed Revolute with great powers, and with the sword in his hand, Aren became known as the protector of the people, unifying them against a dark fright. He was a great leader.” A strange expression settled on Elsa’s face. “History seems to be full of great leaders.”

Anna glanced at her sister. For some reason she did not quite understand, Elsa seemed to have left the room, even though she hadn’t physically gone anywhere. She no longer looked at Anna. Instead, her gaze was fixed on a shelf full of books, bottles, and jars.

“Why were they studying magic? And why did they seal off the room and never tell us about it?” Elsa asked, her voice so soft that Anna wondered if she’d meant to say anything at all. Elsa stood there, with her back impossibly straight, standing the way a queen should. But at that exact moment, Anna didn’t see Elsa, queen of Arendelle. She saw Elsa the lonely child, who’d spent her days alone in her room with only patterns of frost to keep her company.

Anna reached out to touch Elsa’s arm. Her sister was stiff, as if she didn’t just wield cold and snow, but were made of it. “I have the same question,” Anna admitted, glad they were in this together. “But think about it: why do people study art?” she asked. “Why does Baker Blodget spend her entire life in pursuit of baking the best butter biscuits in the world? Why does Kristoff keep trying to sing?”

Elsa remained silent, so Anna answered for her, reaching down to pick up Secrets of the Magic Makers. “Because talents are worth exploring. Because butter biscuits are delicious, singing is fun, and your magic is beautiful, Elsa. Maybe they wanted to know more about it.”

She slipped a hand in Elsa’s, and waited. A few seconds later, Elsa squeezed her fingers, and Anna squeezed back. Without meeting Anna’s eye, Elsa moved away from her and toward the exit.

“I need to go.” Elsa’s voice was quiet. “This place creeps me out.”

“What do you mean?” Anna didn’t think she had ever been in a more beautiful room with still so much to explore. The possibilities were endless!

“It’s all these things in jars.” Elsa waved her hands. “Contained and locked away.”

“Well,” Anna said, tucking Secrets of the Magic Makers under her arm, “maybe that just means it’s time for them all to be brought to the light of day.” Excitement again rose within her. “The answers to how to stop the Blight could be in here! Maybe there’s even more magic out there, magic that can actually help us!”

Elsa flinched.

“I—I didn’t mean it like that,” Anna said. “Your magic is really helpful. Just not in this situation.”

Elsa took a step back. “I need to help the livestock before we can start really delving into this room, okay?” Elsa said. “There’s no time to waste. I…I have to go.”

“Of course. But—but we…I can stay here and keep looking for clues,” Anna suggested. “We may be able to find the answers to what’s happening to—”

Elsa shook her head. “I really think we should leave this place alone for now.”

“Hold on,” Anna said, desperate to keep her plan in place, desperate to help. “There’s so much we haven’t uncovered! The books might have the answers!”

“I have to go now.” Elsa’s voice was sharp as an icicle.

“But we—”

“We should leave this room in the past. There has to be a reason Mother and Father wanted to keep it secret. Besides,” she said as she gestured toward the door, “the answers to our problems are out there.”

No, Anna thought, her fear big and full and pressing against her chest. It was happening again. Her plan to prove herself to Elsa was falling apart! Who cared about being able to go on some silly grand tour? Anna wanted to do what was best for everyone, but she seemed to have a knack for doing the complete opposite these days.

“Stay away from this room, Anna,” Elsa continued, turning away from her and stepping toward the library. “It was left hidden for a reason. Let’s keep it that way.”

“Elsa—”

“Leave it alone.” And when Elsa spoke in that tone, more like a queen than a sister, Anna knew there was no point in arguing.

Silently, Anna nodded. As she placed Secrets of the Magic Makers back onto a shelf, Elsa returned to the library and strode to her next scheduled appointment. But Anna couldn’t bring herself to leave—not just yet. She let herself look one last time at this secret room, imagining how her mother might have sat at that worktable, translating symbols into words, while her father studied the objects on the shelves and cracked a clever joke.

Without really thinking about it, Anna reached her fingers back toward Secrets of the Magic Makers, but they stopped just short of touching the soft leather. Elsa might be really upset with her if she found out what Anna was thinking, but Elsa would be even more upset if the animals kept getting sick. It would be worth it, Anna told herself firmly, when everything had been fixed—when Anna had fixed things. Besides, Elsa had only said that Anna needed to stay out of this room, but she hadn’t said—or at least, hadn’t said specifically—that Anna couldn’t take some of the room with her.

And with that, Anna tugged her mother’s book free and hurried away.
chapters.zh:
艾莎回来了。

尽管安娜知道姐姐比她早起得多，开过村民大会、走访过农场、翻过图书馆，又去了另一座农场，她却依旧清爽干净，金辫像一道阳光，衬在母亲那温暖的酒红围巾上——此刻围巾正搭在她肩上。

艾莎站着不动，张着嘴，只能用“惊愕”来形容地盯着密室里的安娜和奥拉夫。“怎——怎么？

我是说，你们……”艾莎语无伦次。“这是什么地方？”喜悦与释然漫过安娜。

从艾莎脸上的神情和她发颤的声音，安娜知道——就像她知道冰是冷、火是热一样——艾莎并不知道这个特定的秘密。

这一次，安娜不是最后一个知道的。“我们发现了一间秘密（clandestine）房间，”奥拉夫说。“clandestine 意思是秘密。

可我想现在它没那么秘密了。

除非你能保守一个……clandestine 的名词形式是什么？

保守个 clandestiny？”他还是把雪景球攥在手里。“介意我拿给斯文看看吗？”姐妹俩还没答，他就蹦跳着出了房间。“确切说，我也不知道，”安娜回应艾莎的问题。“可这难道不奇妙吗？”她指向密室的架子，强忍笑意——艾莎已走进房间几步，睁大眼环顾，打量着干草药、闪亮的铜望远镜，以及那卷像是独角鲸牙的乳白漩涡。

艾莎凑近架子。“你们怎么找到这地方的？”艾莎问。“奥拉夫，”安娜说。

她把那些物件、地图、笔记，以及她觉得可能藏着答案那本书，一一告诉了艾莎。

一提到父母曾在此，艾莎倒吸一口气。“所以，”安娜总结，“我打赌我们能在这儿找到关于枯萎病的东西。”“这我可不敢说，”艾莎说。“但无论什么影响了小允的牛，也影响了韦斯顿家的山羊。

我没能叫醒它们。

我什么办法都试了。”“我是说，看这书名！”安娜从架上抽出《炼金术士年鉴》转回身，可艾莎的注意力似乎被别处勾住——一幅小心倚墙而立的旧金框。

框里的画被污垢糊住，可安娜觉得自己能勉强辨出一双眼睛和硬朗的下巴：一幅肖像。

艾莎拾起它吹了吹，一团灰腾起，落在安娜脸上。

安娜打了个喷嚏，艾莎则把画伸直手臂举着眯眼细看。“我想这该是阿伦黛尔的阿伦。

不过画太脏，难说清。”安娜把年鉴放回架，从艾莎肩后窥看。“你怎么觉得是阿伦？”阿伦是远古——极远古、甚至在末次冰期之前的传说领袖。

事实上太古，那位著名战士多半根本不存在。“看见没？”艾莎指着一块黑斑。“我想那该是他的剑‘雷伏律特’，剑上镶着‘亮若眼的黄钻’。”安娜盯着姐姐。“你……在引用什么？”“对，”艾莎承认。“那是《阿伦 saga》里的一句，作者是个无名诗人，有人称她实为阿伦的真爱。”安娜听着有点耳熟。

尽管她对阿伦黛尔无所不知，仍有某些细节——像这些——她知道自己曾知道却忘了。

她忘掉的，通常是父母讲过的故事。

尴尬悄悄爬过她。

她讨厌自己忘事！

她努力回想关于阿伦的一切。

关于他英勇事迹的故事与史诗无穷无尽——从帮胡尔德民藏尾巴，到潜海与美人鱼同歌，或登山顶会太阳。

据那个特定的故事，安娜回想，太阳对阿伦如此倾心，便赠他一柄叫“雷伏律特之刃”的剑。

握着太阳之剑，阿伦在群山间凿出了峡湾。

且不止任何峡湾，正是这条：阿伦峡湾，阿伦黛尔王国的脊梁。“可是那句‘旋转的月，飞转的日，铸成弯月之刃’，然后……什么什么什么，‘愿阿伦黛尔的旗帜永飘’？”安娜问。

艾莎点头。“正是。”艾莎指向黑斑上方一点的模糊处，安娜的尴尬消了。“我想那可能是柄头上的黄钻，然后那里”——她移手——“看见剑身怎么弯的吗？

据传说，那弯处正是剑首次劈地之处。

剑名由此而来。‘Revolute’意为‘弯曲’。”“魔法剑什么的都好，”安娜歪着头，用手给自己扇风。

这无窗的房间渐热。“可我真看不出能切开大地有什么用。”艾莎拨弄辫子看着画。“据说，太阳赐雷伏律特以伟力，握剑在手，阿伦成了守护者，团结众人抵御黑暗恐惧。

他是位伟大的领袖。”一种奇怪的神情落在艾莎脸上。“历史似乎满是伟大的领袖。”安娜瞥了姐姐一眼。

因某个她不太明白的原因，艾莎仿佛已离开房间，尽管她人没动。

她不再看安娜。

相反，她的目光定在满是书、瓶与罐的架子上。“他们为何研究魔法？

又为何封起这房间，从不告诉我们？”艾莎问，声音轻得让安娜怀疑她是否真想说出口。

艾莎立在那里，背挺得不可思议地直，正是女王该有的站姿。

可就在那一刻，安娜没看见阿伦黛尔女王艾莎。

她看见孤独的孩子艾莎，终日独处房中，只有霜花图案作伴。

安娜伸手碰了碰艾莎的手臂。

姐姐僵着，仿佛她不仅掌控冰雪，本就是冰雪所造。“我也有同样的疑问，”安娜承认，庆幸他们同在此事里。“可想啊：人们为何学艺术？”她问。“面包师布洛杰特为何毕生追求烤出世上最好的黄油饼干？

克斯托夫为何总想唱歌？”艾莎仍沉默，于是安娜替她答，弯腰拾起《魔法创造者之秘》。“因为才华值得探索。”

因为黄油饼干好吃、唱歌有趣，而你的魔法很美，艾莎。

也许他们想多了解它。”她把手滑进艾莎的手里，等着。

几秒后，艾莎攥了攥她的手指，安娜也回攥。

艾莎不与安娜对视，挪开身朝出口走去。“我得走了。”艾莎声音轻。“这地方让我发毛。”“什么意思？”安娜想，她从没待过一间如此美、却还有那么多可探索的房间。

可能无穷无尽！“全是这些罐里的东西。”艾莎挥着手。“被装着、锁起来。”“唔，”安娜说，把《魔法创造者之秘》夹在臂下，“也许这正意味着，是时候让它们都见见天日了。”兴奋再次在她心中升起。“治愈枯萎病的答案可能就在这儿！

也许外面还有更多魔法，真能帮我们的魔法！”艾莎一缩。“我——我不是那个意思，”安娜说。“你的魔法真的很管用。

只是不在此情此景。”艾莎退了一步。“在我们真正深挖这房间前，我得先去帮牲口，好吗？”艾莎说。“没时间可浪费。

我……我得走了。”“当然。

可——可我们……我可以留在这儿继续找线索，”安娜提议。“我们或许能找到正在发生之事的答案——”艾莎摇头。“我真的觉得，眼下我们该别碰这地方。“等一下，”安娜说，拼命想保住计划、拼命想帮忙。“还有太多我们没揭开！

书里也许有答案！”“我现在得走了。”艾莎声音冷如冰锥。“可我们——”“我们该让这房间留在过去。

父母想保密，必有缘由。

再说了，”她朝门一指，“我们问题的答案在那儿外头。”不，安娜想，恐惧庞大而满溢，压着她的胸口。

又来了。

她向艾莎证明自己的计划要瓦解了！

谁稀罕能去参加什么傻乎乎的环球巡游？

安娜想做对大家最有利的事，可近来她似乎有种反着来的本领。“离这房间远点，安娜，”艾莎继续道，转身朝图书馆走去。“它藏起来是有原因的。

就让它那样吧。”“艾莎——”“别碰它。”当艾莎用那种语气——更像女王而非姐姐——说话时，安娜知道争辩无益。

安娜默默点头。

当她把《魔法创造者之秘》放回架，艾莎已回图书馆，迈步赶向下一场预约。

可安娜无法让自己离开——至少现在不能。

她让自己最后看一眼这密室，想象母亲如何坐在工作台前，把符号译成文字，而父亲研究架上的物件，讲个机灵的笑话。

没多想，安娜伸手又朝《魔法创造者之秘》探去，却停在将触未触那柔软皮革之前。

若艾莎发现安娜所想，或许会真生气；可若动物继续生病，艾莎会更气。

一切都修好时——当安娜修好一切时——这便值得，安娜坚定地对自己说。

再说了，艾莎只说安娜需远离这房间，却没说——至少没明确说——安娜不能带走这房间的一点什么。

于是，安娜把母亲的书抽出来，匆匆离去。

sentences.en: But at that exact moment, Anna didn’t see Elsa, queen of Arendelle.
sentences.zh: 可就在那一刻，安娜没看见阿伦黛尔女王艾莎。

sentences.en: She saw Elsa the lonely child, who’d spent her days alone in her room with only patterns of frost to keep her company.
sentences.zh: 她看见孤独的孩子艾莎，终日独处房中，只有霜花图案作伴。

sentences.en: Anna reached out to touch Elsa’s arm.
sentences.zh: 安娜伸手碰了碰艾莎的手臂。

sentences.en: Her sister was stiff, as if she didn’t just wield cold and snow, but were made of it. “I have the same question,” Anna admitted, glad they were in this together. “But think about it: why do people study art?” she asked. “Why does Baker Blodget spend her entire life in pursuit of baking the best butter biscuits in the world?
sentences.zh: 姐姐僵着，仿佛她不仅掌控冰雪，本就是冰雪所造。“我也有同样的疑问，”安娜承认，庆幸他们同在此事里。“可想啊：人们为何学艺术？”她问。“面包师布洛杰特为何毕生追求烤出世上最好的黄油饼干？

sentences.en: Why does Kristoff keep trying to sing?” Elsa remained silent, so Anna answered for her, reaching down to pick up Secrets of the Magic Makers . “Because talents are worth exploring.
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫为何总想唱歌？”艾莎仍沉默，于是安娜替她答，弯腰拾起《魔法创造者之秘》。“因为才华值得探索。”

sentences.en: Because butter biscuits are delicious, singing is fun, and your magic is beautiful, Elsa.
sentences.zh: 因为黄油饼干好吃、唱歌有趣，而你的魔法很美，艾莎。

sentences.en: Maybe they wanted to know more about it.” She slipped a hand in Elsa’s, and waited.
sentences.zh: 也许他们想多了解它。”她把手滑进艾莎的手里，等着。

sentences.en: A few seconds later, Elsa squeezed her fingers, and Anna squeezed back.
sentences.zh: 几秒后，艾莎攥了攥她的手指，安娜也回攥。

sentences.en: Without meeting Anna’s eye, Elsa moved away from her and toward the exit. “I need to go.” Elsa’s voice was quiet. “This place creeps me out.” “What do you mean?” Anna didn’t think she had ever been in a more beautiful room with still so much to explore.
sentences.zh: 艾莎不与安娜对视，挪开身朝出口走去。“我得走了。”艾莎声音轻。“这地方让我发毛。”“什么意思？”安娜想，她从没待过一间如此美、却还有那么多可探索的房间。

sentences.en: The possibilities were endless! “It’s all these things in jars.” Elsa waved her hands. “Contained and locked away.” “Well,” Anna said, tucking Secrets of the Magic Makers under her arm, “maybe that just means it’s time for them all to be brought to the light of day.” Excitement again rose within her. “The answers to how to stop the Blight could be in here!
sentences.zh: 可能无穷无尽！“全是这些罐里的东西。”艾莎挥着手。“被装着、锁起来。”“唔，”安娜说，把《魔法创造者之秘》夹在臂下，“也许这正意味着，是时候让它们都见见天日了。”兴奋再次在她心中升起。“治愈枯萎病的答案可能就在这儿！

sentences.en: Maybe there’s even more magic out there, magic that can actually help us!” Elsa flinched. “I—I didn’t mean it like that,” Anna said. “Your magic is really helpful.
sentences.zh: 也许外面还有更多魔法，真能帮我们的魔法！”艾莎一缩。“我——我不是那个意思，”安娜说。“你的魔法真的很管用。

sentences.en: Just not in this situation.” Elsa took a step back. “I need to help the livestock before we can start really delving into this room, okay?” Elsa said. “There’s no time to waste.
sentences.zh: 只是不在此情此景。”艾莎退了一步。“在我们真正深挖这房间前，我得先去帮牲口，好吗？”艾莎说。“没时间可浪费。

sentences.en: I…I have to go.” “Of course.
sentences.zh: 我……我得走了。”“当然。

sentences.en: But—but we …I can stay here and keep looking for clues,” Anna suggested. “We may be able to find the answers to what’s happening to—” Elsa shook her head. “I really think we should leave this place alone for now.” “Hold on,” Anna said, desperate to keep her plan in place, desperate to help. “There’s so much we haven’t uncovered!
sentences.zh: 可——可我们……我可以留在这儿继续找线索，”安娜提议。“我们或许能找到正在发生之事的答案——”艾莎摇头。“我真的觉得，眼下我们该别碰这地方。“等一下，”安娜说，拼命想保住计划、拼命想帮忙。“还有太多我们没揭开！

sentences.en: The books might have the answers!” “I have to go now.” Elsa’s voice was sharp as an icicle. “But we—” “ We should leave this room in the past.
sentences.zh: 书里也许有答案！”“我现在得走了。”艾莎声音冷如冰锥。“可我们——”“我们该让这房间留在过去。

sentences.en: There has to be a reason Mother and Father wanted to keep it secret.
sentences.zh: 父母想保密，必有缘由。

sentences.en: Besides,” she said as she gestured toward the door, “the answers to our problems are out there.” No , Anna thought, her fear big and full and pressing against her chest.
sentences.zh: 再说了，”她朝门一指，“我们问题的答案在那儿外头。”不，安娜想，恐惧庞大而满溢，压着她的胸口。

sentences.en: It was happening again.
sentences.zh: 又来了。

sentences.en: Her plan to prove herself to Elsa was falling apart!
sentences.zh: 她向艾莎证明自己的计划要瓦解了！

sentences.en: Who cared about being able to go on some silly grand tour?
sentences.zh: 谁稀罕能去参加什么傻乎乎的环球巡游？

sentences.en: Anna wanted to do what was best for everyone, but she seemed to have a knack for doing the complete opposite these days. “Stay away from this room, Anna,” Elsa continued, turning away from her and stepping toward the library. “It was left hidden for a reason.
sentences.zh: 安娜想做对大家最有利的事，可近来她似乎有种反着来的本领。“离这房间远点，安娜，”艾莎继续道，转身朝图书馆走去。“它藏起来是有原因的。

sentences.en: Let’s keep it that way.” “ Elsa —” “Leave it alone.” And when Elsa spoke in that tone, more like a queen than a sister, Anna knew there was no point in arguing.
sentences.zh: 就让它那样吧。”“艾莎——”“别碰它。”当艾莎用那种语气——更像女王而非姐姐——说话时，安娜知道争辩无益。

sentences.en: Silently, Anna nodded.
sentences.zh: 安娜默默点头。

sentences.en: As she placed Secrets of the Magic Makers back onto a shelf, Elsa returned to the library and strode to her next scheduled appointment.
sentences.zh: 当她把《魔法创造者之秘》放回架，艾莎已回图书馆，迈步赶向下一场预约。

sentences.en: But Anna couldn’t bring herself to leave—not just yet.
sentences.zh: 可安娜无法让自己离开——至少现在不能。

sentences.en: She let herself look one last time at this secret room, imagining how her mother might have sat at that worktable, translating symbols into words, while her father studied the objects on the shelves and cracked a clever joke.
sentences.zh: 她让自己最后看一眼这密室，想象母亲如何坐在工作台前，把符号译成文字，而父亲研究架上的物件，讲个机灵的笑话。

sentences.en: Without really thinking about it, Anna reached her fingers back toward Secrets of the Magic Makers , but they stopped just short of touching the soft leather.
sentences.zh: 没多想，安娜伸手又朝《魔法创造者之秘》探去，却停在将触未触那柔软皮革之前。

sentences.en: Elsa might be really upset with her if she found out what Anna was thinking, but Elsa would be even more upset if the animals kept getting sick.
sentences.zh: 若艾莎发现安娜所想，或许会真生气；可若动物继续生病，艾莎会更气。

sentences.en: It would be worth it, Anna told herself firmly, when everything had been fixed—when Anna had fixed things.
sentences.zh: 一切都修好时——当安娜修好一切时——这便值得，安娜坚定地对自己说。

sentences.en: Besides, Elsa had only said that Anna needed to stay out of this room, but she hadn’t said—or at least, hadn’t said specifically —that Anna couldn’t take some of the room with her.
sentences.zh: 再说了，艾莎只说安娜需远离这房间，却没说——至少没明确说——安娜不能带走这房间的一点什么。

sentences.en: And with that, Anna tugged her mother’s book free and hurried away.
sentences.zh: 于是，安娜把母亲的书抽出来，匆匆离去。

chapters.title: 第5章
chapters.en:
IT WAS VERY LATE NOW, and Anna was hungry.

Stopping to grab a plate of cheese, crackers, and apple slices from the kitchen, she chatted with the castle cooks, catching up on local gossip: who was most likely to grow the biggest pumpkin in the village patch this year, how many people would attend the annual harvest feast, and the very exciting rumor that an engagement ring had been purchased at the jeweler’s shop, but by whom?

Usually, Anna would have loved to stay and muse, but she knew the more time she spent down there, the less time she’d have to research. And so, excusing herself with her cheese plate, Anna rushed into her warm bedroom, clambered into her most comfortable pajamas, and began to read.

Secrets of the Magic Makers was more than just a collection of stories. It almost seemed like a field guide, as if someone had traipsed through the wilderness collecting information on various mythological creatures while also gathering ingredients for turning flowers into frogs. There were histories of enchanted forests, and things that looked like recipes. And while several of the text passages had not been translated by her mother, many had.

Anna followed her mother’s handwriting like a hungry bird trailing crumbs. Crunching on her crackers, she read of shape-shifters who lived with herds of reindeer; talking trees; draugs; and boys who were no larger than a thumb. There were pages and pages of the unknown language, and every so often an illustration accompanied the symbols. Anna wondered if Kristoff would know anything about the runes, or if he had ever come across anything in the Valley of the Living Rock that might help. Were they runes of the mountain trolls? Or something else?

Her mother seemed to have skipped translating the pages with the more creepy-looking sketches. Anna flipped past a sketch of a man seemingly screaming in agony, then one of another man lying on a stone table as blue smoke curled from his head and a troll stood over him with its arms held high. Finally, she landed on a page that, based on its illustrations, seemed to detail the Saga of Aren.

The physical features of the legendary hero were much easier to see in this book than they had been in the portrait Elsa had uncovered. Aren had a shaggy head of yellow hair and a bright blond beard with a few skinny braids tucked into it. His face was more square than it was round, and his hooked nose put Anna in mind of an eagle. Though there were only runes on the page—no translation—Anna recognized some of his more famous exploits. In the corner was a sketch of the waterfall whom Aren had tricked into helping him breathe underwater. And just to the right of that, a sketch of the sun, each ray a delicate sword with a yellow diamond in its pommel, just like Aren’s famed Revolute Blade. And in the last corner, far right and down, lounged a scrawled dragon. Anna turned the page, and cringed.

A sketch of a wolf, so realistic that Anna half thought she could feel its hot breath blasting from the pages, snarled up at her. Her mother seemed to have only gotten to the very beginning of the page, and had translated only a single word: Nattmara. Anna frowned. Yet another one of those once-known-now-forgotten words from her childhood. In frustration, she flipped the page. She’d had enough of not knowing—and enough, as a five-year-old, of that scary recurring nightmare, thank you very much.

The next installment that made her pause her was a recipe. It was a loose page, simply tucked into the binding, but it had been neatly titled in her mother’s handwriting: MAKE DREAMS COME TRUE. There was another word scrawled in the margins in the same handwriting: SPELL? Anna’s fingers traced the word spell. Not a recipe—magic.

She had never known anyone other than Elsa to be able to use magic before, and Elsa certainly didn’t incant words or spells when she created and manipulated snow and ice. The magic was part of Elsa. It ran within her. Shortly after their reunion, Anna had asked Elsa what it felt like when she twirled her hands. Elsa had described it as an overwhelming emotion, a feeling that would eventually grow so big it had to find release in some way.

“Like when you want to cry but you hold on to it because you don’t want others to see?” Anna had asked.

“Yes,” Elsa had said, “but not just crying. Sometimes, it’s the feeling of clamping in a giant laugh in a time you’re supposed to be quiet, like in the chapel. It seems that if I listen to the feeling, to the magic, and release it, I can manage it.”

A poem in a book didn’t seem like the kind of magic Elsa possessed, but that didn’t necessarily mean these words would not hold any power. These words. This spell. Excitement trilled through Anna.

The more she looked at the words, the more certain she felt that everything they needed was right here, in their parents’ research. She just wished she knew what knowledge lay behind the untranslated sections. Anna squinted at the symbols, as though by simply staring at them she would come to understand. But no knowledge came, only heavy eyelids.

She wondered if Kristoff had found out anything helpful on his trek to the valley. She wondered if SoYun was still out in the field, trying to keep her cattle awake through the night. But most of all, she wondered what her parents would have done in this situation.

“Anna and Elsa, always lean on each other for help,” Father had said. He’d have wanted her to tell Elsa about this spell, but first, she just needed to rest her eyes. Anna’s thoughts slipped over and past each other like darting fish as her eyelids drooped lower, and lower, and lower….She needed to fix the Blight….

The court of Royaume was just as beautiful as Anna had always dreamed, and she knew she was dreaming—not only because she’d never been to Royaume, but also because everything felt too perfect and fragile to be real. Besides, Elsa would never be caught dancing in real life, and there she was, spinning on the dance floor, arms flung wide as if she were trying to embrace the chandeliered ceiling above them.

Anna grinned. “You look like a tree caught in a gale!” she shouted over the high song of violins and flutes.

“And you look like you’re dizzy,” Elsa said.

Anna shook her head. “Dizzy? Why—oh!”

Before she could finish her question, Elsa grabbed her hand and began to twirl her, her diaphanous white skirts fanning around her like a skein of sparkling snow.

Anna threw back her head and laughed, imagining what a sight they must make on the dance floor. Elsa, dressed all in white spangled with pearl seeds, was the very embodiment of winter, while Anna’s headdress and gold skirts helped her masquerade as summer.

The grand ballroom blurred around her, seeming to turn into streaks of paint. Her head began to pound, but it was so rare to see Elsa silly and carefree that she didn’t want to tell her to stop. Instead, Anna closed her eyes, trying to hold on to this moment, even if it was only pretend…but was it?

She was feeling really dizzy now. No matter how much fun Elsa was having, it was time to stop.

“Hey, Elsa? That’s enough!” Anna opened her eyes and gasped.

Her sister was no longer twirling her.

Instead, a tall stranger in coattails and a silver wolf mask stood where Elsa had been.

Anna stumbled to a halt. “Pardon me.” She removed her hand. “I need to find my sister.”

The dancer bowed, the silver wolf mask nearly tipping off his nose. “As you wish, Princess Anna.”

The blood in her veins turned to ice. Anna knew that voice. It was a voice she didn’t want to hear again. She peered uncertainly through the dark eyeholes of the mask. “Prince—Prince Hans?”

“The very same.” A diamond ring suddenly materialized in his hand. “Your sister said I should give this to you when I ask for your hand.”

“My—my hand?”

Hans grabbed her wrist and jammed the ring onto her finger. “Your hand in marriage, of course. Your sister has given her blessing. She has no use for you.”

Anna yanked her hand away. “I don’t believe that,” she said, craning her neck to see if she could spot her sister in the glittering hall. But no one was there. The decorations, the musicians, the dancers…all had vanished, leaving her completely alone with the prince of the Southern Isles—her villainous almost-husband, who had tricked her and the rest of the kingdom before Anna uncovered his awful plans to kill Elsa and take over Arendelle.

Hans laughed, an awful sound, made worse by the way it turned up into a howl at the end. As Anna watched, the silver hair of his wolf mask rippled in the draft as if it were real fur, and his nose elongated, becoming more and more snoutlike.

More and more wolflike.

Until suddenly, there was no Hans, just a great white wolf with amber eyes and teeth the size of dinner knives. It was the same wolf that had stalked her childhood dreams. But while most things from childhood seem to become smaller as one grows, the wolf had, in fact, only grown with Anna. He was fiercer now. Hungrier.

The wolf licked his maw and advanced.

Wake up, Anna, she thought frantically, tripping on her skirts as she tried to scramble backward. Wake up! Wake up! Wake up—

“Wake up!” Anna sat straight up. The sound of her own voice shattered her nightmare. Relief, warm and sweet as fresh honey, coursed through her. It had been so long since she’d had this particular dream, this particular nightmare, and the fear it spawned was unfortunately as familiar as the ache of missing her parents. And this time, there was no Mother to tell her a distracting story or Father to bring her hot chocolate.

Always rely on each other for help.

Leaning forward, Anna grabbed Secrets of the Magic Makers, which had slid to the foot of her bed. She tucked it close to her chest and raced into her parents’ old bedroom. Not because she thought they would be there, but because Elsa had moved into it after her coronation, abandoning her childhood bedroom. But looking around the room and at the dying fire, Anna wondered why Elsa had not yet returned. She reassured herself that sometimes queenly duties could last all night.

She walked back to her room. Before clambering into bed, she stopped by her dressing table and took hold of her father’s sketchbook. King Agnarr had been a talented artist, wielding both his pencil and sword with ease. On the bad days, when Anna felt most alone, she liked to open his sketchbook up and see the world as he once had. There were images of Arendelle Castle, as well as the far-off lands he’d seen on his grand tour.

Elsa would leave on her own grand tour in just four—no, now three days—and if Anna could heal the animals before then, there was still a chance she’d be able to sail away with Elsa.

Returning to her bed, Anna decided that she’d wake up extra early to show Elsa the spell first thing. And so, with her father’s sketchbook on one side of her pillow and her mother’s book on the other, she at last dared to close her eyes.

The wolf did not return.
chapters.zh:
此刻夜已深，安娜饿了。

她在厨房顺手取了一盘奶酪、饼干和苹果片，与城堡厨师们闲聊，追着本地八卦：今年村园里谁最可能种出最大的南瓜，多少人会来一年一度的丰收宴，还有个极刺激的传闻——珠宝店卖出了一枚订婚戒指，可会是谁买的？

平时安娜会乐意留下神聊，可她知道在那儿耗得越久，研究的时间就越少。

于是，安娜端着奶酪盘告退，冲进温暖的卧室，套上最舒服的睡衣，开始阅读。

《魔法创造者之秘》不止是故事集。

它几乎像一本野外指南，仿佛有人踏遍荒野，收集各类神话生物的信息，同时也采集把花变蛙的材料。

有魔法森林的历史，也有看似配方之物。

尽管有几段文字母亲未译，许多却译了。

安娜像一只循着面包屑的饿鸟，跟着母亲的笔迹。

她咔嚓嚼着饼干，读到与驯鹿群同住的变形者、会说话的树、draug（僵尸），以及不比拇指大的男孩。

一页又一页的未知文字，偶尔有插图相伴。

安娜想，克斯托夫会懂这些如尼文吗，还是他在活石谷曾见过什么有用的？

它们是山地地精的如尼文吗？

还是别的？

母亲似乎跳过了那些画风更可怖的页未译。

安娜翻过一张似在痛苦尖叫的男人速写，又翻过一张：另一男人躺在石桌上，蓝烟从头顶盘旋，一只地精高举双臂立在他上方。

终于，她落在一页上，从插图看，似乎详述着《阿伦 saga》。

这位传说英雄的体貌，在此书中比在艾莎揭出的肖像里清楚得多。

阿伦顶着一头乱蓬蓬的黄发，亮金色胡须里掖着几缕细辫。

他的脸偏方不偏圆，钩鼻让安娜想起鹰。

尽管页上只有如尼文——没有译文——安娜认得他几件更出名的事迹。

角落里是一幅瀑布的速写，阿伦曾骗它帮自己在水下呼吸。

就在其右，是一幅太阳的速写，每一道光芒都是柄精致的剑，柄头镶着黄钻，正如阿伦那柄著名的雷伏律特之刃。

而在最右下角，懒洋洋趴着一条草草画的龙。

安娜翻页，瑟缩了一下。

一张狼的速写，逼真得让安娜半信自己能感到它从页中喷出的热气，正朝她龇牙。

母亲似乎只译到这页开头，只译了一个词：夜魇（Nattmara）。

安娜皱眉。

又是那些儿时曾知、如今已忘的词之一。

她懊恼地翻过页。

她受够了无知——也受够了五岁时那个吓人的反复噩梦，非常感谢。

让她停下的是下一段：一张配方。

那是张散页，随意夹在装订里，却用母亲清晰的笔迹题了名：美梦成真。

页边用同一笔迹草草写着另一个词：咒语？

安娜的手指描过“咒语”二字。

不是配方——是魔法。

除了艾莎，她从不知别人能用魔法，而艾莎创造、操控冰雪时，绝不会念什么咒语。

魔法本就是艾莎的一部分。

在她的血脉里流淌。

重逢后不久，安娜问过艾莎，转手腕时是什么感觉。

艾莎形容那是一种压倒性的情绪，终会涨大到必须以某种方式释放。“就像你想哭却忍着，因为不想让别人看见？”安娜问。“对，”艾莎说，“可不止哭。

有时，是在该安静的场合——比如礼拜堂——憋住一场大笑的感觉。

似乎只要我倾听那感觉、那魔法，并释放它，就能驾驭。”书中的诗不像艾莎那种魔法，可这不意味着这些字句毫无力量。

这些字句。

这咒语。

兴奋在安娜体内震颤。

她越看这些字，越确信所需一切就在此处，在父母的研究里。

她只愿自己知道未译部分背后藏着什么知识。

安娜眯眼盯着符号，仿佛仅凭凝视便能懂。

可没来知识，只来了沉重的眼皮。

她想知道克斯托夫去谷中的路上可发现了什么有用的。

她想知道小允是否还在田里，整夜试着让牛保持清醒。

但最重要的是，她想知道父母在此境况会怎么做。“安娜与艾莎，永远互相依靠，”父亲说过。

他定愿她把这咒语告诉艾莎，可首先，她只需歇歇眼。

安娜的思绪像窜动的鱼般彼此滑过，眼皮垂得越来越低……她得治好枯萎病……

罗亚姆的宫廷美得一如安娜梦中所见，而她知道自己是在做梦——不只因为她从没去过罗亚姆，也因一切太完美、太易碎，不似真实。

再者，现实里艾莎绝不会被撞见跳舞，可她就在那儿，在舞池旋转，双臂大张，像要拥抱头顶的水晶灯天花板。

安娜咧嘴。“你像一棵被大风刮住的树！”她在提琴与长笛的高亢乐声上喊道。“你倒像晕了，”艾莎说。

安娜摇头。“晕？

为什么——噢！”话没问完，艾莎抓住她的手开始转她，半透明的白裙像一缕闪亮的雪在她四周散开。

安娜仰头大笑，想象她们在舞池该是多惹眼的景象。

艾莎一身白、缀着珍珠籽，是冬的化身；而安娜的头饰与金裙帮她扮成夏。

大舞厅在她四周模糊，仿佛化作画笔的条纹。

她头开始一跳一跳地疼，可难得见艾莎这般傻气无忧，她不愿叫停。

于是安娜闭上眼，想抓住这一刻，哪怕只是假装……可它是吗？

此刻她真觉得晕了。

无论艾莎玩得多开心，是时候停了。“嘿，艾莎？

够了！”安娜睁眼，倒吸一口气。

姐姐不再转她了。

取而代之的，是个穿燕尾服、戴银狼面具的高个陌生人，立在艾莎方才的位置。

安娜踉跄停住。“失陪。”她抽回手。“我得找我姐姐。”舞者鞠躬，银狼面具几乎从鼻尖滑落。“如您所愿，安娜公主。”她血管里的血成了冰。

安娜认得那声音。

那是她不想再听到的声音。

她不安地从面具的暗眼孔里窥看。“汉斯——汉斯王子？”“正是。”一枚钻戒忽然在他手中显形。“你姐姐说，我向你要手时，该把它给你。”“我的——我的手？”汉斯抓过她手腕，把戒指硬套上她手指。“当然是婚约。

你姐姐已赐下祝福。

她用不着你了。”安娜猛抽回手。“我不信，”她说，伸长脖子想在那闪亮的厅里找出姐姐。

可没有人在。

装饰、乐师、舞者……全消失了，只留她与南方群岛的王子独处——那个险些成为她丈夫的恶棍，曾在安娜揭穿他欲杀艾莎、篡夺阿伦黛尔的恶计前，骗了她与举国上下。

汉斯笑了，一声可怕的音，末了还上扬成嗥叫，更显狰狞。

安娜看着，他狼面具的银发在气流中起伏，像真毛，鼻子拉长，越来越像口鼻。

越来越像狼。

直到忽然，汉斯不见了，只剩一头琥珀眼、牙如餐刀般大的白狼。

正是那头潜入她童年梦境的狼。

可尽管童年之物常随人成长而变小，这狼实则只随安娜长大。

他如今更凶。

更饿。

狼舔了舔嘴，逼上前。

醒来，安娜，她慌乱地想，被裙子绊着，想往后爬。

醒来！

醒来！

醒来——“醒来！”安娜猛地坐直。

自己声音击碎了噩梦。

如新蜜般温暖甘甜的释然流遍全身。

她许久未做这特定的梦、这特定的噩梦了，而它催生的恐惧，不幸地如思念父母的痛般熟悉。

而这一次，没有母亲讲个分神的故事，也没有父亲端来热可可。

永远互相依靠。

安娜前倾，抓起滑到床脚的《魔法创造者之秘》。

她把它紧贴胸前，冲进父母从前的卧室。

不是以为他们会在，而是因艾莎加冕后搬了进去，弃了童年卧室。

可环顾房间与将熄的火，安娜疑惑艾莎为何还没回来。

她安慰自己，女王的职责有时能持续整夜。

她走回房。

爬上床前，她在梳妆台边驻足，拿起父亲的素描本。

阿格瑞国王是个有才的画家，铅笔与剑都使得从容。

在糟糕的日子，当安娜最觉孤独，她爱翻开他的素描本，看他曾眼里的世界。

有阿伦黛尔城堡的画，也有他巡游所见远方之地的画。

艾莎再过四天——不，如今是三天——就要启程自己的巡游，若安娜能在那前治好动物，仍有机会随艾莎扬帆。

回到床上，安娜决定明日格外早起，第一件事就把咒语给艾莎看。

于是，父亲素描本在一侧枕边、母亲的书在另一侧，她终于敢合上眼。

狼没有回来。

sentences.en: IT WAS VERY LATE NOW, and Anna was hungry.
sentences.zh: 此刻夜已深，安娜饿了。

sentences.en: Stopping to grab a plate of cheese, crackers, and apple slices from the kitchen, she chatted with the castle cooks, catching up on local gossip: who was most likely to grow the biggest pumpkin in the village patch this year, how many people would attend the annual harvest feast, and the very exciting rumor that an engagement ring had been purchased at the jeweler’s shop, but by whom?
sentences.zh: 她在厨房顺手取了一盘奶酪、饼干和苹果片，与城堡厨师们闲聊，追着本地八卦：今年村园里谁最可能种出最大的南瓜，多少人会来一年一度的丰收宴，还有个极刺激的传闻——珠宝店卖出了一枚订婚戒指，可会是谁买的？

sentences.en: Usually, Anna would have loved to stay and muse, but she knew the more time she spent down there, the less time she’d have to research.
sentences.zh: 平时安娜会乐意留下神聊，可她知道在那儿耗得越久，研究的时间就越少。

sentences.en: And so, excusing herself with her cheese plate, Anna rushed into her warm bedroom, clambered into her most comfortable pajamas, and began to read.
sentences.zh: 于是，安娜端着奶酪盘告退，冲进温暖的卧室，套上最舒服的睡衣，开始阅读。

sentences.en: Secrets of the Magic Makers was more than just a collection of stories.
sentences.zh: 《魔法创造者之秘》不止是故事集。

sentences.en: It almost seemed like a field guide, as if someone had traipsed through the wilderness collecting information on various mythological creatures while also gathering ingredients for turning flowers into frogs.
sentences.zh: 它几乎像一本野外指南，仿佛有人踏遍荒野，收集各类神话生物的信息，同时也采集把花变蛙的材料。

sentences.en: There were histories of enchanted forests, and things that looked like recipes.
sentences.zh: 有魔法森林的历史，也有看似配方之物。

sentences.en: And while several of the text passages had not been translated by her mother, many had.
sentences.zh: 尽管有几段文字母亲未译，许多却译了。

sentences.en: Anna followed her mother’s handwriting like a hungry bird trailing crumbs.
sentences.zh: 安娜像一只循着面包屑的饿鸟，跟着母亲的笔迹。

sentences.en: Crunching on her crackers, she read of shape-shifters who lived with herds of reindeer; talking trees; draugs; and boys who were no larger than a thumb.
sentences.zh: 她咔嚓嚼着饼干，读到与驯鹿群同住的变形者、会说话的树、draug（僵尸），以及不比拇指大的男孩。

sentences.en: There were pages and pages of the unknown language, and every so often an illustration accompanied the symbols.
sentences.zh: 一页又一页的未知文字，偶尔有插图相伴。

sentences.en: Anna wondered if Kristoff would know anything about the runes, or if he had ever come across anything in the Valley of the Living Rock that might help.
sentences.zh: 安娜想，克斯托夫会懂这些如尼文吗，还是他在活石谷曾见过什么有用的？

sentences.en: Were they runes of the mountain trolls?
sentences.zh: 它们是山地地精的如尼文吗？

sentences.en: Or something else?
sentences.zh: 还是别的？

sentences.en: Her mother seemed to have skipped translating the pages with the more creepy-looking sketches.
sentences.zh: 母亲似乎跳过了那些画风更可怖的页未译。

sentences.en: Anna flipped past a sketch of a man seemingly screaming in agony, then one of another man lying on a stone table as blue smoke curled from his head and a troll stood over him with its arms held high.
sentences.zh: 安娜翻过一张似在痛苦尖叫的男人速写，又翻过一张：另一男人躺在石桌上，蓝烟从头顶盘旋，一只地精高举双臂立在他上方。

sentences.en: Finally, she landed on a page that, based on its illustrations, seemed to detail the Saga of Aren .
sentences.zh: 终于，她落在一页上，从插图看，似乎详述着《阿伦 saga》。

sentences.en: The physical features of the legendary hero were much easier to see in this book than they had been in the portrait Elsa had uncovered.
sentences.zh: 这位传说英雄的体貌，在此书中比在艾莎揭出的肖像里清楚得多。

sentences.en: Aren had a shaggy head of yellow hair and a bright blond beard with a few skinny braids tucked into it.
sentences.zh: 阿伦顶着一头乱蓬蓬的黄发，亮金色胡须里掖着几缕细辫。

sentences.en: His face was more square than it was round, and his hooked nose put Anna in mind of an eagle.
sentences.zh: 他的脸偏方不偏圆，钩鼻让安娜想起鹰。

sentences.en: Though there were only runes on the page—no translation—Anna recognized some of his more famous exploits.
sentences.zh: 尽管页上只有如尼文——没有译文——安娜认得他几件更出名的事迹。

sentences.en: In the corner was a sketch of the waterfall whom Aren had tricked into helping him breathe underwater.
sentences.zh: 角落里是一幅瀑布的速写，阿伦曾骗它帮自己在水下呼吸。

sentences.en: And just to the right of that, a sketch of the sun, each ray a delicate sword with a yellow diamond in its pommel, just like Aren’s famed Revolute Blade.
sentences.zh: 就在其右，是一幅太阳的速写，每一道光芒都是柄精致的剑，柄头镶着黄钻，正如阿伦那柄著名的雷伏律特之刃。

sentences.en: And in the last corner, far right and down, lounged a scrawled dragon.
sentences.zh: 而在最右下角，懒洋洋趴着一条草草画的龙。

sentences.en: Anna turned the page, and cringed.
sentences.zh: 安娜翻页，瑟缩了一下。

sentences.en: A sketch of a wolf, so realistic that Anna half thought she could feel its hot breath blasting from the pages, snarled up at her.
sentences.zh: 一张狼的速写，逼真得让安娜半信自己能感到它从页中喷出的热气，正朝她龇牙。

sentences.en: Her mother seemed to have only gotten to the very beginning of the page, and had translated only a single word: Nattmara .
sentences.zh: 母亲似乎只译到这页开头，只译了一个词：夜魇（Nattmara）。

sentences.en: Anna frowned.
sentences.zh: 安娜皱眉。

sentences.en: Yet another one of those once-known-now-forgotten words from her childhood.
sentences.zh: 又是那些儿时曾知、如今已忘的词之一。

sentences.en: In frustration, she flipped the page.
sentences.zh: 她懊恼地翻过页。

sentences.en: She’d had enough of not knowing—and enough, as a five-year-old, of that scary recurring nightmare, thank you very much.
sentences.zh: 她受够了无知——也受够了五岁时那个吓人的反复噩梦，非常感谢。

sentences.en: The next installment that made her pause her was a recipe.
sentences.zh: 让她停下的是下一段：一张配方。

sentences.en: It was a loose page, simply tucked into the binding, but it had been neatly titled in her mother’s handwriting: MAKE DREAMS COME TRUE .
sentences.zh: 那是张散页，随意夹在装订里，却用母亲清晰的笔迹题了名：美梦成真。

sentences.en: There was another word scrawled in the margins in the same handwriting: SPELL?
sentences.zh: 页边用同一笔迹草草写着另一个词：咒语？

sentences.en: Anna’s fingers traced the word spell .
sentences.zh: 安娜的手指描过“咒语”二字。

sentences.en: Not a recipe— magic .
sentences.zh: 不是配方——是魔法。

sentences.en: She had never known anyone other than Elsa to be able to use magic before, and Elsa certainly didn’t incant words or spells when she created and manipulated snow and ice.
sentences.zh: 除了艾莎，她从不知别人能用魔法，而艾莎创造、操控冰雪时，绝不会念什么咒语。

sentences.en: The magic was part of Elsa.
sentences.zh: 魔法本就是艾莎的一部分。

sentences.en: It ran within her.
sentences.zh: 在她的血脉里流淌。

sentences.en: Shortly after their reunion, Anna had asked Elsa what it felt like when she twirled her hands.
sentences.zh: 重逢后不久，安娜问过艾莎，转手腕时是什么感觉。

sentences.en: Elsa had described it as an overwhelming emotion, a feeling that would eventually grow so big it had to find release in some way. “Like when you want to cry but you hold on to it because you don’t want others to see?” Anna had asked. “Yes,” Elsa had said, “but not just crying.
sentences.zh: 艾莎形容那是一种压倒性的情绪，终会涨大到必须以某种方式释放。“就像你想哭却忍着，因为不想让别人看见？”安娜问。“对，”艾莎说，“可不止哭。

sentences.en: Sometimes, it’s the feeling of clamping in a giant laugh in a time you’re supposed to be quiet, like in the chapel.
sentences.zh: 有时，是在该安静的场合——比如礼拜堂——憋住一场大笑的感觉。

sentences.en: It seems that if I listen to the feeling, to the magic, and release it, I can manage it.” A poem in a book didn’t seem like the kind of magic Elsa possessed, but that didn’t necessarily mean these words would not hold any power.
sentences.zh: 似乎只要我倾听那感觉、那魔法，并释放它，就能驾驭。”书中的诗不像艾莎那种魔法，可这不意味着这些字句毫无力量。

sentences.en: These words.
sentences.zh: 这些字句。

sentences.en: This spell .
sentences.zh: 这咒语。

sentences.en: Excitement trilled through Anna.
sentences.zh: 兴奋在安娜体内震颤。

sentences.en: The more she looked at the words, the more certain she felt that everything they needed was right here, in their parents’ research.
sentences.zh: 她越看这些字，越确信所需一切就在此处，在父母的研究里。

sentences.en: She just wished she knew what knowledge lay behind the untranslated sections.
sentences.zh: 她只愿自己知道未译部分背后藏着什么知识。

sentences.en: Anna squinted at the symbols, as though by simply staring at them she would come to understand.
sentences.zh: 安娜眯眼盯着符号，仿佛仅凭凝视便能懂。

sentences.en: But no knowledge came, only heavy eyelids.
sentences.zh: 可没来知识，只来了沉重的眼皮。

sentences.en: She wondered if Kristoff had found out anything helpful on his trek to the valley.
sentences.zh: 她想知道克斯托夫去谷中的路上可发现了什么有用的。

sentences.en: She wondered if SoYun was still out in the field, trying to keep her cattle awake through the night.
sentences.zh: 她想知道小允是否还在田里，整夜试着让牛保持清醒。

sentences.en: But most of all, she wondered what her parents would have done in this situation. “Anna and Elsa, always lean on each other for help,” Father had said.
sentences.zh: 但最重要的是，她想知道父母在此境况会怎么做。“安娜与艾莎，永远互相依靠，”父亲说过。

sentences.en: He’d have wanted her to tell Elsa about this spell, but first, she just needed to rest her eyes.
sentences.zh: 他定愿她把这咒语告诉艾莎，可首先，她只需歇歇眼。

sentences.en: Anna’s thoughts slipped over and past each other like darting fish as her eyelids drooped lower, and lower, and lower….She needed to fix the Blight….
sentences.zh: 安娜的思绪像窜动的鱼般彼此滑过，眼皮垂得越来越低……她得治好枯萎病……

sentences.en: The court of Royaume was just as beautiful as Anna had always dreamed, and she knew she was dreaming—not only because she’d never been to Royaume, but also because everything felt too perfect and fragile to be real.
sentences.zh: 罗亚姆的宫廷美得一如安娜梦中所见，而她知道自己是在做梦——不只因为她从没去过罗亚姆，也因一切太完美、太易碎，不似真实。

sentences.en: Besides, Elsa would never be caught dancing in real life, and there she was, spinning on the dance floor, arms flung wide as if she were trying to embrace the chandeliered ceiling above them.
sentences.zh: 再者，现实里艾莎绝不会被撞见跳舞，可她就在那儿，在舞池旋转，双臂大张，像要拥抱头顶的水晶灯天花板。

sentences.en: Anna grinned. “You look like a tree caught in a gale!” she shouted over the high song of violins and flutes. “And you look like you’re dizzy,” Elsa said.
sentences.zh: 安娜咧嘴。“你像一棵被大风刮住的树！”她在提琴与长笛的高亢乐声上喊道。“你倒像晕了，”艾莎说。

sentences.en: Anna shook her head. “Dizzy?
sentences.zh: 安娜摇头。“晕？

sentences.en: Why—oh!” Before she could finish her question, Elsa grabbed her hand and began to twirl her, her diaphanous white skirts fanning around her like a skein of sparkling snow.
sentences.zh: 为什么——噢！”话没问完，艾莎抓住她的手开始转她，半透明的白裙像一缕闪亮的雪在她四周散开。

sentences.en: Anna threw back her head and laughed, imagining what a sight they must make on the dance floor.
sentences.zh: 安娜仰头大笑，想象她们在舞池该是多惹眼的景象。

sentences.en: Elsa, dressed all in white spangled with pearl seeds, was the very embodiment of winter, while Anna’s headdress and gold skirts helped her masquerade as summer.
sentences.zh: 艾莎一身白、缀着珍珠籽，是冬的化身；而安娜的头饰与金裙帮她扮成夏。

sentences.en: The grand ballroom blurred around her, seeming to turn into streaks of paint.
sentences.zh: 大舞厅在她四周模糊，仿佛化作画笔的条纹。

sentences.en: Her head began to pound, but it was so rare to see Elsa silly and carefree that she didn’t want to tell her to stop.
sentences.zh: 她头开始一跳一跳地疼，可难得见艾莎这般傻气无忧，她不愿叫停。

sentences.en: Instead, Anna closed her eyes, trying to hold on to this moment, even if it was only pretend…but was it?
sentences.zh: 于是安娜闭上眼，想抓住这一刻，哪怕只是假装……可它是吗？

sentences.en: She was feeling really dizzy now.
sentences.zh: 此刻她真觉得晕了。

sentences.en: No matter how much fun Elsa was having, it was time to stop. “Hey, Elsa?
sentences.zh: 无论艾莎玩得多开心，是时候停了。“嘿，艾莎？

sentences.en: That’s enough!” Anna opened her eyes and gasped.
sentences.zh: 够了！”安娜睁眼，倒吸一口气。

sentences.en: Her sister was no longer twirling her.
sentences.zh: 姐姐不再转她了。

sentences.en: Instead, a tall stranger in coattails and a silver wolf mask stood where Elsa had been.
sentences.zh: 取而代之的，是个穿燕尾服、戴银狼面具的高个陌生人，立在艾莎方才的位置。

sentences.en: Anna stumbled to a halt. “Pardon me.” She removed her hand. “I need to find my sister.” The dancer bowed, the silver wolf mask nearly tipping off his nose. “As you wish, Princess Anna.” The blood in her veins turned to ice.
sentences.zh: 安娜踉跄停住。“失陪。”她抽回手。“我得找我姐姐。”舞者鞠躬，银狼面具几乎从鼻尖滑落。“如您所愿，安娜公主。”她血管里的血成了冰。

sentences.en: Anna knew that voice.
sentences.zh: 安娜认得那声音。

sentences.en: It was a voice she didn’t want to hear again.
sentences.zh: 那是她不想再听到的声音。

sentences.en: She peered uncertainly through the dark eyeholes of the mask. “Prince—Prince Hans?” “The very same.” A diamond ring suddenly materialized in his hand. “Your sister said I should give this to you when I ask for your hand.” “My—my hand?” Hans grabbed her wrist and jammed the ring onto her finger. “Your hand in marriage, of course.
sentences.zh: 她不安地从面具的暗眼孔里窥看。“汉斯——汉斯王子？”“正是。”一枚钻戒忽然在他手中显形。“你姐姐说，我向你要手时，该把它给你。”“我的——我的手？”汉斯抓过她手腕，把戒指硬套上她手指。“当然是婚约。

sentences.en: Your sister has given her blessing.
sentences.zh: 你姐姐已赐下祝福。

sentences.en: She has no use for you.” Anna yanked her hand away. “I don’t believe that,” she said, craning her neck to see if she could spot her sister in the glittering hall.
sentences.zh: 她用不着你了。”安娜猛抽回手。“我不信，”她说，伸长脖子想在那闪亮的厅里找出姐姐。

sentences.en: But no one was there.
sentences.zh: 可没有人在。

sentences.en: The decorations, the musicians, the dancers…all had vanished, leaving her completely alone with the prince of the Southern Isles—her villainous almost-husband, who had tricked her and the rest of the kingdom before Anna uncovered his awful plans to kill Elsa and take over Arendelle.
sentences.zh: 装饰、乐师、舞者……全消失了，只留她与南方群岛的王子独处——那个险些成为她丈夫的恶棍，曾在安娜揭穿他欲杀艾莎、篡夺阿伦黛尔的恶计前，骗了她与举国上下。

sentences.en: Hans laughed, an awful sound, made worse by the way it turned up into a howl at the end.
sentences.zh: 汉斯笑了，一声可怕的音，末了还上扬成嗥叫，更显狰狞。

sentences.en: As Anna watched, the silver hair of his wolf mask rippled in the draft as if it were real fur, and his nose elongated, becoming more and more snoutlike.
sentences.zh: 安娜看着，他狼面具的银发在气流中起伏，像真毛，鼻子拉长，越来越像口鼻。

sentences.en: More and more wolflike.
sentences.zh: 越来越像狼。

sentences.en: Until suddenly, there was no Hans, just a great white wolf with amber eyes and teeth the size of dinner knives.
sentences.zh: 直到忽然，汉斯不见了，只剩一头琥珀眼、牙如餐刀般大的白狼。

sentences.en: It was the same wolf that had stalked her childhood dreams.
sentences.zh: 正是那头潜入她童年梦境的狼。

sentences.en: But while most things from childhood seem to become smaller as one grows, the wolf had, in fact, only grown with Anna.
sentences.zh: 可尽管童年之物常随人成长而变小，这狼实则只随安娜长大。

sentences.en: He was fiercer now.
sentences.zh: 他如今更凶。

sentences.en: Hungrier.
sentences.zh: 更饿。

sentences.en: The wolf licked his maw and advanced.
sentences.zh: 狼舔了舔嘴，逼上前。

sentences.en: Wake up, Anna, she thought frantically, tripping on her skirts as she tried to scramble backward.
sentences.zh: 醒来，安娜，她慌乱地想，被裙子绊着，想往后爬。

sentences.en: Wake up!
sentences.zh: 醒来！

sentences.en: Wake up!
sentences.zh: 醒来！

sentences.en: Wake up— “Wake up!” Anna sat straight up.
sentences.zh: 醒来——“醒来！”安娜猛地坐直。

sentences.en: The sound of her own voice shattered her nightmare.
sentences.zh: 自己声音击碎了噩梦。

sentences.en: Relief, warm and sweet as fresh honey, coursed through her.
sentences.zh: 如新蜜般温暖甘甜的释然流遍全身。

sentences.en: It had been so long since she’d had this particular dream, this particular nightmare, and the fear it spawned was unfortunately as familiar as the ache of missing her parents.
sentences.zh: 她许久未做这特定的梦、这特定的噩梦了，而它催生的恐惧，不幸地如思念父母的痛般熟悉。

sentences.en: And this time, there was no Mother to tell her a distracting story or Father to bring her hot chocolate.
sentences.zh: 而这一次，没有母亲讲个分神的故事，也没有父亲端来热可可。

sentences.en: Always rely on each other for help.
sentences.zh: 永远互相依靠。

sentences.en: Leaning forward, Anna grabbed Secrets of the Magic Makers , which had slid to the foot of her bed.
sentences.zh: 安娜前倾，抓起滑到床脚的《魔法创造者之秘》。

sentences.en: She tucked it close to her chest and raced into her parents’ old bedroom.
sentences.zh: 她把它紧贴胸前，冲进父母从前的卧室。

sentences.en: Not because she thought they would be there, but because Elsa had moved into it after her coronation, abandoning her childhood bedroom.
sentences.zh: 不是以为他们会在，而是因艾莎加冕后搬了进去，弃了童年卧室。

sentences.en: But looking around the room and at the dying fire, Anna wondered why Elsa had not yet returned.
sentences.zh: 可环顾房间与将熄的火，安娜疑惑艾莎为何还没回来。

sentences.en: She reassured herself that sometimes queenly duties could last all night.
sentences.zh: 她安慰自己，女王的职责有时能持续整夜。

sentences.en: She walked back to her room.
sentences.zh: 她走回房。

sentences.en: Before clambering into bed, she stopped by her dressing table and took hold of her father’s sketchbook.
sentences.zh: 爬上床前，她在梳妆台边驻足，拿起父亲的素描本。

sentences.en: King Agnarr had been a talented artist, wielding both his pencil and sword with ease.
sentences.zh: 阿格瑞国王是个有才的画家，铅笔与剑都使得从容。

sentences.en: On the bad days, when Anna felt most alone, she liked to open his sketchbook up and see the world as he once had.
sentences.zh: 在糟糕的日子，当安娜最觉孤独，她爱翻开他的素描本，看他曾眼里的世界。

sentences.en: There were images of Arendelle Castle, as well as the far-off lands he’d seen on his grand tour.
sentences.zh: 有阿伦黛尔城堡的画，也有他巡游所见远方之地的画。

sentences.en: Elsa would leave on her own grand tour in just four—no, now three days—and if Anna could heal the animals before then, there was still a chance she’d be able to sail away with Elsa.
sentences.zh: 艾莎再过四天——不，如今是三天——就要启程自己的巡游，若安娜能在那前治好动物，仍有机会随艾莎扬帆。

sentences.en: Returning to her bed, Anna decided that she’d wake up extra early to show Elsa the spell first thing.
sentences.zh: 回到床上，安娜决定明日格外早起，第一件事就把咒语给艾莎看。

sentences.en: And so, with her father’s sketchbook on one side of her pillow and her mother’s book on the other, she at last dared to close her eyes.
sentences.zh: 于是，父亲素描本在一侧枕边、母亲的书在另一侧，她终于敢合上眼。

sentences.en: The wolf did not return.
sentences.zh: 狼没有回来。

chapters.title: 第6章
chapters.en:
ANNA HEARD THE SOUND of chimes and footsteps from somewhere in the castle.

Dawn had broken, spilling warm autumn sunlight across her face. Keeping her eyes closed, Anna stretched, enjoying the coziness of her quilt and the softness of her pillow. Just a few more minutes. She could afford to wait before she found Elsa, asked more about the Westens’ goats, and told her about what she’d found last night in their mother’s book. After all, she was so comfortable that it would be a crime to untuck herself, and—

Her thoughts screeched to a halt.

Secrets of the Magic Makers. The book with spells in it. The book with a potential cure for the animals.

Anna lurched up, eyes flying open—only to be blinded not by the light of dawn, but by golden mid-morning sun. She’d overslept again!

Faster than Sven could chomp a carrot, Anna tumbled out of bed before she could even untwist herself from her quilt. She grabbed Secrets of the Magic Makers, and with her blanket flapping behind her, she sprinted through the dressing room and downstairs. Not bothering to knock, she flung open the door to her parents’ old bedroom. The bed was neatly made, the ashes cold in their hearth.

Of course—her sister would have been up for hours at this point. Elsa, for some strange reason, enjoyed mornings. She said they made her feel fresh as new snow, while they made Anna feel as fresh as chicken droppings. A headache pounded at her temples. Even though she’d overslept by hours, it had been a restless sleep, as it had taken her long hours to relax after the return of the childhood nightmare.

Think. Where would Elsa be at this time of day? Whirling from the bedchamber, Anna ran down the hallway to peer through open doors. Elsa wasn’t in the library or council chambers. Maybe the portrait gallery? Anna flew downstairs and made a sharp turn on the landing—and barreled into something warm and solid.

Anna flew backward, sprawling onto the ground. A dull pain rattled through her backside, but thankfully, the majority of her fall had been cushioned by the carpet. Ow.

“Hey!” the warm wall grumbled from above. “Watch where you’re going!”

“You watch where you’re going!” Anna replied, and instantly regretted it. That’s not what someone hoping to be a royal ambassador on a grand tour should say. “I’m sorry,” she added, looking up to see the old, wrinkled face of Madam Eniola staring down at her.

“Anna!” Madam Eniola bobbed a curtsy, her long brown skirt contrasting with the bundle of white ribbons she held in her arms. “My apologies, I didn’t recognize you in your…” Her eyes swept up and down. “Quilt?”

Anna winced. Royal ambassadors should also probably remember to put on proper clothes before carrying out their important missions—and to comb their hair, too. Her hair didn’t look so much like hair as it resembled a bird’s nest. “That’s all right.” Anna clambered to her feet. “I should have been paying attention.” Like always. She pulled her quilt tighter around her and hoped it looked more dignified than her ruffled pale green nightgown and bare feet.

Anna knew Eniola as one of the new villagers who’d moved to Arendelle from Tikaani, and specifically as the one who had taught Tikaani’s national anthem to Anna. Eniola lived in a cozy cottage on the outskirts of the farmlands. Holding her chin up, Anna asked, “What brings you to the castle, Madam Eniola?”

Eniola sighed, and the creases on her face, which already held more lines than King Agnarr’s old sailing charts, seemed to increase tenfold as she frowned. “I’m here to speak to the queen.” She pursed her lips. “We all are.”

Anna arched an eyebrow. “We?”

Eniola stepped back to reveal more villagers lined up outside the Great Hall, staring at Anna. She recognized many of her friends—the candymaker, the farmer, the gas lamp lighter, the miller, the two blacksmiths, and many more. Many, many more.

Anna’s eyes widened as she saw that the line of villagers extended from the double doors that led into the Great Hall all the way through the second great hall and into the portrait gallery. Anna’s mouth went dry, and she cleared her throat. “Why do you need to see Elsa? Erm, Queen Elsa?” she asked.

Eniola held out her bundle of ribbons, which Anna saw now were not actually ribbons at all. They were strands of wheat, but instead of the long golden straws Anna was used to seeing from the tower window, these strands were short and mottled white—moldy and rotten all the way through and recognizable only by the heads of grains at the tops. Even as Anna stared, a few seeds crumbled off into white dust. First the animals, then the crops. What was going on?

“We woke this morning,” Eniola said, “and it’s all like this—everything!”

The villagers grumbled in agreement behind her.

Anna needed to tell Elsa about all these villagers—now.

“Excuse me.” Anna tore her eyes away from the pitiful bundle in Madam Eniola’s arms and hurried downstairs in the direction of the Great Hall. “Pardon me, coming through!” The line shifted to allow Anna to wiggle by, and as she did, she saw that each and every person held white bundles similar to the one that Madam Eniola held: the pumpkins, usually the color of the sunset, had large unsightly splotches splashed across them, while the apples, usually red, round, and crisp, seemed to have the same consistency as raw dough. Up and down the line, Anna saw dried corn husks, white-mottled potatoes, and carrots as pale as cream. Every crop, every vegetable, every grain Anna could think of, was destroyed. Rotten.

The Blight.

Anna picked up the pace. Squeezing past a harried-looking woman, she at last made it through the doors and into the Great Hall.

The Great Hall, as its name suggested, was exactly that: great. It was the largest room in the castle, with tall windows and a gleaming chandelier, capable of fitting a hundred dashing lords and twirling ladies, Elsa’s throne, and a massive chocolate fountain all at the same time. Once, it had even hosted an entire ice skating rink when a late winter storm had threatened the annual ice dance competition.

But now, for the first time Anna could remember, the Great Hall felt small. The single file line cutting through the portrait gallery hadn’t prepared her for the absolute crush of people that filled the Great Hall. Even on the busiest market day on record—shortly after Elsa’s coronation, when everyone had come to see their new magical sovereign—there had not been this many people. Or maybe there had been, but joy didn’t take up nearly as much room as fear. Fear filled the hall, as large and present as one of the Earth Giants in her mother’s tales. The voices all around Anna were pulled tight, sounding as if they would break at any moment.

“Everything is gone! It’s been ruined!”

“My cattle! They won’t wake up!”

“Never in all my days! It’s as if the very earth has gone awry!”

“Do you think this has to do with the Northuldra?”

“No,” someone grunted. “King Runeard, may he rest in greatest peace, made sure they would never trouble Arendelle again.”

“And the animals…”

Anna heard a strange noise from outside. It sounded like a mix of children learning how to play the violin crossed with the sounds of a zoo. Peering through the window, Anna gasped. The courtyard was just as full as the Great Hall, filled to the brim with farmers and animals. Sheep had broken loose from their shepherds, and the herding dogs, usually so careful, seemed distracted, following something in the air that no one else could see. All the animals looked like walking ghosts, their fur and hides the same sickly yellow-white. And even as Anna watched, a cow and two horses knelt to the ground, their eyes as large and black as lumps of coal, their mouths open and tongues lolling out until, suddenly, they fell asleep.

Anna’s stomach turned. “Excuse me,” she said over and over again as she tried to wade her way to the front of the hall, toward the throne where Elsa must be. Grumbling people followed in her wake as she wove in and out of the crowd, and more than once, she had to tug her quilt from beneath someone’s boot.

But with one last push, she made it to the throne, relief washing over her as she found Elsa standing there, just as Wael, the local journalist, yelled out, “That’s not going to help us!”

“Wael,” Elsa said, “if you would please only just—”

“Ah-hem! Winter is fast approaching.” Wael’s ink-stained fingers gestured wildly. “We will have nothing to eat! We deserve answers—and it’s your responsibility as queen to give us answers and take care of your people! We don’t have enough food to last the week!”

A hush fell over the Great Hall at his words.

Elsa stood tall, not backing down, but Anna knew her sister. She could see the overbright sheen of her eyes. It wasn’t just ice that could sparkle in chandelier light. Tears could, too.

Anger, bright and hot, swept through Anna. “Don’t speak to my sister that way!” she burst out as she reached Elsa’s side.

“Anna,” Elsa said, her voice low, “I’ve got this, it’s fine—”

Anna glared at Wael. “No, it’s not!”

The man glared right back.

“Elsa is doing her best,” Anna plowed on, her words coming fast and furious. “She has a plan! She’ll fix everything before she leaves on the grand tour!”

Next to her, she heard Elsa’s breath catch. “Anna—”

“That’s in just three days,” a tired-looking villager said, her arms full of what Anna thought was supposed to be emerald zucchini but now looked more like great white slugs. “Can the queen really—”

“Anna—” Elsa tried again.

But Anna didn’t listen. She was going to stick up for her sister. Elsa might be able to stand there and listen to people doubt her, but Anna wasn’t going to have any of it.

“Of course Elsa can!” Anna said, holding on to their glowing secret, the promise of the mysterious book.

“ANNA.” Elsa flung out her hand. There was a time when icy spears would have sprouted from the floor, but Elsa had control of her magical powers now. Instead of a dangerously pointed ice spear, it was now just a gesture—to remind her sister to watch what she said. “I apologize for my sister,” Elsa said to the Great Hall at large. Her chin had lifted in the exact same way Anna remembered her father lifting his during special ceremonies, when he was trying to be his most regal.

Anna opened her mouth to protest, but one glance at Elsa’s expression squashed any words she had left. Her cheeks flushed. Burning anger transformed into burning embarrassment. What had she done?

“I understand your concern,” Elsa continued, her voice steady and cool. “And I share it. What I’ve been trying to say is, to show my commitment to solving the problem of the ruined crops and sick animals, I’m postponing my grand tour until I can sort out this troubling matter at hand.”

“What?” Anna gasped before she could stop herself, shocked her sister would cancel her grand tour. She didn’t understand what Elsa was thinking—what if postponement convinced the dignitaries and people from other lands that Arendelle wasn’t, in fact, opening its gates, but closing them once again? And from the shocked look on Wael’s face and the murmur of the crowd, Anna knew she wasn’t the only one surprised by this announcement.

If they hadn’t been standing in front of a large crowd of stressed villagers, Anna imagined Elsa would be rubbing her temples and sighing right about now. But they were standing in front of stressed villagers, and her sister never failed to live up to what was expected of her: she was queen, regal and unflappable.

“Because,” Elsa said, speaking loud enough for all to hear, “the royal ship is loaded with rations of food, apples, wheat, dried vegetables, cheeses, cans of pickled herring, and sausages. We need to share our surplus, or else the villagers with Blight-stricken farms will suffer further.” Once again, Elsa had come up with the perfect solution—one so obvious Anna wondered why she hadn’t thought of it herself. Elsa was so good at seeing the larger tapestry, while Anna let herself get distracted by whatever thread was dangling in front of her at that very moment.

“That amount of food will only last us all three days at the most,” Wael protested. “And what makes you think the food on your ship hasn’t soured, Your Majesty?” There was something about his all-knowing attitude that made Anna want to release Marshmallow, Elsa’s dangerous giant snowman—and Olaf’s little brother—on him. But seeing as that wasn’t an option, since Marshmallow was currently the housekeeper for the ice palace on top of the North Mountain, she’d settle for glaring at Wael instead.

“I’ll scour our kitchen here,” Elsa offered.

Beside her, Kai scribbled a note onto a ream of parchment, while brown-haired and kind Olina, in charge of overseeing the kitchen staff, clasped her gloved hands together in deep thought. Nothing ever missed Olina’s careful eye, and Anna knew that she was probably already running through a mental list of food the castle kitchen could provide.

“What if that food’s gone bad, too?” cried a voice from the crowd.

Anna held her breath while everyone stared at Elsa.

Elsa, however, looked at only one person: Olina. The woman gave a slight shake of her head: the kitchen was still fine. Anna exhaled, thankful that at least this one piece of news wasn’t terrible.

“As your queen,” Elsa said loudly, her voice strong, “I will see to it that you have food.”

The crowd murmured, but Anna could hear the shift in tone. The conversation around her no longer vibrated with the intensity of a string pulled too tight. Instead, the words loosened and the conversation relaxed as the villagers considered Elsa’s proposal.

“I think it’s a good idea,” Tuva called out. “My wife and I accept.” And the two blacksmiths nodded in agreement.

“I accept, too,” Eniola called out, and soon other villagers voiced their agreement as well. All except for Wael, who only reluctantly nodded, but not before adding, “Fine—but the Village Crown will make sure that you keep Anna’s promise that the solution will be found before three days are up.”

Pride filled Anna as Kai led the disgruntled villagers back out of the castle and toward the harbor to collect the supplies from the royal ship. She felt like cheering, but instead she settled on a quiet squeal, and whispered to Elsa, “That was brilliant.”

But Elsa didn’t smile back. Instead, she walked to one of the more secretive side entrances to the Great Hall, hidden from view by a tapestry. “Anna,” she said without turning around, “can we talk for a minute, please?”

Anna’s smile slipped away as she followed her older sister. She might not know why the farm animals were sleeping or why their fur was turning white, or why the kingdom’s food seemed to be turning to dust and ash, but she did know one thing: she was absolutely, completely, 100 percent in trouble.

“Three days?!” Elsa whirled on Anna as soon as the tapestry fell back in place, obscuring them from view. “Anna of Arendelle, how on earth can I fix this mess, and so soon?” Even though Elsa didn’t raise her voice, Anna could hear her frustration boiling underneath. “Between this and Kristoff—”
