太阳明晃晃地挂在天上，像个扁平的亮盘，把秋叶斑斓的盛景照得闪闪发亮。

平常，安娜最爱晴朗的秋日，那些天空蓝得不能再蓝、四周一切都金灿灿的午后。

平常。

可今天，太阳太刺眼了。

它照出太多东西：小路上的脚印、在地上爬行的影子、艾莎头发亮眼的光泽。

全都无所遁形。

简直像给狼立了路标，恨不得喊一声"美味大餐往这边走"。

尽管他们都猜狼白天不会动，而且它还困在城堡里，可谁也不敢打包票。

于是他们避开顺着咆哮河的大车路，改走森林深处，在倒木和埋在落叶堆里的石头间磕磕绊绊地挑路走。

安娜被横生的树根绊了好几回。

想象着狼在后面追、偷偷溜过树林，对安娜来说再熟悉不过。

走了一会儿，安娜红着脸向克斯托夫坦白了她的所作所为。

他非但没生气，还抱了抱她。

他明白她只是想帮忙，也对救斯文的计划充满信心。"我不明白，"安娜说，尽量压低声音，既不想引人注意，又要盖过踩落叶的声响，让克斯托夫和艾莎听见，"我常做美梦啊。

我梦到过飞，梦到过住在巧克力做的城堡里，梦到过独角兽的探险，还有——""还有我，显然，"克斯托夫带着促狭的笑提议。

安娜轻轻撞了下他的胳膊。"专心，"她说，努力装出严肃，尽管知道自己脸颊正发烫，"我庆幸你没梦到真正吓人的东西——比如会走路的鲨鱼，"他说。

安娜笑了。"那是你最可怕的噩梦？""不是，"克斯托夫摇头，"我小时候，总做布尔达要拿蘑菇汤勺喂我的噩梦。"安娜停下，把斗篷从荆棘丛上解下来。"那一点都不可怕。""你让地精拿勺子喂过你吗？"克斯托夫调整了下行囊。安娜咯咯笑着转向艾莎，想把她也拉进话题，可艾莎连笑都没笑一下。

自从离开奥肯的商栈，她几乎没开口，安娜越来越强烈地觉得姐姐在生她的气。"那……你呢，艾莎？"安娜尽量让语气轻快，"你最怕的噩梦是什么？"艾莎拨开一根树枝。"我没有噩梦。"安娜用眼角看见克斯托夫加快了脚步。

他向来能躲就躲，不愿起争执。

和他一样，安娜也察觉到一场争吵正在酝酿。"得了吧，艾莎。"安娜迅速往旁边一闪，避开艾莎松手后弹回来的树枝，"谁都有噩梦。

我是你妹妹。

你可以跟我说。

你们现在都知道我的噩梦了——一只巨大的、专盯着我追的狼。"艾莎把母亲的围巾甩到肩后。"我不知道跟你说什么，安娜，只能说我没有噩梦。"安娜那种"不祥的预感"不再只是下沉。

它已经沉到底，锚在了她胃的最深处。

艾莎肯定在生她的气，而最糟的——绝对最糟的——是安娜并不怪她。

安娜对自己有点恼火。

阳光从树叶间漏下，雪片在其中飘。

安娜抬起头。

天空依旧湛蓝如故，这意味着雪只可能来自另一处。"艾莎，你为什么要弄出雪花？"安娜伸出手指，接住一颗极小的冰晶，"我们不能下雪。

会留下脚印。

比我们在泥里留下的还多。"艾莎停下，看着她。"不是我。""那你说这是什么？"安娜伸出手指。

艾莎端详着那片雪，苍白的脸更没血色了。"那不是雪。""安娜！

艾莎！"克斯托夫在前头喊。

他站在一座林中小丘顶上，望着另一边的什么东西。"快过来！"他们顾不上谁——或什么——会听见，撒腿就跑，在克斯托夫身旁刹住脚。

安娜倒吸一口气。

小丘顶上森林到了头，一座红顶农舍立在眼前，被一片麦田拥着；麦子全白了，在烈日下甚至透着半透明。

安娜看着，一阵风吹过田野，抖落谷粒，扬起像灰烬般的阵阵白烟。

枯萎病在蔓延。"我们不能再这样蹑手蹑脚了，"克斯托夫说，安娜看得出他想起了斯文那身白毛，正和这可怕的白粉一个样，"这样东躲西藏太慢了。

我们得加快速度！"他说得对。

可安娜不知道该怎么办。

即便隔着这么远，她也能在田里看见一团团小小的白影。

是睡着了的牛。

是倒在路上的马。

任何能让他们走得快、跑得远的牲口都病倒了。

在这片褪了色的秋景里，唯一看起来正常的，是远处蜿蜒流向矿工山山脚的咆哮河那道藏蓝的细线。"你能把河冻住吗？"安娜问艾莎，"那样我们也许能过去。""哈，"艾莎偏了偏头，"这倒是个主意！

也许这些也能帮上忙。"艾莎挥挥手，安娜觉得自己长高了三寸。

低头看脚，她明白为什么了：艾莎把安娜的步行靴变成了冰鞋。

安娜摇摇晃晃，克斯托夫一把扶住她胳膊，让她站稳。

艾莎朝奔流的河扬了扬下巴。"我们可以滑冰。"这可不是安娜想的那种办法。

她咽了口唾沫。

主意是好，可会滑冰的是艾莎，不是她。

而且安娜滑冰时，喜欢在平整结实的地面上滑。

在河上，冰随时可能裂，把她摔进刺骨的冷水里。"在开阔的河面上我们会暴露，"安娜慢慢说，"躲都没处躲。""好在，"艾莎顺着小丘走向河边，"你身边有位冰的专家。

我能让冰薄到刚好托住我们的重量，可更重的——比如一只巨狼——会直接踏破它。"说完，她一脚踩上水面。

艾莎冰鞋的鞋尖触到水面，河面绽开一朵冰晶。

冰晶开了两倍，又四倍，再成倍地长，直到整条河面变成一整张野生的冰花，在正午刺眼的阳光下反复折射。

安娜暗自承认，这又是艾莎一个绝妙的主意和魔法杰作。

只是她实在喜欢不来。

不过她信姐姐，于是走到河边。

冰薄得能一眼看穿，像她卧室那扇精致的窗玻璃。"快呀，安娜，"克斯托夫说，"我们在浪费时间！"他穿着自己的冰鞋跳上河面。

冰面像蹦床一样在他脚下弹了弹，可它撑住了，正如艾莎保证的那样。"我不会让你有事的，安娜，"艾莎看穿姐姐担忧的神情，说道，"这是我们最好的机会，而修补这场噩梦，时间不多了。"艾莎说得对。

安娜把他们拖进了这团乱子。

现在她得把它补好。

她吸了口气，踏上了冰面。

艾莎在前领路，每一步都在水面洒下冰晶。

两岸排着盛装的秋树，河流像一条钻石项链，镶在红色的衬垫上。

等安娜脚下站稳，她觉得心情轻快了些。

被风刮得沙沙作响的落叶，像在鼓掌。

她从这声音里借了勇气。

仿佛阿伦黛尔在为她欢呼，盼她成功。

而她会的。

不把阿伦黛尔救安顿，她绝不罢休。

几小时过去了。

风把安娜的头发吹得乱糟糟，不断的冷风让她开始流鼻涕。

她的脚开始发酸。

艾莎的魔法冰鞋平时正合脚，今天却有点挤，仿佛艾莎忘了安娜已经长大。

想到这，她有点泄气，想甩掉心里的低落。

安娜踩到一个凹坑——绊倒了。

还没等她鼻子砸在冰上，一只手拽住了她的胳膊。"还行吧，软脚虾？"克斯托夫问。"完全行，"安娜说，"我是故意的。"虽说她的滑冰自第一次跟艾莎学以来进步很大，短期之内还赢不了比赛。"抱歉，"克斯托夫说，"我不是故意毁了那个'安娜阿克塞尔'。"安娜把鼻子一扬，哼了一声。"我想我可以不计较你。""你确定？"克斯托夫咧嘴一笑，手滑进她掌心，接着他转身就滑，能滑多快滑多快，把安娜拽在身后。

他带着她转圈，四周的景物都模糊了，他在冰上和在地上一样从容。

他们越滑越快，在掌控与失控的薄刃上保持着平衡。

前头的艾莎轻松滑行，没注意到他们倾斜、打滑、飞起，直到——"小心！"安娜喊，河面毫无预兆地拐了个弯。

可警告来得太迟。

克斯托夫来不及带他们转向，他们打着滑冲出河面，扎进一堆高高的枫叶里。

安娜仰面躺着，看一簇簇金叶在身边飘落。"我是故意的，"克斯托夫说。"嗯哼。

就像我'故意'来那个安娜阿克塞尔？"她问。

他点头。"没错。""安娜！"艾莎的声音划破空气，"我在这儿！"安娜站起身，抖了抖旅行斗篷，让叶子簌簌落地。"我们稍微失了下足。

呃，失了下冰。"艾莎的冰刀在他们面前猛地停住，扬起一片粉末。"这不是玩闹的时候！"安娜熟悉的世界慢了下来，然后凝固。

尽管艾莎没使任何魔法——没有转手，没有迸发寒冰，没有冰锥钻进安娜心里——艾莎的话却把安娜心里某种东西冻住了。

她的希望。

而冻结的东西……会碎。

安娜能感到碎掉希望的碎片像碎玻璃般在自己体内翻滚，每一次呼吸、每一次眨眼都生疼，她望着姐姐——阿伦黛尔的女王，再没有地方容纳妹妹那些傻气胡闹。"我知道这不是游戏，"安娜回嘴，"我觉得你不知道。""我想你不知道，"艾莎说，声音克制得恰到好处。

安娜想摇醒这个完美的姐姐，想看她裂开一道缝，想让她知道自己把她当平起平坐的人。

可那种语气——那种失望的语气——把艾莎对安娜的看法暴露得淋漓尽致。

接着安娜不再受伤，不再麻木，不再冻结。

她沸腾了。"我不是小孩，"安娜说。

她庆幸冰鞋的刀刃让她比平时高了几分。"你以为我不明白？"每个字她都越说越响，到最后简直在喊，"你以为我没在努力？"没等听见艾莎回话，安娜就把自己甩上了冰面。

冰刀深深咬进冰里，她一下下蹬，越来越快。

安娜感受太多。

她太满。

问题就在这。

她太分心。

太无忧无虑。

太荒唐，让任何人——连她姐姐——都看不出她能怎么帮上王国。

风把她的斗篷吹在身后，她却迎风倾身，想感受冰凉贴着发热发怒的皮肤。

有那么一刻，她仿佛听见艾莎在喊她，可她没停。

她想滑离这一切。

离开艾莎声音里那失望的调子，离开克斯托夫不该给的温柔体贴，离开自己那团乱麻般的情绪。

离开她那巨大而受了诅咒的过错。

冰在她体重下呻吟，冰刀刮出一声哀怨的调子，安娜逃不开。

快，快，快！

要是她能滑得和风一样快，也许会融进风里，被卷离她做下的一切。

就在这时，冰裂了。

sentences.en: THE SUN SHONE with intensity in the sky, a bright flat disk that sparked the colorful splendor of autumn leaves.
sentences.zh: 太阳明晃晃地挂在天上，像个扁平的亮盘，把秋叶斑斓的盛景照得闪闪发亮。

sentences.en: Usually, Anna loved nothing more than sunny fall days, those afternoons when the sky was as blue as could be and everything around her was golden.
sentences.zh: 平常，安娜最爱晴朗的秋日，那些天空蓝得不能再蓝、四周一切都金灿灿的午后。

sentences.en: Usually.
sentences.zh: 平常。

sentences.en: Today, though, the sun was too bright.
sentences.zh: 可今天，太阳太刺眼了。

sentences.en: It showed too many things: their footprints on the path, their shadows creeping across the ground, the bright gleam of Elsa’s hair.
sentences.zh: 它照出太多东西：小路上的脚印、在地上爬行的影子、艾莎头发亮眼的光泽。

sentences.en: All were as visible as could possibly be.
sentences.zh: 全都无所遁形。

sentences.en: Beacons for the wolf that might as well have screamed DELICIOUS MEALS WENT THAT WAY.
sentences.zh: 简直像给狼立了路标，恨不得喊一声"美味大餐往这边走"。

sentences.en: Even though they had all guessed that the wolf would not move during the day, and that it was still trapped in the castle, there was no real way to be sure.
sentences.zh: 尽管他们都猜狼白天不会动，而且它还困在城堡里，可谁也不敢打包票。

sentences.en: So they stayed away from the cleared wagon path that followed the Roaring River, and instead stuck to the interior of the forest, picking their way over fallen logs and stumbling against rocks hidden by piles of leaves.
sentences.zh: 于是他们避开顺着咆哮河的大车路，改走森林深处，在倒木和埋在落叶堆里的石头间磕磕绊绊地挑路走。

sentences.en: Anna tripped more than a few times over wayward roots.
sentences.zh: 安娜被横生的树根绊了好几回。

sentences.en: Sneaking through the woods while imagining a wolf chasing her was all too familiar to Anna.
sentences.zh: 想象着狼在后面追、偷偷溜过树林，对安娜来说再熟悉不过。

sentences.en: After a little while, an embarrassed Anna admitted to Kristoff what she had done.
sentences.zh: 走了一会儿，安娜红着脸向克斯托夫坦白了她的所作所为。

sentences.en: And instead of being upset at her, he hugged her.
sentences.zh: 他非但没生气，还抱了抱她。

sentences.en: He understood that all she had wanted to do was help, and he was optimistic about their plan to save Sven. “I don’t get it,” Anna said, trying to keep her voice quiet enough not to attract attention, but loud enough for Kristoff and Elsa to hear her over the crunching of leaves. “I have good dreams all the time.
sentences.zh: 他明白她只是想帮忙，也对救斯文的计划充满信心。"我不明白，"安娜说，尽量压低声音，既不想引人注意，又要盖过踩落叶的声响，让克斯托夫和艾莎听见，"我常做美梦啊。

sentences.en: I’ve dreamed about flying, and living in a castle made of chocolate, and unicorn quests, and—” “And me, obviously,” Kristoff suggested with a cheeky grin.
sentences.zh: 我梦到过飞，梦到过住在巧克力做的城堡里，梦到过独角兽的探险，还有——""还有我，显然，"克斯托夫带着促狭的笑提议。

sentences.en: Anna nudged his arm. “Focus,” she said, trying to sound stern, though she knew her cheeks were turning pink. “I’m just glad you didn’t dream of something really scary—like a land-walking shark,” he said.
sentences.zh: 安娜轻轻撞了下他的胳膊。"专心，"她说，努力装出严肃，尽管知道自己脸颊正发烫，"我庆幸你没梦到真正吓人的东西——比如会走路的鲨鱼，"他说。

sentences.en: Anna smiled. “Is that your most terrifying nightmare?” “No.” Kristoff shook his head. “When I was little, I used to have nightmares about Bulda trying to spoon-feed me mushroom soup.” Anna paused to unhook her cloak from a thorny bush. “That’s not scary at all.” Kristoff adjusted his traveler’s pack. “Have you ever had a troll try to spoon-feed you?” Anna giggled and turned to Elsa, trying to invite her to the conversation, but Elsa didn’t so much as crack a smile.
sentences.zh: 安娜笑了。"那是你最可怕的噩梦？""不是，"克斯托夫摇头，"我小时候，总做布尔达要拿蘑菇汤勺喂我的噩梦。"安娜停下，把斗篷从荆棘丛上解下来。"那一点都不可怕。""你让地精拿勺子喂过你吗？"克斯托夫调整了下行囊。安娜咯咯笑着转向艾莎，想把她也拉进话题，可艾莎连笑都没笑一下。

sentences.en: She’d been practically silent since they’d left Oaken’s trading post, and Anna had the sinking suspicion her sister was upset with her. “H-how about you, Elsa?” Anna tried to keep her tone light and airy. “What’s your worst nightmare?” Elsa pushed back a branch. “I don’t have nightmares.” From out of the corner of her eye, Anna saw Kristoff pick up the pace.
sentences.zh: 自从离开奥肯的商栈，她几乎没开口，安娜越来越强烈地觉得姐姐在生她的气。"那……你呢，艾莎？"安娜尽量让语气轻快，"你最怕的噩梦是什么？"艾莎拨开一根树枝。"我没有噩梦。"安娜用眼角看见克斯托夫加快了脚步。

sentences.en: He always liked to avoid spats whenever he could.
sentences.zh: 他向来能躲就躲，不愿起争执。

sentences.en: And he, like Anna, could detect one brewing. “Come on, Elsa.” Anna took a quick side step to avoid the branch whipping back toward her as Elsa released it. “ Everyone has nightmares.
sentences.zh: 和他一样，安娜也察觉到一场争吵正在酝酿。"得了吧，艾莎。"安娜迅速往旁边一闪，避开艾莎松手后弹回来的树枝，"谁都有噩梦。

sentences.en: I’m your sister.
sentences.zh: 我是你妹妹。

sentences.en: You can tell me.
sentences.zh: 你可以跟我说。

sentences.en: You all know my nightmare now—a massive, girl-stalking wolf.” Elsa flung their mother’s scarf over her shoulder. “I don’t know what to tell you, Anna, except that I don’t have nightmares.” Anna’s sinking suspicion was no longer sinking.
sentences.zh: 你们现在都知道我的噩梦了——一只巨大的、专盯着我追的狼。"艾莎把母亲的围巾甩到肩后。"我不知道跟你说什么，安娜，只能说我没有噩梦。"安娜那种"不祥的预感"不再只是下沉。

sentences.en: It had hit rock bottom, and anchored in the pit of her stomach.
sentences.zh: 它已经沉到底，锚在了她胃的最深处。

sentences.en: Elsa was definitely upset with her, and the worst part—the absolute worst part—was that Anna didn’t blame her.
sentences.zh: 艾莎肯定在生她的气，而最糟的——绝对最糟的——是安娜并不怪她。

sentences.en: Anna was a little furious at herself.
sentences.zh: 安娜对自己有点恼火。

sentences.en: Snowflakes drifted in the shafts of sunlight that trickled down through the trees.
sentences.zh: 阳光从树叶间漏下，雪片在其中飘。

sentences.en: Anna looked up.
sentences.zh: 安娜抬起头。

sentences.en: The sky remained as blue as ever, which meant there could only be one other source of snow. “Elsa, why are you making flurries?” Anna held out a finger to capture a miniscule ice crystal. “We can’t have snow.
sentences.zh: 天空依旧湛蓝如故，这意味着雪只可能来自另一处。"艾莎，你为什么要弄出雪花？"安娜伸出手指，接住一颗极小的冰晶，"我们不能下雪。

sentences.en: We’ll leave footprints.
sentences.zh: 会留下脚印。

sentences.en: More than the ones we’re already leaving in the mud.” Elsa stopped and looked at her. “It’s not me.” “Then what do you call this?” Anna held out her finger.
sentences.zh: 比我们在泥里留下的还多。"艾莎停下，看着她。"不是我。""那你说这是什么？"安娜伸出手指。

sentences.en: Elsa inspected the flake, and her pale cheeks grew even paler. “That’s not snow.” “Anna!
sentences.zh: 艾莎端详着那片雪，苍白的脸更没血色了。"那不是雪。""安娜！

sentences.en: Elsa!” Kristoff yelled from ahead.
sentences.zh: 艾莎！"克斯托夫在前头喊。

sentences.en: He stood on top of a wooded knoll, looking down at something on the other side. “Come quick!” They stopped caring who—or what—might hear them, and ran, coming to a halt beside Kristoff.
sentences.zh: 他站在一座林中小丘顶上，望着另一边的什么东西。"快过来！"他们顾不上谁——或什么——会听见，撒腿就跑，在克斯托夫身旁刹住脚。

sentences.en: Anna gasped.
sentences.zh: 安娜倒吸一口气。

sentences.en: The forest ended on top of the knoll, and a red farmhouse sat before them, cradled by fields of wheat; wheat that was all white, translucent even, in the sun’s sharp light.
sentences.zh: 小丘顶上森林到了头，一座红顶农舍立在眼前，被一片麦田拥着；麦子全白了，在烈日下甚至透着半透明。

sentences.en: As Anna looked, a breeze rippled through the field, dislodging the grains and sending up billows of what looked like ash.
sentences.zh: 安娜看着，一阵风吹过田野，抖落谷粒，扬起像灰烬般的阵阵白烟。

sentences.en: The Blight was spreading. “We can’t keep tiptoeing around,” Kristoff said, and Anna could tell he was thinking of Sven’s white coat that matched the terrible white powder. “All this darting and dodging is taking way too long.
sentences.zh: 枯萎病在蔓延。"我们不能再这样蹑手蹑脚了，"克斯托夫说，安娜看得出他想起了斯文那身白毛，正和这可怕的白粉一个样，"这样东躲西藏太慢了。

sentences.en: We have to move way faster!” He was right.
sentences.zh: 我们得加快速度！"他说得对。

sentences.en: But Anna didn’t know what to do.
sentences.zh: 可安娜不知道该怎么办。

sentences.en: Even from this distance, she could spot little white huddles among the fields.
sentences.zh: 即便隔着这么远，她也能在田里看见一团团小小的白影。

sentences.en: Cows that had fallen asleep.
sentences.zh: 是睡着了的牛。

sentences.en: Horses that had dropped in their tracks.
sentences.zh: 是倒在路上的马。

sentences.en: Any animal that could take them farther or faster had fallen sick.
sentences.zh: 任何能让他们走得快、跑得远的牲口都病倒了。

sentences.en: The only thing that looked normal in the bleached autumn landscape was the navy thread of the Roaring River that wound its way to the base of Miner’s Mountain in the distance. “Can you freeze the river?” Anna asked Elsa. “Then maybe we could cross it.” “Huh.” Elsa tilted her head. “ That’s an idea!
sentences.zh: 在这片褪了色的秋景里，唯一看起来正常的，是远处蜿蜒流向矿工山山脚的咆哮河那道藏蓝的细线。"你能把河冻住吗？"安娜问艾莎，"那样我们也许能过去。""哈，"艾莎偏了偏头，"这倒是个主意！

sentences.en: Maybe these will help, too.” Elsa waved her hands, and Anna felt like she’d grown three inches.
sentences.zh: 也许这些也能帮上忙。"艾莎挥挥手，安娜觉得自己长高了三寸。

sentences.en: Looking down at her feet, she realized why: Elsa had transformed Anna’s walking boots into a pair of ice skates.
sentences.zh: 低头看脚，她明白为什么了：艾莎把安娜的步行靴变成了冰鞋。

sentences.en: Anna wobbled, but Kristoff grabbed her elbow, keeping her upright.
sentences.zh: 安娜摇摇晃晃，克斯托夫一把扶住她胳膊，让她站稳。

sentences.en: Elsa nodded at the rushing river. “We can ice-skate.” That was not what Anna had had in mind.
sentences.zh: 艾莎朝奔流的河扬了扬下巴。"我们可以滑冰。"这可不是安娜想的那种办法。

sentences.en: She gulped.
sentences.zh: 她咽了口唾沫。

sentences.en: It was a good idea, but Elsa was the skater, not Anna.
sentences.zh: 主意是好，可会滑冰的是艾莎，不是她。

sentences.en: And when Anna did skate, she preferred to skate on smooth, solid ground.
sentences.zh: 而且安娜滑冰时，喜欢在平整结实的地面上滑。

sentences.en: On a river, there was always the chance the ice could break, pitching her into icy water. “We’ll be exposed on the open river,” Anna said slowly. “We won’t be able to hide.” “Luckily,” Elsa said as she made her way down the knoll and to the river’s edge, “you’re traveling with an expert in ice.
sentences.zh: 在河上，冰随时可能裂，把她摔进刺骨的冷水里。"在开阔的河面上我们会暴露，"安娜慢慢说，"躲都没处躲。""好在，"艾莎顺着小丘走向河边，"你身边有位冰的专家。

sentences.en: I can make the ice just thin enough that it’ll support our weight, but anything heavier—like a giant wolf—will crash right through it.” And with that, she stepped out onto the water.
sentences.zh: 我能让冰薄到刚好托住我们的重量，可更重的——比如一只巨狼——会直接踏破它。"说完，她一脚踩上水面。

sentences.en: As the toe of Elsa’s skate touched the surface, a bloom of ice crystals appeared on the river.
sentences.zh: 艾莎冰鞋的鞋尖触到水面，河面绽开一朵冰晶。

sentences.en: The crystal blossoms doubled, then quadrupled, then further multiplied, until the entire surface of the river had transformed into a sheet of wild ice blossoms refracting over and over and over again in the blinding midday sun.
sentences.zh: 冰晶开了两倍，又四倍，再成倍地长，直到整条河面变成一整张野生的冰花，在正午刺眼的阳光下反复折射。

sentences.en: It was, Anna admitted to herself, another one of Elsa’s great ideas and magical creations.
sentences.zh: 安娜暗自承认，这又是艾莎一个绝妙的主意和魔法杰作。

sentences.en: But just not one she really cared for all that much.
sentences.zh: 只是她实在喜欢不来。

sentences.en: She trusted her sister, though, and so she moved to the river’s edge.
sentences.zh: 不过她信姐姐，于是走到河边。

sentences.en: The ice was so thin she could see straight through it, as though it were the delicate pane of her bedroom window. “Come on, Anna,” Kristoff said, “we’re losing time!” He jumped out onto the river with his own ice skates.
sentences.zh: 冰薄得能一眼看穿，像她卧室那扇精致的窗玻璃。"快呀，安娜，"克斯托夫说，"我们在浪费时间！"他穿着自己的冰鞋跳上河面。

sentences.en: The sheet of ice jounced like a trampoline beneath him, but it held, just as Elsa promised it would. “I won’t let anything happen to you, Anna,” Elsa said, reading her sister’s worried expression. “This is our best chance, and we don’t have much time to fix this nightmare.” Elsa was right.
sentences.zh: 冰面像蹦床一样在他脚下弹了弹，可它撑住了，正如艾莎保证的那样。"我不会让你有事的，安娜，"艾莎看穿姐姐担忧的神情，说道，"这是我们最好的机会，而修补这场噩梦，时间不多了。"艾莎说得对。

sentences.en: Anna had gotten them into this mess.
sentences.zh: 安娜把他们拖进了这团乱子。

sentences.en: And now she needed to fix it.
sentences.zh: 现在她得把它补好。

sentences.en: Taking a breath, she stepped out onto the ice.
sentences.zh: 她吸了口气，踏上了冰面。

sentences.en: Elsa led in front, each stroke of her feet scattering ice crystals across the surface.
sentences.zh: 艾莎在前领路，每一步都在水面洒下冰晶。

sentences.en: Lined on either side by trees in their autumn splendor, the river looked like a diamond necklace set against a cushion of red.
sentences.zh: 两岸排着盛装的秋树，河流像一条钻石项链，镶在红色的衬垫上。

sentences.en: And as Anna got her feet under her, she felt her heart lighten, just a bit.
sentences.zh: 等安娜脚下站稳，她觉得心情轻快了些。

sentences.en: The rattling, windswept leaves sounded like applause.
sentences.zh: 被风刮得沙沙作响的落叶，像在鼓掌。

sentences.en: She took courage in the sound.
sentences.zh: 她从这声音里借了勇气。

sentences.en: It was as though Arendelle were cheering for her, wanting her to succeed.
sentences.zh: 仿佛阿伦黛尔在为她欢呼，盼她成功。

sentences.en: And she would.
sentences.zh: 而她会的。

sentences.en: She wouldn’t stop until Arendelle was safe.
sentences.zh: 不把阿伦黛尔救安顿，她绝不罢休。

sentences.en: Hours passed.
sentences.zh: 几小时过去了。

sentences.en: Wind snarled Anna’s hair, and the constant rush of cold wind meant her nose had started to drip.
sentences.zh: 风把安娜的头发吹得乱糟糟，不断的冷风让她开始流鼻涕。

sentences.en: Her feet were beginning to ache.
sentences.zh: 她的脚开始发酸。

sentences.en: Elsa’s magical skates usually fit just right, but today they squeezed a bit too tight, as though Elsa had forgotten Anna had grown up.
sentences.zh: 艾莎的魔法冰鞋平时正合脚，今天却有点挤，仿佛艾莎忘了安娜已经长大。

sentences.en: Disheartened by the thought, she tried to shake away her melancholy.
sentences.zh: 想到这，她有点泄气，想甩掉心里的低落。

sentences.en: Anna hit a divot—and tripped.
sentences.zh: 安娜踩到一个凹坑——绊倒了。

sentences.en: Before she could smash her nose into the ice, a hand caught her arm. “You okay there, Twinkle Toes?” Kristoff asked. “Totally,” Anna said. “I meant to do that.” Even though her ice-skating had much improved since her first lesson with Elsa, she wasn’t winning a competition anytime soon. “Sorry,” Kristoff said. “I didn’t mean to ruin the Anna Axel.” Putting her nose in the air, Anna sniffed. “I guess I can forgive you.” Kristoff grinned, his hand slipping into hers. “Are you sure?” And then he was off, skating backward as fast as he could, pulling Anna after him.
sentences.zh: 还没等她鼻子砸在冰上，一只手拽住了她的胳膊。"还行吧，软脚虾？"克斯托夫问。"完全行，"安娜说，"我是故意的。"虽说她的滑冰自第一次跟艾莎学以来进步很大，短期之内还赢不了比赛。"抱歉，"克斯托夫说，"我不是故意毁了那个'安娜阿克塞尔'。"安娜把鼻子一扬，哼了一声。"我想我可以不计较你。""你确定？"克斯托夫咧嘴一笑，手滑进她掌心，接着他转身就滑，能滑多快滑多快，把安娜拽在身后。

sentences.en: The world around them blurred as he whirled her around, as confident on the ice as he was on solid ground.
sentences.zh: 他带着她转圈，四周的景物都模糊了，他在冰上和在地上一样从容。

sentences.en: Faster and faster they skated, balancing on a thin edge between control and out-of-control.
sentences.zh: 他们越滑越快，在掌控与失控的薄刃上保持着平衡。

sentences.en: Ahead of them, Elsa cruised with ease, not noticing them tilting, slipping, flying, until— “Look out!” Anna shouted as the river took an unexpected bend.
sentences.zh: 前头的艾莎轻松滑行，没注意到他们倾斜、打滑、飞起，直到——"小心！"安娜喊，河面毫无预兆地拐了个弯。

sentences.en: But the warning came too late.
sentences.zh: 可警告来得太迟。

sentences.en: Kristoff didn’t have time to pull them to a new course, and they skidded off the river and into a tall pile of maple leaves.
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫来不及带他们转向，他们打着滑冲出河面，扎进一堆高高的枫叶里。

sentences.en: Lying back, Anna watched as a swirl of golden leaves fell around them. “I meant to do that,” Kristoff said. “Mm-hmm.
sentences.zh: 安娜仰面躺着，看一簇簇金叶在身边飘落。"我是故意的，"克斯托夫说。"嗯哼。

sentences.en: The same way I meant to do the Anna Axel?” she asked.
sentences.zh: 就像我'故意'来那个安娜阿克塞尔？"她问。

sentences.en: He nodded. “Exactly.” “ANNA!” Elsa’s voice tore through the air. “I’m here!” Anna stood up and shook out her travel cloak to send leaves skittering to the ground. “We had a bit of a misstep.
sentences.zh: 他点头。"没错。""安娜！"艾莎的声音划破空气，"我在这儿！"安娜站起身，抖了抖旅行斗篷，让叶子簌簌落地。"我们稍微失了下足。

sentences.en: Er, mis- skate .” Elsa’s blade sent a spray of powder over them as she came to an abrupt stop in front of them. “This isn’t a time for game-playing!” The world as Anna knew it slowed, then froze.
sentences.zh: 呃，失了下冰。"艾莎的冰刀在他们面前猛地停住，扬起一片粉末。"这不是玩闹的时候！"安娜熟悉的世界慢了下来，然后凝固。

sentences.en: And though Elsa hadn’t done any magic—there had been no twirl of her hand, no blast of her ice, no ice shard burrowing its way into Anna’s heart—Elsa’s words froze something deep within Anna.
sentences.zh: 尽管艾莎没使任何魔法——没有转手，没有迸发寒冰，没有冰锥钻进安娜心里——艾莎的话却把安娜心里某种东西冻住了。

sentences.en: Her hope .
sentences.zh: 她的希望。

sentences.en: And things that are frozen…shatter.
sentences.zh: 而冻结的东西……会碎。

sentences.en: Anna could feel the splinters of her broken hope tumbling through her like smashed glass, making every breath, every blink, painful as she looked at her sister, queen of Arendelle, who no longer had any place for her sister’s silly antics. “I know it’s not a game,” Anna retorted. “I don’t think you do,” Elsa said, her voice carefully controlled.
sentences.zh: 安娜能感到碎掉希望的碎片像碎玻璃般在自己体内翻滚，每一次呼吸、每一次眨眼都生疼，她望着姐姐——阿伦黛尔的女王，再没有地方容纳妹妹那些傻气胡闹。"我知道这不是游戏，"安娜回嘴，"我觉得你不知道。""我想你不知道，"艾莎说，声音克制得恰到好处。

sentences.en: Anna wanted to shake her perfect sister, to see some sort of crack, to show her that she saw her as an equal.
sentences.zh: 安娜想摇醒这个完美的姐姐，想看她裂开一道缝，想让她知道自己把她当平起平坐的人。

sentences.en: But that tone—that disappointed tone—revealed all too well exactly what Elsa thought of Anna.
sentences.zh: 可那种语气——那种失望的语气——把艾莎对安娜的看法暴露得淋漓尽致。

sentences.en: And then Anna was no longer hurt, no longer numb, no longer frozen.
sentences.zh: 接着安娜不再受伤，不再麻木，不再冻结。

sentences.en: She boiled . “I’m not a child,” Anna said.
sentences.zh: 她沸腾了。"我不是小孩，"安娜说。

sentences.en: She was grateful that the ice skates’ blades made her taller than she usually was. “Do you think I don’t know?” With each word, her voice got louder and louder until she practically shouted. “Do you think I haven’t been trying ?” And before she could hear Elsa’s reply, Anna flung herself out onto the ice.
sentences.zh: 她庆幸冰鞋的刀刃让她比平时高了几分。"你以为我不明白？"每个字她都越说越响，到最后简直在喊，"你以为我没在努力？"没等听见艾莎回话，安娜就把自己甩上了冰面。

sentences.en: Digging the blades in deep, she pushed and pushed, going faster and faster.
sentences.zh: 冰刀深深咬进冰里，她一下下蹬，越来越快。

sentences.en: Anna felt too much.
sentences.zh: 安娜感受太多。

sentences.en: She was too much.
sentences.zh: 她太满。

sentences.en: That was the trouble.
sentences.zh: 问题就在这。

sentences.en: She was too distracted.
sentences.zh: 她太分心。

sentences.en: Too carefree.
sentences.zh: 太无忧无虑。

sentences.en: Too ridiculous for anyone—even for her sister—to see how she could be helpful to the kingdom.
sentences.zh: 太荒唐，让任何人——连她姐姐——都看不出她能怎么帮上王国。

sentences.en: The wind whipped her cloak behind her, but she leaned into it, wanting to feel the fresh iciness against her hot, angry skin.
sentences.zh: 风把她的斗篷吹在身后，她却迎风倾身，想感受冰凉贴着发热发怒的皮肤。

sentences.en: For a moment, she thought she heard Elsa calling out to her, but she didn’t stop.
sentences.zh: 有那么一刻，她仿佛听见艾莎在喊她，可她没停。

sentences.en: She wanted to skate away from it all.
sentences.zh: 她想滑离这一切。

sentences.en: Away from that disappointed note in Elsa’s voice, away from Kristoff’s undeserved gentle kindness, and away from her own messy, tangled emotions.
sentences.zh: 离开艾莎声音里那失望的调子，离开克斯托夫不该给的温柔体贴，离开自己那团乱麻般的情绪。

sentences.en: Away from her giant, cursed mistake.
sentences.zh: 离开她那巨大而受了诅咒的过错。

sentences.en: The ice groaned beneath her weight, her blades scratching out a mournful note that Anna couldn’t escape.
sentences.zh: 冰在她体重下呻吟，冰刀刮出一声哀怨的调子，安娜逃不开。

sentences.en: Faster, faster, faster!
sentences.zh: 快，快，快！

sentences.en: If only she could skate as quick as the wind, maybe she’d melt into it and be swept away from all that she’d done.
sentences.zh: 要是她能滑得和风一样快，也许会融进风里，被卷离她做下的一切。

sentences.en: And that’s when the ice cracked.
sentences.zh: 就在这时，冰裂了。

chapters.title: Chapter Thirteen
chapters.en:
ONE SECOND, everything was cold and dry.

The next second, everything was cold and wet.

The water dragged at Anna like it had fingers.

She gasped once—a single great breath of air—before it pulled her under.

The world below the ice was dark and quiet, peaceful even, except for the wild scream that worked through Anna.

She was cold again! She would freeze again! And if she died…would the wolf win? Anna kicked. She couldn’t let everyone down! But no matter how much she willed her feet to propel her back up to the surface, the heavy blades of her skates dragged her down…

down…

down into the dark.

Or was it up? Sideways? The dark, ice-cold quiet was disorienting, and her thoughts began to slow. And then, a beam of light shot past her as someone chopped through the ice from somewhere above. Anna felt the water underneath her move like a giant horse, a black wave of water that surged beneath her, and she was flying up through the water and toward the surface with all the strength of a geyser. The water didn’t have the temperature of a hot spring, though, but of an icy slush. Elsa. Moments later, after much spluttering and coughing, Anna was in the arms of Kristoff and Elsa.

“Thank you for saving me,” Anna whispered, shivering.

But Elsa didn’t acknowledge her words. Instead, her sister said, “Kristoff, you need take her back to Oaken’s.”

“What?! No,” Anna croaked. “I’m fine. I’ll be fine.”

“But Anna,” Elsa said, throwing her hands up in protest, “you almost drowned.”

“Almost,” Anna protested. “I’ve almost done a lot of things. I have to help with this!”

Elsa shook her head. “I’m just not sure.”

“Why are you always trying to push me away?” Anna asked.

Elsa looked stung. “What? Anna, what are you talking about? When do I push you away?”

Anna grew quiet. “I’m sorry. I…Please, I need to accompany you.” For a second, Anna thought Elsa would say no, but then something seemed to melt in Elsa.

She wrapped Anna in a hug. “I’m sorry, too. I didn’t mean to yell—I just…I’m upset, I guess.”

“I didn’t mean to cast a spell,” Anna said, needing to get the words out now. “I had no way of knowing it would bring my nightmare about the wolf to life.”

Elsa shook her head. “It just…When did you start having the nightmares?”

“When I was a little girl, and then, this week the nightmare came back.” Ever since I realized that you were going to leave me behind for the grand tour. But Anna didn’t say that last bit out loud.

There was the scritch of a match as Kristoff lit a small pile of branches he’d gathered. He gestured the sisters over to the fire.

“When did you first have the nightmare?” Elsa prodded as they huddled close to the flames. Steam rose from Anna’s clothes as they slowly dried.

Anna thought back. “I think it was the night you…you know.” She touched the spot in her hair where the white streak had once been, recalling once more when Elsa had accidentally struck her there with magic as a young girl. “I can’t believe you’ve never had bad dreams.”

Elsa shrugged. “The last time I had a bad dream, I must have been eight years old. I woke up and my entire room had turned into a winter landscape.” She shook her head. “I felt so bad! Everything got wet and they had to bring in new furniture and carpets for me.”

“And you never had the nightmare again?”

“No.” Elsa leaned her head back and looked up. “Father taught me a bunch of tricks to try to control my emotions, my magic. I remember he came into my room once with a mug of hot chocolate—”

“He used to do that for me, too!” Anna said.

Elsa smiled, and Anna smiled back, enjoying the surprise bridge that linked them.

“And Mother joined him and told me to imagine bunching up all the nightmares and throwing them out the window,” Elsa said. “I used to think that when I balled them up, I would throw them and pretend to feed them to the constellations in the sky.”

“I used to do that, too!” Anna said, feeling closer to her sister than ever. “I’d pretend to give them to Frigg the Fisherman so he could fish for them. But the trick didn’t stop me from having nightmares.”

Elsa shrugged. “Mother’s trick worked for me. I haven’t had a nightmare since.”

“I’m sorry to interrupt,” Kristoff said, “but speaking of stars…it’s getting late.”

The sisters smiled, and Anna felt a little bit better, if not completely. Her clothes were still damp, but no longer dripping.

After putting out the fire, Kristoff stepped back on the ice, and Anna followed after him. But the bright hope that had been so certain before now seemed to have been left behind in the maple leaf pile at the riverbank.

Soon enough, the sun began to set, casting long shadows on the ice as they continued to skate up the rest of the Roaring River. Anna couldn’t help thinking that their shadows looked like drowning figures trapped beneath the ice.

They were quiet as they skated. Anna didn’t want to accidentally step on the tenuous peace between her and Elsa, while Kristoff seemed to be lost again in his own worries. Kristoff’s birth parents had died long ago, and for the early part of his life, Sven had been his only family—until they’d both been adopted by the mountain trolls. The farther they glided away from Sven, the quieter Kristoff became, until, at last, it became unbearable for Anna. She needed a distraction—for all of them.

“Kristoff, have you ever met the Huldrefólk?” she asked, blurting out the first thing she could think of. “Did they ever visit the trolls?”

He shook his head. “Not that I know of,” he said. “The trolls like to hide, but the Huldrefólk—well, they really like to hide, right? I don’t think anyone’s ever seen one.”

“They’re known for finding lost things, too,” Elsa said, slowing down so the other two could catch up with her. No one in Arendelle, or probably in the whole world, for that matter, was as comfortable on the ice as Elsa. While Elsa always moved with grace, when she skated, she was more than grace. She became someone with wind in her veins and wings on her feet. “It’s said that Aren of Arendelle once went to visit them.”

“But his adventures led him to many make-believe creatures,” Anna said as his tales gradually came back to her. “Like mermaids and dragons.”

“Right,” Elsa said with a nod. “So maybe the Huldrefólk are like dragons and don’t exist at all. Maybe Aren never even existed.”

Kristoff made a face. “So why do you two know so much about this guy if he may or may not have existed? He’s just a legend, right? A myth?”

“Possibly. It’s said he did a lot of great things for the land,” Anna said. “He carved Arenfjord himself, you know. Or so the old myths go.”

Kristoff snorted. “Yeah, right. That’s the most ridiculous thing I’ve ever heard.”

“You’ve never heard the story?” Anna asked in surprise. “I thought everyone knew it.”

Kristoff jabbed a thumb at his chest. “Raised by trolls, remember? Some of us didn’t have fancy lessons growing up.” There was something strange lurking in his voice, as though Anna had hit a nerve. It must have had to do with his worry for Sven. She turned to Elsa and asked, “You know the saga verbatim, right?”

Elsa nodded. “It helped pass the time when I was growing up.” She paused a moment, seeming to collect herself, and then spoke the familiar lines that signified the beginning of a story: “‘A long time ago, in the time before time, a great darkness swept over the land…’”

Anna held her breath as Elsa recited the ancient tale and described how an everlasting night had set over the mountains, and how humankind had fled to their boats for safety. Humans then lived on the waters for hundreds of years, until the day a strange sickness smote them. Scared, the people had asked the most ancient of water spirits for help, and the Water Spirit had told them that they were withering away without a place to plant their roots—they needed to return home. But all were too scared, except for a young boy.

“‘Young as the morning, as fierce as a twig, Aren stepped out onto the land…’” Elsa recited.

They skated in rhythm to Elsa’s voice, a stroke of one leg, then the other, a beat that flowed through Anna, and calmed her. Impossible things had happened in the past. So why couldn’t they happen in the future?

She took heart as Elsa described how Aren had climbed up the highest mountain to bargain with night and bring back the sun, and how when he’d finally freed the sun, the sun had gifted him the Revolute Blade and told him how to bring his people home: by carving a new path for them, right between the protective mountains.

Elsa’s voice picked up speed as she reached the crescendo of Aren’s very first quest, and Anna couldn’t help mouthing along with the words as she suddenly remembered.

“‘Revolving moon and spinning sun, forged a crescent blade. From light and dark within the heart, the burnished sword was made. The curving arc of Revolute shimmered in his hand. He raised it high above his head, and smote the edge of land.’”

Without missing a beat, Elsa reached out a hand for Anna, gesturing for her to join her on the final stanza of Aren’s first adventure, which Anna found herself happily able to recall. Together, the sisters finished telling the tale: “‘The sea rushed in as hidden power flowed from the gleaming sword, and shaped the rock and forest crown of the first majestic fjord!’”

Their voices rang out as one, the words triumphantly echoing across the ice.

“Not too shabby,” Kristoff said. “It kind of reminds me of the troll ballad about Dagfinn the Dusty, a troll who was allergic to mountains and would accidentally cause avalanches wherever he went by sneezing boulders out of his nose.”

“Wait, what?” Anna giggled. “That’s what trolls say boulders are? Troll boogers?”

Kristoff shrugged. “Well, yeah. I can sing it for you, if you’d like.”

“Maybe later,” Elsa cut in, stopping with a spray of ice. “We’re here.” She pointed up at a sign:

MINER’S MOUNTAIN

WARNING: KEEP OUT

NO TRESPASSERS OR GOATS

HULDREFÓLK ARE WATCHING!

Anna looked up at the sparkling summit of Miner’s Mountain. If she squinted her eyes just so, she thought she could make out the mystic’s tower. But it was so high up and so far away that from where she stood it looked more like a chimney that had been stuck on top of a roof rather than a tower on a mountain. It would take days to climb all that distance.

For people who didn’t have a magical sister, that is.

Elsa waited for Kristoff and Anna to step off the frozen river before she did so herself. As soon as Elsa was on the bank, the ice cracked, and blue water began to flow once more. With a twirl of Elsa’s hand, Anna’s ice skates melted away to reveal her boots beneath, but Anna hardly realized it because of the great whirlwind that kicked up around her, snow climbing into the air higher and higher, until solidifying into a grand icy staircase.

Elsa had done it again. While the staircase of ice was long and ever so high, with nothing but a curving, slender handrail, it would be much easier to navigate than a treacherous and tedious rocky trail. There must have been at least a thousand steps in the ice staircase—Anna couldn’t be bothered to count. Either way, they were going to climb it, because, at the very top, answers were waiting for them.

“Classic,” Kristoff said to Elsa.

“Thanks,” she replied.

One step, then another, they ascended.

At first, Anna didn’t bother holding on to the fragile railing, but about two-thirds of the way to the top, she looked down and gripped it tight. The staircase was clear as glass, and Anna—though brave—wasn’t entirely comfortable with the sight of her feet seemingly dangling above thin air. From this height, the pines seemed to shrink, smaller and smaller and smaller. As they moved up, the sun moved down.

At long last, in the blazing sunset, they reached the top. From there, the tower was much taller than Anna had realized—and much more jumbled. The rocks that made up the tower seemed to be haphazardly arranged, and certain stones seemed to be on the verge of slipping out of place. In fact, the tower did not look unlike the staggered piles of books Anna had left in the library. Elsa reached the door to the tower first, and paused. Her hand remained still, raised out in front of her, as if she couldn’t decide whether she should knock.

Anna pulled her cloak to her chest as the wind sang around them. “What’s wrong?”

“What do I say?” Elsa asked.

“You knock and say hi, and we’ll go from there,” Kristoff called. “Hurry.”

“What Kristoff said,” Anna said, watching the sun sink over the horizon.

Elsa threw back her shoulders and knocked.

Then the three of them stared at the door and waited, but nothing happened. Was no one home? The thought filled Anna with a heavy dread. They had come all this way, and Sorenson was not there.

Elsa knocked again. Nothing.

“Stand back,” Kristoff said. He moved in front of Elsa and put his shoulder to the door. But it was sturdier than it looked. He lifted his pickax high.

“Why don’t you try the handle?” Elsa asked.

Kristoff raised an eyebrow and did just that. The door swung easily open.

“Huh,” he said as he put his pickax away. Without saying another word, he went inside.

Anna exchanged an amused glance with her sister, and they followed him through the doorway and into the tower. From the outside, the tower had looked about to topple, but the inside seemed solid enough, made up of rock and wood and books.

Anna had always imagined a mystic to be exacting, the kind of person who might label the spices in their kitchen cabinet, but everything seemed to be randomly placed. Plants sprawled on top of books, and books on top of statues. On the far side of the circular room was a spiral staircase. There was practically everything under the sun in the tower room.

Except for a mystic.
chapters.zh:
前一秒，一切都又冷又干。

下一秒，一切都又冷又湿。

水像长了手指，拽着安娜。

她猛吸一口气——一大口空气——然后就被拖了下去。

冰下的世界黑暗、安静，甚至安稳，只有安娜体内发出的那声狂叫例外。

她又冷了！

她又要冻僵了！

而要是她死了……狼会赢吗？

安娜蹬腿。

她不能让大家失望！

可不管她怎么拼命让脚把自己推回水面，冰鞋沉重的刀刃却把她往下拖……往下……往黑暗深处。

还是往上？

斜着？

冰冷黑暗的寂静让人辨不清方向，她的思绪也慢了下来。

接着，一道光柱从上方某处穿过冰层，朝她射来。

安娜感到身下的水像一匹巨马，一股黑色的水浪在身下翻涌，她借着喷泉般的力量，从水里朝水面飞升。

可那水不是温泉的温度，而是冰碴般的凉。

艾莎。

片刻之后，在一阵呛水咳嗽中，安娜落进克斯托夫和艾莎的怀里。"谢谢你救我，"安娜颤抖着，小声说。

可艾莎没接她的话。

姐姐只说："克斯托夫，你得带她回奥肯那儿。""什么？！"

不，"安娜沙哑地说，"我没事。

我会没事的。""可安娜，"艾莎举手抗议，"你差点淹死。""差点，"安娜争辩，"我'差点'做过的事多了。

我得帮忙！"艾莎摇头。"我只是不确定。""你为什么总想把我推开？"安娜问。

艾莎像被刺了一下。"什么？

安娜，你在说什么？

我什么时候推开过你？"安娜安静下来。"对不起。

我……求你了，让我陪你去。"有那么一瞬，安娜以为艾莎会拒绝，可接着艾莎心里像化开了什么。

她抱住安娜。"我也对不起。

我不是故意吼的——我只是……我有点心烦，我想。""我不是故意念咒的，"安娜说，这话现在非说不可，"我哪知道它会把我关于狼的噩梦变成真的。"艾莎摇头。"只是……你从什么时候开始做这些噩梦的？""我小时候就有，然后这周，噩梦又回来了。"从我意识到你要丢下我去巡游那时起。

可安娜没把最后这句说出口。

克斯托夫划着一根火柴，点燃一小堆捡来的树枝，发出"嗤"的一声。

他招手让姐妹俩到火边。"你第一次做这个噩梦是什么时候？"他们凑近火苗，艾莎追问。

安娜的衣服冒起蒸汽，慢慢干着。

安娜回想。"我想是你……你明白的那晚。"她摸了摸头发上曾经那道白痕的地方，又想起小时候艾莎不小心用魔法击中那儿的事。"我真不敢相信你从没做过噩梦。""艾莎耸耸肩。"我最后一次做噩梦，一定才八岁。

我醒来，整个房间变成了冬天的景象。"她摇摇头，"我心里好难受！

一切都湿了，他们只好给我换新的家具和地毯。""那以后再也没做过噩梦？""没有。"艾莎仰起头。"父亲教了我好多法子，试着控制情绪、控制魔法。

我记得他有一次端着杯热可可进我房间——""他也常那样对我！"安娜说。

艾莎笑了，安娜也回以微笑，享受着这道意外连起两人的桥。"母亲也来了，叫我想象把噩梦都揉成一团，从窗口扔出去，"艾莎说，"以前我总想着揉成团扔出去时，假装喂给天上的星座。""我也那样做过！"安娜说，觉得和姐姐从未这么亲近，"我假装把它们送给渔夫弗里格，让他替我钓走。

可这法子没止住我的噩梦。""母亲的法子对我管用，"艾莎耸肩。

"从那以后我就没再做噩梦。""抱歉打断，"克斯托夫说，"可说到星星……天不早了。"姐妹俩笑了，安娜觉得好受了些，虽不彻底。

她的衣服还潮，但不再滴水。

灭了火，克斯托夫踏回冰上，安娜跟在后面。

可先前那份笃定的明亮希望，似乎被留在了河岸的枫叶堆里。

很快，太阳开始落下，在他们继续滑完咆哮河余下路程时，在冰上投下长长的影子。

安娜忍不住想，他们的影子像冰下溺着的人形。

他们滑得安静。

安娜不想不小心踩碎她和艾莎之间那点脆弱的平和，克斯托夫则又陷进自己的忧思里。

克斯托夫的亲生父母早逝，他生命最初那段，斯文是他唯一的家人——直到他们都被山地地精收养。

他们离斯文越远，克斯托夫越沉默，到最后安娜再也受不了。

她需要点事——为所有人——分散注意力。"克斯托夫，你见过胡尔德精灵吗？"她脱口而出，问出能想到的第一件事，"他们去过地精那儿吗？"他摇头。"据我所知没有，"他说，"地精爱躲，可胡尔德精灵——嗯，他们才真叫爱躲，对吧？

也许没人真见过他们。""他们也以能找回失物出名，"艾莎说，放慢速度让另外两人赶上。

整个阿伦黛尔，或者大概全世界，都没人比艾莎在冰上更自在。

艾莎一向优雅，可她一滑起冰，就不只是优雅了。

她成了个血管里淌着风、脚上生着翅膀的人。"据说阿伦岱尔的阿伦曾去拜访过他们。""可他的冒险把他带向许多虚构的生灵，"安娜说，那些故事渐渐回到她脑中，"比如美人鱼和龙。""对，"艾莎点头，"所以也许胡尔德精灵和龙一样，根本不存在。

也许阿伦压根没存在过。"克斯托夫做了个怪脸。"那你们俩要是他可能存在也可能不存在，怎么这么了解这家伙？

他不过是个传说，对吧？

一个神话？""有可能。

据说他为这片土地立过大功，"安娜说，"阿伦峡湾就是他亲手开凿的，你知道。

老神话是这么讲的。"克斯托夫嗤笑。"得了吧。

我听过最荒唐的话。""你没听过这故事？"安娜惊讶地问，"我以为谁都知道呢。"克斯托夫竖起拇指戳自己胸口。"地精带大的，记得吗？

我们有些人小时候可没上过那种精致的课。"他声音里藏着古怪的东西，仿佛安娜戳到了他的痛处。

一定和他对斯文的担忧有关。

她转向艾莎，问："你能一字不差地背出那篇史诗，对吧？"艾莎点头。"它帮我打发过小时候的时光。"她顿了顿，像在整理自己，然后念出标志故事开头的熟句："'很久以前，在时间之前的时代，一团巨大的黑暗席卷了大地……'"安娜屏住呼吸，听艾莎吟诵这古老的故事，讲永不消散的黑夜怎样笼罩群山，人类怎样逃上船只求生。

人类在水上生活了数百年，直到一天怪病袭来。

人们惊慌，去向最古老的水灵求助，水灵告诉他们，没有根可扎，他们正渐渐枯萎——他们需要回家。

可大家都怕，只有一个小男孩例外。"'如晨之稚，如枝之韧，阿伦踏上了陆地……'"艾莎吟诵。

他们踩着艾莎的节奏滑，一腿，又一腿，那节拍流过安娜，让她平静。

过去发生过不可能的事。

那未来为何不能？

艾莎讲阿伦怎样爬上最高的山，与黑夜谈判、唤回太阳，安娜听得心里一振；讲他终于放出太阳时，太阳怎样把回旋之刃赠他，并告诉他怎样带人民回家：在守护的山峦间，为他们开出一条新路。

讲到阿伦第一次冒险的高潮，艾莎语速加快，安娜忽然想起，忍不住跟着默念："'旋转的月，流转的日，锻出一把弯刃。

由心中光暗，铸成此柄亮剑。

回旋之刃的弧光在他手中闪烁。

他高高举过头顶，劈向大地的边缘。'"艾莎不慌不忙，伸手邀安娜，示意她一起念阿伦第一段冒险的最后一节，安娜惊喜地发现自己竟还记得。"'海水涌入，隐秘的力量从闪亮的剑中流出，雕琢出岩石与森林冠冕，成就了第一道壮丽的峡湾！'"两人同声说完这故事，声音合而为一，词句在冰面上胜利地回荡。"不赖嘛，"克斯托夫说，"倒让我想起地精那首关于'灰尘达格芬'的歌谣——那是个对山过敏的地精，走到哪儿打喷嚏就喷出石头，引起雪崩。""等等，什么？"安娜咯咯笑，"地精管石头叫那个？

地精擤鼻涕？"克斯托夫耸肩。"嗯，对。

他笑了，可笑着笑着，看清她脸上认真的神情，摇了摇头。"抱歉，可阿伦本人——连同他神话里的神剑——多半从没存在过。

也许很久以前真有过一位勇士，可他大概从没见过太阳，没面对过巨龙，也没开凿过阿伦峡湾。

那只是传说——像胡尔德精灵或山地地精。""可地精是真的，"克斯托夫耸肩，"他们把我养大。"索伦森死死盯着克斯托夫。

接着他捂住嘴，凑到艾莎耳边低语："那山地汉子没事吧？""克斯托夫，"安娜纠正，"他棒极了。

而且地精真的存在。

纳特玛拉也存在。

胡尔德精灵嘛，嗯，他们大概也存在！"索伦森往后一靠，啪地合上书。"魔法和神话不存在，"他说。

艾莎撇嘴，手腕一弹。

一秒钟后，安娜感到脸颊上一阵冰凉的吻。

她抬头，看见他们头顶悬着一场精致的雪。

索伦森从凳子上摔下来，哐当一声。"活了这么大！

传言是真的！"艾莎笑了。"你可是很久没下过山了，对吧，索伦森？"于是，艾莎把过去三年发生的一切讲给索伦森听。

每听一件新事，索伦森就多一个问题。

克斯托夫不耐烦地用手指敲桌子，直到安娜把手覆上他的，他才停。"抱歉，"他低声说，"可我们说话的当儿，斯文还病着！"安娜知道克斯托夫是对的。"我们再找找，"她轻声说。

克斯托夫蹑手蹑脚走到书架边，安娜则翻开桌上的书。

她跳过会说话的树和顽皮风灵的段落，终于找到要找的：纳特玛拉。

果然，索伦森说的都在上面，还多了几条：纳特玛拉生于孩子的恐惧大到藏不住，孩子恐惧的心向它们呼救之时。

再往下一点：地精在纳特玛拉的嚎叫下发抖，而纳特玛拉像影子一样从太阳身边逃开。

这一节没提任何能召唤或驱散纳特玛拉的咒语。

但知道纳特玛拉不喜欢阳光，很有用。

这也解释了地精为何多半不见了。

安娜皱眉，翻着书页，重读一条关于胡尔德精灵的条目。

她停在一行：胡尔德精灵总能寻回失物。

失物……安娜的心怦怦快起来。

也许，她越想越兴奋，那也意味着胡尔德精灵能找来一把失落于历史的神话之剑。

这希望渺茫，却是她紧抓不放的希望。

也许他们该去矿井找胡尔德精灵——不顾那些警告。

可时间不多了。

离咒语永久生效，只剩两个日出——而夜已不年轻。"你知道吗，"索伦森对艾莎说，"你母亲来过一次，寻答案。

其实，天花板上那幅就是她画的。"安娜僵住。

他们的母亲来过这儿？

不可能。

母亲到底为什么要来见索伦森？

寻什么答案？

忽然，她明白为何那画着的天花板眼熟了。

它让她想起密室天花板上那幅北极光与星座的画。

安娜把书塞进克斯托夫的行囊，张嘴想多问索伦森，也把去矿井的念头告诉大家。

可她一抬头，看见塔屋那头有点不对劲：一队黑蚁从门底下涌进来。

她闭了嘴。

不。

不是蚂蚁。

是黑沙。

纳特玛拉终于找到他们了。

圆形房间另一头是一道螺旋楼梯。

塔楼房间里简直应有尽有。

除了那位神秘人。

sentences.en: The water didn’t have the temperature of a hot spring, though, but of an icy slush.

sentences.zh: 姐姐只说："克斯托夫，你得带她回奥肯那儿。""什么？！"

sentences.en: No,” Anna croaked. “I’m fine.

sentences.zh: 我会没事的。""可安娜，"艾莎举手抗议，"你差点淹死。""差点，"安娜争辩，"我'差点'做过的事多了。

sentences.en: I have to help with this!” Elsa shook her head. “I’m just not sure.” “Why are you always trying to push me away?” Anna asked.
sentences.zh: 我得帮忙！"艾莎摇头。"我只是不确定。""你为什么总想把我推开？"安娜问。

sentences.en: Anna, what are you talking about?
sentences.zh: 安娜，你在说什么？

sentences.en: I…Please, I need to accompany you.” For a second, Anna thought Elsa would say no, but then something seemed to melt in Elsa.
sentences.zh: 我……求你了，让我陪你去。"有那么一瞬，安娜以为艾莎会拒绝，可接着艾莎心里像化开了什么。

sentences.en: She wrapped Anna in a hug. “I’m sorry, too.

sentences.en: I didn’t mean to yell—I just…I’m upset, I guess.” “I didn’t mean to cast a spell,” Anna said, needing to get the words out now. “I had no way of knowing it would bring my nightmare about the wolf to life.” Elsa shook her head. “It just…When did you start having the nightmares?” “When I was a little girl, and then, this week the nightmare came back.” Ever since I realized that you were going to leave me behind for the grand tour.
sentences.zh: 我不是故意吼的——我只是……我有点心烦，我想。""我不是故意念咒的，"安娜说，这话现在非说不可，"我哪知道它会把我关于狼的噩梦变成真的。"艾莎摇头。"只是……你从什么时候开始做这些噩梦的？""我小时候就有，然后这周，噩梦又回来了。"从我意识到你要丢下我去巡游那时起。

sentences.en: But Anna didn’t say that last bit out loud.

sentences.en: He gestured the sisters over to the fire. “When did you first have the nightmare?” Elsa prodded as they huddled close to the flames.

sentences.en: Steam rose from Anna’s clothes as they slowly dried.

sentences.zh: 安娜回想。"我想是你……你明白的那晚。"她摸了摸头发上曾经那道白痕的地方，又想起小时候艾莎不小心用魔法击中那儿的事。"我真不敢相信你从没做过噩梦。""艾莎耸耸肩。"我最后一次做噩梦，一定才八岁。

sentences.en: Everything got wet and they had to bring in new furniture and carpets for me.” “And you never had the nightmare again?” “No.” Elsa leaned her head back and looked up. “Father taught me a bunch of tricks to try to control my emotions, my magic.

sentences.zh: 艾莎笑了，安娜也回以微笑，享受着这道意外连起两人的桥。"母亲也来了，叫我想象把噩梦都揉成一团，从窗口扔出去，"艾莎说，"以前我总想着揉成团扔出去时，假装喂给天上的星座。""我也那样做过！"安娜说，觉得和姐姐从未这么亲近，"我假装把它们送给渔夫弗里格，让他替我钓走。

sentences.en: But the trick didn’t stop me from having nightmares.” Elsa shrugged. “Mother’s trick worked for me.

sentences.en: I haven’t had a nightmare since.” “I’m sorry to interrupt,” Kristoff said, “but speaking of stars…it’s getting late.” The sisters smiled, and Anna felt a little bit better, if not completely.

sentences.en: Anna couldn’t help thinking that their shadows looked like drowning figures trapped beneath the ice.
sentences.zh: 安娜忍不住想，他们的影子像冰下溺着的人形。

sentences.en: They were quiet as they skated.

sentences.en: Anna didn’t want to accidentally step on the tenuous peace between her and Elsa, while Kristoff seemed to be lost again in his own worries.

sentences.zh: 克斯托夫的亲生父母早逝，他生命最初那段，斯文是他唯一的家人——直到他们都被山地地精收养。

sentences.en: The farther they glided away from Sven, the quieter Kristoff became, until, at last, it became unbearable for Anna.

chapters.title: Chapter Fourteen
chapters.en:
KRISTOFF GROANED, letting his traveler’s pack thump to the floor. “He’s not here. Now what?”

“I’m sure he’ll come back,” Anna said, unclasping her cloak. The tower felt especially stuffy after being in the wind all day long. “In the meantime, we wait.”

Arooooooooooooooo!

A long, low howl wrapped around the tower, carving a pit in Anna’s stomach—was it the wolf? Had it escaped Elsa’s ice dome?

Kristoff, however, remained calm. “It’s just the wind. Trust me.” He picked up a small guitar that leaned next to a potted plant. “Growing up with trolls, you know what’s the wind, and what’s a wolf.” He strummed the guitar. The tinkling sound filtered through the air, pretty, if a bit off-key.

Anna’s fear receded a little, and she hoped he was right. “I’d rather the wolf be stalking us here and leaving the villagers alone,” she admitted.

“Very noble of you,” Elsa said. “We’ll stay, but just until we figure out a plan in case Sorenson doesn’t come back soon.”

“Maybe there’s a book or something here that can undo the curse,” Anna said. “One that’s already been translated.”

“That’s a good idea,” Kristoff said. “I’ll take the upstairs. You two search down here.” And with a nod at the girls, he lit his lantern and disappeared into the swirl of dark steps above them. Anna thought she knew why he wanted to search a floor by himself. When Anna was upset, she always sought company, but when Kristoff was upset, he liked to be by himself or with Sven. And with Sven in trouble, she knew Kristoff was having a hard time, too.

Elsa sighed. “Ugh. I knew coming here was a bad idea.”

Anna felt herself bristle like the gray barn cat, but she didn’t want to fight, not again, not so soon. They had come a long way, and they had more of a way to go. So she kept her voice light. “We don’t know that yet. Let’s just give this room a chance. Please?”

Elsa crossed her arms, but after a second, Anna knew she’d won. This round, anyway. They divided up the circular room. In the light of a dying fire, she could see the walls were plastered with detailed star charts and strange silver instruments that hummed, and a delicate gold miniature of the solar system that was so beautifully done, Anna thought it was a shame that she couldn’t study it for hours and tell the children of the village all about it. She also found a calendar with all the phases of the moon laid out, three miniature telescopes, powder-filled glass vials, and an old sundial, its copper face green from the years it must have spent out in the harsh elements. And last but not least, a hunk of blue-black rock that was labeled METEORITE.

“This mystic seems to really like the night sky,” Anna called to Elsa.

“I noticed,” Elsa said as she straightened a frame. “Did you see the ceiling?”

Anna tilted her head back and gasped. A star map had been painted above them in deep blues and indigos. Delicate lines of silver paint connected some of the stars, tracing the outlines of fantastical beasts, crowns, and heroes. They were familiar images, and Anna recognized them as constellations. But there was something else about the illustrations that seemed familiar to her, though she couldn’t quite place her finger on it….

“It’s so pretty,” Anna said. “It’s the prettiest ceiling I’ve ever seen.”

Elsa nodded. “I like it, too. It even has my favorite constellation—Ulf.” She looked over at Anna and smiled. “Ulf the Wolf was always my favorite. I made Mother tell me all his stories.”

The sisters kept searching.

Sorenson’s thinking seemed random, and his shelves didn’t appear to be organized in any particular order that Anna could tell. Though, when she peeled back the first book’s cover, she wondered if maybe he had ranked them by stench. Many of the books had dark stains on their pages, and a couple of them even had their own furry patch of mold. But for someone who was known to be an expert in myths and lore, Sorenson didn’t appear to have many books on those topics. The closest thing was a small slate covered with strange symbols in chalk, but upon examining it, Anna saw it wasn’t magic, but physics.

Wandering over to the last bookshelf, Anna skimmed the titles: Book of Later Han by Zhang Heng, Almanack by Richard Saunders, and Book of Optics by Hasan Ibn al-Haytham. Picking up the first title, Anna flipped through the pages to see sketches of instruments that looked quite similar to those sitting on the mystic’s shelves, along with annotations of water clocks and wind flows. No mention of curses, or of dream spells gone awry.

“It’s funny,” Anna called out to Elsa as she tapped the book back onto the shelf. “I wouldn’t think that a mystic would have so many books on science. I thought he would have more spell books and stuff. You know?” She paused, waiting for her sister’s response. But when Elsa didn’t say anything, Anna called again. “Hey, Elsa?”

“Anna, can you come here?” Elsa asked.

Anna followed her sister’s voice to where she stood in a back room, more of an alcove really, that contained a tiny kitchen. Anna hurried over to her sister to find her gaping open-mouthed at a table. It looked ordinary enough, but then Anna saw it: on the center of the table was a pot of soup.

A steaming pot of soup.

Anna’s stomach flipped. For that twist of steam to exist, someone had to have been there recently.

“Where’s Kristoff?” Anna whispered. She’d planned on checking on him, but had become distracted by the many books and treasures. The mystic’s mind seemed just as distracted as her own. And now Kristoff had been gone upstairs for at least ten minutes, and he’d not come back down.

“Anna,” Elsa whispered, “I don’t think we’re alone here.”

“Exactly so,” said a low, raspy voice.

Anna spun around as a man stepped off the staircase landing and into the tower room. He was short, barely up to Anna’s shoulders, and he wore his long silver beard down to the floor. Anna had the fleeting thought that he looked a bit like the nisse from her mother’s tales, those tiny gnomelike creatures that would adopt a family to both hinder and help. The only thing he was missing was a nisse’s traditional pointy red hat, but he did have a sharp, glinting spear—and it was aimed directly at her heart.

Anna stopped breathing. In the corner, she saw Elsa raise her hands. They were trembling. But there was Elsa, once again ready to step in. Anna knew better than anyone how much Elsa never again wanted to use her powers to harm another—not after the disastrous consequences that had occurred the last time, when she had turned Anna to ice by accident. But Anna also knew that Elsa would use her powers to protect Anna—and Anna could not allow that. Not when Anna could do something about it herself.

“Hi! I’m Anna! This is Elsa!” Anna smiled, trying to inject as much cheer and goodwill into her voice as possible. “We’re sorry to intrude. We promise we weren’t going to eat your soup—it smells a bit funny—er, that’s so rude of me. I’m sorry. I mean, it doesn’t smell bad, but I’m not really sure I recognize that spice? But we’re not here for spices. Please don’t hurt us!”

“Hurt you?” The man looked dizzy from trying to follow Anna’s words. “Why would you think I would want to hurt you?” His voice was deep and grating like gravel.

“Umm.” Anna’s eyes flew to his hand. “Because of the spear you’re holding?”

“What sp—? Oh!” The man lowered the point of his spear. “This isn’t a spear, it’s part of a weather vane. That mountain man upstairs broke it when he barged onto my peaceful observation deck unannounced! He’s exceedingly lucky I finished my Highly Flammable and Very Dangerous Combustion Powder last night, or he might not have ten fingers. Hmph.”

Anna blinked as the man shoved the pointed weather vane under her nose, and she took in the large golden N that twinkled in front of her. N for north. “Ha ha,” she said, and pushed the golden point away from her. “What a silly mistake. Is the, er, mountain man…all right?”

“He will be, once he cleans up the mess he made,” the short man said, shooting her a glare. “He’s also lucky he didn’t come next month and disturb my view of the meteor shower. But that’s what I’m doing here. I live here. Always have. My question is: what are you doing here?”

“We’re looking for the great mystic Sorenson,” Anna said, trying to sweep a curtsy, but her knees were still shaky from misinterpreting the weather vane, and she almost knocked over a nearby bust of a man in round reading glasses. “We’re assuming that’s you?”

The old man snorted. “I’m Sorenson, but I’m no mystic.”

Elsa stepped forward, her hands no longer raised, but now clenched in the folds of her cloak. “But the villagers say you are a mystic.”

“I’m a scientist,” the man said, using the weather vane to reach through his thick beard and scratch the underside of his chin. “Though I suppose the villagers might not see that much of a difference between me and the old mystics of legendary tales.”

A scientist. Anna tried not to let her disappointment show. It was great to be a scientist, but not when one needed a mystic to save a kingdom from a vicious magical wolf. How would a scientist be able to help with a terrible curse? “We’re sorry to have bothered you.” Anna stepped aside as Sorenson shuffled past her to check on his soup. “Oaken had told us that you’re an expert in myths and lore.”

“Oh, but I am.” Sorenson gave his pot a stir. “Mythology and science are familiar friends—both seek for the why behind things. Both look to provide an explanation for the natural phenomena of the world around us. And all myths contain a kernel of hard truth.” He took a sip of his soup and winced before tossing in a pinch of salt. Only after he took another sip and nodded his head in satisfaction did he look back at the sisters. “Though I am curious as to why the queen and princess of Arendelle are here seeking an expert in myths and lore. Something must be truly wrong.”

“Because,” Elsa said, her voice low but steady, “Arendelle has been cursed.”

“And we need your help to figure out how to undo it,” Anna added, attempting to gloss over the fact that she’d been the one who’d cursed it. She tried not to look at anyone, but Elsa caught her eye and nodded. For a moment, it felt like an ember from the fireplace had broken away from the logs and settled somewhere in Anna’s heart. Even though snow and ice flowed through Elsa, she always made Anna feel the warmest. Maybe everything wasn’t lost, after all.

Except, Sorenson’s reaction wasn’t exactly encouraging. His bushy eyebrows shot up so fast that they almost skidded off his face, and Anna wondered for a minute if he would laugh. Instead, he opened an old trunk and began pulling out empty bowls.

“In that case,” Sorenson said, “someone please fetch the mountain man from the observation deck and have him rebuild my fire. It seems as though you have a story to tell, and I’d rather be warm while I listen.”

A few minutes and a roaring fire later, Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff gathered around Sorenson’s table, each taking turns sharing all they knew. Anna heard Elsa describe the unnatural quiet that had befallen SoYun’s farm and the way the trees in the kingdom’s orchards were not only producing mushy gray apples, but had also become gnarled, as though they were twisting away from something—the wolf, Anna guessed—as it had passed by. But did that mean the wolf had been present before she read the spell? And if so, how?

Then it was Kristoff’s turn, and he described how the forest, too, had been quiet, though he did not mention the trolls or their surprising absence. Arendelle’s mountain trolls were private creatures, and for the most part, they liked to keep themselves hidden from humans, with a few special exceptions. Kristoff wouldn’t mention them to just any person, and though Sorenson was now feeding them warm soup that tasted of mushrooms and roots, Kristoff was still protective of the concealed trolls who had raised him as part of their family, and, after all, Sorenson had forced Kristoff to clean up his mess out on a chilly observation deck.

Finally, it was Anna’s turn. She began with the crumpled piece of paper with the “Make Dreams Come True” spell on it, and how she’d had a nightmare, and gone to the kitchen to make some hot chocolate. She told him how she’d seen something out of the corner of her eye and followed it to the Great Hall, where she’d seen a wolf—the same wolf from her nightmare. And how her friends’ eyes had turned inky black and then glowing yellow while they seemed to have lost themselves in the strong hold of a nightmare sleep. As she completed her tale, Sorenson stood and went to his shelves. Pulling out two books, he returned to the table, the wooden floorboards beneath his boots creaking slightly as he walked.

“I think,” Sorenson said, placing the books on the table and slipping back into his stool, “that the answer can be found in one of these.”

Anna looked at the books. One was a tome called Psychologia. The other was a slim leather volume with block letters stamped across its cover:

NATTMARA

“‘Nattmara,’” Elsa read out loud. “I know that word.”

Anna knew the word, too. She’d heard the word before, long, long ago, but she had seen that word recently as well, as a non-translated entry in Secrets of the Magic Makers. A vision sprang to her mind: a sketch of a man screaming in agony, and the drawing of the wolf…

“Yes.” Sorenson nodded. “You probably do. Nattmara often show up in the sagas of old, and those stories are often told to children as warning tales.” Flipping open the ancient book, he pointed to an illustration of a child sleeping in bed. “Another name for a Nattmara is ‘Nightmare,’ because that’s what it is—the embodiment of our deepest fear.”

“Embody-what?” Kristoff asked.

“It means that nightmares can take on a physical shape and exist outside of your mind,” Elsa said.

“Precisely.” Sorenson held up his pointer finger. “The act of burying fear is what manifests the Nattmara. And eventually, the fear is too big to keep inside. They can take the shape of anything, and this particular one seems to have taken the form of a wolf. Nattmara tend to roam the world, leaching energy from all living things. Their very presence can cause trees to twist away from them. They feed on fear, and so they seek to create fear.”

Anna’s eyes widened as she listened, trying to grasp onto the strange ideas.

Sorenson flipped the page to another illustration, this one of a swirling storm of black sand. “A Nattmara is also able to turn itself into black sand in order to slip through cracks—cracks in doors, and cracks within the heart. There is no escaping them, unless you’re brave enough that there is no weakness for the Nattmara to enter through.”

He looked up, his brown eyes locking on Anna. “And if a Nattmara is allowed to run loose for too long, then a kingdom and everyone in it can fall into an eternal nightmare sleep. And as it grows more powerful, more people can become afraid, and it can gorge itself on fear, becoming bigger and bigger.” He tapped the page. “Or so the age-old myth goes.”

Anna blinked, breaking away from Sorenson’s deep gaze. “You don’t sound like you believe in this myth,” she said, puzzled. “But doesn’t what’s happening in Arendelle now prove that the myth is real?”

“Not at all,” Sorenson said, shaking his head and sending his long beard swaying. “What do they teach in schools these days? The Nattmara is a creature of myth, and like all myths, it’s an explanation to a greater mystery. In this instance: where do nightmares come from?”

“Pardon me,” Elsa said, while Anna and Kristoff exchanged puzzled glances, “but I don’t understand your question.”

Sighing, Sorenson shook his head. “Let’s look at it a different way. Did you see the signs for the mines that warn to be wary of Huldrefólk?” He paused, and when they nodded, he continued. “The mines were abandoned nearly twenty years ago, because of strange and mysterious things that kept going wrong. Cave-ins started to occur with increased frequency, and miners that had worked their entire lives in these tunnels began to get lost. Now, what was the explanation?” Sorenson looked from Anna to Elsa to Kristoff.

“Huldrefólk,” Anna said, thinking back to the sign they had passed and Oaken’s warning. “The mysterious, elf-like people known as the Huldrefólk are rumored to live throughout Arendelle in mounds and under rock. They are a mischievous bunch, not necessarily bad, but they enjoy pranks above all else. They have a bit of a reputation for being thieves, but some stories insist they are simply collectors, borrowers of lost things. But unlike the mountain trolls, they are just a story that parents tell their young ones to go to sleep.”

“Exactly,” Sorenson nodded. “The miners believed the Huldrefólk were angry that they were impeding on their territory. They thought the Huldrefólk were creating the cave-ins to scare the humans away.”

“It seemed to have worked,” Kristoff remarked. “I noticed some boards over the mines’ entrance.”

“It did work,” Sorenson agreed. “And a good thing, too, because the mines had been overworked. The miners weren’t in danger from territorial Huldrefólk. The human miners were in the middle of a danger of their own making. It was their pickaxes that had made the rock walls too thin to hold the weight of a mountain. Nothing mythical about it; just old-fashioned greed.”

“So,” Elsa said slowly, “you’re saying the Nattmara probably has a simple explanation, too?”

“A scientific one,” Sorenson clarified. “Most likely, our answer is in this.” He tapped the book labeled Psychologia with a grimy fingernail.

Anna turned this information over. What Sorenson had said seemed simple enough, but she had seen the wolf. She had seen Kai’s and Gerda’s eyes. The “myth” had seemed very real as it had chased her and her friends through the rooms and halls of the castle.

“But say it is a Nattmara that is doing all of this,” Anna argued, not wanting to leave empty-handed, not wanting to leave without at least one answer. “How can we defeat it?”

“That’s easy enough,” Sorenson said, pulling out another book, this one titled Mythica Explainia. “You can only defeat a myth with a thing of myth. But it’s not like Revolute exists. None of it really truly does.”

“Revolute?” Kristoff asked. “That was Aren’s sword, right?”

“The very one.” Sorenson nodded. “Aren was said to have defeated many a mythical beast with his sword. The very sword, some say, that the sun herself gifted to him for ripping holes in the night sky so that she could watch her children during the day. Those rips, of course, are what we call stars.” He smiled up in the direction of his painted ceiling. “See? Another myth seeking to answer how things came to be.”

“Great!” Anna felt hope lift within her for the first time since they’d arrived at the tower. “So we need Revolute! Where is it?”

Sorenson burst into laughter, but as he did, he took in the serious expression on her face, and shook his head. “I’m sorry, but it’s unlikely that Aren himself ever existed—or his mighty sword of myth. It’s likely that there was a strong warrior from way back when, but he probably never met the sun or faced a great dragon, or carved out the Arenfjord. That’s just legend—like the Huldrefólk or the mountain trolls.”

“But the trolls exist,” Kristoff said with a shrug. “They raised me.”

Sorenson stared hard at Kristoff. Then he cupped his hand around his mouth and whispered in Elsa’s ear, “Is the mountain man okay?”

“Kristoff,” Anna corrected, “is amazing. And the trolls do exist. And the Nattmara exists. And the Huldrefólk, well, they probably exist, too!”

Sorenson sat back, snapping his book shut. “Magic and myth don’t exist,” he said.

Elsa smirked and flicked her wrist. A second later, Anna felt a cold kiss on her cheek. She looked up to see a delicate snow flurry hovering above their heads.

There was a loud clatter as Sorenson tumbled from his stool. “In all my days! The rumors are true!”

Elsa smiled. “You haven’t come down your mountain in a very long time, have you, Sorenson?” And so, Elsa began to tell Sorenson all that had happened in the last three years. And with each new thing he learned, Sorenson had another question.

Kristoff drummed his fingers on the table impatiently, and only when Anna laid her hand over his did he stop. “Sorry,” he whispered, “but while we’re talking, Sven is still sick!”

Anna knew that Kristoff was right. “Let’s keep looking,” she said quietly.

Kristoff crept over to the bookshelves while Anna cracked open the volume on the table. She skipped past passages about talking trees and a playful wind spirit until, finally, she found what she had been looking for: NATTMARA.

Sure enough, all that Sorenson had said was written there, including a few additional pieces of information:

The Nattmara is created when a child’s fear grows too big to be contained and the child’s fearful heart calls out to them.

And then, a little below that:

Trolls tremble at the Nattmara’s howl while the Nattmara flees from the sun like a shadow.

Nothing in the section said anything about a spell that was able to manifest a Nattmara, or banish it. But it was useful to know that the Nattmara didn’t like sunlight. And it explained why the trolls had most likely gone missing. Frowning, Anna thumbed through the pages and reread an entry about the Huldrefólk. She stopped upon a line:

Huldrefólk always find that which is lost.

That which is lost…Anna’s heart quickened. Maybe, she thought with rising excitement, that also meant the Huldrefólk could find a mythical sword that was lost to history. It was a slim hope, but a hope she clung to nevertheless. Maybe they needed to go to the mines to find the Huldrefólk—despite the warnings.

But they didn’t have much time.

They only had two more sunrises left before the spell became permanent—and the night was no longer young.

“You know,” Sorenson said to Elsa, “your mother came here once, seeking answers. In fact, she was the one who painted my ceiling.”

Anna froze. Their mother had been here? It couldn’t be. Why on earth would their mother come to visit Sorenson? Answers to what? And suddenly, she realized why the painted ceiling looked familiar. It reminded her of the painting of the northern lights and constellations that decorated the ceiling of the secret room.

Slipping the book into Kristoff’s traveler’s pack, Anna opened her mouth to ask Sorenson more, and to tell the others her idea about going to the mines. But as Anna looked up, she noticed something strange across the tower room: an army of black ants pouring in from under the door. She shut her mouth.

No. Not ants.

Black sand.

The Nattmara had found them at last.

安娜尽量不露出失望。

当科学家挺好，可当你需要一位秘术师把王国从恶毒的魔法狼手里救出来时，就不怎么好了。

一个科学家能怎么帮上可怕的诅咒？"很抱歉打扰您。"安娜侧身让索伦森趿拉着走过她去照看汤。"奥肯告诉我们您是神话与传说的专家。""哦，我确实是，"索伦森搅了搅锅，"神话和科学是老相识——都探求事物背后的'为什么'。

都为周遭自然现象寻找解释。

而所有神话都含有一粒硬邦邦的真相。"他抿了口汤，皱皱眉，撒了撮盐。

等再抿一口、满意地点头，他才回头看姐妹俩。"不过我好奇，阿伦黛尔的女王和公主为何来寻神话与传说的专家。

一定出了什么大事。""因为，"艾莎说，声音低却稳，"阿伦黛尔被诅咒了。

我们需要您帮忙找出怎么解除它，"安娜补道，努力掩饰是她自己下了诅咒。

她尽量不看任何人，可艾莎对上她的眼，点了点头。

有那么一刻，像壁炉里一颗火星脱离了木柴，落在安娜心里的某处。

尽管艾莎体内流淌着冰雪，她总让安娜觉得最暖。

也许终究不是全完了。

只可惜，索伦森的反应不太鼓舞人。

他浓密的眉毛飞快扬起，差点滑下脸，安娜有一瞬以为他会笑。

可他打开一口旧箱子，开始往外拿空碗。"那样的话，"索伦森说，"谁去把观测台那山地汉子叫来，让他把我的火重新生上。

看来你们有故事要讲，而我宁愿听着暖和点。"几分钟后，一团旺火烧起，安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫围在索伦森桌边，轮流把知道的一五一十说出来。

安娜听艾莎讲SoYun农场那不寻常的安静，讲王国果园里的树不光结出软塌塌的灰苹果，还扭曲了，像在躲避什么——安娜猜是狼——从旁经过时那样。

可那意味着狼在她念咒之前就出现了？

若是，怎么可能？

接着轮到克斯托夫，他讲森林也曾如何安静，虽没提地精和他们出奇的消失。

阿伦黛尔的山地地精是怕生的生灵，多半喜欢躲着人，只有几个特殊的例外。

克斯托夫不会随随便便对谁提起他们，尽管索伦森此刻正喂他们喝着蘑菇和根茎味的热汤，克斯托夫仍护着那些把他当家人养大的隐秘地精；再者，索伦森刚逼克斯托夫在冷飕飕的观测台上收拾残局。

终于轮到安娜。

她从那张揉皱的、写着"美梦成真"的纸讲起，讲她怎样做了个噩梦，去厨房煮热可可。

讲她怎样眼角瞥见什么，跟到礼堂，看见一只狼——和她噩梦里一样的狼。

讲她朋友们的眼睛怎样变成墨黑，又变成发光的黄，仿佛陷进噩梦沉睡里出不来。

她讲完，索伦森站起，走向书架。

他抽出两本书回来，木靴下的地板吱呀轻响。"我想，"索伦森把书放桌上、坐回凳子，"答案就在其中一本里。"安娜看着书。

一本是叫《心理学》的厚册子。

另一本是皮面小书，封面上印着大写字母：纳特玛拉。"'纳特玛拉，'"艾莎念出声，"我知道这个词。"安娜也知道这词。

她很久很久以前听过，可最近也见过——作为《魔法制造者之秘》里一条未译的条目。

一个画面跳进脑海：一个男人痛苦尖叫的素描，还有那只狼的画……"对，"索伦森点头，"你们大概知道。

纳特玛拉常出现在古老的史诗中，那些故事常当警示童话讲给孩子听。"他翻开古书，指向一幅小孩睡在床上的画。"纳特玛拉另一个名字叫'噩梦'，因为它就是——我们最深恐惧的化身。""化……身什么？"克斯托夫问。"意思是噩梦能具成形，存在于你脑外，"艾莎说。"正是，"索伦森竖起食指，"把恐惧埋起来，才生出纳特玛拉。

而终有一天，恐惧大得藏不住。

它们能变成任何形状，这只偏偏成了狼的模样。

纳特玛拉爱在世间游荡，从一切活物身上吸取精力。

它的存在本身就能让树扭身躲开。

它以恐惧为食，所以才制造恐惧。"安娜睁大眼听着，努力抓住这些古怪的念头。

索伦森翻到另一幅画，这次是一团打着旋的黑沙风暴。"纳特玛拉还能把自己变成黑沙，从缝里钻过——门缝，还有心里的裂缝。

你躲不开它，除非你勇敢到没有弱点供它钻入。"他抬头，棕眼锁住安娜，"而若放任纳特玛拉游荡太久，整个王国和所有人都会陷入永恒的噩梦沉睡。

它越强大，怕它的人越多，它便能大啖恐惧，越长越大。"他敲了敲书页，"老神话是这么讲的。"安娜眨眨眼，移开与索伦森深邃目光的对视。"听上去你不大信这神话，"她困惑地说，"可阿伦黛尔现在发生的事，不正好证明神话是真的吗？""才不，"索伦森摇头，长胡子跟着晃，"如今学校都教些什么？

纳特玛拉是神话里的生灵，和所有神话一样，是对更大谜团的解释。

这回的谜团是：噩梦从哪来？""抱歉，"艾莎说，安娜和克斯托夫交换着困惑的眼神，"我不懂你的问题。"索伦森叹气摇头。"换个角度看。

你们看见矿上警告当心胡尔德精灵的牌子了吗？"他顿了顿，见他们点头，继续，"矿井大约二十年前废弃，因为不断出怪事。

塌方越来越频繁，在矿里干了一辈子的矿工开始迷路。

那么，解释是什么？"索伦森从安娜看到艾莎，再到克斯托夫。"胡尔德精灵，"安娜说，想起路过的牌子和奥肯的警告，"传说中淘气、像精灵的胡尔德精灵，住在阿伦黛尔各处的土丘和岩石下。

他们爱捣蛋，不算坏，却最爱恶作剧。

他们有点贼名，可有些故事坚称他们只是收藏家，借走丢失的东西。

不过和山地地精不同，他们只是父母哄小孩睡觉的故事。""正是，"索伦森点头，"矿工们以为胡尔德精灵恼他们占了地盘。

以为胡尔德精灵制造塌方，想把人吓走。""看来奏效了，"克斯托夫说，"我看见矿口钉了些木板。""是奏效了，"索伦森同意，"而且幸好，因为矿开采过度了。

矿工不是被占地盘的胡尔德精灵害的。

是人类矿工自己把自己置于险境。

是他们自己的镐，把石壁挖得太薄，撑不住一座山的重量。

没什么神话的，不过是老式的贪心。""所以，"艾莎慢慢说，"你是说纳特玛拉大概也有个简单的解释？""科学的解释，"索伦森澄清，"答案最可能在那儿。"他用脏指甲敲了敲标着《心理学》的书。

安娜把这话在心里转了转。

索伦森说的似乎很简单，可她见过那只狼。

她见过凯和格尔达的眼睛。

那"神话"追着她和朋友们穿过城堡的厅堂时，可真实得很。"可要是真有纳特玛拉在干这些，"安娜争辩，不想空手而归，不想连一个答案都没有，"我们怎么打败它？""那容易，"索伦森说，抽出另一本叫《神话释疑》的书，"你只能用神话之物，打败神话之物。

可回旋之刃又不是真存在。

那些东西没一样真存在过。""回旋之刃？"克斯托夫问，"那是阿伦的剑，对吧？""正是，"索伦森点头，"据说阿伦用他的剑打败过许多神话猛兽。

有人说，正是这把剑，太阳亲手赠他，因为他撕开夜空，好让她白天能照看孩子们。

那些裂缝，当然，就是我们叫的星星。"他朝画着的天花板方向笑了笑，"看？

又是一个解'万物从何而来'的神话。""太好了！"安娜自他们到塔后，头一回心里升起希望，"那我们需要回旋之刃！

它在哪儿？"索伦森大笑，可笑着笑着，看清她脸上认真的神情，摇了摇头。"抱歉，可阿伦本人——连同他神话里的神剑——多半从没存在过。

也许很久以前真有过一位勇士，可他大概从没见过太阳，没面对过巨龙，也没开凿过阿伦峡湾。

那只是传说——像胡尔德精灵或山地地精。""可地精是真的，"克斯托夫耸肩，"他们把我养大。"索伦森死死盯着克斯托夫。

接着他捂住嘴，凑到艾莎耳边低语："那山地汉子没事吧？""克斯托夫，"安娜纠正，"他棒极了。

而且地精真的存在。

纳特玛拉也存在。

胡尔德精灵嘛，嗯，他们大概也存在！"索伦森往后一靠，啪地合上书。"魔法和神话不存在，"他说。

艾莎撇嘴，手腕一弹。

一秒钟后，安娜感到脸颊上一阵冰凉的吻。

她抬头，看见他们头顶悬着一场精致的雪。

索伦森从凳子上摔下来，哐当一声。"活了这么大！

传言是真的！"艾莎笑了。"你可是很久没下过山了，对吧，索伦森？"于是，艾莎把过去三年发生的一切讲给索伦森听。

每听一件新事，索伦森就多一个问题。

克斯托夫不耐烦地用手指敲桌子，直到安娜把手覆上他的，他才停。"抱歉，"他低声说，"可我们说话的当儿，斯文还病着！"安娜知道克斯托夫是对的。"我们再找找，"她轻声说。

克斯托夫蹑手蹑脚走到书架边，安娜则翻开桌上的书。

她跳过会说话的树和顽皮风灵的段落，终于找到要找的：纳特玛拉。

果然，索伦森说的都在上面，还多了几条：纳特玛拉生于孩子的恐惧大到藏不住，孩子恐惧的心向它们呼救之时。

再往下一点：地精在纳特玛拉的嚎叫下发抖，而纳特玛拉像影子一样从太阳身边逃开。

这一节没提任何能召唤或驱散纳特玛拉的咒语。

但知道纳特玛拉不喜欢阳光，很有用。

这也解释了地精为何多半不见了。

安娜皱眉，翻着书页，重读一条关于胡尔德精灵的条目。

她停在一行：胡尔德精灵总能寻回失物。

失物……安娜的心怦怦快起来。

也许，她越想越兴奋，那也意味着胡尔德精灵能找来一把失落于历史的神话之剑。

这希望渺茫，却是她紧抓不放的希望。

也许他们该去矿井找胡尔德精灵——不顾那些警告。

可时间不多了。

离咒语永久生效，只剩两个日出——而夜已不年轻。"你知道吗，"索伦森对艾莎说，"你母亲来过一次，寻答案。

其实，天花板上那幅就是她画的。"安娜僵住。

他们的母亲来过这儿？

不可能。

母亲到底为什么要来见索伦森？

寻什么答案？

忽然，她明白为何那画着的天花板眼熟了。

它让她想起密室天花板上那幅北极光与星座的画。

安娜把书塞进克斯托夫的行囊，张嘴想多问索伦森，也把去矿井的念头告诉大家。

可她一抬头，看见塔屋那头有点不对劲：一队黑蚁从门底下涌进来。

她闭了嘴。

不。

不是蚂蚁。

是黑沙。

纳特玛拉终于找到他们了。
