chapters.title: Chapter Seventeen
chapters.en:
THE CHILD’S—Hulder’s—melody flew off on invisible wings and faded again into silence.

Anna burst into applause; she couldn’t help it. After all, the little Hulder didn’t seem dangerous.

“That was incredible!” she exclaimed. “What’s your name?”

For a moment, the Hulder seemed to stare at Anna in the glow-light, luminescent eyes boring into hers, and then the Hulder tumbled backward off the crystal.

“No!” Anna said as she rushed behind the crystal to check on the child, hoping the tiny Hulder hadn’t hurt themselves.

But as she rounded the tree-trunk-sized crystal, she saw that the Hulder was no longer behind it. The child had disappeared, except for the sound of footsteps pattering down the dark passage up ahead. Without a second thought, Anna took off.

“Anna!” Elsa called from behind. “Wait! Slow down! You’re going too fast!”

“Anna!” Kristoff shouted. Their warnings echoed off the rocks around them, but Anna disagreed with them both: she was going too slow.

The Hulder was quick—Anna wasn’t sure if it was footsteps she was following now, or just the quiet drip of stalactites in the distance. Still, they had come to look for the Huldrefólk, the only ones who might be able to help them find the Revolute Blade, the only ones of myth who might be able to save them all from Anna’s terrible mistake. And so Anna ran on, only just missing the occasional low-hanging rocks. Suddenly, the Hulder screeched. It sounded frightened, and Anna hoped the Hulder wasn’t in trouble.

“Hang on!” Anna shouted. She ran faster and faster, and then her foot caught—on a rock, a divot, or a root, it was too dark to tell—and she toppled to the ground, her hands out to cushion her fall.

Pain cracked through Anna’s ribs as she slammed into the solid rock. She was going to have one giant bruise in an hour. Everything hurt. Everything but her right arm, which she’d flung out far in front of herself to try to break her fall. And as Anna looked at the glowworm bracelet dangling from her wrist, she saw why: her right arm had not hit any rock at all. All that hand had hit was thin air. Anna was glad she was already lying on the ground, because she thought she might faint if she were still standing. She’d followed the Hulder—and had almost run off a cliff and into an abyss.

She could still hear the Hulder’s cry. Tuva’s warning from the trading post came back to her. They’re tricky. Sometimes, they help. Other times, they lure humans off the safest paths. And maybe, Anna thought, lure them into an abyss. There was always a chance that the Hulder child had done this on purpose, had perhaps meant to distract Anna and Elsa and Kristoff away from the Huldrefólk’s home.

But even as these dark thoughts gathered into a cloud, Anna scooted forward on her belly, toward the sound of the Hulder’s cry. It didn’t matter what the Hulder’s intentions had been—but it did matter that the Hulder was stuck and scared. Once she wiggled to the edge, Anna leaned her chin out and peered down. The Hulder had tumbled over the edge, but by some luck or miracle, the child had caught themselves on a small ledge five feet down. It would be easy for Kristoff to lean over and reach the Hulder, but even as Anna watched, the rocky ledge was crumbling away under the child’s weight.

“Elsa! Kristoff! Help!” Anna shouted as she inched forward even more, letting herself dangle over the edge, her hand outstretched. “Grab my hand!” she called down.

The Hulder raised a hand, but Anna was still too far away. She had to get closer. Wiggling forward, Anna lowered herself down inch by fraction of an inch. Just a little bit farther now…She strained her fingers forward, willing them to lengthen—and that’s when she felt the crumbling of the earth beneath her own weight. What was once solid ground turned to gravel, and Anna skidded forward, headfirst into the dark abyss. She screamed.

But before she could shoot past the Hulder and plummet into the vast void, two pairs of hands grabbed her ankles from above. Kristoff! Elsa!

She lurched to a stop, face to face with the little cat-eyed Hulder, who was still mostly in shadow, and who, if Anna had to wager a guess, looked terrified of her.

“Hi,” Anna said, trying hard to iron out the quiver in her voice. “My name is Anna, and I’m not going to hurt you.” She offered out her hand. “Come with me!”

The Hulder hesitated a moment, then gripped Anna’s palm. The child’s skin was smooth and dry, like one of the little lizards Anna had read about that populated the Chatho deserts. But even with the Hulder so close to her, it was hard to see them properly. It was almost as though the child had been made of shadow or carved from a mirror. Trying to make out the details was a little like trying to hold tight to a bar of soap: the harder one squeezed, the quicker the soap slid away; the harder one looked, the quicker the Hulder seemed to vanish.

Gripping the child with all her strength, Anna called, “Pull us up!”

There was a grunt, and then Anna and the Hulder rose to safety, just as the little ledge deteriorated into nothingness. She and the child were dragged back onto solid rock. Before Anna had a chance to release the Hulder, Elsa and Kristoff wrapped Anna into a tight hug, and she leaned into their warmth.

“Anna,” Elsa said, voice tight. “I couldn’t…I mean, you almost—”

“Key word: almost,” Kristoff cut in with a wink.

Anna smiled at him. He always seemed to understand her, to know that if she thought too much about what had just almost happened, she would sit there forever and turn into a fossil.

“I’m here,” Anna said. She could have stayed there forever in their arms, but for the wiggling Hulder she held.

The child pushed out of the group and plopped onto the floor—still far enough away that all Anna could really make out was a pointy elbow, but in more detail than before. Now Anna could see that the Hulder’s skin was the exact color of the bluish rock that filled the mines. Anna frowned. When she’d first spotted the Hulder, she’d thought the child’s skin was a smoky white, similar to the crystal the Hulder had been sitting on. A funny, tickling idea crawled into Anna’s mind: she’d been right both times. The Hulder had been smoky white and then a bluish gray. The Hulder’s body had first looked smooth, then as rough as the stone wall. Maybe the Huldrefólk were like octopuses in the deeps of the Southern Sea, able to change not only their color but also their texture.

“Wow,” Anna said, trying to collect herself even as a stream of rapid thoughts dashed through her mind. First thought: This is so cool! She was thrilled to learn about this wonderful trait of the Huldrefólk. The second thought came fast on the heels of the first: if Anna could change color and texture, she’d head to the portrait gallery, stand in front of all her favorite paintings, and feel what it was like to be Lieutenant Mattias, her father’s old official Arendellian guard, for an afternoon. And finally, her third thought: the last time she’d been in the castle, she’d seen the wolf, and everything had changed. A shudder ran down her spine.

Elsa knelt before the child. “Hi there, little one. I’m Elsa. What’s your name?”

The little Hulder burst into tears that sparkled like gems.

“Oh, no.” Elsa jerked back. “Here!” She conjured a snowflake and presented it.

“Elsa,” Anna hissed. “No magic, remember?”

The snowflake burst into water droplets. Elsa’s cheeks turned pink and her hands clenched at her sides. “I’m sorry,” she whispered. “I forgot.” It was sad that Elsa had spent most of her life trying to suppress her magic. It truly seemed a part of her, as natural as breathing and blinking. Having to refrain from using it again was probably taking some getting used to.

Anna felt sorry about it. She took a deep breath. They had to get out of there. They had to find Revolute and defeat the Nattmara, not only for Arendelle, but for her sister. She couldn’t let Elsa shut herself away again.

“Ow!” Elsa yelped.

Looking down, Anna saw her sister’s thick braid held tight in a chubby fist.

“Ow-ow!” the little Hulder repeated, and gave another pull, as if Elsa’s braid were a rope.

“Owowowow!” Elsa unwound her hair from the child’s fists. “I’m not a horse.”

“Horse!” the little Hulder said. “Horse! Horse! Horse!”

Elsa sighed while Anna covered her mouth to hide a giggle. She understood the Hulder’s fascination with Elsa’s braid. When she’d been little, she, too, had pretended Elsa was a racehorse and had ordered her sister to charge up and down the castle hallways. Once, she’d even gotten Elsa to neigh.

The little Hulder let go of Elsa’s hair and toddled over to Kristoff. “Horse!” the child proclaimed.

“Hey,” Kristoff protested as the Hulder ran around him. “You’re one to talk.”

“Hey! Hey! Hey!” the little Hulder said. “Talk, talk, talk!” Though the Hulder was running in circles around Kristoff, the child ran sideways, long gallops, keeping their back to the wall at all times.

To hide the tail! Anna realized with delight. Maybe she would finally be able to find out the answer to her childhood question about whether they all had tails.

“They’re a bit…hyper?” Elsa tugged her cloak so that it would hang neatly again.

“No more than any other child,” Anna said, thinking of the children she’d often run into in the village. “But most children wouldn’t know how to get around a cave, while this little one might be able to lead us to the older Huldrefólk who can help us.”

Tucking strands of hair back into her braid, Elsa looked doubtful. “Maybe?”

Taking note of what had happened to Elsa, Anna pushed her own hair back to make sure it wasn’t easily accessible before getting on her hands and knees. “Hi,” she said. “Do you remember my name?”

“Anna! Anna! Anna!” the Hulder screeched.

Anna blinked. She hadn’t been expecting quite so much enthusiasm. “Yes, that’s right. What’s your name?”

“What’s your name?” the Hulder repeated.

“Anna,” Anna said.

“Anna,” the Hulder repeated.

“Wait.” Anna rubbed her forehead. “Your name is Anna, too?”

“Wait.” The Hulder mimicked her again. “Your name is Anna, too!”

“Like I said,” Elsa said, her lips twitching, “hyper.”

“I might be wrong,” Kristoff observed, “but I think they’re just repeating everything you say.”

“Hyper! Everything you say!” the Hulder echoed back.

Taking a deep breath, Anna spoke as quickly as she could, giving the Hulder no chance to repeat her words until she was done. “Hi, I’m Anna! My home is Arendelle, like you, but above the ground.”

The Hulder looked at her in complete astonishment. “Home?”

Anna nodded. “Yes, home. Where do you live? We’d like to meet your family.”

The Hulder looked at Anna, then nodded. “Home!” And then the Hulder was off—running backward as easily as if they had eyes in the back of their head. And maybe they did. After all, as Anna knew from old bedtime stories, no one had ever seen a Hulder’s back.

“Come on!” Anna shot to her feet. “We have to follow!”

The Hulder ran impossibly fast—and unlike Anna and the others, the Hulder was short enough to avoid low-hanging rocks, while Kristoff had to run at a crouch. Up, down, and down again, they sprinted through seemingly endless corridors of crystals and sparkling rocks. Anna couldn’t understand how the Hulder—Dash, as she mentally nicknamed them, taking a page from Olaf’s book—was able to tell the difference between the tunnels. Maybe it was some special Huldrefólk trick. After all, Huldrefólk could always find lost things. Maybe it meant they could never become lost themselves.

A strange thought crossed her mind, and she wondered if that meant the Huldrefólk always knew what they should do next. How fantastic would that be? Maybe that’s how Dash had found them so quickly. Or maybe Dash had found them because Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff were the lost things.

Anna shook her head. She had so many questions, and there was so little time to attend to them all.

But there was one thing she could do. “Kristoff? Elsa?” Anna waited until they both looked at her, and then said, “I think I know what happened to the missing trolls. I read in Sorenson’s tower that they always flee the land when a Nattmara appears.”

Anna heard Kristoff let out a great sigh of relief. “Good,” he said. “Then that means they’re safe.”

Soon enough, another sound began to play under the staccato of their footsteps. A strange, shuffling, creaking sound.

“Do you hear that?” Anna called back between breaths.

“Yeah,” Kristoff said. “Do you think—?”

“Maybe,” Anna replied, slowing to a walk. She didn’t need him to finish his sentence to know what he was thinking: Nattmara.

“We should stop,” Elsa said. “Take a moment to scout out what’s happening. Huldrefólk can be mischievous…especially if they think we’re here to take something that doesn’t belong to us.”

“But if we stop,” Anna said, “we’ll lose Dash!”

The corners of Elsa’s eyes crinkled in confusion as she navigated around a large boulder that Anna had simply scrambled over. “Dash?” she asked.

“The Hulder,” Anna explained. She turned back to see if Kristoff needed any help with the boulder, but he’d simply shoved it to the side, clearing the way.

“It’s too late,” he said. “We already lost them.”

In the two seconds Anna had taken her eyes off Dash, the child had sped out of sight. “No,” Anna breathed. “We have to keep up!” She broke into a run again, fresh fear giving her newfound speed. “Dash doesn’t know about the Nattmara!”

But as Anna rounded the final bend, she saw where the sound had been coming from: an underground city carved out of the rock itself.

The secret home of the Huldrefólk.

Just as the world above, so was the world below. Cozy homes were carved into the blue-gray stone, and orange light spilled out from them, as welcoming as a smile. The pebble-lined streets were alight with glowworms, so it was easy to see what various mine carts pulled: one held a pile of stalactites bundled like firewood, another was filled to the brim with glowing mushrooms the size of sun hats, and another was heaped with water-clear rocks that Anna thought might be large diamonds.

And the Huldrefólk. The adults appeared to be tall, built more like sapling trees than people, with long limbs and long necks. And similar to Dash, they were hard to see in the light of the underneath realm.

The glow-light wasn’t the same as sunlight, bright and revealing, but the kind of soft glow that Anna associated with romantic candlelit dinners. It illuminated at the same time as it concealed, casting shadows that again helped to obscure the Huldrefólk. Still, even in the dimness, Anna could tell that they camouflaged into whatever it was that they were standing near, from onyx black to marble white and every shade in between. Some of the Huldrefólk looked as though they could be purple, others orange and green with sparkling, black-veined skin. The Huldrefólk—the hidden folk—could blend into any surrounding.

Which was great, Anna thought, but most important, they were real. Real creatures who would have real answers to where they could find the real lost sword of Aren. The thing of myth they needed to save the day.

“Wow,” Elsa whispered. “How beautiful. And peaceful.”

“If Sven were here,” Kristoff said, “I bet he’d eat all those mushrooms, and then his teeth would probably glow for a week.”

Sven. Anna wished the reindeer were with them. The way down to the village looked steep, and Sven was always good about finding the surest path down a craggy mountain. She scanned the side of the rock, looking for a pathway to the dwellings. Somewhere below, she was sure they would find the answers to how to set things right and heal Sven, and the rest of Arendelle, from the Nattmara’s influence.

As she leaned forward to see better, Anna felt a sharp something prod her back.

“Kristoff,” she said, swiping a hand behind her, “stop that. I’m just trying to see.”

“I’m not doing anything,” Kristoff said, standing to her left, a few feet away from easy poking distance.

The back of Anna’s neck prickled.

Elsa stood to her right, her face pensive as she took in the city below them.

Suddenly, Anna became very aware of the feeling that someone was watching her.

Maybe even a few someones.

“Oh,” she heard Elsa squeak.

Anna turned, only to come nose-to-nose with a spear. And not just one spear.

Many spears.
chapters.zh:
那孩子的——胡尔德的——歌声乘着无形的翅膀飞走，再次没入寂静。

安娜忍不住鼓起掌来。

毕竟，小胡尔德似乎并不危险。"太了不起了！"她叫道。"你叫什么名字？"有那么一刻，胡尔德在幽光中盯着安娜，发光的眼睛直直看进她的眼里，接着那孩子从水晶上向后一翻，跌了下去。"不！"安娜说着冲到水晶后面去查看孩子，希望小胡尔德没有受伤。

可当她绕过那树干般粗的水晶，却看见胡尔德已经不在后面了。

孩子消失了，只剩前方黑暗通道里传来的细碎脚步声。

安娜想也没想就追了上去。"安娜！"艾莎在身后喊。"等等！

慢点！

你跑太快了！""安娜！"克斯托夫也喊。

他们的警告在四周岩石间回响，可安娜不认同两人说的：她明明跑得太慢了。

胡尔德动作很快——安娜不确定自己此刻追的是脚步声，还是远处石笋滴落的静谧水声。

不过，他们本是来找胡尔德精灵的，只有他们或许能帮着找到回旋之刃，也只有这神话中的生灵，或许能把大家从安娜可怕的错误中拯救出来。

于是安娜继续奔跑，只险险避开偶尔垂下的矮石。

突然，胡尔德尖叫起来。

那声音听起来很害怕，安娜希望胡尔德没有遇险。"撑住！"安娜喊。

她越跑越快，随后脚下一绊——绊在石头、坑洞还是树根上，天太黑看不清——整个人向前栽倒，双手伸出去缓冲。

安娜撞上坚硬的岩石，肋部一阵刺痛。

一个小时之内，她准会青肿一大块。

浑身都疼。

只有右臂不疼——她为了撑住自己，把右臂远远甩在身前。

安娜看着手腕上晃荡的萤虫手环，才明白原因：她的右臂根本没撞上任何石头。

那只手碰到的，只有空气。

安娜庆幸自己已经躺在地上，因为若是还站着，她觉得自己可能会晕过去。

她追着胡尔德——差点就冲下悬崖，坠入深渊。

她还能听见胡尔德的哭声。

图娃在商栈的警告又回到她脑中。

他们诡计多端。

有时，他们会帮忙。

有时，他们会把人引出最安全的路。

也许，安娜想，还会把人诱进深渊。

胡尔德孩子这么做，也许是有意的，也许是想引开安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫，不让他们找到胡尔德精灵的家。

可即便这些阴郁的念头聚成了乌云，安娜还是趴着向前挪，朝着胡尔德哭声的方向。

胡尔德的意图是什么并不重要——重要的是，胡尔德被困住了，而且害怕。

安娜扭动着凑到边缘，探出下巴往下看。

胡尔德翻下了边缘，但凭运气或奇迹，孩子卡在下方五英尺处一块小突出的岩石上。

克斯托夫只要探身就能够到胡尔德，可就在安娜看着的当儿，那块岩架正在孩子的重压下崩碎。"艾莎！

克斯托夫！

救命！"安娜喊着，自己又往前挪了一点，身子悬在边缘外，手伸向下方。"抓住我的手！"她朝下喊。

胡尔德举起一只手，可安娜还是离得太远。

她得再靠近些。

安娜往前蹭，一寸一寸地往下降。

就差一点点了……她拼命把手指往前伸，巴望着它们能变长——就在这时，她感到自己身下的泥土也开始松动崩落。

原本坚实的地面化作碎石，安娜一头栽进黑暗的深渊。

她尖叫起来。

可还没等她掠过胡尔德、坠入那无底的虚空，上方两双手攥住了她的脚踝。

克斯托夫！

艾莎！

她猛地停住，正对着那只猫眼小胡尔德——那孩子大半还隐在阴影里，若让安娜猜，八成被她吓坏了。"嗨，"安娜说，努力压平声音里的颤抖。"我叫安娜，我不会伤害你。"她伸出手。"跟我来！"胡尔德迟疑了片刻，才握住安娜的手掌。

孩子的皮肤光滑而干燥，像安娜在书里读到的那种生活在查索沙漠的小蜥蜴。

可即便胡尔德离她这么近，还是很难看清。

那孩子几乎像是用影子捏成，或是从镜子里刻出来的。

想看清细节，有点像紧紧攥住一块肥皂：你攥得越紧，肥皂溜得越快；你盯得越用力，胡尔德似乎消失得越快。

安娜用尽全力抓着孩子，喊道："拉我们上去！"一声闷哼，接着安娜和胡尔德被拉到安全处，就在那小块岩架碎成虚无的刹那。

她和孩子被拖回坚实的岩石上。

安娜还没来得及松开胡尔德，艾莎和克斯托夫就紧紧抱住了她，她依偎着他们的温暖。"安娜，"艾莎声音发紧，"我……我是说，你差点——""关键词：差点，"克斯托夫眨眨眼插话。

安娜冲他笑了。

他似乎总是懂她，知道若她多想刚才那险些发生的事，就会一直坐在那儿，变成化石。"我在，"安娜说。

她本可以永远待在他们怀里，要不是怀里那个扭动的小胡尔德。

孩子从人堆里挣脱，一屁股坐到地上——仍离得够远，安娜能看清的不过是一只尖尖的胳膊肘，但比之前清楚些。

这下安娜看清了：胡尔德的皮肤和矿井里那种泛蓝的石头一模一样。

安娜皱起眉。

她刚发现胡尔德时，还以为孩子的皮肤是烟白色，和胡尔德坐着的那块水晶相似。

一个有趣又发痒的念头爬进安娜脑海：她两次都对了。

胡尔德先是烟白色，而后变成蓝灰色。

胡尔德的身体起初光滑，随后又粗粝得像石墙。

也许胡尔德精灵就像南海深处的大章鱼，不仅能变色，还能变纹理。"哇，"安娜说，一边努力镇定下来，脑中却掠过一串飞快的念头。

第一个念头：这太酷了！

能了解到胡尔德精灵这种奇妙的特质，她兴奋极了。

第二个念头紧跟着第一个冒出来：如果安娜能变色变纹理，她就要去画像长廊，站在所有最爱的画前，体会一下当马提亚斯中尉——父亲那位阿伦黛尔老警卫——过一个下午是什么感觉。

最后，第三个念头：她上一次在城堡里，是见到了那只狼，然后一切都变了。

一阵寒意顺着她的脊背而下。

艾莎在小家伙面前跪下。"嗨，小不点。

我是艾莎。

你叫什么名字？"小胡尔德突然哭起来，眼泪像宝石般闪闪发亮。"噢，不。"艾莎往后一缩。"给！"她变出一片雪花递过去。"艾莎，"安娜嘶声道。"别忘了，不能用魔法。"雪花啪地化成水珠。

艾莎的脸颊泛红，双手在身侧攥紧。"对不起，"她轻声说。"我忘了。"艾莎大半生都在努力压抑自己的魔法，想来真让人难过。

那魔法仿佛是她的一部分，自然得如同呼吸和眨眼。

如今又要克制不用，大概得慢慢习惯。

安娜为此感到抱歉。

她深吸一口气。

他们得离开那儿。

他们得找到回旋之刃，打败纳特玛拉，这不仅是为了阿伦黛尔，也是为了姐姐。

她不能让艾莎再次把自己关起来。"嗷！"艾莎叫出声。

安娜低头，看见姐姐粗粗的辫子被一只胖拳头攥得紧紧的。"嗷——嗷！"小胡尔德重复道，又扯了一下，仿佛那辫子是根绳子。"嗷嗷嗷嗷！"艾莎把头发从孩子手里解下来。"我不是马。""马！"小胡尔德说。"马！

马！

马！"艾莎叹了口气，安娜则捂住嘴，藏住一声咯咯笑。

她懂胡尔德为什么对艾莎的辫子着迷。

她小时候也曾假装艾莎是赛马，命令姐姐在城堡走廊里来回冲。

有一回，她甚至让艾莎嘶叫出声。

小胡尔德松开艾莎的头发，摇摇晃晃地走向克斯托夫。"马！"孩子宣称。"嘿，"克斯托夫抗议，胡尔德绕着他跑。"你倒好意思说。""嘿！

嘿！

嘿！"小胡尔德说。"说话，说话，说话！"胡尔德绕着克斯托夫兜圈，却总是侧着身、大步蹦跳，背始终贴着墙。

为了藏尾巴！

安娜欣喜地明白了。

也许她终于能找到童年那个问题的答案——他们是不是都有尾巴。"他们有点……太闹了？"艾莎拽了拽斗篷，让它重新整齐垂好。"不比别的孩子闹，"安娜说，想起村里常碰到的那些孩子。"可多数孩子不认得怎么在洞里穿行，这个小家伙说不定能带我们去找年长的胡尔德精灵帮忙。"艾莎把几缕头发塞回辫子里，一脸怀疑。"也许吧？"吸取了艾莎的教训，安娜也把头发往后拢，确保不会被轻易抓到，然后趴下身。"嗨，"她说。"你还记得我的名字吗？""安娜！

安娜！

安娜！"胡尔德尖声叫。

安娜眨了眨眼。

她没料到会有这么大热情。"对，就是这样。

你叫什么名字？""你叫什么名字？"胡尔德重复。"安娜，"安娜说。"安娜，"胡尔德重复。"等等。"安娜揉了揉额头。"你也叫安娜？""等等。"胡尔德又学她。"你也叫安娜！""如我所说，"艾莎嘴角抽动，"太闹了。""我可能说错了，"克斯托夫观察道，"但我想他们只是把你说的每句话都重复一遍。""太闹了！

你说的每句话！"胡尔德回敬道。

安娜深吸一口气，用最快的语速说话，不给胡尔德重复的机会，直到说完。"嗨，我是安娜！

我的家在阿伦黛尔，和你一样，但在地面之上。"胡尔德难以置信地看着她。"家？"安娜点头。"对，家。

你们住在哪儿？

我们想见见你的家人。"胡尔德看看安娜，然后点头。"家！"接着胡尔德就跑了——倒退着跑，轻松得像后脑勺也长了眼睛。

也许真有。

毕竟，从安娜听过的睡前故事里，没人见过胡尔德的背影。"快！"安娜一下站起来。"我们得跟上！"胡尔德跑得快得不可思议——和安娜他们不同，胡尔德个子矮，能避开低垂的岩石，而克斯托夫得猫着腰跑。

上、下、再向下，他们冲过似乎没有尽头的、满是水晶与闪石的长廊。

安娜想不通，胡尔德——她心里管它叫"飞毛腿"，是跟奥拉夫学的绰号——怎么分得清这些通道。

也许那是胡尔德精灵的某种本事。

毕竟，胡尔德精灵总能找到失物。

也许这意味着他们自己从不会迷路。

一个古怪的念头掠过她心头，她寻思，这是否意味着胡尔德精灵永远知道自己下一步该做什么。

那该多妙啊？

也许飞毛腿就是这样这么快找到他们的。

又或者，飞毛腿找到他们，是因为安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫才是"失物"。

安娜摇了摇头。

她有太多问题，而能顾及的时间太少。

但有一件事她能办。"克斯托夫？

艾莎？"安娜等到两人都看向她，才说："我想我知道失踪的地精怎么了。

我在索伦森的塔里读到，纳特玛拉一出现，他们就会逃离这片土地。"安娜听见克斯托夫长长舒了口气。"好，"他说。"那说明他们安全。"很快，在急促的脚步声之下，又响起另一种声响。

一种奇怪的、拖沓的、吱呀作响的声音。"你们听见没？"安娜在喘息间回头喊。"听见了，"克斯托夫说。"你觉得——？""也许吧，"安娜答，放慢成走路。

她不用等他说完就知道他在想什么：纳特玛拉。"我们该停下，"艾莎说。"花点时间侦察一下情况。

胡尔德精灵可能很调皮……尤其是若他们认为我们是来拿不属于自己的东西。""可要是我们停，"安娜说，"就会跟丢飞毛腿！"艾莎绕过一块大圆石——那石头安娜是直接爬过去的——眼角困惑地皱起。"飞毛腿？"她问。"那胡尔德，"安娜解释。

她回头想看看克斯托夫要不要帮忙搬石头，可他早已把石头推到一边，清出了路。"太迟了，"他说。"我们已经跟丢了。"就在安娜移开视线那两秒，孩子已飞快消失在视线外。"不，"安娜轻声说。"我们得跟上！"她重新跑起来，新的恐惧给了她新生般的速度。"飞毛腿不知道纳特玛拉！"可当安娜转过最后一个弯，她看见那声音的来源：一座从岩石中凿出的地下城。

胡尔德精灵的秘密家园。

地上世界如何，地下世界也如何。

温馨的屋子凿在蓝灰色的石头里，橙色的光从里面漫出，像微笑般招人。

铺着卵石的街道被萤虫照亮，所以能轻易看清各辆矿车拉着什么：一辆堆着像柴火般捆好的石笋，一辆装满了和太阳帽一般大的发光蘑菇，还有一辆堆着水一样清透的石头，安娜想那或许是巨大的钻石。

还有胡尔德精灵。

成年精灵显得高大，身形更像小树苗而非人，四肢和脖颈都长。

和飞毛腿一样，他们在地下国的光里也很难看清。

那幽光不同于明亮、暴露一切的阳光，而是安娜联想起浪漫烛光晚餐的那种柔光。

它既照亮，也遮掩，投下的阴影再次帮着藏起胡尔德精灵。

即便在昏暗里，安娜也能看出，他们能融入所站之物的颜色，从乌木黑到云石白，中间每一层色都有。

有些胡尔德精灵看起来可能是紫色，有些是橙色和绿色，皮肤闪着黑色的脉络。

胡尔德精灵——隐者之民——能融入任何周遭。

安娜想，这很了不起，但最重要的是，他们是真的。

真实的生灵，会对在哪里能找到阿伦那把真正失落的神剑，给出真实的答案。

他们需要这个神话之物来拯救一切。"哇，"艾莎低声说。"真美。

真宁静。""要是斯文在这儿，"克斯托夫说，"我打赌他会把那些蘑菇全吃了，然后牙大概会发光一个星期。"斯文。

安娜希望驯鹿和他们在一起。

下到村庄的路看起来很陡，而斯文总擅长在崎岖山上找出最稳的下山路。

她打量着岩壁，寻找通往住处的路。

她确信在下方某处，能找到如何拨乱反正、治愈斯文以及阿伦黛尔其余地方、解除纳特玛拉影响的方法。

她往前探身想看得更清，忽然感到背后被什么尖利的东西戳了一下。"克斯托夫，"她说着把手往后一挥，"别闹了。

我只是想看看。""我什么也没做，"克斯托夫说，站在她左边几英尺外，远到戳不到她。

安娜的后颈一阵发麻。

艾莎站在她右边，神色若有所思，打量着下方的城。

忽然，安娜强烈地察觉到，有人在盯着她。

也许还不止一个人。"噢，"她听见艾莎一声轻叫。

安娜转过身，正好与一支长矛鼻尖对鼻尖。

而且不止一支长矛。

许多长矛。

sentences.en: THE CHILD’S— Hulder’s —melody flew off on invisible wings and faded again into silence.
sentences.zh: 那孩子的——胡尔德的——歌声乘着无形的翅膀飞走，再次没入寂静。

sentences.en: Anna burst into applause; she couldn’t help it.
sentences.zh: 安娜忍不住鼓起掌来。

sentences.en: After all, the little Hulder didn’t seem dangerous. “That was incredible !” she exclaimed. “What’s your name?” For a moment, the Hulder seemed to stare at Anna in the glow-light, luminescent eyes boring into hers, and then the Hulder tumbled backward off the crystal. “No!” Anna said as she rushed behind the crystal to check on the child, hoping the tiny Hulder hadn’t hurt themselves.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，小胡尔德似乎并不危险。"太了不起了！"她叫道。"你叫什么名字？"有那么一刻，胡尔德在幽光中盯着安娜，发光的眼睛直直看进她的眼里，接着那孩子从水晶上向后一翻，跌了下去。"不！"安娜说着冲到水晶后面去查看孩子，希望小胡尔德没有受伤。

sentences.en: But as she rounded the tree-trunk-sized crystal, she saw that the Hulder was no longer behind it.
sentences.zh: 可当她绕过那树干般粗的水晶，却看见胡尔德已经不在后面了。

sentences.en: The child had disappeared, except for the sound of footsteps pattering down the dark passage up ahead.
sentences.zh: 孩子消失了，只剩前方黑暗通道里传来的细碎脚步声。

sentences.en: Without a second thought, Anna took off. “Anna!” Elsa called from behind. “Wait!
sentences.zh: 安娜想也没想就追了上去。"安娜！"艾莎在身后喊。"等等！

sentences.en: Slow down!
sentences.zh: 慢点！

sentences.en: You’re going too fast!” “Anna!” Kristoff shouted.
sentences.zh: 你跑太快了！""安娜！"克斯托夫也喊。

sentences.en: Their warnings echoed off the rocks around them, but Anna disagreed with them both: she was going too slow .
sentences.zh: 他们的警告在四周岩石间回响，可安娜不认同两人说的：她明明跑得太慢了。

sentences.en: The Hulder was quick—Anna wasn’t sure if it was footsteps she was following now, or just the quiet drip of stalactites in the distance.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德动作很快——安娜不确定自己此刻追的是脚步声，还是远处石笋滴落的静谧水声。

sentences.en: Still, they had come to look for the Huldrefólk, the only ones who might be able to help them find the Revolute Blade, the only ones of myth who might be able to save them all from Anna’s terrible mistake.
sentences.zh: 不过，他们本是来找胡尔德精灵的，只有他们或许能帮着找到回旋之刃，也只有这神话中的生灵，或许能把大家从安娜可怕的错误中拯救出来。

sentences.en: And so Anna ran on, only just missing the occasional low-hanging rocks.
sentences.zh: 于是安娜继续奔跑，只险险避开偶尔垂下的矮石。

sentences.en: Suddenly, the Hulder screeched.
sentences.zh: 突然，胡尔德尖叫起来。

sentences.en: It sounded frightened, and Anna hoped the Hulder wasn’t in trouble. “Hang on!” Anna shouted.
sentences.zh: 那声音听起来很害怕，安娜希望胡尔德没有遇险。"撑住！"安娜喊。

sentences.en: She ran faster and faster, and then her foot caught—on a rock, a divot, or a root, it was too dark to tell—and she toppled to the ground, her hands out to cushion her fall.
sentences.zh: 她越跑越快，随后脚下一绊——绊在石头、坑洞还是树根上，天太黑看不清——整个人向前栽倒，双手伸出去缓冲。

sentences.en: Pain cracked through Anna’s ribs as she slammed into the solid rock.
sentences.zh: 安娜撞上坚硬的岩石，肋部一阵刺痛。

sentences.en: She was going to have one giant bruise in an hour.
sentences.zh: 一个小时之内，她准会青肿一大块。

sentences.en: Everything hurt.
sentences.zh: 浑身都疼。

sentences.en: Everything but her right arm, which she’d flung out far in front of herself to try to break her fall.
sentences.zh: 只有右臂不疼——她为了撑住自己，把右臂远远甩在身前。

sentences.en: And as Anna looked at the glowworm bracelet dangling from her wrist, she saw why: her right arm had not hit any rock at all.
sentences.zh: 安娜看着手腕上晃荡的萤虫手环，才明白原因：她的右臂根本没撞上任何石头。

sentences.en: All that hand had hit was thin air.
sentences.zh: 那只手碰到的，只有空气。

sentences.en: Anna was glad she was already lying on the ground, because she thought she might faint if she were still standing.
sentences.zh: 安娜庆幸自己已经躺在地上，因为若是还站着，她觉得自己可能会晕过去。

sentences.en: She’d followed the Hulder—and had almost run off a cliff and into an abyss.
sentences.zh: 她追着胡尔德——差点就冲下悬崖，坠入深渊。

sentences.en: She could still hear the Hulder’s cry.
sentences.zh: 她还能听见胡尔德的哭声。

sentences.en: Tuva’s warning from the trading post came back to her.
sentences.zh: 图娃在商栈的警告又回到她脑中。

sentences.en: They’re tricky.
sentences.zh: 他们诡计多端。

sentences.en: Sometimes, they help.
sentences.zh: 有时，他们会帮忙。

sentences.en: Other times, they lure humans off the safest paths.
sentences.zh: 有时，他们会把人引出最安全的路。

sentences.en: And maybe, Anna thought, lure them into an abyss.
sentences.zh: 也许，安娜想，还会把人诱进深渊。

sentences.en: There was always a chance that the Hulder child had done this on purpose, had perhaps meant to distract Anna and Elsa and Kristoff away from the Huldrefólk’s home.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德孩子这么做，也许是有意的，也许是想引开安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫，不让他们找到胡尔德精灵的家。

sentences.en: But even as these dark thoughts gathered into a cloud, Anna scooted forward on her belly, toward the sound of the Hulder’s cry.
sentences.zh: 可即便这些阴郁的念头聚成了乌云，安娜还是趴着向前挪，朝着胡尔德哭声的方向。

sentences.en: It didn’t matter what the Hulder’s intentions had been—but it did matter that the Hulder was stuck and scared.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德的意图是什么并不重要——重要的是，胡尔德被困住了，而且害怕。

sentences.en: Once she wiggled to the edge, Anna leaned her chin out and peered down.
sentences.zh: 安娜扭动着凑到边缘，探出下巴往下看。

sentences.en: The Hulder had tumbled over the edge, but by some luck or miracle, the child had caught themselves on a small ledge five feet down.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德翻下了边缘，但凭运气或奇迹，孩子卡在下方五英尺处一块小突出的岩石上。

sentences.en: It would be easy for Kristoff to lean over and reach the Hulder, but even as Anna watched, the rocky ledge was crumbling away under the child’s weight. “Elsa!
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫只要探身就能够到胡尔德，可就在安娜看着的当儿，那块岩架正在孩子的重压下崩碎。"艾莎！

sentences.en: Kristoff!
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫！

sentences.en: Help!” Anna shouted as she inched forward even more, letting herself dangle over the edge, her hand outstretched. “Grab my hand!” she called down.
sentences.zh: 救命！"安娜喊着，自己又往前挪了一点，身子悬在边缘外，手伸向下方。"抓住我的手！"她朝下喊。

sentences.en: The Hulder raised a hand, but Anna was still too far away.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德举起一只手，可安娜还是离得太远。

sentences.en: She had to get closer .
sentences.zh: 她得再靠近些。

sentences.en: Wiggling forward, Anna lowered herself down inch by fraction of an inch.
sentences.zh: 安娜往前蹭，一寸一寸地往下降。

sentences.en: Just a little bit farther now…She strained her fingers forward, willing them to lengthen—and that’s when she felt the crumbling of the earth beneath her own weight.
sentences.zh: 就差一点点了……她拼命把手指往前伸，巴望着它们能变长——就在这时，她感到自己身下的泥土也开始松动崩落。

sentences.en: What was once solid ground turned to gravel, and Anna skidded forward, headfirst into the dark abyss.
sentences.zh: 原本坚实的地面化作碎石，安娜一头栽进黑暗的深渊。

sentences.en: She screamed.
sentences.zh: 她尖叫起来。

sentences.en: But before she could shoot past the Hulder and plummet into the vast void, two pairs of hands grabbed her ankles from above.
sentences.zh: 可还没等她掠过胡尔德、坠入那无底的虚空，上方两双手攥住了她的脚踝。

sentences.en: Kristoff!
sentences.zh: 克斯托夫！

sentences.en: Elsa!
sentences.zh: 艾莎！

sentences.en: She lurched to a stop, face to face with the little cat-eyed Hulder, who was still mostly in shadow, and who, if Anna had to wager a guess, looked terrified of her. “Hi,” Anna said, trying hard to iron out the quiver in her voice. “My name is Anna, and I’m not going to hurt you.” She offered out her hand. “Come with me!” The Hulder hesitated a moment, then gripped Anna’s palm.
sentences.zh: 她猛地停住，正对着那只猫眼小胡尔德——那孩子大半还隐在阴影里，若让安娜猜，八成被她吓坏了。"嗨，"安娜说，努力压平声音里的颤抖。"我叫安娜，我不会伤害你。"她伸出手。"跟我来！"胡尔德迟疑了片刻，才握住安娜的手掌。

sentences.en: The child’s skin was smooth and dry, like one of the little lizards Anna had read about that populated the Chatho deserts.
sentences.zh: 孩子的皮肤光滑而干燥，像安娜在书里读到的那种生活在查索沙漠的小蜥蜴。

sentences.en: But even with the Hulder so close to her, it was hard to see them properly.
sentences.zh: 可即便胡尔德离她这么近，还是很难看清。

sentences.en: It was almost as though the child had been made of shadow or carved from a mirror.
sentences.zh: 那孩子几乎像是用影子捏成，或是从镜子里刻出来的。

sentences.en: Trying to make out the details was a little like trying to hold tight to a bar of soap: the harder one squeezed, the quicker the soap slid away; the harder one looked, the quicker the Hulder seemed to vanish.
sentences.zh: 想看清细节，有点像紧紧攥住一块肥皂：你攥得越紧，肥皂溜得越快；你盯得越用力，胡尔德似乎消失得越快。

sentences.en: Gripping the child with all her strength, Anna called, “Pull us up!” There was a grunt, and then Anna and the Hulder rose to safety, just as the little ledge deteriorated into nothingness.
sentences.zh: 安娜用尽全力抓着孩子，喊道："拉我们上去！"一声闷哼，接着安娜和胡尔德被拉到安全处，就在那小块岩架碎成虚无的刹那。

sentences.en: She and the child were dragged back onto solid rock.
sentences.zh: 她和孩子被拖回坚实的岩石上。

sentences.en: Before Anna had a chance to release the Hulder, Elsa and Kristoff wrapped Anna into a tight hug, and she leaned into their warmth. “Anna,” Elsa said, voice tight. “I couldn’t…I mean, you almost—” “Key word: almost ,” Kristoff cut in with a wink.
sentences.zh: 安娜还没来得及松开胡尔德，艾莎和克斯托夫就紧紧抱住了她，她依偎着他们的温暖。"安娜，"艾莎声音发紧，"我……我是说，你差点——""关键词：差点，"克斯托夫眨眨眼插话。

sentences.en: Anna smiled at him.
sentences.zh: 安娜冲他笑了。

sentences.en: He always seemed to understand her, to know that if she thought too much about what had just almost happened, she would sit there forever and turn into a fossil. “I’m here,” Anna said.
sentences.zh: 他似乎总是懂她，知道若她多想刚才那险些发生的事，就会一直坐在那儿，变成化石。"我在，"安娜说。

sentences.en: She could have stayed there forever in their arms, but for the wiggling Hulder she held.
sentences.zh: 她本可以永远待在他们怀里，要不是怀里那个扭动的小胡尔德。

sentences.en: The child pushed out of the group and plopped onto the floor—still far enough away that all Anna could really make out was a pointy elbow, but in more detail than before.
sentences.zh: 孩子从人堆里挣脱，一屁股坐到地上——仍离得够远，安娜能看清的不过是一只尖尖的胳膊肘，但比之前清楚些。

sentences.en: Now Anna could see that the Hulder’s skin was the exact color of the bluish rock that filled the mines.
sentences.zh: 这下安娜看清了：胡尔德的皮肤和矿井里那种泛蓝的石头一模一样。

sentences.en: Anna frowned.
sentences.zh: 安娜皱起眉。

sentences.en: When she’d first spotted the Hulder, she’d thought the child’s skin was a smoky white, similar to the crystal the Hulder had been sitting on.
sentences.zh: 她刚发现胡尔德时，还以为孩子的皮肤是烟白色，和胡尔德坐着的那块水晶相似。

sentences.en: A funny, tickling idea crawled into Anna’s mind: she’d been right both times.
sentences.zh: 一个有趣又发痒的念头爬进安娜脑海：她两次都对了。

sentences.en: The Hulder had been smoky white and then a bluish gray.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德先是烟白色，而后变成蓝灰色。

sentences.en: The Hulder’s body had first looked smooth, then as rough as the stone wall.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德的身体起初光滑，随后又粗粝得像石墙。

sentences.en: Maybe the Huldrefólk were like octopuses in the deeps of the Southern Sea, able to change not only their color but also their texture. “Wow,” Anna said, trying to collect herself even as a stream of rapid thoughts dashed through her mind.
sentences.zh: 也许胡尔德精灵就像南海深处的大章鱼，不仅能变色，还能变纹理。"哇，"安娜说，一边努力镇定下来，脑中却掠过一串飞快的念头。

sentences.en: First thought: This is so cool!
sentences.zh: 第一个念头：这太酷了！

sentences.en: She was thrilled to learn about this wonderful trait of the Huldrefólk.
sentences.zh: 能了解到胡尔德精灵这种奇妙的特质，她兴奋极了。

sentences.en: The second thought came fast on the heels of the first: if Anna could change color and texture, she’d head to the portrait gallery, stand in front of all her favorite paintings, and feel what it was like to be Lieutenant Mattias, her father’s old official Arendellian guard, for an afternoon.
sentences.zh: 第二个念头紧跟着第一个冒出来：如果安娜能变色变纹理，她就要去画像长廊，站在所有最爱的画前，体会一下当马提亚斯中尉——父亲那位阿伦黛尔老警卫——过一个下午是什么感觉。

sentences.en: And finally, her third thought: the last time she’d been in the castle, she’d seen the wolf, and everything had changed.
sentences.zh: 最后，第三个念头：她上一次在城堡里，是见到了那只狼，然后一切都变了。

sentences.en: A shudder ran down her spine.
sentences.zh: 一阵寒意顺着她的脊背而下。

sentences.en: Elsa knelt before the child. “Hi there, little one.
sentences.zh: 艾莎在小家伙面前跪下。"嗨，小不点。

sentences.en: I’m Elsa.
sentences.zh: 我是艾莎。

sentences.en: What’s your name?” The little Hulder burst into tears that sparkled like gems. “Oh, no.” Elsa jerked back. “Here!” She conjured a snowflake and presented it. “Elsa,” Anna hissed. “No magic, remember?” The snowflake burst into water droplets.
sentences.zh: 你叫什么名字？"小胡尔德突然哭起来，眼泪像宝石般闪闪发亮。"噢，不。"艾莎往后一缩。"给！"她变出一片雪花递过去。"艾莎，"安娜嘶声道。"别忘了，不能用魔法。"雪花啪地化成水珠。

sentences.en: Elsa’s cheeks turned pink and her hands clenched at her sides. “I’m sorry,” she whispered. “I forgot.” It was sad that Elsa had spent most of her life trying to suppress her magic.
sentences.zh: 艾莎的脸颊泛红，双手在身侧攥紧。"对不起，"她轻声说。"我忘了。"艾莎大半生都在努力压抑自己的魔法，想来真让人难过。

sentences.en: It truly seemed a part of her, as natural as breathing and blinking.
sentences.zh: 那魔法仿佛是她的一部分，自然得如同呼吸和眨眼。

sentences.en: Having to refrain from using it again was probably taking some getting used to.
sentences.zh: 如今又要克制不用，大概得慢慢习惯。

sentences.en: Anna felt sorry about it.
sentences.zh: 安娜为此感到抱歉。

sentences.en: She took a deep breath.
sentences.zh: 她深吸一口气。

sentences.en: They had to get out of there.
sentences.zh: 他们得离开那儿。

sentences.en: They had to find Revolute and defeat the Nattmara, not only for Arendelle, but for her sister.
sentences.zh: 他们得找到回旋之刃，打败纳特玛拉，这不仅是为了阿伦黛尔，也是为了姐姐。

sentences.en: She couldn’t let Elsa shut herself away again. “Ow!” Elsa yelped.
sentences.zh: 她不能让艾莎再次把自己关起来。"嗷！"艾莎叫出声。

sentences.en: Looking down, Anna saw her sister’s thick braid held tight in a chubby fist. “Ow-ow!” the little Hulder repeated, and gave another pull, as if Elsa’s braid were a rope. “Owowowow!” Elsa unwound her hair from the child’s fists. “I’m not a horse.” “Horse!” the little Hulder said. “Horse!
sentences.zh: 安娜低头，看见姐姐粗粗的辫子被一只胖拳头攥得紧紧的。"嗷——嗷！"小胡尔德重复道，又扯了一下，仿佛那辫子是根绳子。"嗷嗷嗷嗷！"艾莎把头发从孩子手里解下来。"我不是马。""马！"小胡尔德说。"马！

sentences.en: Horse!
sentences.zh: 马！

sentences.en: Horse!” Elsa sighed while Anna covered her mouth to hide a giggle.
sentences.zh: 马！"艾莎叹了口气，安娜则捂住嘴，藏住一声咯咯笑。

sentences.en: She understood the Hulder’s fascination with Elsa’s braid.
sentences.zh: 她懂胡尔德为什么对艾莎的辫子着迷。

sentences.en: When she’d been little, she, too, had pretended Elsa was a racehorse and had ordered her sister to charge up and down the castle hallways.
sentences.zh: 她小时候也曾假装艾莎是赛马，命令姐姐在城堡走廊里来回冲。

sentences.en: Once, she’d even gotten Elsa to neigh.
sentences.zh: 有一回，她甚至让艾莎嘶叫出声。

sentences.en: The little Hulder let go of Elsa’s hair and toddled over to Kristoff. “Horse!” the child proclaimed. “Hey,” Kristoff protested as the Hulder ran around him. “You’re one to talk.” “Hey!
sentences.zh: 小胡尔德松开艾莎的头发，摇摇晃晃地走向克斯托夫。"马！"孩子宣称。"嘿，"克斯托夫抗议，胡尔德绕着他跑。"你倒好意思说。""嘿！

sentences.en: Hey!
sentences.zh: 嘿！

sentences.en: Hey!” the little Hulder said. “Talk, talk, talk!” Though the Hulder was running in circles around Kristoff, the child ran sideways, long gallops, keeping their back to the wall at all times.
sentences.zh: 嘿！"小胡尔德说。"说话，说话，说话！"胡尔德绕着克斯托夫兜圈，却总是侧着身、大步蹦跳，背始终贴着墙。

sentences.en: To hide the tail!
sentences.zh: 为了藏尾巴！

sentences.en: Anna realized with delight.
sentences.zh: 安娜欣喜地明白了。

sentences.en: Maybe she would finally be able to find out the answer to her childhood question about whether they all had tails. “They’re a bit…hyper?” Elsa tugged her cloak so that it would hang neatly again. “No more than any other child,” Anna said, thinking of the children she’d often run into in the village. “But most children wouldn’t know how to get around a cave, while this little one might be able to lead us to the older Huldrefólk who can help us.” Tucking strands of hair back into her braid, Elsa looked doubtful. “Maybe?” Taking note of what had happened to Elsa, Anna pushed her own hair back to make sure it wasn’t easily accessible before getting on her hands and knees. “Hi,” she said. “Do you remember my name?” “Anna!
sentences.zh: 也许她终于能找到童年那个问题的答案——他们是不是都有尾巴。"他们有点……太闹了？"艾莎拽了拽斗篷，让它重新整齐垂好。"不比别的孩子闹，"安娜说，想起村里常碰到的那些孩子。"可多数孩子不认得怎么在洞里穿行，这个小家伙说不定能带我们去找年长的胡尔德精灵帮忙。"艾莎把几缕头发塞回辫子里，一脸怀疑。"也许吧？"吸取了艾莎的教训，安娜也把头发往后拢，确保不会被轻易抓到，然后趴下身。"嗨，"她说。"你还记得我的名字吗？""安娜！

sentences.en: Anna!
sentences.zh: 安娜！

sentences.en: Anna!” the Hulder screeched.
sentences.zh: 安娜！"胡尔德尖声叫。

sentences.en: Anna blinked.
sentences.zh: 安娜眨了眨眼。

sentences.en: She hadn’t been expecting quite so much enthusiasm. “Yes, that’s right.
sentences.zh: 她没料到会有这么大热情。"对，就是这样。

sentences.en: What’s your name?” “What’s your name?” the Hulder repeated. “Anna,” Anna said. “Anna,” the Hulder repeated. “Wait.” Anna rubbed her forehead. “Your name is Anna, too?” “Wait.” The Hulder mimicked her again. “Your name is Anna, too!” “Like I said,” Elsa said, her lips twitching, “hyper.” “I might be wrong,” Kristoff observed, “but I think they’re just repeating everything you say.” “Hyper!
sentences.zh: 你叫什么名字？""你叫什么名字？"胡尔德重复。"安娜，"安娜说。"安娜，"胡尔德重复。"等等。"安娜揉了揉额头。"你也叫安娜？""等等。"胡尔德又学她。"你也叫安娜！""如我所说，"艾莎嘴角抽动，"太闹了。""我可能说错了，"克斯托夫观察道，"但我想他们只是把你说的每句话都重复一遍。""太闹了！

sentences.en: Everything you say!” the Hulder echoed back.
sentences.zh: 你说的每句话！"胡尔德回敬道。

sentences.en: Taking a deep breath, Anna spoke as quickly as she could, giving the Hulder no chance to repeat her words until she was done. “Hi, I’m Anna!
sentences.zh: 安娜深吸一口气，用最快的语速说话，不给胡尔德重复的机会，直到说完。"嗨，我是安娜！

sentences.en: My home is Arendelle, like you, but above the ground.” The Hulder looked at her in complete astonishment. “Home?” Anna nodded. “Yes, home .
sentences.zh: 我的家在阿伦黛尔，和你一样，但在地面之上。"胡尔德难以置信地看着她。"家？"安娜点头。"对，家。

sentences.en: Where do you live?
sentences.zh: 你们住在哪儿？

sentences.en: We’d like to meet your family.” The Hulder looked at Anna, then nodded. “Home!” And then the Hulder was off—running backward as easily as if they had eyes in the back of their head.
sentences.zh: 我们想见见你的家人。"胡尔德看看安娜，然后点头。"家！"接着胡尔德就跑了——倒退着跑，轻松得像后脑勺也长了眼睛。

sentences.en: And maybe they did.
sentences.zh: 也许真有。

sentences.en: After all, as Anna knew from old bedtime stories, no one had ever seen a Hulder’s back. “Come on!” Anna shot to her feet. “We have to follow!” The Hulder ran impossibly fast—and unlike Anna and the others, the Hulder was short enough to avoid low-hanging rocks, while Kristoff had to run at a crouch.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，从安娜听过的睡前故事里，没人见过胡尔德的背影。"快！"安娜一下站起来。"我们得跟上！"胡尔德跑得快得不可思议——和安娜他们不同，胡尔德个子矮，能避开低垂的岩石，而克斯托夫得猫着腰跑。

sentences.en: Up, down, and down again, they sprinted through seemingly endless corridors of crystals and sparkling rocks.
sentences.zh: 上、下、再向下，他们冲过似乎没有尽头的、满是水晶与闪石的长廊。

sentences.en: Anna couldn’t understand how the Hulder—Dash, as she mentally nicknamed them, taking a page from Olaf’s book—was able to tell the difference between the tunnels.
sentences.zh: 安娜想不通，胡尔德——她心里管它叫"飞毛腿"，是跟奥拉夫学的绰号——怎么分得清这些通道。

sentences.en: Maybe it was some special Huldrefólk trick.
sentences.zh: 也许那是胡尔德精灵的某种本事。

sentences.en: After all, Huldrefólk could always find lost things.
sentences.zh: 毕竟，胡尔德精灵总能找到失物。

sentences.en: Maybe it meant they could never become lost themselves.
sentences.zh: 也许这意味着他们自己从不会迷路。

sentences.en: A strange thought crossed her mind, and she wondered if that meant the Huldrefólk always knew what they should do next.
sentences.zh: 一个古怪的念头掠过她心头，她寻思，这是否意味着胡尔德精灵永远知道自己下一步该做什么。

sentences.en: How fantastic would that be?
sentences.zh: 那该多妙啊？

sentences.en: Maybe that’s how Dash had found them so quickly.
sentences.zh: 也许飞毛腿就是这样这么快找到他们的。

sentences.en: Or maybe Dash had found them because Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff were the lost things.
sentences.zh: 又或者，飞毛腿找到他们，是因为安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫才是"失物"。

sentences.en: Anna shook her head.
sentences.zh: 安娜摇了摇头。

sentences.en: She had so many questions, and there was so little time to attend to them all.
sentences.zh: 她有太多问题，而能顾及的时间太少。

sentences.en: But there was one thing she could do. “Kristoff?
sentences.zh: 但有一件事她能办。"克斯托夫？

sentences.en: Elsa?” Anna waited until they both looked at her, and then said, “I think I know what happened to the missing trolls.
sentences.zh: 艾莎？"安娜等到两人都看向她，才说："我想我知道失踪的地精怎么了。

sentences.en: I read in Sorenson’s tower that they always flee the land when a Nattmara appears.” Anna heard Kristoff let out a great sigh of relief. “Good,” he said. “Then that means they’re safe.” Soon enough, another sound began to play under the staccato of their footsteps.
sentences.zh: 我在索伦森的塔里读到，纳特玛拉一出现，他们就会逃离这片土地。"安娜听见克斯托夫长长舒了口气。"好，"他说。"那说明他们安全。"很快，在急促的脚步声之下，又响起另一种声响。

sentences.en: A strange, shuffling, creaking sound. “Do you hear that?” Anna called back between breaths. “Yeah,” Kristoff said. “Do you think—?” “Maybe,” Anna replied, slowing to a walk.
sentences.zh: 一种奇怪的、拖沓的、吱呀作响的声音。"你们听见没？"安娜在喘息间回头喊。"听见了，"克斯托夫说。"你觉得——？""也许吧，"安娜答，放慢成走路。

sentences.en: She didn’t need him to finish his sentence to know what he was thinking: Nattmara. “We should stop,” Elsa said. “Take a moment to scout out what’s happening.
sentences.zh: 她不用等他说完就知道他在想什么：纳特玛拉。"我们该停下，"艾莎说。"花点时间侦察一下情况。

sentences.en: Huldrefólk can be mischievous…especially if they think we’re here to take something that doesn’t belong to us.” “But if we stop,” Anna said, “we’ll lose Dash!” The corners of Elsa’s eyes crinkled in confusion as she navigated around a large boulder that Anna had simply scrambled over. “Dash?” she asked. “The Hulder,” Anna explained.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德精灵可能很调皮……尤其是若他们认为我们是来拿不属于自己的东西。""可要是我们停，"安娜说，"就会跟丢飞毛腿！"艾莎绕过一块大圆石——那石头安娜是直接爬过去的——眼角困惑地皱起。"飞毛腿？"她问。"那胡尔德，"安娜解释。

sentences.en: She turned back to see if Kristoff needed any help with the boulder, but he’d simply shoved it to the side, clearing the way. “It’s too late,” he said. “We already lost them.” In the two seconds Anna had taken her eyes off Dash, the child had sped out of sight. “No,” Anna breathed. “We have to keep up!” She broke into a run again, fresh fear giving her newfound speed. “Dash doesn’t know about the Nattmara!” But as Anna rounded the final bend, she saw where the sound had been coming from: an underground city carved out of the rock itself.
sentences.zh: 她回头想看看克斯托夫要不要帮忙搬石头，可他早已把石头推到一边，清出了路。"太迟了，"他说。"我们已经跟丢了。"就在安娜移开视线那两秒，孩子已飞快消失在视线外。"不，"安娜轻声说。"我们得跟上！"她重新跑起来，新的恐惧给了她新生般的速度。"飞毛腿不知道纳特玛拉！"可当安娜转过最后一个弯，她看见那声音的来源：一座从岩石中凿出的地下城。

sentences.en: The secret home of the Huldrefólk.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德精灵的秘密家园。

sentences.en: Just as the world above, so was the world below.
sentences.zh: 地上世界如何，地下世界也如何。

sentences.en: Cozy homes were carved into the blue-gray stone, and orange light spilled out from them, as welcoming as a smile.
sentences.zh: 温馨的屋子凿在蓝灰色的石头里，橙色的光从里面漫出，像微笑般招人。

sentences.en: The pebble-lined streets were alight with glowworms, so it was easy to see what various mine carts pulled: one held a pile of stalactites bundled like firewood, another was filled to the brim with glowing mushrooms the size of sun hats, and another was heaped with water-clear rocks that Anna thought might be large diamonds.
sentences.zh: 铺着卵石的街道被萤虫照亮，所以能轻易看清各辆矿车拉着什么：一辆堆着像柴火般捆好的石笋，一辆装满了和太阳帽一般大的发光蘑菇，还有一辆堆着水一样清透的石头，安娜想那或许是巨大的钻石。

sentences.en: And the Huldrefólk.
sentences.zh: 还有胡尔德精灵。

sentences.en: The adults appeared to be tall, built more like sapling trees than people, with long limbs and long necks.
sentences.zh: 成年精灵显得高大，身形更像小树苗而非人，四肢和脖颈都长。

sentences.en: And similar to Dash, they were hard to see in the light of the underneath realm.
sentences.zh: 和飞毛腿一样，他们在地下国的光里也很难看清。

sentences.en: The glow-light wasn’t the same as sunlight, bright and revealing, but the kind of soft glow that Anna associated with romantic candlelit dinners.
sentences.zh: 那幽光不同于明亮、暴露一切的阳光，而是安娜联想起浪漫烛光晚餐的那种柔光。

sentences.en: It illuminated at the same time as it concealed, casting shadows that again helped to obscure the Huldrefólk.
sentences.zh: 它既照亮，也遮掩，投下的阴影再次帮着藏起胡尔德精灵。

sentences.en: Still, even in the dimness, Anna could tell that they camouflaged into whatever it was that they were standing near, from onyx black to marble white and every shade in between.
sentences.zh: 即便在昏暗里，安娜也能看出，他们能融入所站之物的颜色，从乌木黑到云石白，中间每一层色都有。

sentences.en: Some of the Huldrefólk looked as though they could be purple, others orange and green with sparkling, black-veined skin.
sentences.zh: 有些胡尔德精灵看起来可能是紫色，有些是橙色和绿色，皮肤闪着黑色的脉络。

sentences.en: The Huldrefólk—the hidden folk—could blend into any surrounding.
sentences.zh: 胡尔德精灵——隐者之民——能融入任何周遭。

sentences.en: Which was great, Anna thought, but most important, they were real .
sentences.zh: 安娜想，这很了不起，但最重要的是，他们是真的。

sentences.en: Real creatures who would have real answers to where they could find the real lost sword of Aren.
sentences.zh: 真实的生灵，会对在哪里能找到阿伦那把真正失落的神剑，给出真实的答案。

sentences.en: The thing of myth they needed to save the day. “Wow,” Elsa whispered. “How beautiful.
sentences.zh: 他们需要这个神话之物来拯救一切。"哇，"艾莎低声说。"真美。

sentences.en: And peaceful.” “If Sven were here,” Kristoff said, “I bet he’d eat all those mushrooms, and then his teeth would probably glow for a week.” Sven .
sentences.zh: 真宁静。""要是斯文在这儿，"克斯托夫说，"我打赌他会把那些蘑菇全吃了，然后牙大概会发光一个星期。"斯文。

sentences.en: Anna wished the reindeer were with them.
sentences.zh: 安娜希望驯鹿和他们在一起。

sentences.en: The way down to the village looked steep, and Sven was always good about finding the surest path down a craggy mountain.
sentences.zh: 下到村庄的路看起来很陡，而斯文总擅长在崎岖山上找出最稳的下山路。

sentences.en: She scanned the side of the rock, looking for a pathway to the dwellings.
sentences.zh: 她打量着岩壁，寻找通往住处的路。

sentences.en: Somewhere below, she was sure they would find the answers to how to set things right and heal Sven, and the rest of Arendelle, from the Nattmara’s influence.
sentences.zh: 她确信在下方某处，能找到如何拨乱反正、治愈斯文以及阿伦黛尔其余地方、解除纳特玛拉影响的方法。

sentences.en: As she leaned forward to see better, Anna felt a sharp something prod her back. “Kristoff,” she said, swiping a hand behind her, “stop that.
sentences.zh: 她往前探身想看得更清，忽然感到背后被什么尖利的东西戳了一下。"克斯托夫，"她说着把手往后一挥，"别闹了。

sentences.en: I’m just trying to see.” “I’m not doing anything,” Kristoff said, standing to her left, a few feet away from easy poking distance.
sentences.zh: 我只是想看看。""我什么也没做，"克斯托夫说，站在她左边几英尺外，远到戳不到她。

sentences.en: The back of Anna’s neck prickled.
sentences.zh: 安娜的后颈一阵发麻。

sentences.en: Elsa stood to her right, her face pensive as she took in the city below them.
sentences.zh: 艾莎站在她右边，神色若有所思，打量着下方的城。

sentences.en: Suddenly, Anna became very aware of the feeling that someone was watching her.
sentences.zh: 忽然，安娜强烈地察觉到，有人在盯着她。

sentences.en: Maybe even a few someones. “Oh,” she heard Elsa squeak.
sentences.zh: 也许还不止一个人。"噢，"她听见艾莎一声轻叫。

sentences.en: Anna turned, only to come nose-to-nose with a spear.
sentences.zh: 安娜转过身，正好与一支长矛鼻尖对鼻尖。

sentences.en: And not just one spear.
sentences.zh: 而且不止一支长矛。

sentences.en: Many spears.
sentences.zh: 许多长矛。

chapters.title: Chapter Eighteen
chapters.en:
WHILE ANNA, ELSA, AND KRISTOFF had been taking in the sights of the village below, it seemed as though a storm cloud had gathered around them.

Though, of course, storm clouds didn’t exist in the belly of the mines, nor were they capable of holding a spear to one’s throat. No. The roiling, shifting dark shapes gathering around them were none other than Huldrefólk warriors.

Like the littler Dash, these ones, too, stuck to the shadows. In the glow, Anna could only make out the glint of an eye here, and the back of a hand there. But she didn’t need to be able to see their faces to sense how they felt about three human trespassers in their secret city: they were not very happy at all.

“H-h-hi,” Anna stuttered to the spear tips, trying to remember the etiquette of meeting a new group of people. It wasn’t the exact same as meeting the prime minister of Torres, but she knew that dignitaries were sensitive, so polite manners seemed the safest bet.

Step one: Introduce yourself, and announce you are a friend.

She dipped into a curtsy. “My name is Anna of Arendelle, and this is my sis—”

A spearpoint jabbed closer to her, and Anna went silent.

“Stop,” a Hulder hissed. “Say no more, thief.”

“I-I think there’s been a mistake,” Anna said, forcing a cheerful smile on her face. “We’ve come to ask for help. We’re not here to take anything—”

“Take,” the same Hulder spoke again, repeating Anna. “Take, take, take!”

“No,” Kristoff said, his back against Anna’s. “We’re not here to take anything. We followed a little one—”

“Take little one,” the Hulder repeated, and Anna could hear fury swell in the Hulder’s voice. “Take little one!” The cry was repeated by another Hulder, and then another, until the entire shifting mass of spear-wielding warriors took up the chant.

Anna had a bad feeling. A very bad feeling.

“I think that they’re accusing us of trying to steal Dash,” she whispered.

“Ah,” Kristoff said in a low voice, “well, that’s not accurate.”

“Wait!” Anna told the Huldrefólk, holding up her hand. “We weren’t trying to kidnap anyone!”

The Huldrefólk’s chant changed. “Liar, liar, every word!”

Anna shook her head, trying to make sense of them.

“We’re not,” Elsa spoke up, her voice smooth as ice, though Anna could hear the friction beneath the surface. “The little one found us. We were singing, and then my sister rescued the child from falling into a dark abyss—”

“The abyss!” another Hulder with a higher voice interrupted. “The abyss! Take to abyss! Take to abyss! Liar, liar, every word!”

Uh-oh.

“Um,” Anna said with a gulp. “I think they want to—”

“Drop us off in the abyss?” Kristoff finished. “Yeah. I got that, too.”

“Wait!” Anna tried again. “There’s a giant wolf out there that’ll be here before you know—” Anna’s sentence was cut short as a warrior rushed forward and tied what felt like a handkerchief around Anna’s mouth, making it impossible for her to shout.

But even if she could, would it help? They were so far underground, and the villagers who were still awake were far away, likely and hopefully already onboard Elsa’s royal ship. Sorenson was gone, having been left to face the Nattmara. And next to her, Elsa and Kristoff were also being gagged. Hard roots pressed into the soft skin of Anna’s wrists as her hands were pulled behind her back and bound.

After checking to make sure the knot was tight, the Hulder who had bound her nodded. “March.”

Single file, they walked in front of the Huldrefólk. Anna kept her eye on Elsa’s braid as it swung, and was grateful when Kristoff accidentally stepped on her heel. It made her feel better knowing they were both there. At least they were all in this mess together.

Anna thought the Huldrefólk would take them away from their hidden city, back to the abyss from which they’d saved Dash, but instead, the warriors marched them down a narrow path, away from the abyss and the swarm of glowworms and fluorescent gardens. Anna’s bad feeling only grew more insistent the longer they walked away from the city. Sweat beaded on her forehead, and her ribcage felt too tight as she breathed in the stale and stuffy air.

How far underground were they? Then the smell of rotten eggs punched her nose, and her eyes watered. It was the smell of sulfur, or else the Huldrefólk had some major issues with their plumbing. The air grew hotter still until it almost seemed to take on a rosy glow. A red light danced along the walls ahead of them, an unusual color that typically could only be found in the most spectacular summer sunsets, or in Tuva and Ada’s forge, or…no. Anna’s heart flipped.

Or in the center of an active volcano. Liar, liar, every word plus abyss apparently equaled throwing the group of human trespassers from Arendelle into molten rock.

The red glow grew brighter, and while the Huldrefólk seemed as cool as ice cream in the middle of an eternal winter, sweat now drenched Anna. She imagined that if it got any hotter, her eyebrows would slide right off her face. Even if Elsa could use her magic here—even if it wouldn’t draw the Nattmara straight to them—what chance did winter’s cold have against the melting powers of red-hot magma?

Now it was in front of them, a round circle of red that pulsed like a beating heart. Anna stumbled to a stop, but the Huldrefólk shoved her forward, and though she could not believe it was possible, she grew even hotter.

“Stop,” Anna garbled through her gag, her mind racing as she skipped over steps two through ten of diplomacy. “We’ll give you chocolate!” The words came out muffled.

It wasn’t actually a step of etiquette—truly, bribery didn’t belong on the list at all—and nothing in all her reading had prepared Anna for the possibility of being thrown into a river of lava by a hosting nation.

But it didn’t work. They pushed her forward. Even though it was hotter than Oaken’s sauna, Anna went numb as she saw Elsa’s boot hang over the edge, the toe turning red in the glow. Anna struggled harder. If they disappeared on their mission, no one would ever know how the Nattmara came to be or how it could be stopped. No one would survive it. Being thrown into lava wouldn’t just mean the end of Kristoff, Elsa, and Anna—it would mean the end of Arendelle. They would have failed. She would have failed. Emptiness yawned in Anna, threatening to swallow her whole.

All she had wanted—ever wanted—was to always do more and, out of true love for her sister, help her.

Although the whole kingdom had seen Anna save her sister three years ago, she had since wondered who wouldn’t save their sister. And still, Anna couldn’t get past that she was the one who had provoked Elsa into casting an eternal winter then, and now she was the one who had called a Nattmara to the land. She would never feed Sven a carrot again. She would never hear more about Olaf’s warm philosophy on life. She would never get a chance to learn about the natural and celestial worlds from Sorenson. And it was all her fault.

From the corner of her eye, she saw Elsa whip her head so fast that her braid slapped her Hulder captor’s nose, taking them by surprise, while Kristoff flung himself backward, slamming his captor into the wall. The two managed to wrestle out of their binds in the process.

Come on! Anna told herself. They’re still fighting. You can, too! She wanted to cheer them on, but she needed to save her breath. And besides, there was still a gag in her mouth. Her guard dragged her forward, closer to the edge of the molten lake, while Anna freed her hands.

“HALT!” A deep voice reverberated around the rock, sending tremors through the earth.

But there was no way Anna was going to stop fighting. She lunged to the side, free of the Hulder’s stony grip, and tore off her gag. She took a few running steps away from them before realizing she wasn’t being chased. Instead, the Huldrefólk knelt to the ground as a fourth Hulder appeared in the red haze. This Hulder seemed to be the tallest of them all, their hair a wild black mane surrounding their face, and on their head they wore a circlet of something shiny. It took Anna a minute to realize it was gold.

The leader of the Huldrefólk.

And on the Hulder leader’s shoulders sat a small, familiar figure.

“Horse!” Dash yanked on the Hulder leader’s hair.

Anna sank into a curtsy, and after she coughed pointedly in Kristoff’s direction, he bowed. Elsa, however, stayed as upright as an icicle, befitting her rank.

“Psst! Rule number one,” Anna murmured loud enough so that Elsa could hear.

Elsa nodded and spoke. “Greetings. I am Queen Elsa of Arendelle, and this is my sister, Princess Anna, and her…er, our guard, Kristoff Bjorgman of Nowhere in Particular. We greet you in friendship.”

Anna held her breath, wondering if the leader would accept.

“Friendship,” the Hulder leader repeated. And then, to Anna’s utter astonishment, the Hulder continued in full sentences. “I apologize for my family. They can be a bit overprotective.” In the dim light, Anna saw the Hulder pat Dash’s dangling knee. “Young Echo, however, has cleared up the misunderstanding, and she and I welcome you to our domain. I am the king of the Huldrefólk.”

“You’re not repeating everything,” Elsa said, clearly too surprised to worry about manners.

The imposing Hulder king inclined his head. “We like to use other people’s words so that we can wrap ourselves up and hide within them. It’s very rare for Huldrefólk to actually have to compose something new. That’s part of the reason why Echo found you—she wanted to collect your song. Songs are easy to remember. Easy to echo back.”

“Echo!” Dash—now Echo, Anna realized—repeated the word from her perch.

Anna knew she should probably let Elsa do all the talking, but her curiosity was too much. “Why do you talk in your own words?” she asked.

“Because I am not only the king, but also the librarian,” said the Hulder leader. “I’ve spent years visiting the world above, collecting items as well as stories, and I have enough words at my disposal. And so, I would like to apologize again for your initial greeting.” The Librarian King reached for Echo and set the child on the ground.

“That’s it?” Kristoff burst out. “We’re almost thrown into a lake of lava, and all you can say is ‘I’m sorry’?”

“I’m sorry!” Echo squealed, moving toward Kristoff.

“Does ‘We’re very sorry’ make it any better?” the Librarian King asked. “Usually, the only humans who make it down this far want to take precious stones and gems from our mountain, or to capture a member of our domain to make them find iron ore deposits for their weapons and the like.”

“We’re not looking for stones, gems, or iron,” Elsa said. “We’re looking for a sword of myth, the Revolute Blade. Can you please help us find it?”

The Librarian King’s eyes flashed. “‘Revolving moon and spinning sun, forged a crescent blade. From light and dark within the heart, the burnished sword was made.’” He looked down at them. “That’s the one, yes?”

Anna nodded, feeling this was a good sign.

“And,” he continued, “I suppose this has something to do with the Nattmara that has come to Arendelle?”

Anna gaped. “How did you know about the Nattmara?”

“Just because you can’t see us doesn’t mean we’re not always there.” The Librarian King studied them a second more. It was impossible to make out any expression on the leader’s face. The Hulder’s textured skin had taken on the appearance of the cracked rivulets of lava, and was hard to see against the molten backdrop. But then, he must have made a secret signal, because the guards bowed before each of them and then hurried away, keeping their backs to Anna and her friends. It only took the hidden people a couple of steps until they seemed to have disappeared entirely, though Anna knew they must still be there, great masters of camouflage that they were.

The Librarian King turned. “Now, all of you, come with me.”

Anna’s heart leapt. At last—she had not led them astray!

“We don’t always know the answer—but we do know where to find it,” the Librarian King continued.

Allowing the humans to walk in front of them, the Librarian King and Echo escorted Anna, Elsa, and Kristoff away from the lake of molten rock and toward a tranquil tributary of water where rafts bumped and prodded against each other.

Anna looked at Elsa and Kristoff in the gloom, and a smile spread across her face. “This could be it!” she whispered. “We may finally find the sword!”

“Let’s wait and see,” said Elsa, ever the one to freeze the excited mood.

Echo tugged at Kristoff’s tunic, and they began to toss stones into the water.

“My assistant will help. She will take you to the Library of Lost Things,” the Librarian King told them. “If my people ever came across the legendary sword, it will be there—that is, if the sword truly exists.”

Elsa shot Anna a look, and Anna bit her lip. She hoped against hope that it did.

“We are sorry for bringing the Nattmara to your door,” Elsa said. It wasn’t lost on Anna that her sister had used the word we.

The Librarian King shook his head. “The Nattmara is one of the many natural enemies of the Huldrefólk—we both seek to reign the dark. But while the Huldrefólk love the night for its quiet privacy, the Nattmara prefers to use the dark as a weapon. Fear not: the Nattmara cannot pass into the borders of our domain. As long as you’re within the Huldrefólk realm, the Nattmara cannot touch you. We are the hidden people. We keep ourselves hidden, and now that you’re with us, we’ll keep you hidden as well.”

Relief filled Anna, and then a thought stirred. “Umm, I have a question for you,” she said. “We lost a member of our group. Is it possible for the Huldrefólk to find him? He’s kind of short and stocky, with a long silver beard that touches the floor, and he’s grumpy.” Anna paused, then added, “He’s nice!”

The Librarian King inclined his head. “As you know, Huldrefólk are seekers of lost things. Collectors. If your friend is still free of the Nattmara, then I’m sure we can locate him.”

“Land ahoy!”

Anna looked to the water, where a gray raft glided in front of them and bumped against the bank. A cheery-looking Hulder (as Anna thought she could make out a smile in the dim glowworms’ light) waved at them and leaned against the long pole she’d been using to steer the vessel.

“Ahoy! Ahoy! Ahoy!” Echo cried out, and left the game of skipping rocks with Kristoff to fling herself onto the raft and into the new Hulder’s arms.

“This is my assistant, Obscuren,” the Librarian King proclaimed. “She will help you find what you are looking for and will be your guide in my domain.”

Anna scrambled onto the raft, settling herself next to Kristoff. It was only then that she noticed the unusual material it was made of. While rafts were almost always constructed of wood, this one seemed to be made of floating stone. As she peered closer, she saw tiny holes perforating the surface, making the texture of the raft seem more like bread than rock.

“I think this is a pumice raft,” Anna said to Kristoff, who nodded.

“It is,” he said. “Rock from the volcano.”

Anna felt a tug on her hair as Echo crawled into her lap, quietly chanting, “Row, row, row your raft!”

“Say your goodbye,” the Librarian King instructed Echo. “It’s time for dinner.”

The little Hulder’s eyes swam with tears. “Stay!”

“I wish you could,” Anna said, and was surprised when she realized she meant it.

Miner’s Mountain was beautiful, full of unexpected surprises and even more unexpected friendships. She liked the little Hulder and her penchant for flying ahead as fast as possible. Anna bet Echo could show her many things—glowing crystals, ice caves, maybe even a sleeping bat or two—but she needed to fix her mistake before she could explore the wonders of the mountain further.

“Besides, you’d be bored if you joined us,” Anna said. “We won’t be singing anymore, and being on a raft makes it hard for you to dash anywhere.”

Head tilted, the little Hulder considered this bleak reality, then clambered out of the raft to join one of the Huldrefólk guards who’d seemingly materialized out of nowhere.

“Bye!” Echo proclaimed from the riverbank, waving. “Bye-bye-bye!”

Anna’s heart squeezed. “See you later. Stay out of dark abysses, okay?”

Elsa was the last to step onto the raft. When she’d settled her cloak around her, she looked back at the Librarian King. “Thank you,” she said. “For all your help. I promise we’ll keep your secret, and we will keep the mines closed. Your city will remain hidden.”

The Librarian King bowed in thanks, and then Obscuren pushed them across the glassy surface of the river.

The raft rocked as they navigated the underground waterway, the air refreshingly cooler now.

Obscuren took in their drooping eyelids. “You can sleep,” she said. “I know my way around the river. And as the Librarian King said, you are hidden here with me, even from the Nattmara.”

“Are you absolutely…” Whatever Kristoff had been going to say was lost in a yawn.

“The Nattmara cannot find our domain,” Obscuren reminded them. “We are cloaked from it. You can rest here, safely, without any fear of losing yourself over to its influence. Sleep. Rest. I’ll wake you when we reach our destination.”

Obscuren had barely finished before a snore ripped out of Kristoff, and in the next second, Elsa, too, was asleep. Anna, however, stayed awake. Though she had been daydreaming about sleeping, she found she couldn’t close her eyes. Every time she did, her stomach hurt too much. Because each moment asleep was a moment she wasn’t fixing her biggest mistake: the Nattmara she’d accidentally welcomed into Arendelle with a spell. Obscuren’s voice interrupted her thoughts, and Anna pulled herself out of them.

“Sorry, what was that?” Anna asked.

“I said,” the Hulder repeated, “that you should sleep, too.” Obscuren pushed on the pole, and the water sighed as the raft sliced through it. The river flowed through winding tunnels with low ceilings, though here and there little beaches seemed to jut into the waterway, and Anna thought she could make out the distant shape of a Hulder or two watching them. This close to a Hulder who was not trying to kill her, she could finally make out a more definite shape.

Obscuren looked almost human but for an overall spindly appearance, pointed ears, and changing skin. At the moment, the Hulder’s eyes were a beautiful shade of orange, a color that made Anna think of the end of autumn or the start of spring. They seemed to take in everything around them, and as Obscuren looked at Anna, Anna wondered if the seeker of things could find Anna’s deepest secret in her eyes.

“Obscuren,” Anna said, “do you know how the Nattmara came to Arendelle? I think I know, but I’m not entirely sure. The Blight started before the Nattmara arrived. I’m a bit murky on the details.” She held her breath, waiting for Obscuren to somehow say the words that were blaring through her mind as loudly as a goatherd playing the tungehorn: the spell. It must have been the spell, as much as it didn’t make sense that the animals and crops had grown sick before she’d read it. But after she read the spell, the wolf appeared. Of that much Anna was certain—just as she was certain it was her fault.

Obscuren was silent, but it wasn’t the kind of sharp silence of being ignored. This quiet had a thoughtful quality to it, as though she were weighing each word before speaking.

“A Nattmara doesn’t appear out of thin air,” the Hulder said. “They are made, formed from an event in a person’s life that grows so big they can’t keep it inside anymore, and the fear becomes so large that it takes on a life of its own.”

Anna nodded. Yes, that was what Sorenson had said. The fear is too big to keep inside. “Sooo,” Anna said, “you don’t think that someone could have, I don’t know”—she tucked a strand of ruddy hair behind her ear—“said a spell, or something, and brought the Nattmara to Arendelle?”

Obscuren gave a shake of her head. “I don’t believe the poems that humans call spells are really anything other than just that: poems. They may be able to conjure a beautiful image or a moment of time, but that is a different kind of magic entirely.”

Anna wasn’t sure what to say, but she was comforted. Because Anna had read a spell…but it sounded like even if she had never said it out loud, the Nattmara still would have come to the kingdom.

Anna still would have accidentally called it, with or without a poem. Because the night that it had materialized from her dreams was the same night she’d heard Elsa holding a council meeting without her, and she had felt her heart break a little. It was the moment she had realized her greatest fear had come true: that Elsa really and truly had no need for her at all. And because of that, her nightmare—her fear—had manifested in the form of the Nattmara that was now stalking them all.

“And I guess,” she said, trying to keep her voice light, “if there’s no spell to call a Nattmara, then there’s probably no spell to banish one, right?”

Obscuren shook her head. “I wouldn’t think so. I’ve only ever heard of one warrior willing to face the Nattmara, and that was Aren, with his mythical Revolute Blade that contained a strange power.”

Revolute.

With Kristoff and Elsa asleep and nestled against her back, and Obscuren in the front, keeping an eye on Anna and her friends, the mythical curved sword shone like a lighthouse in the dark river of Anna’s worry, and, at last, she let her eyes drift shut to sleep.
chapters.zh:
当安娜、艾莎和克斯托夫还在欣赏脚下村庄的景色时，仿佛一团乌云正悄悄在他们四周聚拢。

当然，矿井深处可没有什么乌云，更不会有乌云把长矛抵在谁的喉咙上。

不。

那些在他们身边翻涌游移的黑色影子，其实是一群胡尔德民（Huldrefólk）的战士。

和那个小不点达什（Dash）一样，这些家伙也紧紧贴着暗处。

在微光里，安娜只能勉强辨认出这儿一只眼睛的反光，那儿一只手背的轮廓。
