sentences.en: It didn’t look so much like a library as it did a too-crammed gift shop.
sentences.zh: 这里不像图书馆，倒更像一个塞得太满的礼品店。

sentences.en: Sure, there were a few books scattered here and there, with bleached covers that looked like they’d been forgotten long ago and left out to wither in the sun.
sentences.zh: 当然，这儿那儿散落着几本书，封皮泛白，像是早被遗忘、搁在太阳下晒得发蔫。

sentences.en: But mostly there were items .
sentences.zh: 但更多的，是物件。

sentences.en: There were sideways chairs lying on top of rolled-up rugs next to a careful stack of mirrors.
sentences.zh: 横倒的椅子压在卷起的毯子上，旁边是一摞码得齐整的镜子。

sentences.en: There was a pile of gardening tools, broken clay figurines, and more than one pile of rusted old keys.
sentences.zh: 还有一堆园艺工具、破碎的泥偶，以及不止一堆锈迹斑斑的旧钥匙。

sentences.en: And there were socks—lots and lots of mismatched socks. “Welcome to the Library of Lost Things,” Obscuren said.
sentences.zh: 还有袜子——许许多多配不成对的袜子。“欢迎来到失物图书馆，”奥布斯基伦说。

sentences.en: Above the ground and in the warm light of the turf house, the Hulder seemed to look less like rock and more like a tree, softly sprouting leaves where before there had been the rough texture of a pebble. “Before you say anything, we did not steal any of these things.
sentences.zh: 在地面上、在草皮屋暖洋洋的光里，这名胡尔德看着没那么像石头了，倒更像一棵树，原本粗糙如卵石的纹理处，悄悄抽出了叶芽。“在你开口之前，我们可没偷过这里任何东西。”

sentences.en: We simply find things that are lost and give them homes.
sentences.zh: “我们只是找到丢失的东西，给它们一个家。”

sentences.en: That includes everything from missing spectacles, to hair bands, to legendary swords.
sentences.zh: “从失踪的眼镜、发带，到传说中的宝剑，统统包括在内。”

sentences.en: Please,” the Hulder continued, stepping aside, “feel free to roam.” “Thank you!” Anna cheered. “Can the Nattmara find us up here ?
sentences.zh: “请吧，”胡尔德侧过身，继续说道，“随便逛。”“谢谢！”安娜欢快地应道。“纳特玛拉能在这里找到我们吗？”

sentences.en: Or are we still hidden and all that?” Kristoff asked, peering out a window. “With me, you are still hidden from the Nattmara,” Obscuren said. “Phew!” Kristoff said. “That’s a relief,” said Elsa, peering through the mess of objects. “We should split up,” Anna said, then looked at Elsa. “Right?” Elsa nodded, and so the three of them began their search.
sentences.zh: “还是说我们仍然藏得好好的？”克斯托夫问，从窗口往外张望。“有我在，你们仍对纳特玛拉隐身，”奥布斯基伦说。“呼！”克斯托夫说。“总算松口气，”艾莎透过满屋杂物望出去，说道。“我们分头找吧，”安娜说，又看向艾莎，“对吧？”艾莎点点头，于是三人开始分头搜寻。

sentences.en: Some of the lost objects were beautiful—bronze vases from another age and even a necklace of heavy sapphires that Anna thought would complement Gerda’s eyes—if Anna were able to turn them back from yellow, that is.
sentences.zh: 有些失物很美——来自另一个时代的青铜花瓶，甚至还有一条沉甸甸的蓝宝石项链，安娜觉得衬格达（Gerda）的眼睛正合适——当然，得她先把格达的眼珠从黄色变回来才行。

sentences.en: She set the necklace down and hurried to the next pile.
sentences.zh: 她放下项链，赶向下一堆。

sentences.en: She picked up a round mirror.
sentences.zh: 她捡起一面圆镜。

sentences.en: It was little, meant to slip into a pocket, and clasped cleverly to look like a clamshell.
sentences.zh: 镜子很小，本是要塞进衣袋的，搭扣做得巧妙，看着像只蛤壳。

sentences.en: She opened it, then set it to the side.
sentences.zh: 她打开看了看，便放到一旁。

sentences.en: It was pretty, but not what she was looking for.
sentences.zh: 是漂亮，可不是她要找的东西。

sentences.en: Scanning the room, Anna searched for a glint of metal, trying to find anything that could possibly be the sword of myth.
sentences.zh: 安娜扫视全屋，搜寻着金属的微光，想找出任何可能是那柄神话之剑的东西。

sentences.en: She moved aside a rickety chair and a mountain of missing socks and tried to push down her disappointment, but it kept rising, like a hot-air balloon, not wanting to be weighed down.
sentences.zh: 她拨开一把摇摇晃晃的椅子和一座由失踪袜子堆成的山，想压下失望，可它却像热气球般不断升起，不愿被压住。

sentences.en: There had to be something in this library.
sentences.zh: 这间图书馆里，必定有什么吧。

sentences.en: Anna’s thoughts skidded to a halt.
sentences.zh: 安娜的思绪猛地刹住。

sentences.en: Her eye had caught on a statue in the center of the room.
sentences.zh: 她的目光被屋子中央的一座雕像攫住了。

sentences.en: It was a figure of a human girl in a sky-blue dress with a glittering train, and a platinum blond braid.
sentences.zh: 那是一个人类女孩的像，穿着天蓝色长裙，裙裾流光溢彩，还编着一头铂金色的辫子。

sentences.en: It looked to be about as tall as Elsa’s knee, and it also happened to look a lot like Elsa.
sentences.zh: 它大约只到艾莎的膝盖高，而且——巧的是——长得很像艾莎。

sentences.en: Anna gasped as she stepped closer.
sentences.zh: 安娜走近一步，倒吸一口气。

sentences.en: It was a statue of Elsa.
sentences.zh: 那是一座艾莎的雕像。

sentences.en: Specifically, the one the sisters had installed in the town cuckoo clock a few years before.
sentences.zh: 确切地说，是姐妹俩几年前装进城里布谷鸟钟里的那一尊。

sentences.en: Last spring, the Elsa figure had disappeared in a sudden storm, blown away by unusually strong winds.
sentences.zh: 去年春天，这尊艾莎像在一场突如其来的风暴中失踪，被异常猛烈的风吹走了。

sentences.en: Anna peered at the statue.
sentences.zh: 安娜端详着雕像。

sentences.en: A little green wreath with candles had been perched on top of statue Elsa’s head, and Anna had the briefest thought that the statue looked more comfortable here, surrounded by other wondrous things, than it had looming above the masses, day in and day out.
sentences.zh: 雕像艾莎的头上搁着一圈点着蜡烛的小绿冠，安娜闪过一个念头：比起日复一日高踞众人头顶，这尊雕像待在这儿、被其他奇物环绕，似乎更自在些。

sentences.en: She was glad the Huldrefólk had found a new home for it, and so she kept searching.
sentences.zh: 她很高兴胡尔德民给它找了新家，于是继续搜寻。

sentences.en: But no matter how hard or long they looked, they did not find the coveted sword in the turf house.
sentences.zh: 可不管他们找得多卖力、多久，都没在那间草皮屋里找见那柄梦寐以求的剑。

sentences.en: The closest things to a mythical sword they’d managed to unearth were a few shields and helmets from the time of King Runeard, but nothing older than that.
sentences.zh: 他们翻出来的、最接近的所谓神话之剑，不过是鲁内尔德王（King Runeard）时代的几面盾牌和头盔，再没有更古老的东西。

sentences.en: Anna’s shoulders slumped.
sentences.zh: 安娜的肩膀垮了下来。

sentences.en: If the Huldrefólk didn’t have Revolute, and if Sorenson was lost, and if the trolls had fled the Nattmara…what were they going to do?
sentences.zh: 如果胡尔德民没有回旋之刃，如果索伦森下落不明，如果地精们也逃离了纳特玛拉……他们还能怎么办？

sentences.en: They were running out of places to find answers. “There’s not a single sword in this library!” Elsa said to Obscuren an hour later as the gang flopped in front of a large fireplace to eat from Kristoff’s traveler’s pack.
sentences.zh: 他们能去找答案的地方，快要用光了。“这图书馆里一把剑都没有！”一小时后，艾莎对奥布斯基伦说道，几个人正瘫在巨大的壁炉前，吃着克斯托夫行囊里的干粮。

sentences.en: Obscuren sighed. “So it appears.” The Hulder’s skin had taken on the runes of the turf house walls, and speaking to Obscuren now almost felt like talking to alphabet soup.
sentences.zh: 奥布斯基伦叹了口气。“看来是这样。”胡尔德的皮肤已染上草皮屋墙上的符文，此刻跟奥布斯基伦说话，几乎像在和一锅字母汤对话。

sentences.en: She seemed to droop slightly, and it was clear to Anna that Obscuren wasn’t used to having to converse so much. “Why not?” Kristoff asked. “Arendelle’s history seems to be full of swords, as far as I can tell.
sentences.zh: 她似乎微微耷拉着，安娜一眼就看出，奥布斯基伦不习惯说这么多话。“为什么没有？”克斯托夫问，“据我所知，阿伦黛尔的历史里好像满是剑啊。”

sentences.en: Why didn’t the Huldrefólk ever find one?
sentences.zh: 胡尔德民怎么就一把都没找到呢？

sentences.en: Maybe it’s at another location?” “Sometimes,” Obscuren said, settling down onto the dirt floor to rest, “great swords are buried with their heroes.” “ARRGH!” Anna’s heart began to pound furiously as a cry that sounded a bit like a seagull reverberated through the turf house.
sentences.zh: “也许在别的什么地方？”“有时候，”奥布斯基伦在泥地上坐下歇息，说道，“伟大的剑会和它们的英雄一起下葬。”“啊啊啊！”一声有点像海鸥的呐喊在草皮屋里回荡，安娜的心猛地狂跳起来。

sentences.en: Wide-eyed, Anna turned to see what had made such a terrifying sound—expecting to see the Nattmara or a mob of yellow-eyed villagers coming for them—but all she saw was Elsa, who’d leapt to her feet. “Well, that’s just great!” Elsa’s blue eyes flashed and her cheeks reddened.
sentences.zh: 安娜瞪大眼睛转头，想看清是什么发出这可怕的声响——她本以为会看见纳特玛拉，或一群黄眼村民杀过来——可她只看见艾莎，已经一跃而起。“这下可好了！”艾莎蓝眼睛一闪，脸颊涨得通红。

sentences.en: For the first time in a long time, Anna thought that her sister looked visibly upset. “What’s wrong?” Anna scrambled to her feet, too. “We just need to find out where Aren was buried—” Elsa snorted, and it was such an un-Elsa-like sound that Anna grew quiet. “We can’t find where he was buried.” Elsa paced the floor. “Don’t you remember the story?
sentences.zh: 这是长久以来头一回，安娜觉得妹妹明显心烦意乱。“怎么了？”安娜也慌忙站起。“我们只要弄清阿伦葬在哪儿就行——”艾莎哼了一声，那声音太不像艾莎了，安娜顿时安静下来。“我们找不到他葬在哪儿。”艾莎在地板上踱步，“你不记得了吗，那个故事？”

sentences.en: Aren was swallowed by a dragon!” Anna blinked. “He was ?” She’d forgotten that.
sentences.zh: “阿伦被龙吞了！”安娜眨了眨眼。“他被吞了？”她把这事忘了。

sentences.en: She glanced over at Kristoff, who was looking at Elsa with something like awe, as though he couldn’t quite believe that calm and collected Elsa was panicking. “Yes,” Elsa said, exasperated. “A dragon came to the fjord, and it threatened to eat everyone!
sentences.zh: 她瞥了克斯托夫一眼，他正带着几分敬畏望着艾莎，仿佛不敢相信冷静自持的艾莎居然也会慌神。“对，”艾莎懊恼地说，“一条龙来到峡湾，威胁要把所有人都吃掉！”

sentences.en: And so Aren, our greatest leader besides King Runeard, who loved his home and people more than anything, decided to go face the dragon…who”—Elsa paused, then changed to her most dramatic voice—“‘lives where the sea is a sky,’ and never came back.” Elsa took a deep breath. “Because the dragon swallowed him.
sentences.zh: “于是阿伦——除了鲁内尔德王之外我们最伟大的领袖，他爱家乡和百姓胜过一切——决定去直面那条龙……那条龙”——艾莎顿了顿，换上最戏剧化的腔调——“‘住在大海化作天空的地方’，再也没回来。”艾莎深吸一口气，“因为龙把他吞了。”

sentences.en: And dragons don’t exist, and neither does this sword, and Anna, oh, I’ve tried listening, but there’s nothing we can do!” “Curious,” Obscuren called out.
sentences.zh: “而龙根本不存在，这把剑也不存在，安娜，唉，我试过倾听了，可我们无能为力！”“有意思，”奥布斯基伦喊道。

sentences.en: During Elsa’s tirade, the Hulder had gone to a stone wall. “That’s not what all stories say.” She waved a delicate arm at the walls around them. “In that long-ago time when Huldrefólk and humans were more comfortable with each other, we would meet here, in a place of compromise between earth and sky.
sentences.zh: 方才艾莎长篇大论时，胡尔德走到了一面石墙前。“并非所有故事都这么讲。”她纤细的手臂朝四周的墙壁一挥，“在很久以前，胡尔德民和人类还相处得更自在，我们会在此相会，在这天地之间折中的一处地方。”

sentences.en: Each community carved their stories into these walls.
sentences.zh: 每个族裔都把自己的故事刻在这些墙上。

sentences.en: This is one of the oldest turf houses.
sentences.zh: 这是最古老的草皮屋之一。

sentences.en: And here, the myth of Aren changes, slightly. “This”—the Hulder pointed at a carved rune that looked like a sideways S -shape—“according to our legend, says that a great danger came from the waters, and in order to save his home and people that he loved, Aren set out in a boat and was never seen again.” “How is that any better?” Elsa asked, and Anna was shocked to see her sister’s foot twitch, as though she had just resisted the urge to stomp her feet. “That just means Revolute is probably somewhere at the bottom of the ocean, and even if it were possible to scour all the waters, we just don’t have time.” Elsa turned sharply, sending her braid whipping out behind her and almost smacking a shocked Kristoff across the nose. “So you see,” she addressed Anna, “we’re never going to find Revolute!” But actually…Anna did see.
sentences.zh: 而在这里，阿伦的神话略有不同。“这个——”胡尔德指着一道刻成横卧S形的符文——“按我们的传说，意思是：巨大的危险自水中而来，为了拯救他深爱的家乡与百姓，阿伦乘船出海，从此再没出现。”“这又有什么好？”艾莎问；安娜惊讶地看见妹妹的脚抽动了一下，像是刚忍住跺脚的冲动。“那只说明回旋之刃多半沉在海底某处，而就算搜遍所有水域是可能的，我们也根本没时间。”艾莎猛地转身，辫子甩在身后，差点抽中一脸震惊的克斯托夫的鼻子。“所以你看，”她对安娜说，“我们永远找不到回旋之刃了！”可实际上……安娜看懂了。

sentences.en: Anna opened her mouth. “Elsa—” “The Nattmara is still out there, the Blight chokes the land, and all of our friends are probably stuck in a nightmare by now!” Kristoff flinched at her words. “You wanted to visit the Huldrefólk because they were supposed to be able to tell us something,” Elsa continued, “to show us the way to a made-up sword.
sentences.zh: 安娜张了张嘴。“艾莎——”“纳特玛拉还在外面，枯萎病扼住了大地，而我们所有的朋友这会儿怕是都困在噩梦里了！”克斯托夫被她的话刺得缩了一下。“你执意要拜访胡尔德民，是因为他们本该能告诉我们些什么，”艾莎接着说，“给我们指出那把子虚乌有的剑的方向。”

sentences.en: Is there anything else, any other clue—” “Elsa—” Her sister threw her hands in the air. “The people are all counting on me!” “ELSA!” Elsa’s furor stumbled to a halt, and, panting, she looked over at Anna, who pushed away a smile. “How can you be so calm at a time like this?” Elsa demanded, and Anna had to stop from giggling. “I’m calm because I learned from the best,” Anna said, and she could feel a fiery hope burning bright in her chest. “And because I know where Revolute is.”
sentences.zh: “还有什么别的吗，任何别的线索——”“艾莎——”妹妹把双手往空中一摊。“子民们都指望着我呢！”“艾莎！”艾莎的怒火戛然而止，她喘着气看向安娜，而安娜把笑意压了下去。“这种时候你怎么还能这么镇定？”艾莎质问道；安娜差点笑出声。“我镇定，是因为我向最棒的人学过，”安娜说，胸口能感到一团炽热的希望在燃烧，“还因为我知道回旋之刃在哪儿。”

chapters.title: Chapter Twenty
chapters.en:
“WAIT, WHAT?” ELSA SAID.

Anna couldn’t help smiling now at hearing her signature line coming from Elsa’s mouth.

“What do you mean, you know where Revolute is?”

Somewhere along the way, it had clicked as Anna stared at the carvings on the walls and listened to Obscuren’s tale. The Arendellians’ story and the Huldrefólk’s story were different, but the same. Like Anna and Elsa. And just like the royal sisters, the stories made the most sense when they were together.

“Why can’t both things be true?” Anna suggested. “Why can’t he have been eaten by a dragon, as our story says, and be sent out on a boat? It’s all in the stories—Aren was swallowed by a dragon who lived in a place where the sea is a sky.”

“But for the sea to be a sky, you have to be under the…” Elsa’s voice trailed off and her eyes lit up. “The Earth Giant’s Passage! It goes under the fjord, which means the sea is the sky. And that’s where the dragon boat is!” Elsa’s hand flew to her mouth in wonder. “The tumulus,” she said softly. “It’s Aren’s tumulus, which means…”

“That’s where Revolute is buried,” Anna finished with a nod. “Exactly.”

“Way to go, Anna!” Kristoff said. “You solved it!”

“Thanks!” She flashed him a smile. “This means we have to go back to the castle,” Anna said, looking up at the Hulder, who stood there tall and impassive as they spoke. “And we need to get there as soon as possible! Elsa, can you…” Anna twirled her finger.

“Magic? But it’ll draw the Nattmara right to us,” Elsa said.

Obscuren chimed in. “If you wanted to use your magic without the Nattmara sensing it, I think it would need to be now.”

Elsa nodded. In the safety of the turf house, she crafted a sleigh of ice—ice so clear that Anna could see right through it. It was practically invisible. And then Anna felt a whoosh of cold air blow by her, and she shivered as snowflakes danced in the air, shaping themselves into a massive snow bear, who loomed much too large in the tiny turf house.

“Elsa,” Anna said, taking in the snow bear with wonder, “he’s beautiful.”

The bear growled.

“He says his name is Bjorn,” Obscuren translated.

“I can hear my reindeer, Sven, talk, too,” Kristoff said to the Hulder. His voice sounded glum, and Anna knew he was still worried about his best friend. She hoped Sven was all right, and, at the very least, safe on the royal ship.

Obscuren rested a hand on Kristoff’s arm and flashed a sad smile. “The Huldrefólk are known for finding things that are lost, because we know how to listen,” she said. “But we’re not the only beings who listen. Animals can, too. They can tell a kind heart from one filled with cruelty. And I suspect, Kristoff, that you’re someone who knows exactly what Sven is saying to you.”

Kristoff shook his head. “I just hope he’s okay.”

“If we leave right now, he will be,” Anna said, trying to say it with so much confidence that it would just have to be true.

As quickly as they could, they buckled the snow bear up to the sleigh, and then said their farewells to Obscuren.

“In my family,” the Hulder said, “we don’t say goodbye.”

“What do you say, then?” Anna asked.

“We say, ‘Till we see you again.’”

Anna smiled. “Till we see you again.”

“Maybe,” Obscuren said, already disappearing behind a stack of lost and broken plates. “But I’ll probably see you first. Unless you look very, very closely.”

Obscuren reached out an arm and cracked open the door. There was a second while the Hulder took in the land, and then she flung the door open wide for the bear and the sled. “Remember,” the Hulder called as they slipped from the safety of the turf house and slid out under the sky. “Home is where the heart is. Good luck, friends of Arendelle.”

“Goodbye, friend,” Anna said.

But Obscuren was gone.

As Bjorn loped away from the turf house, home did not look like home anymore. Anna saw a haze had settled over Arendelle as color drained from the world. It was as though the earth itself were afraid, turning pale with fear. Anna held out her hand, studying it in the sunlight. It still looked pink in the cold. Glancing at Elsa, Anna was comforted by the fact that her mother’s scarf, wrapped around Elsa’s shoulders, was still burgundy, while Kristoff’s hair was still the color of wheat. The color that wheat was supposed to be, Anna corrected herself. But there was still time before sunset. There was still time to remedy this all.

“It looks like the forest after a fire,” Kristoff said, glancing at the terrain as he guided the snow bear around a bend with a careful tug of the reins.

“What do you mean?” Elsa asked.

“The way the ash drifts,” Kristoff explained. “It floats on the air instead of falling.”

“Maybe,” Anna said, trying to force cheer into her words, “that’s a good thing. I read in the library that forest fires are necessary to clear the bramble and make way for new life.”

Kristoff shook his head. “Tell that to the people who’ve lost their homes.” He jounced the reins, and the sleigh went faster.

Anna held a spyglass of ice from Elsa up to her eye, scanning the horizon for any sign of the Nattmara. So far, so good. There was no sign of the wolf. Well, no signs other than this pale shadow of their home and the fearful thump of Anna’s own heart.

Except, what was that? A dark smudge seemed to move from the washed-out green of the spruces.

“Elsa,” Anna whispered, and slipped the spyglass back to her sister. “Something’s moving. Over there.”

Elsa peered over her shoulder, then looked ahead again. “You’re right,” she said. “I think it’s following us.”

Kristoff snapped the reins harder and Bjorn veered right, sending a swirl of pale white leaves into the air. Anna looked back. The smudge also veered right. Yes. Whatever it was, it was definitely following them. Bjorn’s ears swiveled, and then Anna heard it.

A cry: Ahhhhhhhh! It seemed to come from the direction of the smudge. And it wasn’t the bone-cold howl of the Nattmara. This noise sounded almost human, as though someone were trying to call out a name. In fact…Ahhhhhh! Naaaaaaaa!

“Stop!” Anna lurched upright. “It’s Sorenson!”

Elsa gasped. “What?”

Kristoff pulled the reins, flinging Anna into Elsa as they sped back to the scientist. As they got closer, the cry became clearer. “Annaaaa! Elsaaaaa!”

“Sorenson!” Anna shouted, relieved he was okay.

Or was he? The scientist looked the worse for wear. His coat was torn, shredded by the Nattmara’s claws, and he limped, his ankle swollen. But he was alive, and not only that, his eyes didn’t appear to be either pitch black or yellow.

“Stop the sleigh!” Anna said, and Kristoff pulled Bjorn to a walk.

The snow bear snorted, protesting the change in pace.

“Sorenson!” Anna called as she swung out of the sleigh and hurried toward him. “We’re so glad to see you! How did you escape?”

“Hello to you, Anna, and to you, Your Majesty,” Sorenson said. He spoke in a strange cadence, as if he had somehow managed to twist his tongue as well as his ankle. “I’ll tell you all about it in a minute. Just let me catch my breath.”

“We don’t really have time,” Elsa said, looking to the sky. The sun was definitely low now, approaching dinnertime. “How about you tell us in the sleigh?”

He nodded. “That’s a good idea, but we can’t take a sleigh where we need to go.”

“And where do we need to go?” Anna asked. She stepped over to Kristoff’s traveler’s pack and sifted around for a spare splint. Aha! There it was. She knew Kristoff rarely left home without it. The splint was for ice mountain emergencies, but Kristoff liked to tease her that he needed to make sure he had one on hand at the castle for the amount of times she’d managed to trip or stumble over something.

Anna sat down and offered the scientist the splint. “How did you escape the Nattmara?”

Sorenson said, “I found a thing of myth.”

Anna’s eyebrows shot upward. “You found Revolute?”

Sorenson tilted his head, and with his long silver beard, he looked a little bit like a confused dog. “Did you figure out where it was hidden?”

Anna grinned. “Yes! Well, we know where to look. It’s in—”

“What did you find, Sorenson?” Elsa asked, stepping in between them. She’d arranged their mother’s scarf around her shoulders like a cape.

“Ah, I found a cure,” Sorenson said, and he tapped his fingertips excitedly together. “But it’s hard to explain. I’d rather show it to you first. It won’t defeat the Nattmara, but I believe it will clear up the Blight from the animals and the crops.”

“What?” Kristoff, who’d been waiting in the sleigh, jumped out. “There’s a cure? We can help Sven?”

“Allegedly, yes,” Sorenson said. “And the Huldrefólk have it.”

“I don’t know about that,” Elsa said, tugging on the fringe of her scarf. “They’re our friends, I think, and they didn’t say anything about having a cure.”

“Yes.” Anna nodded. “And they are definitely our friends.”

Sorenson’s face crinkled and he shook his head while he sighed. “Whatever they told you is wrong,” he said. “The Huldrefólk are thieves. You should not have trusted them.”

“No,” Anna said, standing up for Echo, the Librarian King, and Obscuren. “They find lost, unwanted things and give them homes. They find ‘that which is lost,’ like your book says, sir.”

But Sorenson kept shaking his head, his long beard waving like one of the windswept pennants on the castle wall. In the lengthening light, his beard looked more white than silver. “Then my book must be wrong, because the Huldrefólk have a thing of myth hidden in their hot springs, not more than a mile away. I discovered that if a Nattmara-touched animal drinks the water, they will be cured, even if you don’t defeat the Nattmara by sunrise of the third day.”

“Let’s go!” Kristoff said, the hope so bright on his face that it hurt Anna to see. “If it’s only a mile, we could get a cup of the water from the hot springs, just in case, and still make it back without losing that much time!”

Bjorn’s snuffle was louder now. The bear wanted to move. He wanted to go. Yet Anna was torn…until she saw the expression on Kristoff’s face.

Kristoff’s best friend was sick. And he had no way to know what had happened to Sven in the time they’d been gone, but he’d risked his life over and over again just for the chance that he could help make Sven feel better. How could Anna say no to that?

“Elsa,” she said, turning from Sorenson, who still nursed his ankle on the splint, and from Kristoff, who looked like he was about to go sprinting in any direction as soon as he heard where these curing springs were. “I think we should get the water, as a precaution.”

Again, Elsa looked at the sky and bit her lip. As Anna saw her sister take a deep breath, she knew she wasn’t going to like whatever she was about to hear.

“We can’t risk it,” Elsa said, still keeping her gaze on the sky, and on the floating bits of ash that looked like snow but weren’t. “I’m so sorry, Kristoff, but we can’t. Even if the spring water does work, there’s no way we can bring back enough for everyone in all the kingdom…and what about the sword?”

The look on Kristoff’s face was unbearable. “So now you think the sword is real?”

“Elsa!” Anna said, looking between her sister and the man she loved.

“I understand your responsibility to the kingdom,” Kristoff told Elsa, “but Sven is family to me.”

“Kristoff,” Elsa cut in, and her eyes were wide with hurt, though Anna didn’t know why her sister would be upset. “I’m saying no because it endangers too many people!”

Anna took a deep breath, ready to argue more, when Bjorn let out a great bellow.

Whirling around, she turned to see that Sorenson had taken Kristoff’s pickax from the sleigh and was trying to yank the bear out of his harness.

“Sorenson?” Anna said, forgetting her frustration with Elsa as she took in the man’s peculiar actions. “What are you doing?”

“Nothing, nothing,” Sorenson said, reaching down to fiddle with a buckle. But as he bent down, Anna noticed something falling from his pocket.

If the world had been its normal color—dark emerald hues mixed with the rich blue of the mountains and the oncoming colors of fall—she would never have noticed it. But the world had turned ashy white, so what tumbled from Sorenson’s pocket stood out like a stain. It was sand.

Black sand.

“等等，什么？”艾莎说。

听到这句自己的口头禅从艾莎嘴里冒出来，安娜忍不住笑了。“你说你知道回旋之刃在哪儿，是什么意思？”在盯着墙上的刻纹、聆听奥布斯基伦讲述的途中，安娜心里忽然开窍了。

阿伦黛尔人的故事和胡尔德民的故事，看似不同，其实一样。

就像安娜和艾莎。

而正如这对王室姐妹，两个故事放在一起才最说得通。“为什么不能两件事都真呢？”安娜提议，“为什么不能是：他既被龙吞了——正如我们故事里说的，又被送上船出海？”

“全在故事里呢——阿伦被一条住在‘海即是天’之地的龙吞了。”“可要让海变成天，你得身处……”艾莎的声音低了下去，眼睛却亮了起来。“大地巨人之道（Earth Giant’s Passage）！”

它从峡湾底下穿过，也就是说，海就是天。

“而那正是那条龙船所在！”艾莎难以置信地捂住嘴。“那是冢（tumulus），”她轻声说，“那是阿伦的冢，也就是说……”“回旋之刃就埋在那里，”安娜点头接了下去，“正是。”“干得好，安娜！”克斯托夫说，“你解开了！”“谢谢！”她冲他粲然一笑。“这意味着我们得回城堡去，”安娜抬头望着那名高而沉静的胡尔德说道，“而且得尽快赶到！”

“艾莎，你能……”安娜手指一绕，“用魔法吗？”

“可那会把纳特玛拉直接引到我们这儿，”艾莎说。

奥布斯基伦插话道：“若你想用魔法又不让纳特玛拉察觉，我想就得趁现在。”艾莎点点头。

在草皮屋的安全里，她造出一辆冰橇——那冰通透至极，安娜能一眼看穿。

几乎隐形了。

接着安娜感到一阵冷风拂过，雪花在空中起舞，自行凝成一只巨大的雪熊，在小小的草皮屋里显得过于庞大，她冻得打了个哆嗦。“艾莎，”安娜惊叹地端详着雪熊，“他真美。”雪熊低吼一声。“他说他叫比约恩（Bjorn），”奥布斯基伦翻译道。“我也能听见我的驯鹿斯文说话，”克斯托夫对胡尔德说。

他的声音听着闷闷不乐，安娜知道他还在担心最好的朋友。

她希望斯文平安无事，至少，安稳地留在皇家船上。

奥布斯基伦把手搭在克斯托夫臂上，露出一个苦涩的微笑。“胡尔德民以寻找失物闻名，是因为我们懂得倾听，”她说，“可会倾听的，并不只有我们。”

动物也会。

它们分得清善良的心与残忍的心。

“而我猜，克斯托夫，你是那种确切懂得斯文在说什么的人。”克斯托夫摇摇头。“我只希望他没事。”“只要我们现在就出发，他就会没事的，”安娜说，语气里的笃定，让人不得不信以为真。

他们以最快的速度给雪熊套上橇具，然后向奥布斯基伦道别。“在我们族里，”胡尔德说，“我们不说再见。”“那你们说什么？”安娜问。“我们说：‘后会有期。’”安娜笑了。“后会有期。”“也许吧，”奥布斯基伦说，人已经隐没在一摞丢失和破碎的盘子后面，“但多半会是我先看见你们。”

“除非你们看得非常、非常仔细。”奥布斯基伦伸出手臂，咔哒一声推开了门。

胡尔德打量了门外大地片刻，随即把门大大敞开，让熊和雪橇出去。“记住，”他们滑离草皮屋的庇护、溜到天空之下时，胡尔德喊道，“心在哪儿，家就在哪儿。”

“祝好运，阿伦黛尔的朋友们。”“再见，朋友，”安娜说。

可奥布斯基伦已经不见了。

当比约恩小跑着离开草皮屋，家园已不再是原来的模样。

安娜看见一层阴霾笼罩着阿伦黛尔，世界的色彩正在褪去。

仿佛大地自己也害怕了，吓得脸色发白。

安娜伸出手，在阳光里端详着。

冷空气中，它看上去仍是粉红的。

安娜瞥了眼艾莎，心里一慰：母亲那条围在艾莎肩上的围巾仍是酒红色，而克斯托夫的头发也还是麦子的颜色。

麦子本该有的那种颜色，安娜纠正自己。

不过，离日落还有时间。

还有时间弥补这一切。“看着像火灾后的森林，”克斯托夫望着地形说道，小心一扯缰绳，引着雪熊绕过一道弯。“什么意思？”艾莎问。“灰飘散的样子，”克斯托夫解释，“它不是往下落，而是浮在空气里。”“也许，”安娜努力让语气欢快些，“那是件好事。”

“我在图书馆读到，林火是必要的，能清掉荆棘，为新生命让路。”克斯托夫摇摇头。“去跟那些无家可归的人说这话吧。”他抖了抖缰绳，雪橇加快。

安娜举起艾莎给的冰制望远镜凑到眼前，扫视地平线，寻找纳特玛拉的踪影。

目前为止，一切安好。

没有那头狼的影子。

嗯，除了家乡那苍白的残影，以及安娜自己那颗忐忑狂跳的心。

不过，那是什么？

一个黑斑似乎从褪了色的云杉绿里移动出来。“艾莎，”安娜低语，把望远镜递回妹妹，“有什么东西在动。”

“在那边。”艾莎扭头望了望，又看向前方。“你说得对，”她说，“我觉得它在跟踪我们。”克斯托夫猛地一扯缰绳，比约恩向右一拐，卷起一阵苍白的落叶。

安娜回头望去。

那黑斑也向右拐了。

没错。

不管那是什么，它确确实实在跟着他们。

比约恩的耳朵转了转，接着安娜听见了。

一声喊：啊————！

那声音似乎来自黑斑的方向。

而且，那不是纳特玛拉那刺骨冰冷的嚎叫。

这声响几乎像人声，仿佛有人在竭力喊出一个名字。

事实上……啊————！

娜————！“停下！”安娜猛地直起身。“是索伦森！”艾莎倒吸一口气。“什么？”克斯托夫一拉缰绳，雪橇直冲回科学家那儿，把安娜甩进了艾莎怀里。

靠近些后，喊声清晰起来。“安————娜！”

“艾————莎！”“索伦森！”安娜喊道，见他无恙，松了口气。

还是说，他并不好？

这位科学家看起来狼狈不堪。

他的外套被撕破，是被纳特玛拉的利爪抓烂的，他一瘸一拐，脚踝肿着。

可他活着，而且不只如此，他的眼睛既不像全黑，也不像发黄。“停下雪橇！”安娜说，克斯托夫便让比约恩放慢成步行的速度。

雪熊喷着鼻息，对这变化表示抗议。“索伦森！”安娜一边喊，一边跳出雪橇朝他奔去，“见到你真好！”

“你是怎么逃出来的？”“你好啊，安娜，还有您，陛下，”索伦森说。

他说话节奏古怪，像是舌头和脚踝一样，不知怎么扭到了。“我待会儿全告诉你们。”

“先让我喘口气。”“我们其实没多少时间，”艾莎望着天空说。

太阳明显低了，快到晚饭时分。“你在雪橇上边走边说，行吗？”他点点头。“好主意，可我们要去的地方，雪橇进不去。”“那我们得去哪儿？”安娜问。

她走到克斯托夫的行囊边，翻找着备用的夹板。

啊哈！

找到了。

她知道克斯托夫出门几乎从不落了它。

这夹板本是为冰山急用准备的，可克斯托夫爱打趣说，看她多少次绊倒或磕着碰着，他在城堡里也得随身备一个才安心。

安娜坐下，把夹板递给科学家。“你是怎么从纳特玛拉手里逃出来的？”索伦森说：“我找到了一件神话之物。”安娜眉毛一挑。“你找到了回旋之刃？”索伦森歪了歪头，配上他那把银白长须，看着有点像只困惑的狗。“你弄清它藏在哪儿了？”安娜咧嘴一笑，“是的！”

嗯，我们知道去哪儿找了。

它在——”“你找到了什么，索伦森？”艾莎插到两人中间问道。

她把母亲的围巾像披风般裹在肩上。“啊，我找到了解药，”索伦森说，兴奋地指尖相击，“可这不好解释。”

我宁愿先给你们看。

“它制服不了纳特玛拉，但我想它能除去动物和庄稼身上的枯萎病。”“什么？”一直在雪橇里等候的克斯托夫跳了下来，“有解药？”

“我们能救斯文了？”“据说是的，”索伦森说，“而且胡尔德民手里就有。”“这我可说不好，”艾莎扯着围巾的流苏说，“我想他们是我们的朋友，而且他们只字未提有解药。”“对，”安娜点头，“而且他们绝对是我们的朋友。”索伦森皱起脸，摇着头叹气。“他们跟你说的都是错的，”他说，“胡尔德民是贼。”

“你不该信他们。”“不对，”安娜说，为回声、图书管理员国王和奥布斯基伦辩护，“他们找到丢失、无人要的东西，给它们一个家。”

“他们找的是‘失之所失’，正如你书里写的，先生。”可索伦森不住摇头，长须像城堡墙上被风卷动的旗帜般摆动。

在渐长的光线里，他的胡子看来更白而非银了。“那我的书准是错了，因为胡尔德民把一件神话之物藏在他们的温泉里，离这儿不到一英里。”

“我发现，被纳特玛拉碰过的动物只要喝下这水，就能痊愈，哪怕你们没在第三日日出前打败纳特玛拉。”“走吧！”克斯托夫说，脸上希望之光亮得让安娜看了心疼，“如果只有一英里，我们就能去温泉取一杯水备着，照样能赶回来，耽误不了多少时间！”比约恩的鼻息更响了。

熊想动身了。

它想走。

可安娜左右为难……直到她看见克斯托夫脸上的神情。

克斯托夫最好的朋友病着。

他无从得知他们离开的这段时间里斯文发生了什么，可他一次次拿命去赌，只为换得一个能让斯文好起来的机会。

安娜怎么忍心拒绝？“艾莎，”她转身离开仍在夹板上一揉脚踝的索伦森，也离开那副一得知疗愈温泉在哪儿就随时要冲出去的克斯托夫，说道，“我想我们应该去取水，以防万一。”艾莎又望向天空，咬住嘴唇。

安娜见妹妹深吸一口气，便知道自己不会喜欢接下来听到的话。“我们不能冒这个险，”艾莎说，目光仍停在天空，以及那些像雪却不是雪的浮灰上，“我很抱歉，克斯托夫，可我们不能去。”

“就算泉水真管用，我们也没法带够全王国每个人的份……那剑又怎么办？”克斯托夫脸上的神情让人不忍看。“这么说你现在相信剑是真的了？”“艾莎！”安娜看看妹妹，又看看她爱的人。“我理解你对王国负有的责任，”克斯托夫对艾莎说，“可斯文是我的家人。”“克斯托夫，”艾莎打断他，眼睛因受伤而睁大——尽管安娜不懂妹妹为何难过，“我说不行，是因为这危及太多人！”安娜深吸一口气，正要再争，比约恩却发出一声巨吼。

她猛地转身，只见索伦森已从雪橇上取了克斯托夫的镐，正想把熊从挽具里拽出来。“索伦森？”安娜说，顾不上对艾莎的恼火，只盯着男人古怪的举动，“你在干什么？”“没什么，没什么，”索伦森说着，弯下身去摆弄一个扣环。

可他一弯腰，安娜注意到有东西从他口袋里掉出来。

要是世界还是平常的颜色——深翠绿混着群山浓郁的蓝，以及渐起的秋色——她绝不会注意到。

可世界已变成灰白，所以从索伦森口袋里滚落的东西，就像一块污渍般显眼。

那是沙。

黑沙。
